1.title: A Social-Hydrological Systems (SHS) based approach to Local Resilient Development (LRD) and Drought Risk Management in Islands.
1.abstract:
Contemporary approaches to insular development unilaterally consider islands as tourism destinations and focus on top-down oriented short-term solutions that often place stress on local water resources and disregard the particularities of insular societies and resources. Such practices raise questions on the long-term sustainability of development trajectories, especially as regards the resilience to drought risk of insular societies and hydrological systems.
With respect to drought risk, LRD is understood as development that enhances the resilience of local communities, businesses and infrastructure against drought stress through strategies that promote self-sustenance, adaptability and sustainability. Implementation of such strategies requires shifting from linear approaches aimed at meeting specific objectives to approaches that accommodate uncertainty, acknowledge feedback and embrace re-evaluation of adaptation interventions.
Utilizing a SHS approach, the paper attempts to highlight the interplay between local development trajectories and their impact on drought resilience of vulnerable social groups and the hydrological systems on which they depend. Social-Hydrological Systems’ (SHS), a special category of SES, consist of a social and at least one hydrological subsystem that interact, co-evolve and are inter-determined through adaptation and feedback. SHSs are characterized by their resilience and have spatial boundaries that transform in time.
Focusing on two Greek island cases, the author uses a fit-for-purpose methodology to (a) spatially identify the SHS(s) and their respective subsystems, (b) identify vulnerable social groups, their resources and adaptation options to drought risk, (c) understand the connections between local development, resource allocation and building drought resilience through feedback relations, (d) highlight the importance of adaptive governance in building LRD and (e) justify the appropriateness of SHS approach as a tool to implement LRD in islands with respect to drought risk management.

1.title: IS EVERYTHING CULTURE? THE CONTRIBUTION OF SELECTED CULTURAL ELEMENTS TO URBAN PLANNING AND SUSTAINABILITY

authors.name: Alex Deffner
authors.affiliation: Department of Planning and Regional Development, University of Thessaly, Volos Greece

1.abstract:
This presentation examines the role of culture in urban planning and connects it to geography and sustainability. It raises fundamental questions: Can urban planning be understood as an outstanding cultural practice? How is this relationship made concrete? What challenges lie ahead for Europe, especially under socioeconomic crisis? Urban planning is shown as a field of dilemmas, where resources and constraints coexist. In this context, culture serves both as a means of understanding and as a tool for intervention.
A central figure in this analysis is Klaus Kunzmann, who recognised early on the importance of culture in urban planning and emphasised the dual relationship between culture and education. The contribution of culture draws its roots from classical theorists, evolves through postmodernism, and is today dynamically expressed through urban regeneration, the creative city, the slow city, cultural heritage, and place marketing and branding.
Emphasis is placed on creativity, which Kunzmann approaches more broadly than dominant theories, characterising it as a “friendly virus,” “postmodern Zeitgeist,” and “vague concept.” Creativity requires strong human resources and is closely linked to the concept of the slow society, where quality of life, tradition, and innovation coexist.
Cultural heritage is analysed as a key element of identity, quality of life, and place marketing and branding. It is also seen as a field of tension between the local and the global, particularly under the pressure of globalisation and tourism. Finally, the presentation highlights future challenges in urban planning with a focus on sustainability. It proposes a strategic interconnection of creativity, innovation, heritage, lifestyles, and culture to improve the quality of life and strengthen social cohesion in Europe.

1.title: Feminist approaches to climate change (mal)adaptation: critical insights from seawater desalination for human consumption in Chile
1.abstract: Water security under climate change remains a pressing sustainability challenge, and drinking water supply is particularly demanding, as non-compliance with strict quality and service norms directly affects public health and wellbeing. Desalination has emerged as one of the most prominent technical responses to water scarcity across the MENA region and the Americas. Chile is a pioneer in this regard: desalination is the country's main adaptation strategy, particularly for urban centres along the hyper-arid coast of the Atacama Desert. Drawing on feminist and gendered approaches to domestic water security, the climate change maladaptation literature, and critical social research on desalination, I develop an integrative framework for evaluating water security through a gendered and intersectional lens on maladaptation. I apply this framework to reassess desalination in Chile not as an isolated adaptation intervention with neutral or negative impacts, but as embedded within long-standing neoliberal water policies that privilege market-based solutions and capital-intensive mega-infrastructure, and that produce or sustain water insecurity for women and other vulnerable groups. Empirically, I examine how domestic water insecurity is constituted in the everyday lives of urban Chilean women who drink desalinated water, drawing on household surveys, in-depth interviews, focus groups, and a targeted literature review. The analysis shows that desalination operates as maladaptation in three interrelated ways: (1) it does not guarantee water security at the household level; (2) it displaces conflict geographically, temporally, and socially; and (3) it contributes to the very climate change it is meant to help societies adapt to. The paper contributes to interdisciplinary debates in geography by bridging physical understandings of water with feminist political ecology and critical adaptation studies, surfacing justice concerns often invisible within technocratic sustainability agendas.

1.title: Mapping Territories of Urban Mobility Corridors: A Case Study of Thessaloniki, Greece
1.abstract:
Arterial roads are key urban spaces hosting essential infrastructures and shaping development patterns, yet they are often analysed linearly through a traffic-centric lens. Research typically emphasizes technical cross-sections, neglecting spatial, functional, social, and ecological interconnections with the surrounding urban fabric. Amid mobility transitions, climate adaptation, and calls for equitable spaces, arterial roads require reconceptualization as integrated urban spaces.
This study introduces "Territories of Urban Mobility Corridors," reframing arterial roads as dynamic assemblages embedded in the city across morphological, systemic, and relational dimensions and scales. It extends beyond linear streetscapes to highlight spatial relations, ecological systems, and social interdependencies between street segments and adjacent fabric, avoiding traffic-oriented terms like "street" or "road."
Thessaloniki exemplifies car dependency with minimal unsealed areas, exacerbating air pollution, urban heat islands, flooding, and inhospitable spaces . Arterial roads connect dense fabric but disrupt pedestrian networks, blue-green links, and neighbourhoods . Focusing on selected arterials, this research identifies attributes to derive Territories of Urban Mobility Corridors, revealing potentials and challenges for both strategic and spatial urban planning.
As part of PhD research at TU Wien's Institute of Urban Design and Landscape Architecture , the mixed-methods approach integrates Situational Analysis and critical cartography. Methods include document analysis, urban-design assessments, promenadology, spatial observations, mappings, and expert interviews. Findings synthesize via joint spatial displays for academic, professional, and community dialogue.
Expected outcomes delineate territories like ecological networks, heritage-tourism landscapes, residential zones, and productive areas, aiming to uncover thematic-spatial interactions, situational dynamics, and relational ties between streetscapes and fabric. Results inform a typology advancing mobility corridors as relational, multi-scalar urban spaces. By rendering territorial complexity legible, the study fosters regenerative urbanism through context-sensitive knowledge, supporting reimagined corridors in the Symbiocene.

1.title: The Future of Olive Production in Rural Greece: Sustainability Challenges and Interdisciplinary Evidence from Messenia
1.abstract:
Across Europe, rural regions are undergoing profound socio-ecological transformations, including demographic decline, land abandonment, and increasing environmental pressures linked to climate change. In Greece and the wider Mediterranean, these dynamics are particularly acute in remote rural areas, where depopulation and ageing populations are reshaping land use and agricultural activity. Climate change and water scarcity further exacerbate these trends, raising critical questions about the long-term sustainability of olive cultivation – the region’s most economically and culturally significant permanent crop.

This contribution presents findings from an interdisciplinary field-based research experience conducted in Messenia, Greece. Students worked in four semi-mountainous villages in West Mani to examine processes of olive grove abandonment and landscape change, combining GIS-based spatial analysis with farmer survey data. In parallel, they explored transformative adaptation pathways in the olive sector through semi-structured interviews with policymakers, local stakeholders, and cooperative actors, identifying key governance challenges and opportunities.

Beyond these findings, the presentation reflects on interdisciplinarity as both a research and pedagogical process. It shows how an interdisciplinary project design, developed at the faculty level, is translated into a field-based learning experience in which students actively engage in data collection, interpretation, and the combination of methods. In this context, student-led fieldwork becomes a key site of knowledge production, where spatial analysis, environmental governance, and rural development perspectives are brought into interaction.

Finally, the contribution explores the implications of this experience in the context of sustainability education in Geography. It shows how field-based, experiential and situated learning can support more grounded understandings of rural sustainability transformations, while also making visible the difficulties of combining approaches and perspectives. In this sense, interdisciplinarity emerges not as a given outcome, but as something that is learned, tested, and negotiated in practice.

1.title: Navigating the Eastern Aegean Border Archipelago: Contested Ecologies at Europe’s Edge
1.abstract:
Over the past fifteen years, the Eastern Aegean archipelago has emerged as one of the most perilous border zones in the Mediterranean and as a site of intensifying socio-ecological change. Across this island complex, EU border sovereignty is materialized through hostility-by-design processes, including Closed Controlled Access Centers (CCACs) and violent pushbacks. These processes not only govern mobility but also reconfigure local ecologies through land dipossession, resource extraction, and militarized infrastructure. While research has largely focused on the socio-political dimensions of forced migration, the environmental effects of border regimes within EU territories remain underexplored.
Building on its expanded use in geography, this presentation introduces the ‘archipelago’ as an analytical and methodological framework to capture these entanglements. It proposes archipelagic thinking as a methodology of encounter to examine how ecological and socio-political processes unfold across fragmented yet interconnected island complexes. This approach challenges continental perceptions of seemingly unified or dichotomized worlds while highlighting the relational dynamics of environmental harm and care. In an area such as the Mediterranean basin, where geopolitical conflicts, bordering practices and technological monopolies reinforce violence, segregation and ecological degradation this approach appears particularly urgent.
Drawing on a multi-sited research conducted between 2024–2026 across seven islands as part of the ERC funded project ‘The Game: Counter-mapping Informal Refugee Mobilities along the Balkan Route’, the presentation advances two arguments. First, it proposes archipelagic methodologies as a tool for challenging harmful regimes. It repositions the Aegean as a critical site for investigating the intersections of mobility, sovereignty, and ecology. Second, it examines how border regimes intersect with environmental degradation and resource inequalities. To do so it focuses on three cases: the deforestation of Vastria region in Lesvos, water scarcity and land dispossession in Leros, and solidarity practices in Tilos, exploring how bordering regimes but also forms of solidarity reshape our worlds.

1.title: Integrating geographic knowledge with climate litigation in India: opportunities and challenges at the intersection of spatial-legal interface.

authors.name: Kiran Kumari Singh
authors.affiliation: Department of Geography, University of Allahabad, Prayagraj, India.

authors.name: Ramakant Singh
authors.affiliation: Departmetn of Law, Mahatma Gandhi Kashi Vidyapeeth, Varanasi, India.

1.abstract:
The climate crisis, reflected in climate vulnerability, impacts, and vulnerable population groups, is fuelling climate litigation in India. With many people relying on climate-sensitive sectors and recent Supreme Court rulings recognizing that Article 21 — the right to life — includes the right "to be free from adverse effects of climate change," climate litigation is likely to grow in India. India's long-standing connection between law and geography frequently centers on land disputes, where determining property ownership depends on accurately measuring land boundaries. Today, geography can play a role in legal processes beyond land conflicts.

This study explores the potential and challenges of integrating geographical knowledge with climate litigation via a spatial–legal interface by analyzing 13 climate litigations from India. This perspective article argues that geographic tools such as Geographic Information Systems (GIS), remote sensing, spatial modelling, and vulnerability mapping can greatly improve judicial understanding of risks, location-specific and community-specific vulnerabilities, and the various impacts faced by communities and ecosystems. A spatial approach in the judiciary can be helpful in cases involving extreme weather events, climate disasters, environmental degradation, and displacement, making legal assessments more informed. Besides, Geographic Information Systems can improve compliance monitoring.
Additionally, the paper highlights challenges that hinder spatial-legal integration, such as a lack of knowledge about geospatial data, difficulty in managing complex geospatial data, issues with data reliability and standardization, and concerns about whether courts can consider it as evidence. The paper concludes that fostering collaboration among legal scholars/practitioners, geographers, and policymakers can enhance climate governance and climate justice in India.
Keywords: GIS; Climate litigations; climate justice; spatial-legal interface; India.

1.title: Wickedness and Complexity in Spatial Planning: Towards a Systematic Convergence: Implications for the Just Green Transition, Mega Projects, and the Socio-Political Foundations of Policy.
1.abstract: Theories of spatial planning have frequently engaged with the concepts of wickedness and complexity. Although these notions occasionally intersect, they are typically examined in isolation, without a systematic account of their relationship. Each carries distinct implications for planning practice and policy. This paper seeks to establish a theoretical connection between the two by identifying points of convergence in their constituent characteristics. In doing so, it formulates a complex condition that defines particularly challenging planning contexts—most notably the just green transition as a generalized policy exercise, as well as mega and large-scale projects as specific planning cases. By tracing the presence of this condition in planning practice, the paper draws conclusions about the nature of complexity and its implications for the foundations of planning policy, particularly at the social level, re-examining central questions and their socio-political outcomes.

1.title: Discussing Geography in the Era of Sustainability Science: Bridging Approaches and Knowledge Systems
1.abstract:
Addressing sustainability challenges such as climate change, biodiversity loss, and socio-environmental inequalities requires forms of knowledge production that move beyond disciplinary boundaries and engage with real-world complexity. This is reflected in sustainability science, a field defined less by disciplines than by the challenges it seeks to address. Geography, positioned at the interface of natural and social sciences and grounded in human–environment interactions, is well suited to contribute to these efforts. This orientation is increasingly institutionalized in European universities through interdisciplinary research centers, laboratories, and specialized degree programs. Yet, translating this integrative potential into coherent research practices and policy-relevant outcomes remains a challenge.

This contribution stages a dialogue between two complementary approaches: ecosystem services and social-ecological systems research, which focuses on the attribution of ecosystem functions values for society, and environmental social science, which examines governance processes, social inequalities, and collective action in sustainability transformations. Drawing on selected empirical cases from our research, it explores how these approaches frame key issues and generate different forms of knowledge. It further highlights how methodological choices – from quantitative indicators and spatial modelling to qualitative and participatory approaches – shape not only research outcomes but also their relevance for policy and practice. By placing these perspectives in conversation, the contribution identifies both complementarities, misconceptions and tensions, particularly in integrating data, engaging actors across knowledge systems, ontological framings, and navigating differing epistemologies.

The paper argues for the value of working through disciplinary differences as a productive basis for collaboration. Such engagement can support more reflexive methodological choices, strengthen knowledge integration, and enhance the societal relevance of geographical research. As an opening contribution to this session, it aims to stimulate dialogue on how interdisciplinary and transdisciplinary approaches can be advanced in Geography.

2.title: Urban Resilience in the Era of Polycrisis: Rethinking Governance, Vulnerability, and Collective Action
2.abstract:
In the current era of intersecting housing, energy, climate, and socio-economic crises, urban
vulnerability is increasingly understood as spatially concentrated and structurally produced.
Rising housing costs, energy poverty, inadequate housing conditions, and uneven access to
infrastructure are not isolated phenomena but interconnected expressions of a broader
condition of urban polycrisis. These overlapping pressures challenge conventional
understandings of resilience, which often conceptualise it as adaptive capacity or system
stability in the face of external shocks.
This paper offers a conceptual contribution by rethinking resilience through the lens of urban
polycrisis and bottom-linked governance. It argues that dominant resilience frameworks tend to
depoliticise vulnerability by focusing on recovery and adaptation, while underemphasising the
structural and institutional arrangements that generate uneven exposure to risk. In contrast, this
paper conceptualises resilience as a politically embedded and socially mediated process
shaped by governance configurations operating across multiple scales.
Central to this argument is the role of non-state and multi-sectoral alliances as meso-level
governance infrastructures. Rather than acting solely as service providers or emergency
responders, such alliances can be understood as institutional mediators that connect
fragmented actors, mobilise resources, and produce alternative forms of coordination in
contexts of crisis. In doing so, they may contribute to reconfiguring governance logics toward
more egalitarian and inclusive urban futures, although their transformative capacity remains
uneven and contested.
By linking resilience theory with scholarship on urban governance and polycrisis, the paper
reframes urban vulnerability not as a discrete policy problem but as a relational condition
produced through the interaction of housing systems, energy regimes, and socio-spatial
inequalities. It ultimately argues that understanding resilience in the era of polycrisis requires
shifting attention from systems of recovery to the governance infrastructures that structure
exposure, mediation, and collective action in the urban realm.

2.title: The Hidden Diagnosis: Why Athens and Thessaloniki Strategised Resilience Differently

authors.name: Ersi (Varsami) Zafeiriou
authors.affiliation: Dresden Leibniz Graduate School (DLGS),Institute for Ecological Urban & Regional Development (IÖR);Environmental Studies, Technische Universität Dresden (TUD)

2.abstract:
Urban resilience strategies have become a dominant paradigm for urban development in cities navigating protracted crises. Nevertheless, they often fail to critically engage with the social vulnerabilities that precondition a city’s capacity to cope, adapt, or transform in the face of shocks or stressors. This research argues that a resilience pathway is shaped by a prior diagnostic act: how a city identifies and prioritises its social vulnerabilities. It applies the VISIBLE framework – disaggregating vulnerability into seven core groups (Voice and Power, Information and Awareness, Socioeconomic Disparities, Infrastructure and Services, Belonging and Social Conditions, Land and Housing, and Exposure) – to conduct a comparative analysis of Athens' and Thessaloniki's resilience strategies, Greece.
Despite sharing a context of austerity, migration challenges, and climate risks at the time of strategy-making, the analysis reveals their divergent pathways. Athens’ strategy, forged in overlapping emergencies, perceived vulnerability as requiring immediate triage, resulting in a pathway of pragmatic improvisation that prioritises acute deficits in infrastructure, shelter, and critical services. In contrast, Thessaloniki’s strategy, shaped by institutional constraints and economic stagnation, views vulnerability as a structural deficiency, producing a pathway of strategic projection that foregrounds issues of voice, information asymmetries, and long-term socioeconomic disparities.
Through structured comparison, the research empirically demonstrates that the scope of vulnerability diagnosis preconfigures the substance of resilience planning. Furthermore, it advances the argument for “planning from vulnerability” methodologically by showcasing VISIBLE as a plausible critical tool for making diagnostic choices explicit, comparable, and open to scrutiny. The findings underscore that just resilience planning cannot begin with technical solutions, but must start with a structured diagnosis of a city’s vulnerability profile – including how access to infrastructure, land and housing, exposure to hazards, and differential positionality intersect on the ground.

2.title: Tackling urban injustices and shaping Resilience Imaginaries through Participatory Mapping and other data practices
2.abstract: This paper critically re-examines the relationship between data and urban resilience by shifting attention from data as a neutral technical artefact to data practices as socio-spatial processes that shape how vulnerability, risk, and futures are imagined and governed. Drawing on social constructivist perspectives and critical scholarship on urban imaginaries, the paper conceptualises “resilience imaginaries” as socially produced visions of urban futures that influence policy priorities, resource allocation, and whose vulnerabilities are rendered visible or invisible across urban space. Empirically, the paper synthesises findings from multiple research projects conducted over the past five years in contexts characterised by housing precarity, personal vulnerability, and climate risk in both the Global South and the Global North In and attempts to examines three interrelated domains of data practice: data consumption, where data supports risk management, housing and energy planning and ultimately the process of urban resilience; data circulation, where information flows shape governance coordination and public participation across institutional and territorial scales; and data generation, focusing on participatory and dialogical mapping with marginalised communities experiencing compounding forms of vulnerability ad through the process of mapping nurture a resilience spirit. Our analysis demonstrates how data practices can simultaneously reproduce spatialised injustices and open up possibilities for more inclusive, situated, and equitable urban futures. The paper proposes a holistic framework that positions data as product, flow, and process, highlighting the importance of connecting quantitative spatial analysis with participatory and qualitative approaches. It concludes by arguing that socially embedded, process-oriented data practices are essential for addressing cumulative urban vulnerabilities and advancing more just resilience imaginaries in places dealing with multiple and overlapping crises.

2.title: The Geography of Urban Vulnerability in Athens: Material Deprivation and Spatial Inequalities

authors.name: Antigoni Faka
authors.affiliation: Department of Geography, Harokopio University of Athens

authors.name: Elli Aikaterini Lytra
authors.affiliation: Department of Geography, Harokopio University of Athens

authors.name: Angeliki Paidakaki
authors.affiliation: Department of Geography, Harokopio University of Athens

authors.name: Agapi Pouli
authors.affiliation: Department of Sociology, University of Crete

authors.name: Georgia Stylianeli
authors.affiliation: Social and Political Sciences, Panteion University of Athens

2.abstract:
This study examines material deprivation in the Municipality of Athens through a spatial lens of urban vulnerability, focusing on the intersections between housing deprivation, energy poverty, and homelessness. The research is theoretically grounded in multidimensional approaches to poverty and social exclusion, conceptualizing deprivation as a dynamic and spatially uneven process shaped by unequal access to housing, infrastructure, and essential services. Drawing on geographical perspectives, the study situates material deprivation within broader processes of urban inequality and spatialized injustice. In alignment with European homelessness research, it adopts the ETHOS framework to capture a continuum of housing exclusion, including hidden forms of homelessness.
Methodologically, the research employs a mixed-methods design combining quantitative spatial analysis and qualitative inquiry. Census and socio-economic data are analyzed using GIS and cluster analysis to map the spatial distribution and co-location of deprivation indicators at a fine urban scale. Qualitative data are collected through interviews and focus groups with residents, service users, and social actors in high-deprivation areas, exploring lived experiences of housing precarity, energy insecurity, and social exclusion.
The findings reveal pronounced spatial concentrations of vulnerability in central-western Athens, where housing deprivation, energy poverty, and precarious employment overlap. These areas are characterized by poor housing conditions, overcrowding, limited energy access, and forms of hidden homelessness, reflecting cumulative and mutually reinforcing disadvantages. The analysis demonstrates that these dimensions are deeply interconnected, forming a complex geography of urban vulnerability.
The study emphasizes the need for place-based interventions, including strengthened street outreach to detect hidden homelessness, improved accessibility of social and housing services, and the development of integrated local housing strategies. It further supports coordinated action among municipalities, civil society, and local actors, alongside targeted measures in affordable housing provision and energy upgrading to tackle housing exclusion.

2.title: The Tourist City and Its Shadows: Gentrification Risk in Athens, Greece using GIS & Spatial Analysis

authors.name: Georgia Elisavet Chatzopoulou
authors.affiliation: University of West Attica / Department of Surveying and Geoinformatics Engineering

authors.name: Kleomenis Kalogeropoulos
authors.affiliation: University of West Attica / Department of Surveying and Geoinformatics Engineering

authors.name: Stefanos Tsigdinos
authors.affiliation: University of West Attica / Department of Surveying and Geoinformatics Engineering

authors.name: Andreas Tsatsaris
authors.affiliation: University of West Attica / Department of Surveying and Geoinformatics Engineering

2.abstract: This paper explores the phenomenon of touristification in Athens through the lens of spatial analysis and the Rent Gap theory. The main research hypothesis focuses on the comparison between “potential rent,” captured through an attractiveness index based on proximity to cultural points of interest following the logic of the 15-minute city, and “current rent,” expressed by the existing Quality of Life (QoL) index. By utilizing GIS tools and data from short-term rental platforms such as Airbnb, the analysis seeks to identify areas where low quality of life and correspondingly low rents coexist with high tourist attractiveness, creating strong investment incentives and increased displacement pressures on permanent residents. In the methodological section, a cartographic subtraction of the two indices is applied to produce a composite spatial index. The resulting map highlights zones with different levels of gentrification risk. Areas with high positive values, such as Metaxourgeio, are identified as "gentrification frontiers", where the dynamic of converting housing into tourist accommodation is more intense due to the large profit margin. Conversely, areas with negative values function as "residential refuges", where a high quality of life prevails over tourist pressure, contributing to the maintenance of social cohesion. Overall, the paper offers a quantitative and cartographic documentation of the spatial manifestations of residential pressure in Athens, contributing to the understanding of the mechanisms that lead to the transformation of urban space.

2.title: Quantifying gendered energy precarity: A longitudinal analysis from Southeast Europe

authors.name: Jasna Hivziefendic
authors.affiliation: Sarajevo School of Science and Technology

2.abstract: ‘Gendered energy precarity’ sits at the intersection of SDG 5 (gender equality) and SDG7 (affordable and clean energy), yet it remains rarely examined through integrated quantitative analysis, limiting understanding of how gendered inequalities in energy precarity are patterned across households and regions. Grounded in feminist political ecology, critical energy geographies, and energy precarity debates, this paper develops a framework to challenge the traditional gender-energy nexus by showing how socio-political, economic, and environmental factors intersectionally shape politically-induced energy vulnerability. Gender inequality and energy precarity, often treated separately, are deeply intertwined: unequal access to resources, decision-making power, and social protection reinforces women’s vulnerability to energy deprivation. Robust quantitative analyses remain scarce, particularly in post-socialist Southeast Europe, where gender and energy vulnerabilities are pronounced. To address this gap, we developed the ‘gendered energy precarity’ framework (GEPF), building on ‘energy precarity’ theorisation to link material energy conditions with structural gender and other social dimensions of marginalisation. Applying GEPF to Bosnia and Herzegovina (BiH), a post-socialist country with political fragmentation, socio-economic disparities, uneven energy infrastructure, and entrenched gender inequalities, this study provides the first systematic quantitative analysis of ‘gendered energy precarity’ in the region. We analysed longitudinal data (2004-2021) from the Agency for Statistics of BiH, the United Nations Development Programme, and the International Renewable Energy Agency using Principal Component Analysis and clustering. GEPF integrates three domains: socio-economic background, gender inequality, and energy precarity, covering housing, expenditure, education, employment, political representation, and energy access. Results show reliance on traditional fuels, insecure housing, and energy-inefficient assets drive energy precarity, while persistent gender inequalities in education, labour-force participation, political representation, and unpaid care work exacerbate vulnerability. Temporal analysis reveals improvements in energy provision and housing post-2015, yet enduring gendered disadvantages persist. GEPF is transferable, supporting gender-responsive energy policy and comparative research on energy precarity in underrepresented regions.

2.title: “Summerless" Greece: heat, housing, and the unequal right to a liveable city
2.abstract: This contribution emerges from our lived experience of the last two Greek summers, among the hottest and most unbearable on record. Writing as scholar-activists and critical housing and climate researchers based in urban Greece, we combine a vignette-based methodology grounded in participant-personal reflection with a critical mapping approach to examine how housing precarity, energy poverty, and intensifying climate risk converge in the embodied geographies of the Greek city. We approach urban heatwaves not as neutral natural hazards but as socially produced disasters rooted in speculative urbanisation, fragmented horizontal property ownership, deteriorating concrete building stock, and the systematic neglect of environmental justice and housing rights. We construct a comparative heat vulnerability index for Athens and Thessaloniki at the scale of municipal units, integrating population data, socio-economic indicators, green space distribution, and building stock characteristics. Initial mapping for Athens identifies the Municipality of Athens as the most acutely vulnerable area within the wider metropolitan region, confirming the spatial concentration of compounded risk in the dense urban core. Both cities rank among the least green in Europe, far below WHO thresholds; combined with the urban heat island effect and unequal access to cooling, this produces an uneven geography of exposure in which the elderly, women performing invisible care labour, and precarious residents in poorly insulated dwellings absorb a disproportionate share of climate harm. We argue that quantitative spatial analysis and embodied, situated narratives are mutually constitutive ways of knowing climate injustice: the map locates vulnerability; the vignettes inhabit it. Drawing on political ecology and radical housing studies, we close by calling for a transformative approach that re-frames housing policy as a field of collective struggle over the right to a liveable city.

2.title: Impacts of Impoverishment Risks on Sustainable Housing Affordability: A Case Study of Kenya’s Slum Upgrading Programme in Kibera
2.abstract:
Housing adequacy and the proliferation of informal settlements are some of the major urban struggles in Nairobi. For this reason, the Kenyan State has engaged in multiple types of housing interventions, such as slum upgrading programmes. However, there is evidence that beneficiaries of such housing programs are vacating their assigned housing units, due to affordability constraints.
To interrogate this phenomenon, the research selected the case study of Soweto East A public housing in Kibera, Nairobi, which is an example of on-site resettlement, implemented through slum upgrading. For this purpose, two theoretical models were selected, namely Impoverishment Risks (Cernea, 1997; Patel et al, 2014) and Sustainable Housing Affordability (Mulliner & Maliene, 2011; Ezennia et al, 2021). Impoverishment Risks can be described as the impact of resettlement on capital assets that enable people to pursue their livelihood (natural, physical, financial, human and social capital) (Cernea, 1997; Patel et al, 2014). Sustainable Housing Affordability pursues a comprehensive assessment of affordability that integrates social, environmental, and economic criteria (Ezennia et al, 2019; Elghandour, 2024). The aim of the research was to determine how Impoverishment Risks affect Sustainable Housing Affordability in the case study. For this purpose, it employed a combination of qualitative and spatial methods, assessing primary and secondary data.
The main findings were that Impoverishment Risks and Sustainable Housing Affordability are theoretically compatible and have valid application potential on precarious realities. Through this research, it was also concluded that Impoverishment Risks were directly affected by resettlement distance. In the case study, residents were not notably impoverished by resettlement and their access to housing and infrastructure was generally enhanced. However, Sustainable Housing Affordability struggles related to the inability of slum upgrading to holistically upgrade the slum-dwellers’ lives and directly address the proliferation of poverty in the informal settlements.

2.title: Energy as social relation: Refugees’ energy commons for infrastructuring beyond the grid
2.abstract: This paper reconceptualizes energy as a social relation of (re)production, focusing on the overlooked intersection of refugees, housing precarity, and energy practices. Despite the importance placed by both policy and academia on energy poverty and energy transitions, both academic research and policy practice have systematically overlooked issues related to energy provision and consumption in refugees’ housing. Our research addresses this significant gap in research and analysis. Drawing on extensive ethnographic research conducted with refugees squatting in abandoned buildings in Thessaloniki, Greece, we provide new empirical and theoretical insights into the nexus of housing and energy access among refugees. By examining the improvised energy landscapes that refugees are compelled to construct, we advance a critical understanding of energy as a social relation, namely, the ability to access social relations of production and reproduction which eventually can give access to energy. We introduce the concept of refugees’ energy commons, to explain how refugees’ communities self-organize to meet their energy needs -repairing, maintaining, and improvising energy infrastructures to provide heating, cooling, insulation, cooking, and communication. We also examine the different meanings that energy provision can have, how refugees perceive energy, what practices and activities they engage in and how energy constitutes not only a means for meeting basic needs, but also a means of building practices of solidarity and mutual support. These collective energy infrastructuring practices which act as means to reclaim disrupted life trajectories, question the dominant discourses around energy poverty revealing that access to energy is not simply a matter of technical adaptation or ability to pay bills; rather, it is a matter of being embedded into a set of social relations of (re)production, within which communities, institutions, and technologies, enable or disable access to the housing-energy nexus.

2.title: “It’s On Us Now”: Upholding a Solidary “Living Room” for People on the Move within Thessaloniki’s Eroding Infrastructural Field
2.abstract: In the decade following the “long summer of migration,” scholarship documented how citizens, policy makers, and migrant communities built solidarity infrastructures (Schilliger 2020, 2025) to support illegalized people on the move. Today, however, these infrastructures are increasingly destabilized across European cities by political hostility, the criminalisation of aid, and shrinking budgets (Rygiel & Baban, 2019). Greece exemplifies this, with NGOs and grassroots groups facing mounting constraints that undermine their ability to share essential resources. Drawing on an in-depth ethnography of The Harbour House, a Thessaloniki-based community centre cooking meals for people on the move, this paper examines how solidarity is negotiated and sustained within an eroding infrastructural field (Vasileiadi and Swerts 2024). We situate The Harbour House within this field, showing how people on the move are illegalized and rendered invisible in urban space. Moving beyond binary debates on the (a)political nature of humanitarian aid, we argue that The Harbor House responds to pressures on its solidarity infrastructure through infrapolitical spatial, symbolic, and relational strategies (see Scott 1985). Its ability to uphold solidarity despite surveillance, resource scarcity, and policy hostility depends on “unseen, unasked, and unsaid” everyday strategies of resistance that remain intentionally low in visibility yet are deeply political (see Swerts 2017, 2026). Our findings show that such spatially concentrated infrastructures of solidarity function as vital “living rooms” for displaced people with diverse trajectories and personal histories- spaces where they can access material support, momentarily exhale, and recharge. At the same time, we highlight the tensions inherent in offering unconditional welcome under the radar within a hostile migration regime, where providing temporary relief may inadvertently entrench forms of stuckedness (Drangsland 2020; Felder et al. 2023). The paper contributes to debates on urban inequalities by demonstrating how displacement is produced, navigated, and - quietly - resisted through infrastructures under pressure.

2.title: Demolitions, Evictions and Displacement: The Institutional Production of Vulnerability in Mayotte

authors.name: Salah El Dinn Sadeck
authors.affiliation: Lebanese University / Faculty of Fine Arts and Architecture / Urban planning Department

authors.name: Boris Weliachew
authors.affiliation: Ecole National Supérieure d’Architecture Paris-Val de Seine / EVCAU Laboratory

2.abstract:
This paper examines the socio-spatial effects of policies aimed at eradicating informal housing in Mayotte, considering them not only as tools of urban regulation but as mechanisms that may produce, displace, and intensify vulnerability. In a context marked by rapid demographic growth, severe land scarcity, and a structural shortage of affordable housing, informal settlements constitute a central component of the housing system rather than a marginal one. Official data indicate that nearly 40% of dwellings were still made of sheet metal in 2017, highlighting the scale of housing deprivation and inequality.

Focusing on Mamoudzou and its peripheries, the paper analyzes the 2023 “Wuambushu” operation, which represents a significant intensification of demolition and eviction practices. Framed as a response to insalubrity, insecurity, and irregular land occupation, this intervention provides a critical lens for examining the effects of state action on residential trajectories, social networks, and exposure to risk. Its legal foundation, particularly Article 197 of the French ELAN law, enables accelerated clearance procedures, often without sustainable or secure rehousing solutions for affected populations.

The central question is whether such policies genuinely reduce vulnerability or instead contribute to its institutional production. Three hypotheses structure the analysis. First, evictions do not eliminate vulnerability but displace it, forcing households to resettle under more precarious conditions. Second, these displacements tend to redirect populations toward areas more exposed to environmental hazards, thereby intensifying inequalities. Third, these policies reinforce urban fragmentation by deepening divides between formal and informal spaces.

The impact of Cyclone Chido (2024) illustrates how disasters amplify pre-existing socio-spatial inequalities. A comparative perspective with French Guiana situates Mayotte within a broader framework of displacement-oriented governance. The paper ultimately calls for policies that secure housing pathways and reduce risk sustainably.

2.title: The fragile matter of care: towards a subject-centered political economy of homelessness in Athens, Greece
2.abstract:
What is the role of things in the experience of homelessness? How do subjects engage with objects and what are the performative nuances of situated engagements of the kind? Can we talk about a political economy of things in a context of urban poverty management?

This contribution revisits the core years of the Greek socio-economic crisis so as to suggest a re-materialisation of the homeless geographies of Athens. The suggestion is based on a multi-sited ethnographic practice conducted in the city's spaces of care, the latter being approached as spatialities in which care is performed in material ways. Therein, and after having experienced a "material schism" from their personal belongings, homeless subjectivities are actively involved in processes of rematerialisation through situated practices of care. Rematerialisation here consists of two major dialectical processes: first, a material provision of things of care; and second, a new, negotiated relationship of the homeless subjects with their own objects.

For the analysis and presentation of the empirical findings materiality -as the active matter in spaces of care for homeless people- gets fractured into three interrelated typologies, namely, materiality as things, materiality as qualities, and materiality as practice (between subjects and objects).

Overall, the contribution suggests that, by generating various material conduits throughout urban space, a specific political economy of things is enabled by Athens' spaces of care, actively shaping the ways care for "the homeless" is performed in the city. In such everyday performances, materiality as things, as qualities and as practices, produces subjectivities that might be characterised by the re-production of a material fragility which is -paradoxically enough- centred upon care.

2.title: Homeless Shelter Realities: From Regulation to Vulnerability through Shelter Policy Interventions
2.abstract:
Researchers and policy makers have focused on developing policies to support the resettlement of homeless shelter residents (HSRs). Shelter policies aim to ensure safety and order, yet inflexible regulations can unintentionally increase HSRs’ vulnerabilities. By analysing institutional policy implementation across three global cities, Athens (Greece), Manchester (UK), and Santiago (Chile), we aim to provide a deeper understanding of the interplay between regulation and HSRs’ wellbeing.
This study introduces a three-level model: regulations create and shape the shelter space, which in turn shapes the risk environments residents experience, ultimately reproducing structural vulnerabilities. Regulations determine conditions of shelter stays, which influence daily experiences and well-being, and collectively reinforce structural inequalities, amplifying rather than alleviating residents’ challenges. This study explores institutional level policy, analysing key guidelines in shelters, including zero-tolerance substance use policies, payment for shelter accommodation, inflexible limits on shelter stays, and subsequent shelter transition for HSRs. The interconnection between safety and zero-tolerance substance policies in shelter settings, the detrimental effects of frequent transitions on HSRs’ wellbeing and substance use, and the need for a more individualized approach to permitted stay durations have emerged as key challenges in shelter spaces. This study highlights that vulnerability in shelters is environmentally produced, structurally patterned, and spatially regulated. We argue that managing substance use within shelters requires a closer examination of the impact of common policies, as well as the shelter transitions.
Shelters should provide individualized support, flexible regulations, and harm-informed approaches while minimizing transitions to improve stability, well-being, and residents’ pathways towards social reintegration.

2.title: The Shelter as an “Open Prison”: Care, Control, and the Spatialization of Urban Vulnerability in Athens
2.abstract:
The experience of homelessness is not shaped solely by the absence of housing, but also by the institutional spaces designed to address it. Within this context, local actors operate as key service providers, functioning simultaneously as mechanisms of protection for the homeless and as instruments for safeguarding the image of the continuously transforming city.
A paradigmatic example of such spaces is homeless shelters, which emerge as inherently ambivalent sites. On the one hand, they articulate a discourse of care, albeit residual, within the framework of an emergency-oriented model of homelessness management. On the other hand, they operate as spaces that obscure and render poverty invisible, while contributing to the reproduction of marginalization. At the same time, shelters constitute sites where social relations, identities, and practices, including forms of resistance and exclusion, are actively produced and negotiated under conditions of constraint.
Drawing on ethnographic observation and in-depth interviews conducted in a municipal shelter in central Athens, this paper examines how the spatial position and regulatory framework of the facility shape the lived experiences of its residents. The shelter is approached as a socially produced space that, at both material and symbolic levels, determines who deserves to inhabit it, under what conditions, and at what cost.
Situated within the broader urban context of crisis, the shelter is analyzed as part of the urban management of marginality: a mechanism that absorbs the most visible manifestations of housing deprivation without challenging the structural conditions that produce it. In doing so, the paper contributes to debates on the spatialization of urban vulnerability and the limits of temporary housing policies.

3.title: Sick of Waiting: Historical Disease and the Demographic Transition Dynamics

authors.name: Evi Antonopoulou
authors.affiliation: PhD (c) Athens University of Economics and Business

3.abstract:
This paper examines whether the historical disease environment shaped the timing and structure of the First Demographic Transition and the accumulation of human capital. Drawing on Unified Growth Theory, we test whether historical pathogen prevalence acted as a structural constraint on education, fertility behavior, and demographic takeoff.
Using a three-tiered cross-country empirical strategy, we first assess the relationship between pathogen stress and pre-transition human capital and fertility (1870–1930). We then analyze its effect on the timing of demographic transition onset across distinct transition waves. Finally, we examine whether historical morbidity influenced the stock of human capital at the moment of transition onset.
We find that higher historical pathogen prevalence is associated with lower educational attainment and higher fertility prior to the transition. For early-transitioning countries, pathogen stress significantly delayed demographic takeoff. In contrast, for later transition waves, this effect is partially reversed, consistent with the role of post-war international health interventions that compressed demographic change. Countries with heavier historical disease burdens also entered the transition with lower human capital stocks. These findings suggest that the epidemiological environment constituted a deep structural factor shaping demographic timing and long-run development trajectories.

3.title: Implementation of Health Policy and Contemporary Inequality

authors.name: Iya Dehtyarova
authors.affiliation: Dnipro Institute of Medicine and Public Health, Ukraine

3.abstract:
Globally, healthcare constitutes a central domain of human development and remains embedded in patterns of systemic social inequality. The healthcare sector performs a critical social function by shaping population health outcomes. Key determinants include socioeconomic status, environmental conditions, education, spatial organization (urban versus rural), and housing quality. At these levels, a robust scholarly debate has emerged concerning both the persistence and expansion of inequality. Disparities are evident in access to high-quality healthcare services, including prevention and treatment; to adequate nutrition; and to the broader capacity to maintain a healthy lifestyle - particularly in urban areas, which tend to be most vulnerable.
In response to unequal access to healthcare, national and regional authorities in the European Union and Ukraine have initiated the development and implementation of public health strategies and programs at multiple governance levels.
The objective of this study is to examine the public health sector within the EU and compare it with Ukraine to formulate policy recommendations aimed at mitigating inequalities in access to healthcare services. The study also seeks to contribute to the development of new standards and a comprehensive framework for effective public health policymaking.
A crucial component involves the synthesis of information regarding public policy instruments designed to improve population health, extend life expectancy, enhance quality of life, prevent disease, and promote healthy lifestyles. The study adopts an interdisciplinary and systemic approach, employing methods of analysis, synthesis, generalization, comparison, and economic-statistical evaluation.
The empirical basis includes survey data from Ukrainian and international scholars, as well as statistics from national agencies in the EU and Ukraine. Key indicators include urbanization levels, gross domestic product, environmental pollution, mortality rates, and other relevant economic, social, and health-related variables.

3.title: Pandemic crisis from epicenter to periphery: territorial inequalities and mortality during covid-19 in northern Portugal.
3.abstract:
Territorial inequalities in health and mortality constitute a structural feature of long-term demographic regimes. From the nineteenth century to the present, differences in exposure to disease, vulnerability, and survival have been closely associated with place, socio-economic conditions, and unequal access to healthcare. The COVID-19 pandemic once again demonstrated that health crises tend to amplify pre-existing inequalities, as was also observed during the 1918 influenza pandemic.
This study examines the territorial impact of COVID-19 in Northern Portugal, focusing on the regions of Tâmega e Sousa and the Ave Valley, with particular attention to the municipality of Vizela during the initial phase of the pandemic. At the national level, in March 2020, 143 out of 308 municipalities recorded a number of deaths above the reference period, corresponding to approximately 46% of the total, highlighting differentiated territorial patterns in mortality. At the regional level, significant inequalities in access to healthcare are observed. While municipalities such as Vizela show average travel times to hospital care of less than ten minutes, more peripheral areas, such as Mondim de Basto, exceed thirty minutes. At the same time, asymmetries in the distribution of medical resources persist, reflecting structural inequalities in access to care.
Through an approach combining demographic and spatial analysis, this study demonstrates that factors such as healthcare accessibility, age structure, and territorial organization contributed to differentiated pandemic outcomes. Rather than representing an exceptional rupture, COVID-19 is interpreted as a critical episode that reveals and reinforces persistent patterns of health inequality.
By linking contemporary evidence with a historical-demographic perspective, this study contributes to understanding the relationships between territory, population vulnerability, and access to healthcare, highlighting the importance of long-term and spatial approaches in shaping more equitable public policies.

4.title: Disorientation, Un-homing, and the Criminalization of Memory: Rethinking Urban Displacement in Sur (Amed/Diyarbakır)
4.abstract:
This paper examines urban displacement in Sur (Diyarbakır) not merely as the physical relocation of populations, but as a multi-layered process that reconfigures the relationship between space, memory, and belonging. Building on critical urban geography and forced migration studies, it argues that displacement unfolds through intersecting regimes of violence, including militarization, legal-administrative intervention, and neoliberal urban restructuring. These processes do not operate sequentially but simultaneously, producing overlapping forms of dispossession and spatial reordering.

Drawing on the concepts of “homeplace” (bell hooks,1997) and the “hunted home” (Nadera Shalhoub-Kevorkian,2015), the paper conceptualizes displacement as a form of un-homing that targets the home as both a material and mnemonic infrastructure. In Sur, the destruction of housing during the 2015–2016 military operations, followed by state-led reconstruction and commodification, not only displaced residents but also disrupted spatial familiarity and collective memory. This paper introduces the concept of disorientation to capture how the erasure of streets, landmarks, and everyday spatial references undermines inhabitants’ ability to navigate, recognize, and reinhabit urban space.

Furthermore, the paper argues that displacement in Sur involves the criminalization of memory, where acts of remembering, witnessing, and narrating are subjected to legal and political repression. In this context, displacement extends beyond forced mobility to encompass epistemic and affective dimensions, reshaping how space is inhabited and remembered. At the same time, the paper highlights counter-processes of emplacement, including local memory practices, digital archiving, and everyday forms of staying, through which displaced subjects attempt to reconstitute relations to place.

By foregrounding disorientation and memory as central to urban displacement, the paper contributes to ongoing debates on intersecting displacements and calls for a rethinking of place as a contested and continuously reconfigured socio-spatial relation.

4.title: Contesting displacement: staying, returning, and the politics of place in post-disaster settings
4.abstract: While displacement has been extensively studied in urban contexts, this paper extends the discussion to post-disaster settings, examining how displacement and emplacement are shaped through the interaction of place-based relations, infrastructures, and recovery processes. It presents the conceptual foundations of ongoing doctoral research on post-disaster (im)mobility in Southern Europe. In the context of a changing climate, the paper argues for an expanded understanding of displacement, one that goes beyond forced mobility to encompass a spectrum of (im)mobility across both urban and rural settings. Displacement after disaster is thus approached not as a single outcome, but as a contested process through which place is disrupted and re-made. Challenging dominant frameworks that equate displacement exclusively with physical relocation, the paper positions (im)mobility as a central analytical lens for understanding how communities navigate trajectories of staying, moving, or returning. In doing so, it contributes to debates on climate (im)mobility by foregrounding the relational dimensions of displacement, including care practices, place attachment, and everyday negotiations of belonging. In dialogue with recent flood events in Southern Europe, including Storm Daniel in Thessaly and the Valencia floods, the paper proposes that the rupture of place is produced not only through physical destruction, but also through uneven recovery processes and infrastructural failure. In this context, the paper argues that austerity legacies and uneven infrastructural maintenance shape uneven possibilities of staying, moving, or returning. The paper examines practices of care and place attachment as forms of emplacement that reconstitute socio-spatial relations. These practices are shown to operate under–and in tension with–conditions of uneven recovery. By integrating insights from critical geography, disaster governance, and climate (im)mobilities scholarship, the paper contributes to broader debates on how post-disaster (im)mobility is lived and contested–and how place, far from being simply lost, is actively remade through everyday practices of staying, moving, and returning.

4.title: Places lost, places found, places displacing: narrative constructions of place at Viktoria Square
4.abstract:
The proposed announcement is based on early findings of the doctoral research I conduct at Viktoria Square in Athens, using field observation, informal discussions and semi-structured walking interviews with a variety of respondents that have lived or worked in the area.

We take as principle that places are not synonymous with the geographical and material site they occupy; they are created through narratives and are neither universal nor objective. A usual hypothesis among relevant bibliography proposes that place comes to being through an influx of memory into space.

Guided by these propositions, we analyse the construction of two different “places” at Viktoria Square.
- A lost place of a middle-class, prestigious, homogeneously Greek neighbourhood which is often invoked by elderly respondents. This place is created in a contrast with todays’ multinational, working-class.
- A place of resistance and solidarity which, across different narratives, may be considered lost, persisting or imminent. This place is found on the remarks of progressive, politicised respondents and in posters, slogans on the wall, pamphlets and demonstrations. It is narratively constructed around squats, the movement of solidarity towards immigrants and the response to the development of fascist groups in the area.

By addressing these “places” we can then ask how places can actually displace; the constructed place of one group can act as a rejecting discourse for another group. In Viktoria, the discourse surrounding the lost place of affluence and homogeneity is engulfed in a sentiment of rejection towards immigrants, often utilised by extremist groups and government practices of intimidation and control.

Thus, we discuss how places concurring at the same geographical site can be oppositional to each other. The imbalance in power between the social groups that construct them is translated in material consequences, with the danger of material displacement always present.

4.title: Urban transformations and elective minorities: Creative individuals on survival mode in the city centre, First findings and discussion of empirical research in Istanbul

authors.name: Eirini Oraiopoulou
authors.affiliation: AUTH, Faculty of Engineering, School of Architecture, Department of Urban and Regional Planning and Development

4.abstract:
Since the vast opening of Turkey in the global economy, the inner areas of Istanbul’s historical center have been going under urban transformations in different and multiple spatio-temporal waves, resembling a complex domino effect.
The proposed presentation is based on an empirical research that took place in Istanbul and focuses on a group of people: “intersectionally creative” -associated (in international and Istanbul’s bibliography) with urban transformations -mostly gentrification studies and often identified with pioneer gentrifiers.
As living within the city’s central areas forms a structural element for the lives of the people in focus- the research (which was mainly conducted in situ, through in-depth interviews) follows their residential biographies as “habitation trajectories” in relation to the centre’s urban transformations and their everyday lives.
The notion of “surviving /staying alive” in the city, repeatedly appears in their narratives, tracing a state of constant precariousness, and resembling aspects of the “minority” concept – which is an idiosyncratic element of Istanbul- now revisited in the context of the contemporary- under transformation city, forming an active oxymoron in relation to aspects of elective belonging (M. Savage) which also emerge from the same narratives.
Within the expected reasons for organizing a living there -centrality, affordability, social heterogeneity (diversity/ superdiversity), the latter is further examined - within the scope of everyday life and co-habitation co- existence with reference to D.Massey’s approach on the event of place and throwntogetherness.
Through this examination issues of “difference” and intersectionality emerge (gender, cultural, social, the status of a “creative”, being single, being a woman, being all of the above together, unmarried couple, etc.) that reflect the groups’ s position and precariousness within the city and within the contemporary Turkish society- thus questioning and tracing aspects of belonging beyond the area and the city.

4.title: Beyond Camp vs Market: Housing Regimes and Multiplied Displacement in Athens and Berlin
4.abstract: Displacement in European cities does not end upon arrival but unfolds as an ongoing and multiplied process across institutional, spatial, and everyday domains. This paper examines how different urban configurations of refugee accommodation—camp clearance in Athens and camp expansion in Berlin—produce distinct yet intersecting trajectories of displacement, reshaping relations to place and housing and producing instability across both mobility and enforced stasis. Based on qualitative and ethnographic research with affected populations and institutional actors, we juxtapose two seemingly opposed housing regimes that, in practice, converge in generating dispossession. In Athens, the closure of urban camps such as Eleonas has not marked a transition to inclusion but a displacement into a highly segregated system of extra-urban confinement camps. As a result, more than half of the asylum seekers seek refuge in the city through informal, overcrowded, and extractive rental arrangements, where exploitation substitutes for formal exclusion, and displacement is dispersed and privatized through the market. In Berlin, by contrast, the expansion of large reception facilities, “housing-like” camps and container-based accommodations institutionalize displacement. Refugees—including those with legal status and employment—are frequently unable to exit these facilities due to structural barriers in the housing market. Camps thus function as long-term holding infrastructures, producing a condition of enforced immobility that mirrors forms of urban homelessness. The paper conceptualizes these dynamics as a continuum of multiplied displacement, in which both camps and housing markets operate as mechanisms of racialized control, housing exploitation and banishment. We argue that both models reveal a shared logic: the systematic denial of secure housing through an expansion of campization as means of governing refugee presence in the city. In this sense, housing emerges not as a solution to displacement, but as one of its primary instruments.

4.title: What's in a square meter?

authors.name: Nikolaos Vrantsis
authors.affiliation: Institute for Housing and Urban Research

4.abstract: This text examines how urban land valorization restructures housing relations and class divisions in post-crisis Greece. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork in western Thessaloniki, it situates eviction campaigns by small landowners in 2020 within broader transformations in the political economy of land. It develops a Marxian account of urban ground rent, emphasizing its class character under rising land values and expanded housing assetization. Greece is approached as a historically specific urban land property regime, shaped by possessive familialism and reconfigured after the sovereign debt crisis through austerity and renewed real estate investment. Focusing on western Thessaloniki, the article traces alliances linking developers, construction firms, financial intermediaries, transnational investors and segments of small landownership. It argues that the rent gaps and their closure are linked to the differentiated returns across the actors of this alliance. As these alliances consolidate, pressures vis-à-vis returns are pushed downward, intensifying evictions as moments in the realization of urban ground rent. The text concludes that struggles over urban land constitute a central axis of class conflict in contemporary Greek cities.

4.title: Contesting displacement: Struggles for place in the city of Athens
4.abstract:
What does it mean to be displaced, often more than once, in a city marked by overlapping unsettlements? This paper conceptualizes displacement as a set of processes that rupture the relationship between people and place(s), producing forms of un-homing that unsettle relations, encounters, and practices of belonging. Drawing on an ongoing research project in Athens (H.F.R.I. Project Nο.: 28207), the paper examines intersecting displacement processes across multiple domains, including housing commercialization, touristification, asylum accommodation policies, and everyday racism. It argues that experiences of displacement must be understood alongside practices of contestation, as well as the embodied, everyday strategies through which affected subjects cope and sustain forms of belonging in place. Although settlement/emplacement and displacement are often framed as oppositional, the paper emphasizes their co-constitution.
Empirically, the paper highlights practices such as resistance to involuntary relocation among asylum seekers, everyday homemaking within camps, mobility between isolated camps and urban centers to maintain social ties, translocal connections that exceed displacement pressures, individual usually invisible practices as well as collective actions against housing precarity and gentrification, and informal mutual aid and neighborhood solidarity. These practices are approached as everyday acts of habitation that sustain relationships to people and place, illuminating how affected populations enact their right to the city; in the words of Lefebvre, a right that ‘legitimates the refusal to allow oneself to be removed from urban reality by a discriminatory and segregative organization’ (Lefebvre 1996). Building on Massey’s relational understanding of place, home, and belonging, the analysis explores what it means to struggle for place in a context of intersecting displacements and to attempt settlement within conditions of ongoing unsettlement. It asks how place is reconfigured through displacement and which dimensions of place are crucial for understanding both displacement and emplacement.

4.title: From displacement to emplacement? Rethinking migrants’ relationships to place across times of uncertainty

authors.name: Marina Nikolova
authors.affiliation: Research Associate, Hellenic Foundation for European and Foreign Policy (ELIAMEP)

authors.name: Apostolos G. Papadopoulos
authors.affiliation: Professor, Department of Geography, Harokopio University of Athens

4.abstract:
This paper explores how migrant women’s relationships to place are reconfigured through ongoing and intersecting forms of displacement shaped by migration regimes, labour precarity, and geopolitical change, focusing on women migrants from Ukraine in Athens across two periods marked by extreme uncertainty (2013–2014 and 2022). It examines how shifting socio-political conditions reshape experiences of mobility, inclusion, and belonging over time.
Drawing on qualitative interviews with four distinct groups of respondents - economic migrants (primarily women employed in domestic and care work) in Greece, returnees and family members in Ukraine in 2013 and 2014, as well as newly arrived migrants under temporary protection, and long-term residents in 2022 - the paper adopts a comparative temporal lens to analyse how different migration trajectories, legal statuses, and life-course positions produce uneven and partial forms of emplacement.
These forms of emplacement are reflected in migrants’ fragmented attachments to place across everyday life, including insecure housing, unstable employment in gendered labour sectors, and changing access to social networks and institutional support over time. The findings show that emplacement does not constitute a stable endpoint but remains continuously negotiated under conditions of uncertainty.
This paper contributes to urban geographical debates on migration, displacement, and the production of urban place by interrogating how emplacement is shaped through intersecting regimes of mobility, labour, and crisis over time. In particular, it foregrounds emplacement as an uneven, gendered, and temporally differentiated process that unfolds through everyday practices and shifting socio-political conditions. By focusing on Ukrainian migrant women in Athens across two periods under extreme socio-economic conditions, the paper highlights how legal status, labour precarity, and transnational family arrangements form pathways of belonging in the city.

4.title: Through the gates: place-based education as practice of re-emplacement in touristified Florence
4.abstract:
Processes of sociospatial displacement linked to touristification and housing financialization reshape urban functions, everyday practices, imaginaries and access to “place” in cities. Florence is exemplary of such dynamics with its UNESCO centre being subject to rapid multifaceted transformations. In this context, this contribution focuses primarily on indirect and lengthy forms of displacement to suggest acts of re-emplacement through geography education. It reflects on the Erasmus+ BIP "A Gaze upon the City", coordinated by the University of Florence in collaboration with partners from Portugal and Spain. The project brought together an interdisciplinary group of students and lecturers to investigate the porte (gates) of Florence as physical-symbolic thresholds through which to explore ongoing transformations.

Originally part of the city’s historical fortification system, the gates nowadays survive as fragmented and often overlooked urban remnants, absorbed into the contemporary urban fabric and mobility infrastructures, and overseeing the transforming city in robust silence. Through walking methodologies, observation, mapping, ethnographic inquiry and acoustic explorations, the project explored the changing meanings, uses and imaginaries surrounding these spatialities of passage. Rather than approaching place as fixed or bounded within the displacement processes, the project considered the porte as relational and contested, where displacement-induced dynamics become particularly visible and read from vantage yet ignored viewpoints.

The contribution argues that place-based educational practices can function as forms of re-emplacement within contexts marked by multifacetedf displacements, varying from material to symbolic. Through situated and active forms of geographic knowledge production, students critically engaged with urban transformations while experimenting with alternative ways of relating to and interpreting the city. In such a gate-centered epistemological shift, educational fieldwork thus emerges not only as a methodological tool for urban critical understanding, but also as a pedagogical practice capable of rethinking the transformative role of place and reopening possibilities for situated forms of re-emplacement.

4.title: Reclaiming "Τόπος": Intersecting Urban Displacements and the Erosion of Intangible Place
4.abstract:
Contemporary urban landscapes are increasingly defined by multiple, intersecting forms of displacement that transcend simple physical relocation. This research explores the centrality of "Τόπος"—a concept encompassing the intangible values, memory, aura, and plurality of a location, expressed by Merleau-Ponty and Norberg-Schulz —arguing that the rupture of the relationship between people and place constitutes the core of the experience, even for those who "stay put". Drawing on the theories of Davidson and Zukin, it distinguishes between direct displacement, driven by property demands, and indirect displacement, which occurs when the social fabric, local shops, and communal facilities are replaced by standardized spaces dictated by gentrification and touristification. This "mutation of place" generates an ongoing, non-visible loss of the feeling of belonging and identity, while transforming the living community into a commodified asset.
The rise of the "platform economy," particularly through Airbnb and the influx of "mobility lifestylers" and digital nomads, further complicates these dynamics. These short-term residents redefine gradually, and in a non-direct way, the urban environment to suit their consumption-oriented needs, often at the expense of local "lived space" and "embodied history". In cities like Athens, these forces threaten the very "spirit of place". This study reimagines how the "right to place" can be reclaimed by exploring practices of emplacement and the reactivation of aura and memory as counter-processes to displacement. By foregrounding Τόπος, we can better understand the subjective, intangible "un-homing" that characterizes the contemporary urban polycrisis.

5.title: Shoreline evolution of Naxos Airport Lagoon

authors.name: Eleni Achmakidou
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

authors.name: Evangelos Spyrou
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

authors.name: Anna Karkani
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

authors.name: Giannis Saitis
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

authors.name: Niki Evelpidou
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens
