5.abstract: Coastal lagoons and dunes are highly valuable but vulnerable systems, impacted by sea-level rise, storms and intense human pressures, including tourism and infrastructure development. Robust multi-temporal shoreline mapping is essential for understanding coastal evolution and supporting effective protection and management strategies. This study investigates shoreline evolution at the Naxos Airport Lagoon, located along the western coast of Naxos, within the Cyclades, one of the Mediterranean regions most vulnerable to climate change impacts. The analysis combines historical aerial imagery (1960–1989) with recent high-precision RTK-GNSS shoreline surveys conducted between 2022 and 2024. Historical shorelines are digitized from georeferenced aerial photographs following established photointerpretation approaches. Contemporary shoreline positions are measured using RTK-GNSS techniques. All shoreline datasets are integrated in a GIS environment and analyzed with the Digital Shoreline Analysis System (DSAS), using standard metrics such as End Point Rate (EPR), Net Shoreline Movement (NSM), and Linear/Weighted Linear Regression Rates to quantify erosion and accretion trends over both long (multi-decadal) and short (2022–2024) periods. The combined analysis clarifies how natural processes and human interventions have reshaped the lagoon’s fringe over ~60 years. The results support identification of critical stretches requiring protection or restoration of dunes and wetlands and offer a quantitative baseline for future monitoring, coastal hazard assessment and integrated management of the Naxos Airport Lagoon system.

5.title: Integrating Seascape–Landscape Configuration Metrics into Coastal Protection modelling on Greek Islandscapes
5.abstract:
Greek islands are coastal boundary environments where terrestrial, coastal, and marine processes interact under increasing pressure from sea-level rise, erosion, extreme events, tourism development, and other forms of global environmental change. While these island “edge-scapes” are highly exposed, they host habitats such as dunes, wetlands and seagrass meadows that act as a natural defense against coastal flooding and erosion through wave attenuation, storm surge reduction and sediment stabilization. However, coastal protection assessments often represent habitats mainly through their presence or extent, without considering whether their spatial configuration enhances or limits their protective function. Here we present a workflow that embeds habitat connectivity and fragmentation metrics into an established coastal protection model to better capture where coastal habitats provide effective protection. Habitat distribution data are combined with biophysical and socio‑economic variables describing (i) protection capacity (e.g., geomorphology, slope, sediment accretion, seabed and emerged habitats), (ii) exposure (e.g., wave climate, storm surge, sea‑level change, winds and currents), and (iii) societal demand (e.g., population density, infrastructure and cultural assets). Configuration is quantified using spatial pattern metrics derived from FRAGSTATS to capture patch density, shape, aggregation, and fragmentation of the habitats. Configuration effects are most apparent for seagrass habitats dominated by Posidonia oceanica and Cymodocea nodosa; island coastlines characterized by dense, aggregated, and well‑connected seagrass seascapes are associated with higher modelled capacity, whereas fragmented or sparse patterns correspond to reduced capacity even where habitat presence is recorded. Terrestrial coastal habitats further modulate capacity locally, particularly where dunes and wetlands occur adjacent to high‑exposure shorelines. The approach supports island‑focused marine spatial planning and nature‑based solutions by accounting for both habitat extent and seascape–landscape structure.
Keywords: islands; coastal protection; Posidonia oceanica; connectivity; fragmentation

5.title: Treeline Dynamics: How Much Do We Know? Addressing Local Specificities and Global Trends

authors.name: Stefanos Boutsios
authors.affiliation: Department of Geography, Harokopio University, Athens, Greece

authors.name: George Kefalas
authors.affiliation: Department of Geography, Harokopio University, Athens, Greece

authors.name: Vasileios Detsis
authors.affiliation: Department of Economics and Sustainable Development, Harokopio University, Athens,Greece

authors.name: Panteleimon Xofis
authors.affiliation: Department of Natural Environment and Climatic Resilience, Democritus University of Thrace, Drama,Greece

authors.name: Evangelia G. Drakou
authors.affiliation: Department of Geography, Harokopio University, Athens, Greece

5.abstract:
Treeline ecotones constitute dynamic transitional landscapes that have exhibited global upward altitudinal shifts in recent years, a phenomenon closely linked to climate change. The climatic signal of these dynamics has triggered an explosion of research interest over the last two decades. Changes in forest limits represent complex processes with profound ecological consequences, including changes in biodiversity and carbon storage dynamics.
Despite the general global trend of treeline advancement, the literature frequently documents divergent responses to climate change, including stability or even recession. These discrepancies highlight a prevailing "climate bias," as ecotone dynamics rarely follow climatic warming in a linear manner. Factors such as time lags in tree response, water stress, biotic interactions, and disturbances decisively shape their evolution. Overlooking these processes, combined with short-term time series, often leads to the misinterpretation of transient fluctuations as permanent trends.
This complexity is particularly evident in the Mediterranean basin, a climate change "hotspot," where rising temperatures are accompanied by intensifying aridity that potentially constrains growth in forests at their ecological margins. Despite its significance, the region remains underrepresented in research. Furthermore, in Mediterranean mountain landscapes, distinguishing between climate-driven shifts and secondary forest succession—related to historical land-use changes (e.g., grazing abandonment)—further complicates the interpretation of observed range shift patterns.
Understanding the natural processes of treeline dynamics requires moving beyond single-factor approaches toward multifactorial analytical frameworks, with a particular emphasis on complex and understudied environments.

5.title: Coastal Lagoons of Greece: An inventory and implications for future challenges

authors.name: Georgia Kakoura
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

authors.name: Evangelos Spyrou
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

authors.name: Alexandros Liaskos
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

authors.name: Niki Evelpidou
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

5.abstract: Coastal lagoons are unique ecosystems that provide a wide range of environmental services. However, they are prone to sea-level rise (SLR), due to both human activities and climate change. The Greek coastline is characterized by several coastal lagoons. In this work, we digitized all coastal lagoons along the Greek coastline (a total of 152 lagoons), using satellite images. We calculated their dimensions and physiographical characteristics, such as such as lagoon length, width, area, perimeter and sandspit morphology. We further conducted a multi-temporal analysis using Sentinel-2 imagery (2015–2025) to assess water surface extent and water quality trends for the five largest lagoons. In order to highlight their vulnerability to sea level rise, we considered two Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP1-2.6 and SSP5-8.5) scenarios for future sea-level rise in the Mediterranean context. Where there were available projections also considering Vertical Land Motion (VLM), we used those instead. All lagoons, their computed parameters and projections have been integrated into a freely accessible WebGIS application. Our results show that 8 to 25% of the Greek lagoons will be fully inundated, depending on the scenario considered, while a substantially larger number are expected to experience partial breaching. Regarding the five largest lagoons, remote sensing analysis revealed predominantly stable conditions. However, Tsoukali lagoon exhibited a significant expansion trend; likely linked to sediment starvation caused by dam construction. In terms of water quality, all lagoons remain eutrophic, with Vistonis as the most ecologically stressed with recorded anoxia events. Collectively, these findings underscore the critical susceptibility of Greek coastal lagoons to both climatic and anthropogenic stressors.

5.title: Landscape metrics in relation to ecosystem services and biodiversity across European coastal zone
5.abstract: Coastal landscapes represent highly dynamic socio-ecological systems where terrestrial and marine processes interact, generating complex spatial patterns that strongly influence biodiversity and ecosystem service (ES) provision. Despite their ecological importance, coastal zones are among the most heavily impacted environments globally, experiencing increasing pressure from land-use change, habitat degradation, and cumulative anthropogenic stressors. Understanding how landscape structure shapes ecological processes and multifunctionality is therefore critical for effective ecosystem management. This study examines the relationship between landscape structure, biodiversity, and ecosystem service provision across European coastal zones. Biodiversity–Ecosystem Services (BES) bundles were identified using an unsupervised clustering approach (k-means) applied to harmonized European datasets, incorporating indicators of species and habitat richness alongside provisioning, regulating, and cultural services. Four distinct BES bundles were derived, representing characteristic combinations of biodiversity and ecosystem service supply. To explore how landscape structure influences the spatial distribution of these bundles, a suite of landscape metrics describing composition and configuration was calculated at multiple scales. The relationship between landscape metrics and BES bundle membership was modelled using Geographical Random Forest (GRF), a spatially explicit machine learning approach that accounts for spatial heterogeneity by calibrating local models. Results reveal clear spatial patterns in BES bundle distribution, ranging from low-functioning landscapes to multifunctional systems characterized by high biodiversity and service provision. Landscape metrics related to fragmentation, connectivity, and heterogeneity emerge as key influencing factors, although their importance varies spatially. This highlights the non-stationary nature of landscape–function relationships in coastal environments. The findings demonstrate the potential of landscape metrics as proxies for biodiversity and ecosystem service patterns, while emphasizing the importance of spatially explicit approaches. The proposed framework supports large-scale ecological assessment and provides insights for ecosystem-based management, conservation planning, and restoration across European coastal zones.

5.title: A Mediterranean-Wide Spatial Analysis of Tidal Notches: Calibrating Holocene Relative Sea-Level Changes and Tectonic Drivers.

authors.name: Konstantina Lymperopoulou
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

authors.name: Anna Karkani
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

authors.name: Alexandros Liaskos
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

authors.name: Niki Evelpidou
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

5.abstract:
Tidal notches are among the most reliable geomorphological indicators of past sea levels, providing high-resolution data on the interaction between eustatic changes and regional tectonics. This study presents a comprehensive spatial analysis of a newly developed database comprising over 650 tidal notch sites across the Mediterranean basin, including Greece, Italy, Malta, Croatia, France, Spain and Turkey.
The research employs a multi-proxy approach, integrating morphological parameters such as notch height, vertex depth, and profile geometry with lithological data and bioerosion rates. A key component of this study is the application of a rigorous chronological framework, utilizing calibrated carbon-14 dating and biological markers to establish a precise timeline for Holocene relative sea-level (RSL) changes.
Preliminary results indicate that tidal notches are a widespread geomorphological feature found throughout the Mediterranean basin. The presence of tidal notches throughout the basin, regardless of local tectonic movements, underscores their value as a fundamental tool for understanding the evolution of Mediterranean coasts. Despite the abundance of these landforms, a lot of them remain undated due to the destructive effects of bioerosion on biological markers. The findings offer a refined model for Mediterranean coastal evolution, distinguishing between climate-driven sea-level rise and geodynamic land movements. This work provides essential baseline data for assessing the future vulnerability of coasts in the context of accelerating global sea-level rise.

5.title: Heat at the edge, rethinking urban vulnerability in the coastal city of Kalamata
5.abstract: Under conditions of ongoing global environmental change, coastal cities operate as critical boundary zones where climatic, ecological, and socio-spatial processes intersect. This paper examines Kalamata, a medium-sized coastal city in southern Greece, as an urban “edge-scape” where heat exposure is shaped by the interaction of coastal microclimates, built environments, and seasonal population dynamics. While heat vulnerability assessments have largely focused on metropolitan areas, smaller coastal cities remain underexplored despite experiencing compound pressures. In Kalamata, elevated humidity, proximity to the sea, and limited urban ventilation interact with densely built structures and tourism-driven seasonal intensification, amplifying perceived heat stress and everyday exposure. Methodologically, the paper develops a composite spatial framework and mapping approach using openly available datasets, integrating population distribution, built-up intensity, and relative access to green infrastructure. By operationalizing green space as a proportion of total urban area, the cartographic analysis captures and visualizes unequal access to cooling resources across the city. This approach enables the identification of spatial patterns of vulnerability beyond conventional surface temperature assessments. The paper introduces the concept of coastal amplification of heat vulnerability, arguing that edge conditions, such as humidity, seasonal population fluctuations, and coastal spatial configurations, mediate and intensify the impacts of extreme heat. In this sense, Kalamata functions as a sensitive indicator of emerging socio-environmental pressures in Mediterranean coastal systems. By situating urban heat within a boundary landscape perspective, the study contributes to interdisciplinary discussions on environmental transformation at the edge, highlighting the need to integrate spatial representation, coastal dynamics and socio-spatial inequalities into climate adaptation and spatial planning strategies.

6.title: Reconfiguring Mediterranean invasion landscapes: Future habitat expansion and dispersal dynamics of Myocastor Coypus in Greece

authors.name: Alexandros D. Kouris
authors.affiliation: Department of Sustainable Agriculture, University of Patras, Patras, Greece

authors.name: Apostolos Christopoulos
authors.affiliation: Department of Zoology and Marine Biology, Faculty of Biology, National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, Athens, Greece

authors.name: Yiannis G. Zevgolis
authors.affiliation: Biodiversity Conservation Laboratory, Department of Environment, University of the Aegean, Mytilene, Greece

6.abstract:
Climate-driven environmental change is increasingly altering the spatial dynamics of biological
invasions, particularly for species tightly associated with freshwater systems and human-modified
landscapes. The semi-aquatic rodent Myocastor coypus has expanded rapidly across parts of
southern Europe, where its burrowing activity, herbivory, and occupation of riparian habitats
generate substantial ecological and economic impacts. In Greece, however, the potential for large-
scale range expansion under future climatic conditions remains insufficiently explored despite
growing evidence of establishment in lowland wetlands and drainage networks. A spatial modelling
framework based on Maximum Entropy algorithms was employed to reconstruct the environmental
niche of M. coypus using a nationwide occurrence dataset combined with climatic, hydrological,
edaphic, and land-cover predictors. Variable selection focused on hydroclimatic stability, thermal
tolerance, moisture availability, and landscape connectivity in order to capture the processes
governing dispersal across heterogeneous Mediterranean environments. Model performance
indicated strong predictive capacity, revealing that hydrological proximity and persistent surface
moisture overwhelmingly structure habitat suitability, while warmer thermal regimes substantially
reduce climatic barriers to establishment. Spatial projections under multiple future climate
trajectories revealed a marked reorganization of invasion-prone landscapes during the twenty-first
century. Environmentally suitable areas are projected to expand far beyond the species’ currently
documented distribution, particularly along riparian corridors, irrigated agricultural plains, artificial
water networks, and ecologically sensitive wetland systems. Several projected expansion zones
intersect with protected habitats and biodiversity-rich aquatic ecosystems, indicating an increasing
likelihood of ecological conflict between invasive spread and conservation priorities. The emerging
spatial configuration additionally suggests the formation of interconnected dispersal pathways
capable of accelerating secondary colonization between previously isolated hydrographic basins. The
projected redistribution of suitable habitat indicates that ongoing hydroclimatic change may
transform Greece into an increasingly favorable landscape for the persistence and spread of this
invasive mammal, reinforcing the urgency for spatially targeted surveillance and anticipatory
management strategies.

6.title: Spatial Hotspots and mortality corridors of herpetofauna: A multi-decadal geospatial analysis of wildlife–vehicle collisions in a Mediterranean river basin, Greece

authors.name: Alexandros D. Kouris
authors.affiliation: Department of Sustainable Agriculture, University of Patras, Patras, Greece

authors.name: Apostolos Christopoulos
authors.affiliation: Department of Zoology and Marine Biology, Faculty of Biology, National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, Athens, Greece

authors.name: Yiannis G. Zevgolis
authors.affiliation: Biodiversity Conservation Laboratory, Department of Environment, University of the Aegean, Mytilene, Greece

6.abstract: Linear transportation infrastructure increasingly reshapes ecological processes by generating spatially heterogeneous mortality risks across landscapes. Despite growing recognition of wildlife–vehicle collisions as a major conservation concern, spatially explicit assessments of road mortality in Mediterranean herpetofauna remain limited, particularly at large temporal and landscape scales. This study investigates the spatial configuration, clustering dynamics, and seasonal concentration of amphibian and reptile road mortality within the catchment basin of Spercheios River, a protected Mediterranean ecosystem of high conservation importance included in the Natura 2000 network. Using a long-term dataset (1997–2021), we analyzed 544 wildlife–vehicle collision records involving 23 herpetofaunal species to identify spatial mortality concentrations and landscape-scale collision patterns. Spatial analytical frameworks incorporating Kernel Density Estimation and hotspot analysis were employed to detect non-random aggregations of mortality events and delineate persistent collision corridors. Species-specific road mortality intensity was additionally quantified through a relative mortality index to evaluate differential vulnerability among taxa. Analyses revealed pronounced spatial autocorrelation in road mortality distribution, with distinct mortality hotspots concentrated along ecotonal zones linking wetlands, agricultural mosaics, and riparian habitats. Several statistically significant collision clusters persisted across years, indicating the existence of stable mortality corridors associated with recurrent movement pathways of herpetofauna. Seasonal analysis demonstrated a marked intensification of hotspot formation during spring, suggesting strong associations between road mortality patterns and seasonal behavioral ecology. Mortality intensity was disproportionately higher for large-bodied snake species, particularly the Eastern Montpellier snake, Grass snake, Caspian whipsnake, and the European glass lizard. Our findings demonstrate that herpetofauna road mortality within Mediterranean riverine systems is spatially structured rather than randomly distributed, emphasizing the importance of spatial statistical approaches for identifying high-risk road segments and prioritizing mitigation measures. Integrating hotspot detection and density-based spatial analyses provides a robust framework for conservation-oriented road planning and for reducing biodiversity losses in ecologically sensitive Mediterranean landscapes.

6.title: Movement of Bactrocera oleae Across Olive Grove–Forest Interfaces in a Mediterranean Landscape
6.abstract: Olive fly (Bactrocera oleae) is widely recognized as an important insect pest affecting olive cultivation in Mediterranean agroecosystems, with significant consequences for crop yield and oil quality. Existing management strategies primarily focus on population dynamics within olive groves, while the potential influence of adjacent non-crop habitats on pest ecology remains understudied. In the context of increasing temperatures and more frequent heat events associated with climate change, the role of landscape heterogeneity and microclimatic variability in shaping olive fly movement and persistence warrants further investigation. This study examined the occurrence of B. oleae in olive groves and adjacent forest habitats within a Mediterranean mosaic landscape on Lesvos Island, Greece. Baited McPhail traps were deployed along a spatial gradient extending from grove interiors to forest interiors (up to 300 m), while microclimatic conditions were monitored using fine-scale temperature measurements during the summer and autumn periods. Adult olive flies were consistently detected within olive groves, along grove–forest interfaces, and at distances up to 100 m inside pine forests, whereas captures at 300 m were minimal. Forest habitats exhibited lower temperatures than olive groves, and generally had conditions considered suitable for olive fly activity and survival. In addition, olive fly abundance near grove edges and forest-adjacent locations showed a negative association with temperature, suggesting increased utilization of cooler habitats during periods of elevated thermal stress. These findings indicate that adjacent forest habitats may provide temporary microclimatic shelter for olive flies and facilitate limited cross-habitat movement under high-temperature conditions. The study further demonstrates the ecological relevance of surrounding non-agricultural habitats in olive fly dynamics and highlights the importance of incorporating landscape context and microclimatic variation into integrated pest management approaches under future climatic conditions.

6.title: Agricultural landscapes shape habitat suitability patterns of the European rabbit in a Mediterranean island ecosystem

authors.name: Christina Valeta
authors.affiliation: Biodiversity Conservation Laboratory, Department of Environment, University of the Aegean, Mytilene, Greece

authors.name: Alexandros D. Kouris
authors.affiliation: Department of Sustainable Agriculture, University of Patras, Patras, Greece

authors.name: Foto Konsola
authors.affiliation: Biodiversity Conservation Laboratory, Department of Environment, University of the Aegean, Mytilene, Greece

authors.name: Yiannis G. Zevgolis
authors.affiliation: Biodiversity Conservation Laboratory, Department of Environment, University of the Aegean, Mytilene, Greece

6.abstract:
Mediterranean islands are increasingly experiencing ecological restructuring driven by the expansion
of introduced mammalian herbivores, whose establishment within fragmented insular landscapes
may generate profound consequences for vegetation dynamics, agricultural systems, and ecosystem
functioning. The European rabbit, Oryctolagus cuniculus, has exhibited substantial spatial expansion
on Lemnos Island, Greece, where its growing distribution across heterogeneous agroecosystems and
semi-natural habitats has raised increasing ecological and management concerns. Here, we applied a
species distribution modelling framework based on Maximum Entropy algorithms to investigate
habitat suitability patterns of O. cuniculus using an extensive occurrence dataset derived from
systematic field surveys. Environmental predictors included land-use composition, agricultural cover,
vegetation structure, topographic variables, climatic conditions, and anthropogenic landscape
features in order to identify the ecological factors associated with rabbit occurrence. Model outputs
demonstrated strong predictive performance and revealed substantial spatial heterogeneity in
habitat suitability across the island. Habitat suitability was strongly associated with agricultural
landscapes, cultivated areas, agro-pastoral systems, and lowland environments providing abundant
trophic resources and accessible foraging opportunities. Areas characterized by crop availability and
heterogeneous resource-rich mosaics exhibited particularly high predicted suitability, indicating the
importance of anthropogenic food subsidies in facilitating rabbit persistence and expansion. Spatial
projections identified extensive environmentally suitable areas across large portions of the island,
suggesting that current land-use configurations may facilitate continued expansion of rabbit
populations within Mediterranean insular ecosystems. The predicted distributional patterns indicate
that anthropogenic resource availability rather than climatic limitation may constitute the primary
driver shaping rabbit habitat suitability at the spatial scale examined. These findings highlight the
critical role of agricultural landscape structure in promoting the establishment and persistence of
introduced herbivorous mammals and provide a spatially explicit framework for future monitoring
and management strategies in insular Mediterranean environments.

6.title: Thermal landscapes of hidden architecture: Geospatial detection of thermal heterogeneity associated with European rabbit warrens

authors.name: Christina Valeta
authors.affiliation: Biodiversity Conservation Laboratory, Department of Environment, University of the Aegean, Mytilene, Greece

authors.name: Yiannis G. Zevgolis
authors.affiliation: Biodiversity Conservation Laboratory, Department of Environment, University of the Aegean, GR- 81132 Mytilene, Greece

6.abstract:
Subterranean burrow systems created by fossorial mammals represent concealed forms of biological
architecture capable of influencing environmental conditions beyond the underground spaces they
occupy. Despite their ecological importance, the extent to which these hidden structures generate
organized thermal patterns at the land surface remains poorly understood. In the European rabbit,
warrens form spatially complex subterranean networks whose ecological expression is typically
inferred from the distribution of visible entrances alone, potentially overlooking thermal patterns
associated with the underlying burrow system. To address this gap, we combined infrared
thermography with geospatial analyses to investigate whether rabbit warrens generate structured
thermal mosaics detectable at fine spatial scales. Thermal imagery was collected from multiple
independent warrens and converted into high-resolution thermal surfaces. Spatial analyses were
subsequently applied to quantify thermal clustering, local heterogeneity, and the spatial
configuration of temperature anomalies surrounding burrow entrances and across entire warrens. In
parallel, entrance density and spatial arrangement were used as indicators of subterranean
structural complexity in order to examine whether variation in surface thermal organization reflects
differences in hidden burrow architecture. Our analyses revealed that rabbit warrens generate
distinct and spatially structured thermal mosaics rather than isolated thermal anomalies. Burrow
entrances consistently corresponded to localized thermal hotspots relative to the surrounding
substrate; however, these anomalies were embedded within broader heterogeneous thermal fields
characterized by clear spatial clustering and non-random thermal organization. Furthermore,
warrens exhibiting greater entrance density and more complex entrance configuration displayed
increasingly pronounced thermal heterogeneity and stronger spatial structuring of surface
temperatures. These findings suggest that surface thermal patterning captures important aspects of
the organization of subterranean burrow systems. Overall, our study demonstrates that infrared
thermography integrated with geospatial analysis provides a powerful non-invasive framework for
detecting the thermal imprint of subterranean ecosystem engineering and advances the spatial
understanding of animal-generated microclimatic heterogeneity.

6.title: Landscape complexity rather than climate predicts habitat suitability for the Persian Squirrel

authors.name: Yiannis G. Zevgolis
authors.affiliation: Biodiversity Conservation Laboratory, Department of Environment, University of the Aegean, Mytilene, Greece

authors.name: Alexandros D. Kouris
authors.affiliation: Department of Sustainable Agriculture, University of Patras, Patras, Greece

authors.name: Apostolos Christopoulos
authors.affiliation: Department of Zoology and Marine Biology, Faculty of Biology, National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, Athens, Greece

6.abstract: Understanding the mechanisms governing species distributions is fundamental for predicting biodiversity responses to environmental change, particularly within insular ecosystems where spatial constraints and landscape heterogeneity strongly influence ecological processes. We investigated the habitat suitability patterns of the Persian squirrel (Sciurus anomalus), a regionally Vulnerable arboreal mammal, on Lesvos Island, Greece, using a species distribution modeling (SDM) framework based on the MaxEnt algorithm. To evaluate the relative influence of landscape and climatic drivers, we developed two competing SDMs: an environmental model including landscape composition and anthropogenic variables, and a second model integrating environmental predictors with bioclimatic variables associated with temperature and precipitation regimes. Both models produced high predictive performance, identifying clear spatial gradients in habitat suitability across the island. Suitable habitats were strongly concentrated in areas characterized by heterogeneous vegetation structure and persistent semi-natural landscape mosaics, whereas intensively modified or spatially homogeneous areas exhibited substantially lower predicted suitability. Jackknife analyses revealed that landscape-related variables contributed disproportionately to model gain and predictive stability, while the addition of climatic predictors resulted in only marginal improvements in explanatory power. Response curves further indicated that habitat suitability declined sharply beyond specific thresholds of landscape simplification and increasing isolation from structurally complex habitats. The spatial predictions also revealed a fragmented distribution of highly suitable habitat patches, suggesting potential restrictions in landscape connectivity for insular populations of S. anomalus. In contrast, climatic gradients showed weak spatial correspondence with predicted suitability patterns, indicating limited macroclimatic control at the scale examined. Our findings demonstrate that landscape complexity and habitat configuration are stronger determinants of Persian squirrel distribution than broad-scale climatic conditions within Mediterranean island ecosystems, highlighting the importance of integrating fine-resolution landscape predictors into SDMs for insular mammals and underscores the conservation value of maintaining heterogeneous and structurally connected landscapes for the long-term persistence of vulnerable arboreal species.

6.title: Spatial ecology of mammalian road mortality: hotspot persistence, spatial outliers, and collision risk patterns on a Mediterranean Island

6.abstract: Wildlife–vehicle collisions (WVCs) constitute a spatially structured form of anthropogenic mortality that can disproportionately affect insular mammal populations, particularly within Mediterranean landscapes characterized by ecological heterogeneity and fragmented habitat mosaics. Despite increasing concern regarding road-driven biodiversity loss, the spatial organization and temporal persistence of mammalian road mortality in island ecosystems remain poorly understood. This study examines the spatial ecology of WVCs on Lesvos through a long-term survey conducted across the island's 488.7 km primary road network between 2018 and 2024. Surveys focused on five terrestrial mammalian species: Red Fox, Beech Marten, Northern White-breasted Hedgehog, Least Weasel, and Persian Squirrel. To investigate the spatial structure of mortality events, we employed an integrated spatial-statistical framework combining Kernel Density Estimation (KDE), Getis–Ord Gi* hotspot analysis, and Anselin Local Moran’s I statistics. These approaches enabled the detection of persistent mortality hotspots, statistically significant spatial clusters, and localized outlier events across the transportation network. The analyses revealed strong spatial dependence in WVC occurrence, with recurrent hotspot concentrations primarily distributed in the central and southeastern sectors of the island. Several hotspot zones persisted through multiple survey years, suggesting the existence of chronic collision-risk corridors shaped by road configuration and surrounding landscape structure. Species-specific spatial patterns reflected ecological and behavioral differentiation among taxa. Mortality records of Persian Squirrel were strongly clustered near traditional olive grove systems, whereas Red Fox and Beech Marten exhibited broader and more spatially diffuse mortality distributions. By integrating multi-year monitoring with advanced spatial statistics, this study provides a geographically explicit framework for identifying collision-risk landscapes and informing spatially targeted mitigation planning in Mediterranean insular ecosystems.

7.title: LAND EVOLUTION MODELS: EXAMINING THE MIDTERM LANDSCAPE EVOLUTION OF VOURAIKOS RIVER BASIN, PELOPONNESE, GREECE.
7.abstract:
While the time horizon of the engineering works is about 100 years, the geomorphologist is interested in the long-term evolution of the landscape and the interplay between processes and forms along the course of centuries and even millennia.

Assuming that the governing equations are known, the need to run prolonged periods of simulations (centuries and millennia) based on these differential equations of computational fluid dynamics is limited, at least so far, by the computational cost they require. To this end, the development of a family of LEMs based on the concept of cellular automata has been an interesting and promising endeavor. LEMs utilize a sort of simplified Navier-Stokes equations that control material flow between cells, where each cell is affected only by its neighboring cells. This gives the computational advantage needed to simulate thousands of years within reasonable computing times.

One such LEM is CAESAR (Cellular Automaton Evolutionary Slope and River) model which we utilized to perform simulations in the Vouraikos River basin based on synthetic time series of precipitation. The aim of the work was to forecast the dynamic evolution of the middle part of the river (Kalavryta plain) over a 100 years’ period, and to estimate the average yearly sediment transport across selected cross sections.

The results showed that CAESAR can be useful in such studies despite its great sensitivity in the composition of the sediment, a parameter not easily tractable and largely variable within the domain. The average sediment transport rates proved comparable to existing estimates while it was found that some parts undergo erosion while other parts undergo deposition. CAESAR is indeed capable of providing localized results, but it seems that the model is more trustable for milder slopes than for steeper slopes.

7.title: Low relief, High Impact: Coastal Flood Dynamics in Paralia Katerinis
7.abstract: Here we study the geomorphological impact of the February 2026 flood event in Paralia Katerinis, a coastal area in Northen Greece. Paralia Katerinis is a low-gradient wave dominated coastal setting. The extent of the flooding is primarily attributed to the region’s low topographic relief and chronic sediment starvation caused by anthropogenic structures. Field surveys were conducted five weeks post-event to observe the area and collect sediment samples for grain size analysis. We generated a high-resolution Digital Elevation Model (DEM) using UAV-based photogrammetry to detect micro-topographic terrain changes and identify potential erosion and deposition patterns. Additionally, satellite remote sensing was utilized to map the maximum spatial extent of the flood, while Geographic Information Systems (GIS) are applied for spatial data processing. Our results suggest that the synergistic interaction of intense precipitation and an extreme storm surge, driven by a deep barometric low, astronomical tides, and severe wave run-up led to the flood event. We demonstrate how the combination of these factors can increase flood hazard in coastal settings, offering useful insights for future risk assessments and management in similar environments.

7.title: Assessing the Dispersal of Submarine Mine Tailings and their Ecological Impact on Benthic Foraminifera in Førdefjorden, Norway

authors.name: Panagiotis Bountouroglou
authors.affiliation: Aristotle University of Thessaloniki/ Universitetet i Bergen

7.abstract: Submarine tailing disposal from the mining operations at Engebøfjellet into Førdefjorden (Norway) commenced in 2025, resulting in the deposition of approximately 241,000 tons of mine waste in its first year alone. This active disposal of mine tailings posed significant environmental concerns, as the dispersal of fine sediments and associated pollutants can alter seabed conditions and impact benthic ecosystems. To evaluate these environmental consequences, a research cruise was conducted in Førdefjorden in collaboration with the University of Bergen (UiB). During the cruise, benthic foraminifera were utilized as sensitive bioindicators due to their rapid response to anthropogenic pressure and changing pollution levels. By analyzing both living and dead (fossil) assemblages from the collected sediment samples, both present and past environmental conditions were evaluated. The primary objectives of this cruise were to map the spatial distribution of the active submarine mine tailings in the fjord and to assess their specific ecological impacts on the benthic foraminifera populations. The findings from this investigation crucialy improve our understanding of the environmental footprint of submarine mining activities and provide key data for future environmental impact assessments.

7.title: A Semi‑Automated Framework for Morphosedimentary Connectivity and Sediment Cascade Susceptibility in the Northern French Alps.

authors.name: Anais Fichot
authors.affiliation: EDYTEM, Université Savoie Mont-Blanc, CNRS (UMR 5204), 73370 Le Bourget du Lac, France

authors.name: Laurent Astrade
authors.affiliation: EDYTEM, Université Savoie Mont-Blanc, CNRS (UMR 5204), 73370 Le Bourget du Lac, France.

authors.name: Jean-Luc Peiry
authors.affiliation: EDYTEM, Université Savoie Mont-Blanc, CNRS (UMR 5204), 73370 Le Bourget du Lac, France. & Université Clermont Auvergne, LLSH, F-63000 Clermont–Ferrand, France.

7.abstract:
The degradation of the cryosphere in the headwaters of Alpine catchments is feared to be a source of sediment that fuels extreme torrential events : proglacial margin, rock slope instability and rocky glacier destabilisation. Sediment supply alone is not sufficient to predict a catchment’s response. We therefore propose an analysis based on the morphosedimentary cascade and connectivity to better understand the susceptibility of Alpine torrential basins to generating a major torrential event.

Measurements of sedimentary connectivity are often based on topographic parameters, sometimes leaving out geomorphological components. They are predominantly case studies at the scale of a few catchments.

We propose an approach at the regional scale in the northern French Alps. We have established a semi-automated measure of sediment connectivity at the torrential network scale and a synthesis of the sediment cascade at the catchment scale.
To this end, we rely on measurements of Stream Power every 50 m across the catchment network, as well as on a geomorphological map of the active zone. Each 50-metre cell thus provides information on its susceptibility to supplying material to the event and on its susceptibility to mobilising this material. We also include vegetation as a parameter that relativeises the sediment availability of the cell, as well as upstream-downstream variations in Stream Power, to identify sections where there is a trend towards an increase or decrease in mobilisation ability.

This semi-automated method allows us to prioritise susceptibility to sediment cascades, which we propose to rename ‘morphosedimentary’ as we give central importance to the geomorphology of the catchment.

Finally, nearly 250 catchments affected by cryosphere degradation in the Alps are studied and ranked to support the management of associated glacial, periglacial and torrential hazards.

7.title: Geomorphological Mapping of Lefkada Island (Ionian Islands, Greece)

authors.name: Ariadni-Konstantina Gazi-Stai
authors.affiliation: Department of Geography, Harokopio University of Athens

authors.name: Dimitrios-Vasileios Batzakis
authors.affiliation: Department of Geography, Harokopio University of Athens

authors.name: Efthimios Karymbalis
authors.affiliation: Department of Geography, Harokopio University of Athens

7.abstract: This study examines the geomorphology of Lefkada Island, located in western Greece, with a focus on the geological factors and geomorphic processes that shape its landscape through detailed geomorphological mapping. A geomorphological map at a scale of 1:10,000 was produced based on a review of previous studies at various scales and the application of semi-automated GIS techniques. High-resolution topo-graphic data, including a 5 m resolution Digital Elevation Model (DEM) provided by the Greek Cadastre and 1:50,000 geological maps from the Institute of Geology and Mineral Expolation of Greece, were integrated into a spatial geodatabase. Second-ary datasets, such as hillshade, slope-aspect, and Red Relief Image map (RRIM) lay-ers, were generated and combined with Google Earth imagery to support the initial identification and delineation of landforms across the island. Among these deriva-tives, RRIM proved particularly effective, as it clearly represents terrain features and facilitates the identification of both large- and small-scale landforms. A targeted field survey was conducted to validate the preliminary geomorphological interpreta-tion and to identify features that may have been overlooked during the GIS-based analysis. The final geomorphological map presents the identified landforms, classi-fied according to their dominant formative processes into structural, gravity-induced, fluvial, coastal, karst, and erosional categories. The results reveal a diverse range of landforms formed by the combined influence of tectonic activity, lithology, and exogenous processes, with notable contrasts between the western and the eastern parts of the island. The resulting map contributes to recent advances in ge-omorphological research and serves as a valuable tool for land management, plan-ning, and interdisciplinary studies.

7.title: Cartographic considerations on mapping the geomorphology and labeling of a mountainous village in the Greek island of Naxos

authors.name: John Hatzopoulos
authors.affiliation: Professor Emeritus, University of the Aegean

7.abstract: This work concerns the village of Koronis on the Greek island of Naxos. Such a mountainous village spans a relatively large area, with steep slopes rising from sea level to 1,000 meters. The interesting thing about such a landscape is the diversity of the geomorphological characteristics, which must be identified and cartographically rendered. Another interesting feature is the great variety of local names. Identifying local names at this time is quite difficult because, since 1950, most people from the village have moved to Athens for a better life, most mountainous areas have remained uncultivated, and present-day residents do not know the names of many places. Therefore, several methods were used to collect them for labeling the map and preserving them. Such a map is useful for municipalities to better understand their region, locate highly interesting hiking trails, and support other tourism applications.

7.title: Long-Term Spatial and Landscape Changes Following Peat Extraction in Greater Poland (Poland) Based on Archival Maps and Geospatial Data

authors.name: Tymoteusz Horbiński
authors.affiliation: Adam Mickiewicz University, Poznań / Department of Landscape Ecology

7.abstract:
Peat extraction carried out in the late nineteenth century under Prussian administration left enduring material traces in the landscape of present-day Greater Poland. This article analyses how these historical interventions transformed peatland environments and how their spatial legacy remains legible in the contemporary landscape. The study focuses on three adjacent research areas near Sokołowo in the municipality of Witkowo.

The main objective is to identify, visualise, and interpret long-term spatial and landscape changes associated with peat extraction, and to assess whether these transformations can be regarded as a persistent element of the region’s landscape heritage. The research combines archival maps with geospatial data, including terrain models derived from LiDAR technology, unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery, and satellite data. This integrated approach enables the reconstruction of former extraction zones and drainage patterns, as well as the detection of preserved traces in contemporary landforms, land cover, and spatial structure.

Particular attention is given to morphological changes, hydrological transformations, changes in land cover and land use, and broader functional shifts in the landscape resulting from peat exploitation. Rather than treating peat extraction as a closed episode in economic history, the article interprets it as a process that produced a lasting landscape palimpsest. The results demonstrate that the legacy of nineteenth-century peat extraction remains visible in the contemporary relief, drainage organisation, and landscape structure, while also shaping the cultural interpretation of these areas. More broadly, the study highlights the value of combining historical evidence with multi-source geospatial analysis in research on historical human-environment interactions and landscape heritage.

7.title: Application of the Coastal Vulnerability Index (CVI) to the Gulf of Kechries in the context of climate change.
7.abstract:
In this study, coastal vulnerability along the Kechries Gulf and the western Saronic Gulf was assessed using the Coastal Vulnerability Index (CVI). The study area extends over 71 km of coastline, from Pachi (Attica) to Pefkali (Corinthia), and is characterized by low-relief coastal zones, carbonate and clastic formations, active faulting, and a typical Mediterranean climate.
The CVI methodology, adapted for Greek coastal environments, was applied through GIS-based analysis using datasets from national and international sources, including a digital elevation model, geological maps, satellite-derived shoreline data, and oceanographic records, complemented by targeted field surveys for validation of geomorphological classifications, shoreline conditions, and sediment characteristics. Seven parameters were taken into consideration: coastal slope, lithology, geomorphology, relative vertical sea-level change, shoreline retreat/accretion, mean tidal range, and mean wave height. CVI values (1–16) were classified into vulnerability categories using the Natural Breaks method.
Results indicate that approximately 52.5% of the coastal zone falls within moderate to very high vulnerability classes. These areas are typically associated with gentle slopes, erosion-prone lithologies, and unconsolidated sediments, and they coincide spatially with the majority of settlements, as well as tourism, industrial, and agricultural activities. In contrast, lower vulnerability zones (47.5%) are characterized by steeper slopes, more resistant lithologies, and reduced human presence.
Overall, coastal vulnerability is strongly controlled by geomorphological and geological factors, with significant implications for land use. The concentration of human activities in highly vulnerable areas underscores the need for targeted coastal management and the integration of climate change projections into risk assessment and planning frameworks.

7.title: A GEOGRAPHICAL EXPEDITION TO ACHELΟOS RIVER, WEST GREECE
7.abstract:
This participation intends to be a short narrative of the experiences and findings of an expedition undertaken by the authors in the Acheloos river during the summer of 2008, as part of a study commissioned to the NTUA by DEH. The aim of the study was to estimate the floodplain encroachments under specific flow releases from the -last downstream- Stratos dam. During three days in July 2008 the authors, members of the aforementioned study team, sailed for almost half the length (~30 km) of the river’s low course, with a small boat with a ferryman, measuring depths with a sonar in order to better depict the topography of the riverbed. The depths were measured along (fictional) cross sections in consecutive distances of about one kilometer. It is worth mentioning that the first day the boat entered the river from the rivermouth and, sailing upstream, the team not only had the opportunity of making interesting observations as to the conditions that prevailed, but also to admire the grandiose, paradisial natural riverscape of the delta.
Acheloos is the larger river with its basin entirely within Greek territory and its power producing capabilities are sufficiently exploited by three large hydroelectrical dams. In this report we limit ourselves to general geomorphological and hydrological observations and we present the bathymetry of the lowest reach of the river that, to our knowledge, have never before been presented to the interested audience. It wants to be a romantic -so to speak- return back in the days where geographical expeditions were adventurous and sometimes dangerous undertakings, the findings of which were presented before a knowledge seeking audience.
Also, for the purpose of this presentation newer 2D flow simulations were conducted and will be displayed.

7.title: Multi-Temporal VHR Satellite Assessment and evaluation of their limitations though statistical analysis on Lateral Channel Migration

authors.name: Emmanouil Salas
authors.affiliation: Operational Unit “BEYOND Centre for Earth Observation Research and Satellite Remote Sensing”, Institute for Astronomy, Astrophysics, Space Applications and Remote Sensing, National Observatory of Athens, GR-152 36 Athens, Greece

authors.name: Michail-Christos Tsoutsos
authors.affiliation: Operational Unit “BEYOND Centre for Earth Observation Research and Satellite Remote Sensing”, Institute for Astronomy, Astrophysics, Space Applications and Remote Sensing, National Observatory of Athens, GR-152 36 Athens, Greece

authors.name: Nikolaos Stasinos
authors.affiliation: Operational Unit “BEYOND Centre for Earth Observation Research and Satellite Remote Sensing”, Institute for Astronomy, Astrophysics, Space Applications and Remote Sensing, National Observatory of Athens, GR-152 36 Athens, Greece

authors.name: Charalampos Kontoes
authors.affiliation: Operational Unit “BEYOND Centre for Earth Observation Research and Satellite Remote Sensing”, Institute for Astronomy, Astrophysics, Space Applications and Remote Sensing, National Observatory of Athens, GR-152 36 Athens, Greece

7.abstract:
Assessing channel alterations is of utmost importance regarding their significant implications on fluvial management and river rehabilitation measures. River course changes can be associated with a variety of natural and anthropogenic factors, including hydraulic interventions, gravel extraction, and intense rainfall events triggering floods. Romania is prone to flooding events, with case studies underscoring flood-affected settlements located in close proximity to river corridors. Evaluation of fluvial morphological changes is essential for understanding river dynamics and evaluating hazards associated with channel instability and bank erosion.

The aim of this study is to enable robust detection and detailed delineation of geomorphological changes for the identification and assessment of potential spatiotemporal alterations along the course of the Mureș river and their adjacent floodplain areas, near the Romanian-Hungarian border. Intense rainfall events occurred between 26 May and 6 July 2025; therefore, multi-temporal Very High-Resolution (VHR) satellite imagery acquired before, during, and after the flood event were utilized to assess lateral channel migration through pre- and post-event comparisons, while erosional and depositional zones were identified through pre-during and during-post-event analyses.

The methodology includes: (i) river boundary delineation for each observation period; (ii) identification and mapping of relevant fluvial landform features; (iii) detection of depositional and erosional changes through multi-temporal analysis; (iv) medial-axis centerline extraction across temporal river states. The highlight in this study, is the implementation of a Minimum Mappable Change (MMC) threshold to conduct a proper analysis of the calculated lateral movement; (vi) establishment of reference stationing along the river corridor so as to calculate lateral displacement through the orthogonal offsets. This research highlights how geospatial analysis can be integrated within the context of lateral channel shift analysis, and how the derived results can be associated and validated with the imagery limitations through statistical analysis.

7.title: Mapping pyroclastic formations at the Lesvos Petrified Forest, the pyroclastic sequence of Kotsini, West Lesvos, Greece

authors.name: Loukas Savvelos
authors.affiliation: Natural History Museum of the Lesvos Petrified Forest, University of the Aegean- Geography department

authors.name: Nikolaos Zouros
authors.affiliation: Natural History Museum of the Lesvos Petrified Forest, University of the Aegean- Geography department

7.abstract: The Lesvos Petrified Forest includes massive assemblages of silicified tree trunks located in situ within the Sigri pyroclastic formation. It consists a unique natural monument located in western Lesvos as well as the geological heritage treasure with international significance of the Lesvos Island UNESCO Global Geopark. The Natural History Museum of the Lesvos Petrified Forest is conducting scientific research, excavation and conservation works in the Lesvos Petrified Forest during the last 30 years. Excavations in the Lesvos Petrified Forest revealed a large number of standing and lying silicified tree trunks, root systems, brunches, leaves and cones that belong to conifer and angiosperm tree species. Since 2014 extensive rescue excavation works were carried out by the Natural History Museum of the Lesvos Petrified Forest due to the construction of the Kalloni - Sigri, road crossing the protected area of the Lesvos Petrified Forest. As a result, large amounts of new data in a number of significant fossil sites were collected. As several significant fossil sites are located along the road, a detailed mapping project in Kotsini, west Lesvos was carried out, in order to accurately capture fossiliferous locations. The objective of this study is the identification and mapping of standing and fallen tree trunks, root systems as well as vitric and lithic tuffs. Knowing the exact position of all these fossils and volcanic formations, we can protect and study the Petrified Forest effectively. Kotsini is located at the heart of the protected area, the mapping revealed a substantial amount of fossiliferous locations with standing and fallen petrified trunks. Additionally contributed to a better understanding of the stratigraphy of the pyroclastic formations as soon as the succession of the various fossiliferous horizons, giving us a better understanding of the landscapes geomorphological evolution and the results of the natural processes that taking place.

7.title: The role of aeolian transport in shaping microplastic deposition patterns across the urban landscape: Thessaloniki case study.

authors.name: Nikoletta Soulioti
authors.affiliation: Department of Physical and Environmental Geography, School of Geology, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki

authors.name: Sofia Pechlivanidou
authors.affiliation: Department of Physical and Environmental Geography, School of Geology, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki

authors.name: Kalliopi Koliadimou
authors.affiliation: Department of Physical and Environmental Geography, School of Geology, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki

7.abstract: Microplastics are increasingly recognized not only as pollutants, but also as a novel sedimentary component of the Anthropocene. The massive production of plastics combined with their fragmentation under weathering conditions, has generated vast quantities of particles that can be transported and deposited similarly to natural sediments. Airborne microplastics particularly, are of significant concern due to their potential inhalation by urban populations and associated health risks. In this context, passive atmospheric deposition collectors are placed at five locations across Thessaloniki, Greece, for a six-month period, to investigate the connection between aeolian transport and deposition patterns of microplastics within an urban setting. The collectors are retrieved and replaced monthly, enabling direct comparison between microplastic distribution and meteorological conditions. The collected microplastics are identified and compared through microscopic analysis, focusing on their abundance, type, colour, and size distribution. Preliminary results highlight the spatial differences in deposition patterns of microplastics with thousands of particles being present across all sampling sites within a range of 53.11 items/gr to 235.2 items/gr and fibers dominating 89% of them. The aeolian transport of microplastics is potentially connected to climatic conditions, geomorphology variables and human activity within the complex urban setting of Thessaloniki. Overall, the early findings demonstrate the abundance of airborne microplastics in Thessaloniki that is dynamically shaped by climatic and geomorphological conditions.

7.title: Anthropogenic stream capture: Human-induced geomorphic paradox in the 21st-January flash flood of Glyfada, Athens, Greece

authors.name: Evangelos Spyrou
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

authors.name: Niki Evelpidou
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

7.abstract: On the evening of January 21st, 2026, a high-intensity storm struck Attica, triggering severe flooding. The suburb of Glyfada, situated at the foothills of Mt. Hymettus, was among the most heavily impacted areas, with massive amounts of debris and fluvial sediments transported within the town. In this study, two adjacent basins have been examined, with roughly equal drainage area (0.30 and 0.39 km²), similar slope, drainage density and geological coverage. This study indicated a geomorphic paradox: Despite their similarities, incision, normally comparable, varied significantly, with minimal eroded material in the former and incision reaching – and in parts exceeding – 8 m² per cross-section in the latter. Detailed mapping of flow paths, pre- and post-flood cross-sections and photographic material collected in this study indicated this geomorphic paradox was owed to human activities and, in particular, the construction of mountainous dirt roads, which diverted the flow of lesser streams, normally contributing to the former basin, towards the latter basin. This resulted in an anthropogenic “stream capture”, changing the drainage area of the two basins into 0.61 and 0.08 km², respectively. This capture effectively doubled the peak discharge in the receiving basin, exceeding the critical shear stress required for the entrainment of large cobbles, while simultaneously starving the donor basin of the hydraulic energy necessary for sediment transport. As a characteristic example, a boulder of approximately 1.4 m x 1.2 m x 0.5 m was found transported around 9 m downstream. Overall, this study indicates that human interventions can significantly alter natural stream courses, as well as patterns of erosion and deposition, highlighting the need for effective management strategies to minimize environmental impacts and promote sustainable watershed development.

7.title: Quaternary landscape evolution of the Gulf of Corinth, Greece, inferred through integrated terrestrial and submarine geomorphological mapping

authors.name: Konstantinos Tsanakas
authors.affiliation: Department of Geography, Harokopio University of Athens, Athens, Greece

authors.name: Sofia Rossi
authors.affiliation: Department of Chemical and Geological Sciences, University of Modena and Reggio Emilia, Modena, Italy

authors.name: Monica Giona Bucci
authors.affiliation: Marine Geology and Seafloor Surveying Group, University of Malta, Msida, Malta

authors.name: Dimitris Sakellariou
authors.affiliation: Hellenic Centre for Marine Research, Anavyssos, Greece

authors.name: Mauro Soldati
authors.affiliation: Department of Chemical and Geological Sciences, University of Modena and Reggio Emilia, Modena, Italy

7.abstract:
This study presents a 1:150,000-scale geomorphological map of the Gulf of Corinth (central Greece), integrating terrestrial and submarine landforms. The Gulf, an asymmetric WNW–ESE-trending half-graben, is among the most tectonically active regions in the eastern Mediterranean, characterized by an uplifting southern flank and a subsiding, downward-flexed northern margin. A multidisciplinary approach, combining field surveys with high-resolution seafloor bathymetry, was employed to map both emerged and submerged geological and geomorphological features.
The southern terrestrial sector provides clear evidence of tectonic uplift, including marine terraces, elevated Gilbert-type deltas, raised tidal notches, and locally reversed drainage patterns. In contrast, the northern sector is characterized by the absence of Quaternary marine or lacustrine deposits and by a gently sloping shelf with submerged tidal notches, indicating ongoing tectonic subsidence.
The resulting map offers a comprehensive representation of the region’s complex geomorphology, shaped by Quaternary tectonic activity.

7.title: Tectonic deformation and fault activity on Kythera Island as indicators of offshore subduction dynamics

authors.name: Konstantinos Tsanakas
authors.affiliation: Department of Geography, Harokopio University of Athens, Athens, Greece

authors.name: Julius Jara-Muñoz
authors.affiliation: Institut Hochschule Biberach, Faculty of Civil Engineering, Biberach an der Riß, Germany

authors.name: Dimitrios-Vasileios Batzakis
authors.affiliation: Department of Geography, Harokopio University of Athens

authors.name: Diamantina Griva
authors.affiliation: Department of Geography, Harokopio University of Athens

7.abstract: Offshore islands provide valuable insights into deformation rates, their controlling mechanisms, and the dynamics of the upper crust in offshore subduction zones, where direct observations are otherwise challenging. In this study, active deformation and faulting are investigated over glacial-cycle time scales on Kythera Island, located in the southwestern Hellenic subduction zone between Crete and the Peloponnesus. Kythera Island preserves an exceptional sequence of more than twelve marine terraces, reflecting its active uplift. These terraces are offset by multiple active faults, oriented NNW-SSE and NNE-SSW. High-resolution topography and morphometric analysis are employed to map the marine terraces and estimate the heave and throw rates of the island’s primary faults. The marine terrace sequence is classified into two groups: higher marine terraces (260–480 masl) with composite rasa surfaces and lower terraces (20–220 masl) displaying staircase morphologies. The analysis focuses on two major faults, which exhibit both right- and left-lateral as well as dip-slip displacements, disrupting terrace risers and treads. The activity of these faults is linked to intermediate-depth, high-magnitude earthquakes, such as the Mw 6.6 and 6.7 events that struck Kythera in 1903 and 2006, respectively. Further research will involve dating marine terrace surfaces and conducting structural analysis to correlate the terraces with Marine Isotope Stages and refine estimates of heave and throw rates. This study underscores the importance of island-based observations in quantifying deformation rates in offshore subduction zones.

7.title: Assessing Coastal Vulnerability in Greece: A Review of Methodological Approaches

authors.name: Kanella Valkanou
authors.affiliation: Harokopio University of Greece, Department of Geography

authors.name: Hariklia Skilodimou
authors.affiliation: University of Patras, Department of Geology

7.abstract:
Coastal areas in Greece are increasingly affected by erosion, sea-level rise, and extreme weather events, as a result of both natural processes and climate change. These pressures are particularly significant due to the country’s long and diverse coastline, which includes densely populated urban zones, tourist areas, and environmentally sensitive regions. This has led to the use of different approaches for assessing coastal vulnerability. The aim of this study is to review recent research carried out in Greece, focusing on the methods that have been applied.
The studies examined include the use of Coastal Vulnerability Indices (CVI), GIS and remote sensing techniques, as well as numerical models and, more recently, machine learning approaches. These methods are often applied at different spatial scales depending on data availability and the objectives of each study. Most studies rely on index-based methods, often combined with geoinformatics tools, mainly because they are easier to apply at larger spatial scales. At the same time, more advanced methods are starting to appear, offering new possibilities for improved spatial analysis and prediction of coastal change.
However, differences are observed between studies regarding the selection of parameters, weighting methods, spatial scale, and data availability. Such variations can influence the comparability of results and reflect the diversity of approaches used in the field of coastal vulnerability assessment in Greece.

8.title: Reconfiguring Rural Landscapes under Energy Transition: A Landscape-Based Assessment of a Large-Scale Photovoltaic Project in Western Macedonia, Greece

authors.name: Maria Alebaki
authors.affiliation: Senior Researcher, Agricultural Economics Research Institute, Hellenic Agricultural Organization-DIMITRA

8.abstract:
This paper critically examines the landscape implications of a large-scale photovoltaic (PV) project (60 MW) proposed in the area of Aspri Petra, within the rural region of Xino Nero (Amyndeo) in Western Macedonia, Greece. Drawing on the conceptual framework of landscape as a socio-ecological and experiential system, the study moves beyond conventional Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) approaches that treat landscape primarily as a visual or aesthetic parameter. Instead, it adopts an integrative perspective that considers the structural, functional, symbolic, and experiential dimensions of landscape, in line with the European Landscape Convention.

The analysis is based on a systematic review of the EIA study, combined with spatial interpretation and critical evaluation of its methodological assumptions. Particular emphasis is placed on identifying conceptual and methodological gaps in the treatment of landscape, including the absence of cumulative impact assessment, limited spatial scope, insufficient consideration of geomorphological, biogeographical and hydrological transformations, and the neglect of local socio-cultural and productive systems.

The findings indicate that the project constitutes a profound spatial intervention that reconfigures the landscape from a multifunctional rural system into a predominantly energy-oriented space. Extensive land coverage, terrain modifications, and associated infrastructural networks introduce lasting transformations in geomorphology, microclimate, ecological processes, and land-use patterns. Furthermore, the project appears misaligned with the strategic directions of the Regional Spatial Planning Framework, which prioritizes agricultural specialization, landscape-based development, and the promotion of quality local products, particularly wine and special interest tourism.

The study also highlights limited public participation/consultation and the absence of locally grounded benefit-sharing mechanisms, raising critical questions regarding decision-making processes and the distribution of impacts. Overall, the paper argues that large-scale renewable energy projects, when insufficiently embedded in landscape-sensitive planning frameworks, risk undermining the socio-spatial coherence and long-term development trajectories of rural regions, while its findings may inform more equitable and participatory planning approaches.

8.title: TWIN TRANSITIONS OF THE ENERGY SECTOR IN THE EU PERIPHERY: CONTESTED GEOGRAPHIES IN WESTERN MACEDONIA AND STARA ZAGORA

authors.name: Vasiliki Krommyda
authors.affiliation: Institute of Philosophy and Sociology at the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences & University of the Aegean

8.abstract:
This paper examines the EU's twin digital and green transitions (TTs) through the lens of peripheral political economies, focusing on the electricity sectors in coal regions of Western Macedonia (Greece) and Stara Zagora (Bulgaria). Τhe paper conceptualises TTs as contested processes that reorganise governance, capital allocation, and labour markets, producing deeply unequal geographies of transition. Drawing on Europeanisation and world-ecology perspectives, the TTs function as a form of crisis governance that attempts to stabilise existing political–economic structures while reconfiguring their spatial and institutional expressions, with significant consequences for territorial cohesion and social justice.
Methodologically, the paper employs a mixed research design, combining primary research through interviews with workers, local stakeholders, and energy experts conducted between June and October 2025, with secondary data analysis. Empirically, the analysis shows that Greece's accelerated renewable deployment, coupled with growing dependence on imported gas, large-scale infrastructure investment, and the retreat of vertically integrated public utilities, and Bulgaria's delayed transition, shaped by coal dependence and regulatory inertia, represent different temporalities of the same structural logic. In both cases, decarbonisation advances alongside intensified financialisation of energy systems, weakened public service provision, and the emergence of new forms of energy vulnerability and socio-spatial dependency. These dynamics are acutely felt at the regional and community scale, where coal phase-out reshapes not only employment but access to affordable energy, local fiscal capacity, and the basic conditions of social reproduction. At the same time, early labour market outcomes reveal a shift from territorially embedded, unionised employment toward more fragmented and precarious forms of work, mediated by often inadequate reskilling policies. The paper concludes that the TTs operate as a hegemonic project, mobilising narratives of modernisation and resilience that legitimise infrastructural expansion and market restructuring without challenging extractivist political economies or addressing the unequal distribution of transition costs.

8.title: Who Hosts the Energy Transition? Spatial Inequalities in the Distribution of Renewable Energy Projects in Greece
8.abstract:
Mountainous areas are recognized as important sources of renewable energy, particularly for wind energy and hydropower. However, the rapid deployment of renewable energy projects in these areas raises critical questions regarding spatial justice, environmental protection and the uneven distribution of costs and benefits. In Greece, mountainous areas are increasingly characterized by a high concentration of renewable energy installations, often in landscapes of high ecological value, biodiversity richness and cultural significance. This growing pressure has also triggered a proliferation of local social movements opposing the siting of such energy projects.
This paper investigates the geographic distribution of renewable energy projects in Greece, aiming to identify and quantify emerging territorial inequalities. Based on official data from the Regulatory Authority for Waste, Energy and Water (RAAEY), we compile a comprehensive geospatial dataset regarding energy projects with the occurring data being aggregated at the level of municipalities and municipal units. A set of spatial indicators is further developed, including installed capacity density (MW/km²), capacity per capita (MW/inhabitant), and estimated annual energy production density (MWh/km²).
Using GIS-based spatial analyses, the geographic distribution of renewable energy infrastructure is visualized, while patterns of concentration and clustering across the Greek territory are identified and quantified. The results are expected to reveal significant spatial inequalities, with a disproportionate concentration of projects in mountainous and sparsely populated areas. These findings highlight the emergence of a form of “territorial burden” associated with the energy transition, raising important questions about the fairness and social acceptance of current deployment strategies.
By foregrounding the geographical dimensions of renewable energy development, this study contributes to ongoing debates on just energy transitions, emphasizing the need for more balanced, participatory and territorially sensitive energy planning.

8.title: Crete as an Energy Corridor: Mapping Transition and Conflict in the Eastern Mediterranean
8.abstract:
This paper examines Crete as an emerging energy infrastructure corridor in the Eastern Mediterranean. Official narratives in the country frame energy transition as decarbonisation and green development and a response to climate crisis. Within this context, Crete is increasingly presented as a future energy hub in the Eastern Mediterranean, where interconnections, renewable-energy investments and infrastructural upgrading promise growth and progress. On the island, however, this promise condenses into a dense and contested infrastructural geography.
Drawing on a critical mapping exercise, the paper traces how this transition narrative materialises across Crete’s infrastructural landscape. It maps planned and existing energy infrastructures on and around the island — wind and solar parks, high-voltage lines, substations, interconnections, data centres and offshore energy projects — in order to examine the material geography behind the promise of green development. It then places these infrastructures in relation to collective mobilisations and grassroots initiatives contesting renewable energy and other large-scale investment projects, showing how the island’s infrastructural future has become a terrain of conflict. Finally, by bringing energy projects into relation with tourist and refugee routes, and with the geopolitical context of war and militarisation in the Eastern Mediterranean, the paper asks how Crete is being produced as a Mediterranean corridor: through unequal circulations of energy, capital and people, and through struggles over land, water, development and everyday life in the island. Maps are thus used not as neutral illustrations, but as a critical method for making visible the unequal power relations and situated knowledges obscured by official transition narratives.

8.title: Energy Poverty in Energy-Producing Regions: Renewable Energy Infrastructures, Spatial Inequality and Just Transition in the Upper Tigris Basin
8.abstract: Energy poverty is most often discussed in terms of household income, energy prices, housing conditions, and access to basic energy services. However, this issue is not limited to the realm of consumption; it is also closely linked to the spatial organization of energy systems, infrastructure investments, regional inequalities, and governance processes. This paper aims to discuss the relationship between energy poverty and a just energy transition in energy-producing regions, using the Upper Tigris Basin as a case study. The study’s central premise is that regions hosting energy production infrastructure may not always be in a advantageous position regarding energy access, local benefits, and socio-economic development. In this context, hydroelectric infrastructure is considered not merely as electricity generation systems but as spatial processes that reshape relationships involving water resources, local communities, environmental change, and regional development. The paper is structured as an exploratory case study.
