Through official energy and socio-economic indicators, the spatial distribution of renewable energy infrastructure, and field observations, the following question will be examined: Why and how might a region contributing to energy production experience energy vulnerability, limited local benefits, and exclusion from decision-making processes? Within this framework, the study argues that a just energy transition cannot be evaluated solely through the expansion of renewable energy capacity or the reduction of carbon emissions. If dimensions of distributive justice, participation, recognition, and spatial inequality are not taken into account, renewable energy infrastructure may reproduce existing regional inequalities rather than reduce them. The Upper Tigris Basin example demonstrates that energy poverty must be addressed not only at the household level but also within the contexts of infrastructure, water governance, climate variability, and regional development.

8.title: Oral heat stories. Understanding the multiscalar evolutions of urban thermalscapes in contemporary Athens
8.abstract: The increasing frequency and severity of heatwaves are radically transforming the way people live in major urban centres. Whilst public spaces are at the heart of urban heat adaptation policies, little is known about how people cope with extreme heat in their homes on a day-to-day basis. Drawing on oral history methodologies, and in particular on an in-progress campaign of nearly 50 biographical interviews with people aged between 55 and 90, our research examines how people’s ways of coping with the heat have evolved in the Athens metropolitan area from the 1970s to the present day. This empirical data allows us to describe the gradual reconfigurations of urban thermalscapes in Athens – understood as environmental, material, discursive and cultural constructions, which determines how people perceive and adapt to heat – and to highlight their impact on urban modes of living. The proposition relies on a multiscalar analysis. First, we examine the evolution of bodily experiences of heat over that time period. Then, we consider the domestic experiences of heat and the links between ways of living and cooling down. Finally, we investigate changes at the urban scale, in terms of public space use and energy consumption. More broadly, our analysis invites to understand coolness as the result of a constant negotiation between individuals and their environments, in which energy-intensive technologies are playing an increasingly prominent role. This analysis leads us to argue for the importance of structuring the field of critical heat studies, situated at the intersection of urban climatology, urban studies and energy studies.

8.title: Reassessing the Urban Fabric: Morphology, Energy, Microclimate and Social Processes in Exarcheia, Athens
8.abstract:
The transition towards climate- neutral neighborhood in urban environment brought on the spotlight energy efficiency and larger scale interventions. However, most approaches are exclusively technical, prioritizing building performance while overlooking sociospatial inequalities that energy transition policies usually create. In Mediterranean cities, where mixed land uses, compact urban form and vertical social segregation prevail, energy performance is unevenly distributed and closely linked to urban morphology and everyday practices.

This paper proposes a methodological framework that combines cadastral data analysis, statistical reconstruction, typological classification and microclimatic simulation to investigate the spatial distribution of environmental conditions at neighborhood scale. Using Exarcheia, a central area in Athens, as a case study, the research reconstructs missing building data and develops a detailed urban dataset to support the analysis on thermal comfort, airflow and environmental stress. Building upon these results, the study advances a sociospatial analysis of urban dynamics, examining how environmental performance intersects with patterns of use, housing conditions and social intensity. Preliminary findings suggests that areas of increased thermal stress coincide with highly mixed-use areas, revealing a complex interaction between environmental conditions and everyday life.

The paper, as a first step of ongoing research, argues that energy efficiency and neighborhood scale interventions cannot be expressed exclusively as technical solutions, as their implementation often fails to address the uneven capacity of different social groups to access and benefit from them, while also overlooking specific spatial, social and housing conditions that shape local need and constraints.

As a last step, the research introduces a participatory design approach as an open dialogue with the community of the neighborhood in order to connect environmental analysis with local knowledge to support the development of adaptive and socially inclusive strategies. By integrating morphology, microclimate and sociospatial dynamics, the study contributes to the critical discussion on energy justice and urban transitions.

8.title: PLANNING POLICY FOR URBAN ENERGY POVERTY
8.abstract:
Our biggest challenge in dealing with decaying urban regions regarding social justice and climate change is the "existing". Targeted planning policy for energy efficiency upgrades of neighbourhoods is key to achieving notable, lasting results. To unlock designated funding, these must combine with the rehabilitation of their environment.
In Greece and abroad, attempted interventions in lagging residential areas with socio-spatial disparities address various "R-URBAN" tasks: rehabilitate, reactivate, regenerate, reduce, restructure, refill, recycle, reuse, rethink, etc. However, the nexus of "climate-change/energy/poverty" remains outside mainstream urban planning policy and practice, whereas the energy dimension, constrained by diverse barriers, is not sufficiently embedded in relative doctrines.
In Athenian neighbourhoods with concentrations of vulnerable social groups, urban heat, degrading buildings, shabby environments and diverse poverties feed each other, framing realities within which people interact. Lacking social housing and energy retrofit projects at "scale of impact", people remain exposed to inequalities, as housing precarity and socio-spatial dynamics intensify.
The scale of impact is dependent on planning policy. Planning policy for EP must address regions of different intensities/characteristics (especially in terms of cost/benefit). In crafting policy, one must deal with institutional frameworks (of diverse largely segregated authorities), induce practice shifts by improving planning principles at different scales and building code regulations, and identify facilitating mechanisms for decision-making and types of actions for optimal cost/benefit ratio. Further, funding targeted interventions requires a planning policy to connect with policies of urban and regional development, considering differentiations among regions.
Planning policies leading to more just energy futures need contributions from scientific fields such as environmental physics, urban economics, social sciences and urban geography, whereas targeted multi-criteria spatial mapping and energy assessments valued by empirical wisdom is necessary. A case study of a typical central Athenian neighbourhood may be presented at the Conference.

8.title: Tackling energy poverty through deep renovations: Challenges in supporting vulnerable households
8.abstract:
The presentation summarises the findings and insights gathered from 790 household visits conducted in the Athens Urban Area, in the context of REVERTER, an EU LIFE-funded project aiming to alleviate energy poverty through the deep renovation of dwellings occupied by vulnerable households. The visits, which were organised by EKPIZO’s one-stop shop (OSS), served both as a data collection exercise and as a direct engagement tool, enabling the project team to assess vulnerable households’ conditions related to energy use, comfort, and vulnerability, as well as their awareness, attitudes, and willingness to participate in energy efficiency programmes.
Based on the analysis of the questionnaire’s responses, more than 80% of homes in the assessed housing stock were energy inefficient, resulting in high energy demand and poor indoor comfort. About 50-60% of the households were struggling to make ends meet. Among these households, over 60% failed to meet basic thermal comfort standards, reported cuts in other essentials, such as food purchases and health-related spending and - compared to those living comfortably - damp/mould issues are up to 78% more prevalent and health problems related to energy conditions are up to 12.6 times more common.
Despite the clear need, only 45% of households expressed willingness to participate in subsidised home energy renovation schemes. The primary denial reasons cited include financial constraints (46%), bureaucratic fears (23.2%), scepticism about energy savings (19.3%), lack of awareness (14.7%) and ownership issues (10.2%). Even among those willing to participate, 20.8% cannot afford to contribute anything, and 56.5% could not manage the hypothetical monthly repayment of the retrofit cost, regardless of income group. 
These findings underlined that financial inaccessibility cuts across all income groups, though its effects are most severe for the most vulnerable, and points to the need for integrated social and energy policy responses.

8.title: Energy Democracy in Practice: A Spatial Multi-Indicator Assessment of Energy Communities in Greece

authors.name: Dimitris Kitsikopoulos
authors.affiliation: 1. School of Spatial Planning and Development, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki / 2. Electra Energy cooperative

authors.name: Kyriaki Metaxa
authors.affiliation: 1. Heinrich Boell Stiftung / 2. Giosi Energy Community

authors.name: Vassilios Kostakis
authors.affiliation: Ragnar Nurkse department of Innovation and Governance, Tallin Technical University

8.abstract: Energy communities (ECs) represent a transformative shift in energy systems, prioritising environmental, economic, and social benefits while fostering citizen participation. However, comprehensive frameworks for evaluating their multidimensional impacts remain limited, particularly in Southern European contexts where spatial inequalities and uneven regulatory landscapes shape their development. This perspective article addresses this gap by developing a 22-indicator framework capturing social, economic, environmental, and governance dimensions, and applying it to four Greek ECs across distinct spatial contexts — rural, urban, and island settings. Using a mixed-methods approach, we assessed mature ECs adhering to cooperative principles, explicitly accounting for how place-based conditions and territorial constraints mediate outcomes. Our findings reveal strong democratic innovation and social capital formation; however, these achievements remain constrained by project scale, regulatory barriers, and financing limitations that are themselves spatially uneven in their effects. This tension between democratic excellence and scaling constraints emerges consistently across all four dimensions. ECs performed strongest in governance dimensions while facing universal scaling challenges attributable to systemic policy barriers. The analysis demonstrates that democratic governance and economic efficiency can be complementary rather than competing objectives — a finding with implications for spatially just energy transitions. The framework shows potential applicability beyond Greece, though transferability depends on territorial regulatory context and organisational development stage. While ECs may not fully transform energy systems on their own, they constitute essential, place-sensitive building blocks of democratic, inclusive energy futures.

9.title: Modelled Sprawl and Census Geographies of Housing: Interpreting Thessaloniki’s Urban Expansion

authors.name: Poulicos Prastacos
authors.affiliation: Institute of Applied and Computational Mathematics, Foundation for Research and Technology - Hellas - IACM FORTH

9.abstract:
Urban expansion in Thessaloniki has been increasingly expressed through dispersed residential development, and changing relationships between housing, land use, and the built environment. While urban sprawl models identify spatial patterns of expansion, their interpretation becomes stronger when modelled outputs are examined alongside official census data on buildings and housing. This paper investigates Thessaloniki’s urban expansion by comparing the outputs of Urban Sprawl Models with census-based indicators of housing geography and buildings’ characteristics.

The analysis focuses on the spatial relationship between modelled sprawl zones and census data concerning buildings, dwellings, number of floors, and the distribution of residential uses. Attention is given to the distinction between exclusively residential and mixed-use buildings, as well as to the relative share of housing uses compared with other functions, enabling Thessaloniki’s residential patterns to be interpreted in relation to broader spatial reference levels, including Greece, Northern Greece, and the Regional level. In this way, the paper does not treat urban sprawl only as horizontal land consumption, but also as a differentiated transformation of the residential built environment.

By combining modelled spatial expansion with census indicators, the study seeks to identify where urban growth corresponds with measurable concentrations of housing, where residential development appears vertically intensified through multi-storey buildings, and where mixed-use patterns complicate the interpretation of sprawl. This approach is especially relevant for peri-urban and transitional areas of Thessaloniki, where urbanisation may be fragmented, uneven, and only partially visible through conventional land-use classifications.

The paper focuses on socio-spatial transformations by examining how housing geographies are produced, recorded, and potentially obscured within the expanding urban fabric. It argues that the combined reading of modelled sprawl and census data can provide a more nuanced understanding of Thessaloniki’s urban expansion, revealing not only where the city grows, but also how residential space is structured within that growth.

9.title: The Development of Productive Activities in the Western Peri-Urban Zone of Thessaloniki: Land Transformation and Challenges for Spatial Planning

authors.name: Elisavet Thoidou
authors.affiliation: School of Spatial Planning and Development Engineering, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki

authors.name: Dimitris Foutakis
authors.affiliation: School of Spatial Planning and Development Engineering, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki

9.abstract:
In recent years, the development of productive activities has posed significant challenges for territorial organization and spatial planning, particularly in metropolitan areas. These challenges include securing suitable land for the location of productive activities amid competing land uses and economic functions, as well as addressing locational requirements that, despite technological advances, continue to depend heavily on proximity factors. At the same time, issues concerning the protection of land and the environment are gaining importance, particularly in relation to the impacts of climate change and the risks of natural disasters

The western zone of the Thessaloniki metropolitan area has experienced significant development of productive activities over recent decades, driven by its proximity to the main national road network and the Port of Thessaloniki. In particular, the area of Kalochori has witnessed a considerable expansion of out-of-plan and largely unregulated building activity, mainly for industrial and warehousing purposes, resulting in significant land-use and land-cover transformations and increasing pressures on land resources and the environment. This paper examines transformations in land development in the western peri-urban zone of Thessaloniki, in relation to productive activities and the built and natural environment. It also seeks to identify the challenges these transformations pose for spatial planning and to explore how they may shape the future geography of the area.

9.title: Fragmented Geographies and “Isolated Development” at the Western Entrance of Thessaloniki

authors.name: Paraskevi Tarani
authors.affiliation: Architect - Urban Planner, Major Development Agency Thessaloniki

9.abstract:
The western entrance area of Thessaloniki constitutes one of the city’s most complex and rapidly transforming urban territories. Historically shaped by industrial activities, transport infrastructure, working-class settlements, refugee flows, and logistics functions, the area developed as the productive “backyard” of the city, spatially and symbolically disconnected from its historic and administrative center. Today, this fragmented landscape is undergoing significant socio-spatial transformation through infrastructure upgrades, metro expansion, large-scale real estate investments, and tourism-oriented redevelopment.
Despite increasing investment interest and the area’s strategic metropolitan location, development remains highly uneven. Large flagship projects coexist with degraded open spaces, fragmented urban fabric, environmental pressures, vulnerable social groups, and persistent inequalities. The coexistence of logistics infrastructure, abandoned industrial sites, informal activities, transport hubs, and isolated redevelopment enclaves creates a highly fragmented urban geography, where spatial proximity does not necessarily translate into social, not even functional integration.
This paper explores the contemporary transformation of the western entrance of Thessaloniki through the lens of socio-spatial fragmentation and just transition. Drawing on ongoing research and planning processes developed within the ClimaGen and ReGenWesT projects on regreening and climate resilience, the paper examines how property-led and isolated development patterns interact with green transition policies reshaping the area’s spatial identity and development dynamics. Particular emphasis is placed on the tensions between metropolitan-scale redevelopment strategies and the everyday realities of local communities and vulnerable urban landscapes.
The paper argues that the western entrance of Thessaloniki represents a crucial urban frontier where economic restructuring, climate transition, and socio-spatial inequality intersect. Understanding these fragmented layers and the ways they influence the transformation of a large urban expansion area, developing without an integrated overarching planning framework, may help identify new approaches for the strategic urban planning, and more socially inclusive forms for urban regeneration in the Greek context.

9.title: Transitional morphologies of residential built space. Exploring urban tissues of refugee settlements in Thessaloniki.

authors.name: Maria Oikonomou
authors.affiliation: Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, Dpt. of Urban and Regional Planning and Development Research Unit for the South European Cities

9.abstract:
The study analyses the physical and dynamic processes which produce the actual urban form. Urban tissue has a double role as an element of fundamental importance in shaping the structure of the city. First, it assembles all the physical elements and social fabrics in the intermediate urban scale. Secondly it can adapt or even transform through the continuous changes of urban planning policies, building regulations or even everyday human decisions at the micro-scale. As formations and transformations of the urban tissues are explored the question arises: What are the dynamic processes of production, evolution and transformation of urban form and what are the corresponding transitional morphologies?

A city’s urban form is a complex, overlapping substratum that cannot be fully understood at first glance. In-depth analytical and exploratory research is required to reveal the levels of morphological processes, social and developmental forces that directly concern the design of urban space. Within this framework, the investigation of the urban tissue is organized at two scales: the intermediate scale of the urban parts and the micro-scale of urban blocks.

These scales represent an unexplored level of analysis of the existing urban tissues especially in Greek cities. They become an ideal tool in order to research the complex nature of urban form and for understanding the ways in which built space is composed in a smaller scale. At the centre of the research are two case studies in Thessaloniki with different characteristics but of a historic and socio-cultural significance: Ano Poli and Kato Toumba, both refugee settlements of the 1930s. By analysing their evolution in space and time, we explore specific finds on the evolution and dynamics of residential built space in Thessaloniki and other greek cities.

9.title: From Urban Densification to the Vision of the “New City”: A strategic study for new urban landscape syntax in Neapoli, Thessaloniki, under conditions of multiple pressures

authors.name: Eleftheria Gavriilidou
authors.affiliation: School of Architecture, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki

9.abstract:
Within the broader context of climate change, aging infrastructure, excessive urban density, and mounting housing pressures, the exploration of interventions in urban open spaces—aimed at enhancing sustainability and resilience—emerges as a critical approach for renewing urban identity, restoring ecological balance, rearticulating collective memory, and fostering new forms of social interaction.

In this framework, the post-war district of Neapoli, situated at the western gateway of Thessaloniki—a highly compact urban area characterized by a scarcity of open spaces and among the highest urban densities in Greece—has been examined through a strategic perspective of spatial restructuring and urban repair, grounded in its network of open and residual spaces.

Urban elements such as streets, sidewalks, parks, schoolyards, bus stops, squares, pedestrian routes, sports facilities, and even the smallest vacant or leftover spaces are reinterpreted as integral components of a cohesive spatial strategy. This strategy is rooted in the existing urban fabric, collective memory, and lived experience, while projecting towards the future through the formation of an interconnected network of public and common spaces capable of redefining spatial, perceptual, ecological, and social relationships.

The study was conducted by a multidisciplinary team of researchers and practitioners, commissioned by the Municipality of Neapoli–Sykies between 2023 and 2025. It seeks to expand the discourse on the significance of strategic planning across multiple spatial scales, the centrality of public space design, participatory decision-making processes, and the institutional and procedural frameworks governing the production, commissioning, and implementation of large-scale urban studies within the context of economic austerity in Greece.

9.title: Rendering Thessaloniki's rent conflict politically visible
9.abstract:
Thessaloniki is undergoing a rapid housing transformation, yet some of its most consequential elements remain only partially visible. In the historic centre, the western entrance and other selective pockets of reinvestment, rent gaps are being closed through serviced apartments, student rentals, professionalised short-term rentals and tourism-led redevelopment. Yet rising rents, touristification, real estate investment and severe unaffordability are largely discussed as market trends rather than power imbalances. What remains invisible are the everyday relations through which these processes are experienced, justified and contested: repeated moves, non-renewal of contracts, informal evictions, arbitrary rent increases, abusive clauses, poor housing quality, dependence on family support and household displacement.
Thessaloniki’s housing crisis remains unmapped not only for lack of data, but because dominant property narratives obscure rent as a field of exploitation and political conflict. Unlike contexts where corporate landlordism has produced visible antagonists and strong tenant mobilisation, as in the Catalan case, Thessaloniki’s rental crisis unfolds through dispersed relations of small and medium property ownership, marginal financialisation, tourism-oriented investment and entrenched family-based rent-seeking imaginaries. Through their local organisation, ENIATH, landlords present themselves as the vulnerable next-door neighbour, while tenants remain largely individualised. This makes the crisis harder to politicise.
Yet Thessaloniki also shows signs of institutional and social innovation: the country’s first social rental agency, the first post-war tenants’ union and a municipal party that has placed housing on the city’s agenda. Drawing on my research on the Greek housing property regime and my involvement in tenant organising, I propose rent relations as an entry point into the city’s socio-spatial restructuring. Mapping this crisis requires more than mapping actors, transactions or investment flows. It requires making visible the moral narratives, legal arrangements, social imaginaries and everyday antagonisms that organise access to housing in a city still governed by the common sense of property.

9.title: The gendered everyday production of public space. Encounters of migrant women. The case of Thessaloniki, Greece.
9.abstract: This study explores the gendered everyday production of public space and urban encounters, focusing on migrant women's experiences in public spaces. Engaging with the literature on migration, feminist geography, and urban planning, the research identifies critical gaps in understanding migrant women's experiences through both universal frameworks and individual identities. Drawing on Lefebvre's theory of the production of space and the theoretical framework of intersectionality, the study aims to examine the geographical, social, and planning dimensions of migrant women's interactions with public urban spaces in Thessaloniki, Greece. By integrating intersectionality with the production of space, this approach offers a nuanced exploration of everyday, often overlooked encounters that shape migrant women’s experiences in the city. These encounters are situated within the complex power dynamics of public spaces that influence how migrant women navigate urban environments and negotiate their identities. The study emphasizes how these spaces, both physical and social, can serve as sites of exclusion, appropriation or resistance, revealing the broader societal impacts of urban planning and offering insight in policy. Adopting a qualitative methodology, including walking/go-along interviews and the story completion method, the research collected and analyzed data to provide a comprehensive understanding of these lived experiences. This early-stage study lays the groundwork for further analysis and contributions, offering new insights into the intersection of gender, migration, and public space, and contributing to discussions on urban policy, inclusivity, and spatial justice for marginalized groups. It aims to understand the geographical, social, and planning dimensions of migrant women's experiences in contemporary urban public spaces in Thessaloniki, Greece.

9.title: Housing–Energy Insecurity and Feminist Urban Geopolitics in Thessaloniki: Rethinking Geotrauma

authors.name: Aysegul Can
authors.affiliation: Institute for Regional Sciences, Karlsruhe Institute of Technology

authors.name: Georgia Alexandri
authors.affiliation: Institute of Technology Assessment and System Analysis (ITAS), Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT)

9.abstract:
This contribution develops a feminist urban geopolitics of Thessaloniki by examining how informal labour and care, housing precarity, and energy insecurity intersect within a context of austerity, tourism-led redevelopment, and deepening inequalities. It explores how these dynamics shape everyday life and urban space, while opening up sites of negotiation and contestation.

Drawing on Pain’s (2021) concept of geotrauma, the paper uses it as a lens for understanding the cumulative, spatialised entanglement of intimate and structural forms of violence. It situates geotrauma within ongoing political-economic transformations, such as tightening rental markets, the expansion of short-term rentals, and uneven energy transitions, that produce new forms of urban dispossession. In this way, the paper connects geotrauma to the housing–energy–wellbeing nexus, highlighting how infrastructures and markets become key sites through which these processes are lived and mediated. Rather than centring trauma as a defining condition, we foreground how these processes are navigated, contested, and reworked in everyday life. The analysis builds on five in-depth narrative interviews with migrant women, five expert interviews with municipal actors and NGOs, and a focus group conducted through a mobile urban living lab in a central public space.

These engagements foreground everyday practices through which women navigate housing and energy constraints, mobilise informal networks, and engage in mutual aid and neighbourhood organising. The paper highlights how women shape and sustain their lives under conditions of uncertainty. It shifts attention from vulnerability as a fixed identity to situated agency through which urban life is sustained and reconfigured and argues that housing and energy constitute key terrains of feminist territorial politics, where questions of staying, caring, and belonging are actively negotiated. In doing so, the paper advances a repoliticised understanding of geotrauma and contributes to debates on urban inequality, social reproduction, and feminist geopolitics in Southern European cities

9.title: Unmapped Geographies from Below: Migrant Women, Care, and Feminist Counter-Mapping in Thessaloniki
9.abstract: This paper examines the role of migrant women as everyday actors in the production of urban space in Thessaloniki, through the lens of feminist geography. In a city undergoing uneven and often “unmapped” socio-spatial transformations, it focuses on lived geographies that remain marginal to dominant urban narratives. Drawing on creative interviews and participatory mapping, the research foregrounds the lived geographies of care, desire, and survival that shape migrant women’s everyday experiences. These practices form informal infrastructures of care and solidarity which, although often invisible, are crucial for sustaining urban life and navigating socio-spatial inequalities. The paper argues that feminist counter-mapping redefines the question of “who produces the city” by shifting attention from formal planning processes to embodied experience and everyday practices. In doing so, it challenges dominant representations of the city and makes visible the ways in which urban space is continuously produced “from below.” By tracing these practices, the paper contributes to debates on contemporary socio-spatial transformations in Thessaloniki, highlighting how migrant women actively rework the urban fabric through situated, relational, and often overlooked forms of agency. It thus positions care and everyday spatial practices as key to understanding the city’s emerging, yet largely unmapped, geographies.

10.title: Cohabitation in vertically segregated apartment buildings in Athens
10.abstract: This presentation examines cohabitation in the socially and ethnically mixed apartment buildings in the centre of Athens that were constructed with the “land for flat” system, where the phenomenon of vertical social segregation is pronounced. In contrast with horizontal segregation, the vertical one does lead to spatial proximity. Drawing on the microdata collected through qualitative interview research from 54 residents across 28 apartment buildings, collected within the ISTOPOL project ‘Stories of Athenian apartment blocks’ and analysed in the context of the SeDe research programme ‘Segregation patterns and deprivation areas in Athens 2011–2021’, the study investigates whether spatial proximity leads to harmonious or conflictual forms of cohabitation. The findings indicate that cohabitation in vertically segregated Athenian apartment buildings is multifaceted and not one-dimensional. Relationships range from interpersonal to indifferent, distant, or even hostile relations, often shaped by building management issues, residential mobility, and length of residence. By focusing on social relations at the apartment-building scale, the study contributes to the debates on relations in vertically segregated apartment buildings arguing that spatial proximity does not lead to social interaction or improved community relations.

10.title: Vertical segregation and socio-spatial deprivation in Athens
10.abstract: This presentation will examine and map vertical segregation and socio-spatial deprivation trends in Athens

10.title: Family multi-storey apartment building and urban micro-segregation
10.abstract:
The family multi-storey apartment building is a term that remains mainly in use in spoken discourse. The spatial model which describes it refers to a multi-storey apartment building (ground floor plus two or more upper floors) in which members of the same family reside in its different apartments.

Family apartment buildings were constructed either through self-promotion system —usually 2-storey or 3-storey apartment building mainly located in the periphery of Athens— or through the ‘antiparochi’ system —typical apartment buildings in which the extended family owns the majority of the apartments where it resides.

The family apartment building constitutes a distinct socio-spatial variation of the post-war Athenian ‘polykatoikia’. Its differentiation is evident in its mode of production and the spatial quality of its apartments. It is primarily constructed to address the housing needs of its members. It is structurally distinct from investment-oriented apartment buildings, with the typical antiparochi building positioned between the two.

Focusing on the interior characteristics of family apartment building through self-promotion shows that it is a largely homogeneous residential environment. It is a “Greek” apartment building —with no presence of migrants— where residential use is dominant and owner-occupation is the prevailing residential status.

Micro-segregation can be interpreted in different ways. On the one hand, intergenerational social mobility combined with limited residential mobility due to family ties may lead to increased social mix and increased micro-segregation. On the other hand, within the same building, familial co-residence and practices of mutual support generate tendencies of convergence between households —especially during periods of crisis— which may reduce micro-segregation.

At neighbourhood scale, residence in family apartment buildings and the sense of collective ownership among family members may act as a barrier against apartment abandonment, vacancy, or conversion into short-term rental accommodation.

10.title: Between the anvil and the hammer: Athens' refugees’ housing segregation patterns in times of confinement policies and housing crises
10.abstract:
Based on qualitative and ethnographic research, the contribution analyses Athens' refugees’ segregation patterns, bringing the attention on link between institutional segregation in extra-urban confinement camps and micro-segregation in the informal housing market, through which a large percentage of the refugees seek refuge in the city. It is claimed that the housing deprivation faced by such group is not the result of either the “financial” or the “refugee” crisis, but of the combined effect of a new model of urban development and a new model of migration’s governance, shaping new geographies of mobility and immobility, at both the urban and the international scale. It is argued that such dynamic not only has radicalized the established pattern of both “vertical” and “horizontal” segregation, but has also promoted the growth of a specific segment of the housing market, the underground short-term rental market, deepening the already established patterns of refugees' socio-tenurial segregation. Finally, the contribution analyses how the emergence of the "underground" short-term rental market overlapped with the development of the "legal" short-term rental market, exploring the paradox of the parallel and overlapping growth of both short-term rentals and (wanted and unwanted) human mobilities.

References.
Arapoglou, V.P.; Spyrellis, S.N. (2024). Arrival Infrastructures: Segregation of Displaced Migrants and Processes of Urban Change in Athens. Geographies, 4: 182–202.
Kreichauf, R. (2018). From forced migration to forced arrival: the campization of refugee accommodation in European cities. Comparative Migration Studies. 6. 10.
Tazzioli, M; Garelli, G. (2018). Containment beyond detention: The hotspot system and disrupted migration movements across Europe. Environment and Planning D: Society and Space, 0(0): 1-19.

10.title: Erasmus students' residential patterns in Athens
10.abstract:
This paper examines micro-segregation dynamics in Athens within the "privileged mobility" frameworks. In recent years the Greek capital has become an increasingly popular destination for Erasmus Students (ES), contributing to the reshaping of local housing dynamics in ways that remain largely understudied.
Drawing on original survey data collected among ES enrolling in the main Athenian universities (2023-2025), we focused on their residential patterns. This population, staying in Athens for mostly six months, shares elements with short-term rentals (STRs) and with long-term rental (LTRs), while remaining a distinct case from both.
We analyse the networks through which ES access housing, the type and amenities of the stock they occupy, comparing their residential strategies with those of Athenian students using 2011 and 2021 census data. This comparison seeks to position them within the vertical hierarchy of Athenian apartment buildings and the micro-spatial qualities produced at different floor levels.
Findings reveal that ES access a specific market segment, occupying specific floors and building types, reflecting affordability constraints and informal sorting mechanisms. These micro-scale patterns interact with neighbourhood-level dynamics, raising questions about how spatial proximity to local residents might translate into a socio-economic fracture.
Athens represents a compelling case: a southern European city attractive as a year-round tourist destination, where a real estate crisis is emerging alongside tourism gentrification. Findings suggest that student accommodation is market-driven and concentrated in specific neighbourhoods, shaped less by students' social preferences than by a segmented housing supply targeting foreign temporary residents. This produces a dual housing market between lower-income locals and higher-income foreigners, risking generating rent gaps, displacement pressures, and socio-spatial inequalities.
This presentation advances debates on micro-segregation by showing how privileged mobile populations constitute a distinct layer within urban residential hierarchies, and by highlighting the role of housing policy and urban context in influencing such processes.

10.title: How Transnational Elite Mobility generates new patterns of Urban Micro-segregation : “Offshore Residential Zones” in Mauritius
10.abstract:
In recent years, many cities and states have developed schemes to attract transnational mobile elites, but the effects of these programmes on urban segregation remain poorly understood. By analogy with the ‘special economic zones’ developed to attract foreign companies, the article proposes the new concept of “offshore residendial zones” to designate areas with special status aimed at attracting international investment in real estate. These ORZs have developed significantly over the past 20 years, particularly in tax havens and city-states (Dubaï, Saint Kitts…), where they are often associated with "golden visa" programmes, offering access to citizenship or residency rights in exchange for property purchases. In just 20 years (2002–2022), in Mauritius - a small, densely urbanised and former sugar island transformed into an international financial center and élite tourist destination - more than 183 offshore residential zones have been launched, generating territorial fragmentation at the local scale, and profoundly transforming patterns of urbanisation and forms of micro-segregation. In fact, most of these areas take the form of small gated communities comprising villas with swimming pools or luxury apartments – standardised and tailored to a mobile, international clientele – and stand out sharply from the local built-up environment in terms of population and architecture, as well as in terms of environmental amenities, the quality of urban facilities and legal status.
Our study is based on a mixed method. Between 2023 and 2025, we conducted ethnographic surveys among the ORZ’s intermediaries (policymakers, property developers, wealth managers, etc.) and foreign homebuyers (mainly French and South African). These ethnographic methods were supplemented by cartographic work based on quantitative data (lists of ORZ projects, surveys on the profiles of buyers).
The article shows the new patterns of micro-segregation, of socio-racial hierarchies, and of environmental injustice generated by the transnational élite in urban spaces.

10.title: Low inequality, high segregation? The role of spatial scale in analysing socio-economic stratification

authors.name: Ladislav Novotný
authors.affiliation: Pavol Jozef Šafárik University in Košice, Slovakia, Faculty of Science, Institute of Geography

10.abstract:
Socio-economic segregation is most often studied in large cities, where its development is usually linked to trends in income inequality. Bratislava and Slovakia are usually described as having relatively low-income inequality and low levels of socio-economic segregation. At the same time, recent trends in internal migration suggest that socio-spatial differentiation may be increasing. However, such conclusions strongly depend on the spatial scale at which inequality is analysed.
This study examines how different spatial units influence the observed patterns and development of socio-economic stratification and segregation. Using occupational structure as a proxy for socio-economic status, the analysis adopts a multi-scalar perspective, comparing national, regional and sub-local levels. At higher spatial levels, inequality is typically measured by aggregate indicators such as the Gini coefficient, which usually indicate low and stable disparities. However, these measures can hide important differences within large territorial units.
To address this issue, the study explores how increasing spatial resolution, from national to intra-municipal levels, changes the interpretation of socio-economic inequalities. While the Gini coefficient captures overall distribution, the localization quotient is used at lower spatial levels to identify spatial concentration of specific socio-economic groups. The combination of these measures allows a more detailed view of both vertical inequality and spatial differentiation.
The results show how different spatial scales can lead to different views on inequality trends, including situations where macro-level stability coexists with micro-level disparities. Special attention is given to “hidden segregation”, which becomes visible only at finer spatial scales.

Acknowledgement: Funded by the project VEGA 1/0768/24 “Multiscale assessment of spatial variability of social-economic population stratification”.

10.title: Colonial Planning Legacies and Urban Micro-Segregation: Reproducing Socio-Spatial Hierarchies in Cairo.

authors.name: Lamiaa Ghoz
authors.affiliation: TU Dresden; leibniz institute of ecological urban and regional development

10.abstract:
During colonial rule, urban planning often followed a socio-spatial order intended to segregate colonizers and native populations. Even after the end of colonial regimes, these spatial logics tend to persist and are reproduced over time. This paper examines the urban planning of Heliopolis, a planned district in Cairo developed in the early 20th century, as an early example of such socio-spatial ordering that continues to shape patterns of implicit segregation across the contemporary city.
Developed during the British protectorate under Édouard Empain, Heliopolis was conceived as a planned enclave targeting expatriate and upper-class populations. While its architectural identity reflects eclectic colonial interpretations of local forms, this research shifts the focus toward the city’s underlying planning logic and its socio-spatial implications.
Heliopolis was structured through a deliberate spatial hierarchy, manifested in differentiated housing typologies and street layouts that reinforced social stratification. These planning strategies produced not only neighbourhood-level segregation but also emerging forms of micro-segregation at the street scale, particularly through variations in street hierarchy, accessibility, and the distribution of more and less affluent residential areas. In this context, spatial proximity did not necessarily translate into social integration.
Integrating postcolonial perspectives, this research argues that such implicit segregation logics have been reproduced and adapted across Cairo’s urban fabric. Through spatial mapping of street networks and building typologies, the study identifies comparable patterns across contemporary districts.
Preliminary findings suggest that spatial closeness continues to coexist with social distance, with planning configurations sustaining subtle yet persistent hierarchies. The paper contributes to debates on urban micro-segregation and highlights the importance of critically engaging with inherited planning legacies.

10.title: Urban Form and segregation: Towards a comparative socio-spatial research framework
10.abstract:
Studies on urban segregation have traditionally examined residential patterns and socio-economic characteristics in depth. Nevertheless, segregation is also produced and experienced through everyday practices in public urban space, where the built environment’s characteristics that constitute the city’s urban form shape movement, encounter, visibility, and proximity. However, the explicit role of urban form in urban segregation remains underexplored, particularly within transferable approaches that enable comparative analysis across different urban contexts.
To this end, this submission discusses the theoretical, conceptual, and methodological framework(s) for analysing how urban form patterns interact with socio-economic and socio-demographic typologies to shape urban segregation. More specifically, it explores the core components of a comprehensive research approach that is: i) multi-dimensional, addressing socio-economic and socio-demographic typologies as well as urban form patterns (including urban mobility infrastructure); ii) multi-method, combining quantitative geospatial analysis with qualitative and participatory research methods where appropriate; and iii) multi-scalar, both micro-scale analysis of segregation profiles at block level and below; and meso-scale analysis of urban form types and urban segregation at neighbourhood level.
The proposed framework responds to a double limitation in existing morphological research on urban segregation: studies that provide broad territorial coverage often lack detailed morphological description, while fine-grained morphological or ethnographic works often remain spatially localised and difficult to compare. By focusing on European urban peripheries, this submission sets the scene for a comparative analysis of socio-spatial typologies relevant to urban segregation, to contextualise a critical approach to (spatial and social) proximity planning. Its contribution is to outline a transferable yet context-sensitive approach for identifying how urban segregation is produced, mediated, or facilitated by urban form at different scales, aiming to challenge the recent proximity planning paradigms, such as the “15-minute” city model, that are largely derived from Western and Northern European case studies dominating planning research.

11.title: Towards a Metropolitan Housing Observatory in Athens: data availability, gaps and institutional collaborations
11.abstract:
The intensification of housing unaffordability, tenure insecurity and socio-spatial inequalities in Athens has highlighted the need for robust monitoring tools capable of informing evidence-based and socially responsive housing policy. In this context, the Municipality of Athens has included the establishment of a Municipal Housing Observatory within its recent Housing Policy Strategy, envisioning a permanent mechanism for documenting housing conditions, supporting policy design and evaluation, and improving public access to housing-related information.
This paper sets out a preliminary framework for the design of a Metropolitan Housing Observatory in Athens, examining the opportunities and constraints involved in its institutional and methodological development. It maps the current landscape of available housing data in Greece and the Athens metropolitan area, including administrative registries, census and survey data, taxation records, social policy databases, real-estate market platforms and geospatial sources. Particular attention is given to fragmentation, uneven accessibility, lack of interoperability, and the absence of systematic local-scale indicators.
The presentation also discusses lack of evidence and institutional tools that hinder effective housing policy making, such as the lack of an official rent and housing price index, updated information on use, housing quality, energy upgrade needs and vacancy, as well as displacement pressure or deprivation, tools that would be also necessary for identifying areas under housing stress, as currently discussed at a European level.
Finally, the paper reflects on possible governance models for the Observatory, emphasising collaboration between municipal services, universities, research centres, civil society organisations and national statistical authorities. By articulating dispersed datasets and expertise, a Metropolitan Housing Observatory could become both a technical infrastructure for policy coordination and a democratic instrument for transparency, accountability and housing justice in Athens.

Keywords: housing observatories; Athens; housing data; affordability; housing justice

11.title: Housing Dynamics in Naples: perspective to set and Open Lab
11.abstract:
This contribution addresses the political conditions under which a housing observatory can become an instrument of democratic counter-knowledge, going beyond a monitoring mechanism oriented toward institutional decision-making.
Lately, the discourse around data accessibility has gained a pivotal position both for institutional actors and for grassroots movements dealing with housing inequalities. In contexts of housing precarity and conflict, access to data is never neutral: what gets measured, by whom, and for whom directly conditions the possibility of articulating housing rights as collective claims.
The presentation will reflect on the importance of intersecting multiple sources and actors, as a way to both orient policies toward more community-sensitive approaches and to empower communities by building awareness of the quantitative dimensions of the exclusionary dynamics affecting the right to the city. The context is the municipality of Naples, Southern Italy, where the lack of a coherent and comprehensive dataset constrains the capacity of institutional and civil society actors to measure and analyse the dynamics shaping housing access.
To develop a critical and up-to-date analysis of the housing issue in Naples, the new Open Lab (NaHO), led by the University Federico II of Naples, will process data and analysis on housing dynamics. The NaHO's project aims to collect data on housing conditions in terms of both affected social groups and housing stock quality - integrating background data, often outdated or insufficient, with an analysis of emerging issues and needs. The research outputs will contribute to propose an interactive tool for data elaboration and representation, usable by researchers, institutional actors, and grassroots organisations alike.
The contribution addresses both the methodological challenges of building such an instrument and its political ambition: the observatory as a tool for rendering legible - and therefore contestable - the mechanisms through which financialisation produces housing exclusion.

11.title: Housing beyond metrics: an overview of the ecosystem of civic and institutional local observatories in Italy

authors.name: Laura Colini
authors.affiliation: University Iuav of Venice & Social Forum dell' Abitare

authors.name: Remi Wacogne
authors.affiliation: Ocio Osservatorio CIvicO sulla casa e la residenza Venezia

11.abstract:
Paralleled by a progressive crisis and lack of investments in the public housing sector, civic organisations in Italy are reclaiming housing as common good with a proliferation of strategies, including reframing data about housing as a terrain of political struggle rather than neutral administrative evidence. While housing is increasingly governed through market metrics, asset valorisation, and platform economies, forms of knowledge attentive to social conditions and rights of inhabitation have progressively faded from official systems of recording data.
Analysing local experiences directly or indirectly linked to the national activists network Social Forum dell’Abitare (including civic observatories, counter-mapping practices, and campaigns on vacancy and displacement) the article explains how these grassroots initiatives contest the epistemological frameworks through which urban space becomes governable. It argues that these experiences challenge the technocratic depoliticisation of housing itself, by exposing the inability of institutional housing indicators to capture the issues related housing and reveal lived effects of touristification, financialisation in cities.
Further attention is devoted to the role of academic institutions increasingly involved in collaborative forms of research with civic observatories as much as with local administrations, questioning whether these collaborations have the potential to generate transformative forms of co-knowledge or risk fragmenting, or reabsorbing grassroots critique into managerial instrument of policy neutralisation.
In conclusion, paper argues that the significance of bottom-up local housing observatories lies less in their capacity to improve governance efficiency than in their ability to challenging prevailing assumptions about how urban crises should be recorded, measured, and governed.

11.title: Participatory mapping of vacant and under-used buildings for cooperative and social housing
11.abstract:
Amid intensifying housing pressures and the persistent underuse of urban building stock, vacant and inadequately used properties represent an important yet insufficiently documented resource for cooperative and social housing strategies. This paper presents the action-research methodology developed by CoHab Athens, an open group working for the promotion of cooperative housing in Greece, which focuses on detecting, mapping and reclaiming vacant buildings through collective forms of knowledge production that combine civic engagement with spatial documentation.
Through its “Reclaim” campaign, CoHab tries to mobilise neighbourhood groups, housing activists and residents to identify and record vacant properties using participatory field mapping, direct observation and citizen data collection. The initiative seeks to make vacancy visible not only as a spatial condition but also as a political issue linked to housing exclusion, underinvestment and unequal access to urban resources.
The collected information is visualised through a web-mapping tool (currently based on Google Maps), with plans to migrate to an open-source platform that will support community deliberation and collective claims for the socially beneficial reuse of vacant properties, particularly those under public or charitable ownership. The methodology also includes co-design workshops and collective mapping walks that function simultaneously as data-gathering practices and civic engagement events, fostering local collaboration and awareness around housing under-use.
The paper argues that such bottom-up activist practices can function as alternative housing observatories rooted in community participation and action research, that can complement or even challenge official databases, towards a more socially just (re)activation of urban vacancy.
Keywords: participatory mapping; vacant buildings; cooperative housing; action research

11.title: The Exarcheia Neighborhood Mapping Group
11.abstract: The Exarcheia Mapping Group (Ομάδα Χαρτογράφησης Εξαρχείων) was formed in 2023 to document ongoing socio-spatial transformations in the neighborhood. As a participatory, community-based collective, we engage in counter-mapping as part of broader community responses to touristification and gentrification. Through fieldwork and methods including mapping, GIS, photography, interviews, and sound recordings, we reconstruct these processes from the bottom up, drawing on local knowledge and lived experience. Exarcheia, a historic mixed-use neighborhood of Athens with a strong social and political tradition, has undergone rapid change in recent years. It is significantly affected by the housing crisis, as uncontrolled touristification and real estate speculation displace residents and everyday activities, while weakening social ties. From this perspective, we argue that the housing crisis in Athens extends beyond limited access to affordable housing. Rather, it is a broader and complex crisis of habitation, affecting not only individuals, but also their communities and their ability to exercise their rights ‘within’ and ‘to’ the city. The presentation combines two complementary approaches. First, mapping is used to examine how global dynamics take shape locally, interacting with specific places and processes and shaping everyday urban life. Particular attention is given to vacant buildings and the conversion of residential and mixed-use buildings into tourist accommodation. Second, visual methods, including photography and video, are used to document these changes and explore how they are experienced in space.

11.title: Critical monitoring of social work casefiles for insights into displacement processes
11.abstract:
This contribution reflects on the merits of collaborating with neighbourhood social workers, regionally subsidised organisations, and tenant unions to collect data on residential displacement and housing injustices. It revisits an action research study conducted with Bonnevie, a local housing aid organisation in Old Molenbeek-Saint-Jean, a working-class neighbourhood in Brussels. Using the case files of Bonnevie’s social workers as a situated data source, the research emphasises how such institutional structures can compensate for the lack of systematic data and provide an essential entry point for conceptualising evictions and forced displacement. Taking eviction classifications and causes as an entry point, the study argues for the development of displacement-based eviction monitoring through diversified data collection methods, enabling a critical assessment of institutional interference in the production of precarity.

Engaging with studies and calls to action that denounce the lack of a functioning system for monitoring evictions in Belgium, this contribution intervenes in an ongoing debate on the absence of consistent data on evictions, both nationally and in the Brussels Region. In particular, it refers to a regional eviction monitoring system proposed in a 2023 ordinance to the Brussels Housing Code. Conceptualisations of eviction play an important discursive role, requiring robust data, yet such data production remains embedded in material and institutional realities. This contribution highlights how eviction monitoring is tied to (1) the socio-spatial structures of neighbourhoods and (2) legal frameworks shaped by legislative systems and institutional bodies responsible for regulation, enforcement, prevention, and data collection. It further shows how collecting data through social workers’ frontline positions enables displacement-based monitoring, offering critical insight into the production of precarity and (3) revealing the impacts of displacement pressures from their vantage point.

12.title: Collective actions & Urban commons: Sociocracy as a tool of grassroots governance in Thermi.

authors.name: Giannis Bourantas
authors.affiliation: PhD candidate, School of Spatial Planning and Development, AUTh

authors.name: Naya Tselepi
authors.affiliation: PhD Human Geography, Postdoctoral Researcher & Appointed Lecturer AUTh, Sociocracy Certified Expert, Trainer & Facilitator, Project Manager at Anatoliki S.A

authors.name: Giorgos Gritzas
authors.affiliation: Professor, School of Spatial Planning and Development, AUTh, Director of the Postgraduate Program ‘Social & Solidarity Economy’ HOU

12.abstract:
This study examined whether Sociocracy (also known as the Sociocratic Circle Method) could function as a tool of grassroots governance within the context of commons, focusing on collective action, the production of shared urban commons, and the reconfiguration of power in local governance. The case study focused on the Youth Council of the Municipality of Thermi, a unique case in Greece and Europe where Sociocracy has been implemented as a decision-making method at the municipal level.

Using a combination of autoethnography and unstructured and semi-structured interviews, the research revealed that the Sociocratic Circle Method fosters new forms of collective political subjectivities, governance practices and commons-based social relations emerging through
equal participation, collective decision-making process and consent.

Through this process, participants developed communication, organisational, and deliberative skills, while simultaneously cultivating a collective right to participate in the production and governance of urban space (right to the city) that transcends party frameworks and conventional deliberative practices. Sociocracy served as a tool for personal and collective empowerment, enabling members to overcome an exclusionary mindset and experience collective action as a means of social
change within the urban space of Thermi and beyond. It also fostered inclusion, equality in dialogue, and the recognition of care as a politically productive value within urban commons.

Despite initial reservations regarding its effectiveness and the risk of “partisan exploitation,” the results demonstrated that sociocracy fosters political maturity, critical thinking, and a sense of collective power. The Youth Council of the Municipality of Thermi, operating as a municipal-scale governance practice of the right to the city, exemplified the principles of participation and democratic co-creation. This demonstrates that young people can actively contribute to the development of local policies and promote bottom-up urban transformation through collective action.

Keywords: sociocracy, participatory governance, youth participation, urban commons, collective
action, grassroots urban planning

12.title: The right to centrality: Social struggles and planetary urbanization in the Greek periphery.
12.abstract:
The paper examines the radically transforming rural geographies of the Greek territory under the framing of climate crisis resilience, focusing on the ways the periphery is restructured as an active, contested field of spatial reconfigurations. The analysis is framed within the concept of planetary urbanization (Brenner, 2015; Brenner & Schmid, 2015), drawing from Henri Lefebvre’s proposition of complete urbanization ([1970] 2003), which it critically reinterprets by bringing into focus the transformative dynamics of everyday life and relational space as a multiplicity of trajectories in constant negotiation (Massey, 2005).

The research focuses on Agrafa and North Evia, examined not as external to urbanization processes but as spatialities produced within extended urbanization. Emphasis is placed on climate-accelerated restructuring, such as energy investments and post-disaster reconstruction, which intensify socio-spatial inequalities while creating new grounds for collective struggle.

In this context, local mobilizations—such as the Save Agrafa movement and initiatives against the Northern Evia Reconstruction Plan—are analyzed as practices of reclaiming the commons (Stavros Stavrides, 2016, 2019, 2024), through which landscape and resources are reimagined as use values and fields of collective action.

Using ethnographic methods through the lens of situated knowledge (Donna Haraway, 1988), the research highlights how grassroots practices challenge dominant spatial planning models and contribute to the emergence of alternative forms of spatial organization.

This paper aims to critically reposition the “context of context” framework (Brenner & Schmid, 2015), shifting analysis from the macro-scale of capitalist processes toward situated social action, highlighting the potential for collective production of space and reinterpretation of planetary urbanization through social struggles. The study argues that planetary urbanization is not merely a process of capitalist spatial integration, but also a field of contested spatialities where social struggles redefine the right to centrality as a collective practice, critically expanding Lefebvre’s right to the city.

12.title: Sites of Transcendence: The anti-self place in the century of the self'
12.abstract:
The collective urban domain enables the enactment of values, such as notions of ownership, the right to resources and territory, and ideologies about human life in the realm of existence.
In a world increasingly directed by consumerism, this century has been termed ‘the century of the self’ . Today, as world-class urbanization focuses on market-oriented development, urban space that offers no monetary value is perceived as wasteful by the consumerist mantra.
In a parallel and contrary scenario, alternative modes of personal engagement with place are observed across the Pakistani city. Of the most unique of these is the use of the urban commons for acts of service, such as the street school, the neighbourhood water cooler, the bird-feeding node, the langar (free food distribution). These acts may be termed anti-self-interest, and are largely motivated by the altruistic motive: the unselfish regard for, or devotion to, the welfare of others , at personal risk or personal expense. In the words of Monroe , ‘where the rest of us see a stranger, the altruist sees a fellow human being’.
The research takes the city of Lahore as case, exploring narratives of altruism, and manners in which space in the urban collective domain is appropriated by individuals and communities for these acts. These extend to the appropriation of the road, the street, the footpath, and the green patch- as ‘spaces for all’. The research also brings to light the socio-cultural logic informing the perception of the collective realm in Lahore, a city originating in a traditional urban form.
Taking specific enactments of altruistic practices in the common realm, the research explores engagement and occupation, territory and autonomy, and the broader relationship of altruistic acts in public space with the culturally framed imaginaries of ‘self-and-world’.

12.title: Hidrofeminist commoning in the cracks of Chile's water market: a participatory manual for domestic water self-management in Petorca
12.abstract:
Petorca, in central Chile, has become a global emblem of hydrosocial injustice produced by water privatisation. Since the 1981 Water Code, water rights have been captured by avocado agribusiness, while about 20% of the local population receives water from cistern trucks —100 litres per person per day, against 170 in Santiago— with which households must sustain all reproductive activities. This burden falls disproportionately on women, who daily stretch scarce water across cooking, hygiene, laundry and care work, at the cost of their health, time and well-being.
This contribution reflects on Nuestra casa, nuestro cauce (Our House, Our Watercourse), a community manual for the self-management of domestic water co-produced over two years by La Gota Negra, a hidrofeminist collective of geographers, together with women's organisations and rural water committees of Petorca, supported by the Universidad de Chile. While anchored in women's situated knowledge and reproductive labour, the manual was conceived as an inclusive territorial tool engaging the wider community —men, youth, schools and local organisations.
Drawing on participatory action research and grounded in feminist political ecology and community ecofeminism (Cabnal, Paredes, Federici, Rivera Cusicanqui), it articulates four interwoven axes: ancestral and local water knowledges; legal literacy against water theft and contamination; domestic assessment of drinking water quality; and ecological reuse —dry toilets, efficient plumbing, homemade non-toxic products— that protect water as it flows between bodies, households and territories.
Read through Holloway's theory of cracks and Stavrides' notion of the commons, the manual is interpreted as a feminist commoning practice that prefigures alternative hydrosocial relations within and against the neoliberal regime. The paper places Petorca in dialogue with feminist water struggles across Abya Yala and the Mediterranean —two arid, deeply unequal hydrosocial worlds— offering insights for collective action and feminist territorial pedagogies travelling between both shores.

12.title: When commons meet the state. Encounters, frictions and institutional change
12.abstract:
This contribution presents the key insights of a forthcoming book that examines how commons and state institutions encounter one another across diverse socio spatial contexts. Emerging from a four-year interdisciplinary research project, the book brings together 12 case studies from Europe and beyond, whose transversal and interdisciplinary reading challenges state centric and binary framings of support or opposition that continue to dominate debates on the role of the state in commons governance.
Building on this work, the presentation shifts the debate from whether commons should develop with or without the state to what actually happens in everyday encounters between commoning practices and different forms of state authority. These encounters unfold when commoning practices ‘meet’ planning offices, land registries, municipal agendas, permit systems, policy frameworks and informal negotiations. The analysis shows that commons and states cannot be treated as pre given, coherent entities. Instead, they are understood as relational practices that are continuously reshaped through negotiation, contestation, friction and cooperation. The book reveals a spectrum of state–commons interactions, across which commons may operate within legal frameworks while contesting them, appropriate institutional tools through alternate ethics and for alternative ends, or deliberately keep the state at a distance; often combining these strategies at once.
Recognizing the difficulty of escaping state‑centric vocabularies to study commons, the book develops an action‑oriented vocabulary, organised around verbs such as reclaim, negotiate, embed, generate, and reconfigure, to read encounters as productive sites of institutional innovation and socio-spatial transformation rather than problems to be resolved. By foregrounding situated struggles over land, housing, food, and urban space, the contribution speaks directly to debates on socio‑spatial inequalities, participatory planning, and the politics of commoning, offering critical insights for scholars, activists, and practitioners engaged in struggles for more just and collective urban futures.

12.title: Who Owns the Square? Tales of Tourism, Exclusion, and Reappropriation in Chania

authors.name: Zacharias Ouranos
authors.affiliation: PhD candidate, School of Architecture, Technical University of Crete

12.abstract:
Splantzia Square—officially 1821 Square—constitutes one of the central public spaces in the old town of Chania, retaining its significance since the Ottoman period. The square and its surroundings host a layered assemblage of historical elements, including Venetian churches, an Ottoman minaret, an underground cistern and a centuries-old plane tree as a landmark at the center. Today, however, the square is predominantly occupied by the outdoor seating areas of adjacent commercial establishments, which expand seasonally in alignment with tourism flows, producing a temporally bounded landscape of leisure and consumption.
Over the past decade, municipal interventions have gradually removed the benches that once enabled everyday sociality and non-commercial use. Framed as measures to deter “undesirable” presences, these practices can be understood as forms of exclusionary urban governance that reshape the conditions of access and use. In line with critical debates on the commodification of public space, such transformations undermine inhabitants’ right to the city by restricting possibilities for unmediated presence, encounter, and appropriation.
Within this context, the self-organized carnival initiated by the Yar Aman music collective offers a counter-practice of spatial reclamation. Following a performative procession through the city, participants converge on Splantzia Square, where the space is temporarily reappropriated through music, dance, and collective festivity. For several hours, the square is reactivated through music, dance, and collective celebration, foregrounding alternative modes of belonging and participation. This ephemeral yet recurrent event exemplifies practices of reclaiming public space.
By examining these contrasting dynamics, the paper highlights the tensions between tourism-driven gentrification and grassroots forms of spatial appropriation, contributing to broader discussions on the politics of public space in contemporary cities.

12.title: Plucking the Black Rose of Foucault: Reflections on the common space from a crack of Kasteli Hill
12.abstract:
Drawing from the reclaiming movement of Kasteli Hill (Chania, Creta), in this presentation, we explore the notion of common space, which was adopted by the radical wing of the struggle of reokupation of Rosa Nera, in conversation with Foucault's Heterotopias, Holloway's and Stavride's thinking.
By analyzing –from a militant research perspective– the participants’ discourse, we reflect on common space through the theoretical contributions of Stavrides. We argue that common space constitutes a discourse which: consider space as the material basis of autonomy; removes the barriers that fragment subjects into identities and promotes change as the result of that encounter; focuses on the act of sharing space as a key element for social transformation; implies an internal conflict over the forms that will prevail within it; points to a dialectical conflict between emerging utopias and the capitalist order. Finally, a symbolic transition experience is produced: passengers of the space undergo experiences of individual transformation.
Taking this into account, we return and reconsider the basic assumption of Foucault's Heterotopias considered the Other Spaces not just spaces that, besides they difference with normality, contributes to the constitution of order, but as spatial crisis that crack its robust dimension and presents the space as fragile, full of crisis, spaces that inflame the antagonisms of the city and re-constitute the class composition and thus, class struggle.

Key words: Foucault, Heterotopias, common space, Stavrides, Social movements, Rosa Nera, Holloway

12.title: Reexist-ATLAS: Geo-histories against the grain. Mapping cultures of resistance and struggles for reexistence, cracks in Mexico, Chile, and Greece.
12.abstract:
The concept of re-existence originates from the struggles of seringueiros (rubber tappers) of the Amazon in Brazil (“Aliança dos Povos da Floresta”) and was formulated by the geographer Porto-Gonçalves (1998). The Zapatista uprising that began in Chiapas, Mexico, in 1994 (organizacion from 1984), the struggles of the Indigenous Congress, the recent Zapatista journey to Europe, and the arts and sciences encounters in Zapatista communities have highlighted this relationship in a remarkable way.
The concept of “geo-histories against the grain” is introduced in geography through the speaks of Christy Petropoulou and Alberto Betancourt, which are inspired by the works of Walter Benjamin about historie against the grain and Silvia Rivera Cusicanqui.
The concept of the culture of resistance derives from the work of Stathis Damianakos. The concept of cracks in the system derives from the work of John Holloway. The concept of re-existence in territories with a deep history of rebellious tradition, is understood as the power of a fresh start, of rebirth, of attributing new meanings or renewing the meanings of existence, of life with its own horizons of meaning rather than Agamben’s bare life (Hurtado & Porto-Gonçalves) like cracks in the system (Holloway). And they do this by utilising grassroots cultural actions, street arts, and other “bottom-up” cultural expressions.
In this paper, we will mapping oral geo-histories recorded within the framework of ReexistAtlas in certain cultural geographies related to re-emergence, since for many years they had been rendered invisible, in neighbourhoods and communities with strong characteristics of self-organisation, and anti-patriarchal, anti-colonial, and anti-capitalist approaches, in Greece, Mexico, and Chile. Atlas began with active militant research in Mexico and Chile and was enriched with material from the group’s participation in the assembly for the Zapatistas’ trip to Greece.

12.title: Reexist-ATLAS: Geohistories Against the Grain. Mapping the Struggles for Reexistence in Defense of Land and Freedom in Greece, Mexico, and Brazil.
12.abstract:
“Brushing history against the grain” is a metaphor by Walter Benjamin (“Theses on the Philosophy of History”) that proposes interpreting history in opposition to the dominant narrative of the victors. Adolfo Gilly also used this expression for a collection of texts in his book “History Against the Grain. A Constellation”. The concept of geohistories againthegrain is introduced in geography through the speaks of Petropoulou, Betancourt et al.
