The concept of re-existence stems from the struggles of Amazonian rubber tappers in Brazil (“Aliança dos Povos da Floresta”, Chico Mendes) and was formulated by Porto-Gonçalves (1998). It has since been used to describe social movements that do not merely resist, but rather struggle for concrete forms of existence, for multiple specific ways of living, producing, feeling, acting and thinking.
The “Reexist-ATLAS” examines re-existences as forms of resistance against processes of accumulation by dispossession (Harvey) and land grabbing – monetarization, and how these manifest in cities and on the peripheries through the creation of commons.
Within this framework, the concept of the struggle for Land and Freedom draws on the 1910 Mexican social revolution and the Plan of Ayala, the contemporary Zapatista uprising, and the Zapatista delegation’s visit to Europe. These struggles are understood as efforts to create new worlds “from below.” They oppose the deprivation of land, both within urban environments and in peripheral outskirts. They resist large-scale destructive projects, including so-called “green” industrial energy initiatives and they encompass struggles for water and food, the commons -resources increasingly treated as exploitable commodities. These reflections are also evident in self-sufficiency projects of eco-communities and agroecological initiatives.
Methodologically, this work adopts an activist action research approach, in which the researcher actively participates in the research process in Mexico, Brazil, Greece. The research process both enriches social knowledge and fosters action towards social change.

12.title: Collective actions and the commons against touristification. A comparative study on Venice and Naples

authors.name: Elena Schipani
authors.affiliation: MA in Local and Global Development, University of Bologna, Italy

authors.name: Emiliano Pettenò
authors.affiliation: MA in Local and Global Development, University of Bologna, Italy

authors.name: Christos Bakalis
authors.affiliation: PhD, Cultural and Environmental Sociology, faculty member in the School of Social Sciences, University of the Aegean

12.abstract:
Amid the deepening urban and environmental crisis characterized by touristification, overlapping crises of precarious housing conditions, degradation of social reproduction and climate risk, urban space becomes increasingly perceived as a space of exhaustion, dispossession, and struggles for alternative forms of social organization and social practices. The paper contributes to this discussion by investigating how practices of commoning emerge as locally grounded reactions to neoliberal threats associated with tourism-oriented urbanization processes.
The research is grounded on the theoretical connection between “the right to the city” (Lefebvre; Harvey) and the “societies in movement” described by Zibechi, which offers an empirical lens through which to examine how grassroots resistance reconstructs the urban fabric. Building upon the idea of urban commons proposed by Stavrides and the concept of collective action by Ostrom, the paper builds on the concept of commoning.
Empirically, the analysis is based on the study of two Italian cities, Naples and Venice, which are heavily influenced by tourism development but follow different urban trajectories. Although the Venetian example may be considered as the most radical case of a dependency on tourism, resulting in far-reaching consequences for access to housing and depopulation, the current situation in Naples can be viewed as one where the valorization of intangible cultural heritage is being negotiated against the processes of touristification. In both cases, the growth of vacation rentals and the commodification of urban space have exacerbated conflicts over housing, access, and social reproduction.
The data are collected via a set of semi-structured interviews with actors involved in housing disputes and urban commons projects, including activists, grassroots organizations, and local actors. Special emphasis is put on the ways in which these actors create socio-material infrastructures.Through this process, it identifies the commons as an indispensable space of reinventing the right to the city.

12.title: Radical Rituals. Collective Practices for the Right to the City

authors.name: Alkistis Thomidou
authors.affiliation: Forty five degrees; HafenCity University Hamburg

12.abstract:
This paper draws on the ongoing research project Radical Rituals to explore emerging paradigms of spatial practice grounded in collective agency, care, and justice in contexts marked by infrastructural neglect and environmental stress. Against the backdrop of intersecting ecological, social, and political crises, the paper revisits the concept of “radical design” not as an aesthetic or expert-led intervention, but as a relational, performative, and regenerative process embedded in everyday life. Particular attention is given to mundane and infra-ordinary rituals—often overlooked practices of maintenance, repair, and care—as critical tools through which communities reclaim space, sustain engagement, and contest dispossession.

Based on empirical research with initiatives across Europe and within urban–rural entanglements, the paper examines how local actors engage in shared rituals of commoning, stewardship, and cooperation in response to housing insecurity, uneven access to infrastructure, and exclusion from planning and governance. These practices operate simultaneously as forms of spatial care and political agency: they sustain collective action over time while fostering belonging, resilience, and new forms of social organization. Although rooted in specific localities, such rituals resonate across geographies, suggesting how place-based struggles can connect and scale without losing their situated character.

The paper is informed by an ongoing performative journey along the 45ºN parallel, which functions both as method and metaphor. This axis connects disparate contexts through a shared inquiry into how communities mobilize ritualized practices to claim space and shape alternative urban futures. Rather than producing a static archive, the research adopts the lens of the anarchive—an open, evolving system of knowledge that foregrounds localized expertise, affective labor, and environmental attunement.

Ultimately, the paper argues that collective agency and struggles for the commons are transformative forces in spatial planning, revealing how spatial justice and the right to the city emerge through interdependent practices of care, cooperation, and everyday resistance.

12.title: Contesting Public Space through Collective Action: Urban Struggles in Athens and Caen
12.abstract:
This presentation is grounded in my doctoral research* which aligns with the themes of this panel on urban struggles and the production of space.
Social relations of domination are realized in space and through space. Classes, as well as the various social groups that compose them, require space in order to exist, reproduce themselves, and represent themselves. Conflicts over urban and public space are therefore not merely territorial conflicts over the appropriation of the use value of space, but also existential conflicts. They constitute a confrontation between, on the one hand, a system that relentlessly seeks to integrate or systematically eliminate the spatial practices, representations of space, representational spaces, symbols, and organizational possibilities of the proletariat as well as marginalized and oppressed groups; and, on the other hand, those groups themselves, who survive this onslaught and oppose it through resistance and struggle. The right to the city, collective actions and autonomous experiences stand in opposition to developer-led urbanism and its security-oriented and consumerist ideology.
Space, however, is not merely the product of a power imposed upon it; it may also emerge from the interrelation between social agencies, thereby constituting a field of possibilities for the existence of multiplicities — both a form of rupture and a source of rupture. Spaces of struggle, as well as alternative and oppositional spaces, are (re)produced through this potential for rupture, introducing the possibility of multiplicities both in uses and in representations.
Based on this theoretical stand, I analyze, on the one hand, the strategies of dispossession and appropriation of public space deployed by homogenizing powers and, on the other hand, the strategies of resistance, contestation, and reappropriation of that space developed through urban struggles, drawing on empirical cases of urban struggles in the two cities of Caen (France) and Athens (Greece).

12.title: Gendered Invisibility and Rhizomatic Counter-Memories of Feminicide Across Abya Yala and the Mediterranean
12.abstract: This research engages with debates on the right to the city, the city as commons, and anti-colonial feminist struggles, examining how gender-based violence, in particular femicide, is contested through collective, situated practices of memory-making. It asks how marginalized subjects reclaim presence, visibility and spatial belonging in contexts where dominant regimes of memory erase the geographies of violence. Drawing on anti-patriarchal and anti-colonial perspectives, this research approaches urban space as a contested common shaped through struggle, where everyday practices can open ''cracks'' in hegemonic structures. Within this framework, it explores how grassroots, embodied practices generate alternative spatial knowledges that challenge institutional silencing and dominant narratives. Methodologically, the research combines qualitative and digital approaches. It analyses the feminist protest song Canción sin miedo, which originally emerged in Mexico as a collective act of mourning and resistance against femicides, tracing the transnational circulation of the song across Abya Yala Afro-Latin America and into the Mediterranean, particularly Greece. A dataset of publicly available performances on YouTube is compiled and synthesized into a map that visualizes the geographies articulated through lyrics, translating dispersed, affective narratives into forms of counter-mapping. In addition, the study traces the rhizomatic circulation of the song within Greece between 2022 and 2024 mapping the performances through which it spread. This is complemented by semi-structured interviews with participants involved in this process, providing insights into the rhizomatic spread. The research conceptualizes these practices as rhizomatic, decentralized, iterative and expanding across territories through networks of solidarity. Through song as an embodied, collective practice, collectives produce intangible counter-memorials that inscribe violence and invisibility into space while asserting claims to justice and the commons. It thus highlights how feminist, anti-colonial practices of remembrance reconfigure space and enact the right to the city beyond formal narratives.

13.title: Kessariani and the Social Life of Housing: Demolition, Memory and Urban Value

authors.name: Olga Balaoura
authors.affiliation: School of Architecture, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki

13.abstract:
The neighbourhood of Kessariani, one of the first refugee settlements built in interwar Athens, encapsulates a century-long genealogy of housing, social struggle and urban transformation. Established after the 1922 Asia Minor Catastrophe as part of the first- and arguably last- comprehensive social housing programme in Greece, it evolved from modest brick dwellings and stone units to polykatoikies, reflecting shifting relations between welfare, self-construction and capitalist urbanization.
Within this trajectory, demolition appears not only as a physical process but as an institutional strategy. The post-war antiparochi system dismantled significant parts of the original refugee housing in favour of market-oriented apartment buildings, while also producing the social mixture characteristic of the Greek model of urban development. Today, housing financialization continues this dynamic, while the chronic absence of maintenance acts as a silent form of demolition, eroding material continuity and memory. Under these conditions, publicly subsidised housing- rather than being maintained or reimagined for future generations- is increasingly demolished, turning social infrastructure into an expendable asset. Demolitions thus operate as mechanisms of commodification, facilitating the erasure of lived histories and reshaping what is rendered valuable or expendable in the urban landscape.
Through the physical traces of dismantling, layering and re-inhabitation, one can read a silent social archive: refugee heritage, gendered and collective practices of maintenance and everyday resistance to commodification and erasure. Thus, Kessariani’s residents- despite internal tensions- have asserted their right to inhabit through repair, care and informal construction. Their interventions sustain the memory, scale and social fabric of the neighbourhood, extending the project of Greek modernity beyond official architectural narratives. The presentation reads Kessariani as both a product of modernist planning and a site of endurance shaped by everyday negotiation. It reframes demolition as an instrument of urban transformation, and everyday life as its plural counterforce.

13.title: An AI-Assisted Visual Analysis of Urban Change in the Koukaki Area, Athens
13.abstract: Gentrification remains a persistent theme in discussions of urban restructuring, particularly in relation to housing affordability and residential displacement. Global urban capitalism, the role of the state, and touristification play significant roles in Mediterranean metropolises such as Athens, revealing ongoing gentrification processes. A part of the academic literature examines the social, economic, and physical impacts through both qualitative and quantitative studies, yet comprehensive methodologies remain elusive. Computer vision, machine learning, and Google Street View now provide new tools to identify gentrification in urban areas by capturing expansion through specific visual indicators. In this context, we present a novel methodology to identify signs of gentrification in the Koukaki area, integrating primary and secondary data and employing AI assistance alongside manual validation. Our methodology combines street- level panoramic data collected with LiDAR scanner and historical imagery from Google Street View, comparing present-day panoramas captured in the field with historical imagery from Google Street View (2009), to establish signs, patterns and urban transformations associated with gentrification. Our findings reveal substantial transformations in the economic and physical landscape of the study area, where façade renovation, food and beverage expansion, upgraded commercial uses, and possible Airbnb activity are evident. The presentation documents how and in what terms gentrification visual cues are linked to the growth of touristification in the Greek context, exposing a series of interconnected changes that are transforming the neighbourhood’s profile and offering a near real-time estimation.

13.title: Testing the PRG Index: a comparative assessment of neighbourhood-level socio-spatial change across European urban contexts
13.abstract:
Contemporary socio-spatial transformations are increasingly reshaping urban neighbourhoods across Europe, where processes such as touristification, real estate investment and commercial restructuring interact within the same local spaces. These dynamics have been particularly intense in Southern European cities in the aftermath of economic crises and austerity policies, profoundly affecting housing conditions, commercial activities and everyday life at the neighbourhood scale.

This paper proposes and tests the PRG Index (Potential Risk of Gentrification) as a multidimensional analytical tool for assessing neighbourhood-level socio-spatial change. The PRG Index is designed to identify structural conditions that favour processes of urban revalorisation, integrating economic, social, symbolic and environmental dimensions within a synthetic framework. Rather than focusing solely on observable outcomes, the index aims to capture underlying pressures that shape trajectories of neighbourhood transformation.

The empirical analysis is based on a comparative framework including four European cities representing different urban regimes: Copenhagen and Berlin in Northern Europe, and Madrid and Athens in Southern Europe. Within each city, two types of neighbourhoods are examined—those where processes of revalorisation are already consolidated and those where such dynamics are currently unfolding. This design allows for a dual assessment of the index: ex post, by evaluating its capacity to reflect established transformations, and prospectively, by assessing its ability to identify emerging patterns of change.

The results show that while similar dynamics—such as capital inflows, shifts in commercial land uses and pressures on housing—are present across all contexts, their intensity and configuration vary significantly depending on local structural conditions, including housing regimes, welfare systems and regulatory frameworks. By focusing on the neighbourhood as a space of coexistence where multiple dynamics intersect over time, the paper demonstrates the analytical value of the PRG Index for capturing the complexity of contemporary socio-spatial change and enabling systematic comparison across diverse European urban contexts.

13.title: Changing Geographies of Urban Inequality in Metropolitan Athens: A Socio-Spatial Analysis of Akadimia Platonos and Kypseli
13.abstract:
The paper focuses on the long-term relationship between the structure of urban space and social inequalities, highlighting issues of social polarization, residential segregation and uneven geographies of development in the urban and metropolitan area of Athens. Drawing on census data from 1991, 2001, 2011, and 2021, it analyses changes in the city’s socio-spatial structure through the lens of contemporary processes of urban restructuring.

The analysis of the metropolitan area indicates that historically established patterns of east–west socio-spatial differentiation remain identifiable, while intermediate zones of heightened social fluidity are simultaneously emerging, where tendencies of upgrading, decline, and investment pressures coexist. The research investigates these zones as critical sites for understanding the mechanisms through which socio-spatial inequalities are reproduced or transformed.

Within this framework, the neighbourhood is approached as a critical analytical scale, with particular emphasis on the cases of Akadimia Platonos and Kypseli. The two areas express different dimensions of broader metropolitan transformations: the former as a site of uneven land valorisation and investment-led restructuring, and the latter as a space of complex social recomposition and shifting housing dynamics.

The study argues that the mechanisms transforming these areas are closely linked to capital flows, spatial policies, and processes of selective development that reshape the conditions under which inequalities are produced. By combining longitudinal census analysis with comparative investigation at the neighbourhood scale, the research seeks to illuminate contemporary forms of uneven urban development and the role of spatial planning in shaping them.

Key words: Social polarization, Residential segregation, Uneven development, Metropolitan Athens, Neighborhood scale

13.title: Belonging as Mechanism: Intersecting Mobilities and the Production of Space in Kypseli, Athens
13.abstract:
This paper examines socio-spatial change at the neighborhood scale through an ethnographic study of Kypseli, a densely populated and historically heterogeneous area in Athens. It advances a conceptualization of belonging not merely as an affective attachment or discursive claim, but as a social mechanism with material effects, actively shaping the production and transformation of urban space.

Drawing on participant observation, interviews, and spatial methods, this research traces how these struggles over belonging leave material traces in the built environment. In this sense, belonging is approached as a mediating process that connects everyday practices, social relations, and the physical shaping of the neighbourhood.

Historically, Kypseli has been a site of convergence of different mobilities: internal Greek migrants from the provinces in the 1960s, Balkan, African, Asian and Middle-Eastern migrants after 1990, refugees and asylum seekers during and after the 2015 European "migrant crisis", and since the pandemic a new stream of foreign nationals seeking not only economic opportunities but also a lifestyle of cosmopolitanism and proximity to a vibrant urban environment. These dynamics have been accompanied by growing foreign real estate investment, spurred by state-driven policies such as tax incentives for investors and the Golden Visa program.

Ultimately, by treating belonging as a social mechanism with material effects, this research shows how competing claims to belonging are inscribed in the social production of space, shaping the built environment in which all these categories co-exist. In doing so, it highlights the neighborhood as a key analytical scale for understanding how socio-spatial change unfolds through the entanglement of lived experience and material transformation.

13.title: Kypseli in transition: global changes at the local level
13.abstract:
Cities in Southern Europe are undergoing profound transformations shaped by the interplay between housing crises, tourism expansion, and new forms of transnational mobility. In contexts historically characterized by limited public housing provision, strong reliance on homeownership, and informal welfare mechanisms, these pressures are contributing to the reconfiguration of socio-spatial inequalities, a dynamic particularly visible at the neighborhood scale.
This paper investigates these processes through the case of Kypseli, a central neighborhood of Athens marked by high density and longstanding social and ethnic diversity. The neighborhood is approached not as a bounded entity, but as a space where local specificities intersect with global processes — such as touristification, transnational gentrification, and housing financialization — reshaping both social composition and the everyday use of residential and commercial space.
Particular attention is paid to temporary populations — international students, digital nomads, neo-tourists — situated at the intersection of tourism and migration, as key actors driving recent transformations. Their presence, amplified by the platform economy and short-term rental markets, reconfigures housing uses and everyday practices, generating material and symbolic fractures between long-term and more recent residents.
These dynamics are furthermore reflected in the transformation of Kypseli's commercial landscape. Drawing on mixed methods, systematic on-site recording of business openings and closures between 2019 and 2025, combined with questionnaires and interviews along two commercial streets (Sporades and Zakynthos), this paper traces a gradual shift from diverse, locally oriented retail toward standardized, tourism-driven services. This pattern of functional homogenization points to a broader process of commercial upgrading tightly entangled with the neighborhood's new social composition.
Together, the two research strands reveal how global pressures are rearticulated through context-specific trajectories, making Kypseli a particularly valuable lens for understanding contemporary urban change in Southern Europe.

13.title: Urban Transformations and Inhabitation: The Case of Fokionos Negri from the Pandemic to the Present
13.abstract:
This paper analyzes the complex transformations of urban identity and inhabitation in Fokionos Negri, Kypseli, from the Covid-19 pandemic period to the present. The primary objective is to investigate the imprints left on housing and the "right to the city" through the strategic scale of the neighborhood. Fokionos Negri is selected as a case study as it constitutes a "microcosm" of the broader pressures characterizing South European cities: touristification, shifts in land use, rising rents, and changes in social composition. As a site with a long history of social heterogeneity and dense public life, it emerges as a distinctive field where multi-scale processes intersect.
The ongoing research is based on a qualitative methodology (urban ethnography, on-site observation, semi-structured interviews) with residents, professionals, and street users. Public space is approached as "lived space," where everyday practices negotiate broader urban shifts. Preliminary findings indicate a displacement of the pedestrian zone from a space for the neighborhood's residents into a space of consumption.
The study documents how the "Situated Imaginaries" of the inhabitants function as bulwarks against commodification. The daily coexistence on public benches, the survival of traditional small-scale businesses, and the collective memory of the inhabitants constitute a "poetics of inhabitation" that resists the logic of profit. This presentation explores how the lived experience of diverse subjects undergoes a violent hierarchy, where the imposition of an investment-driven imaginary and a monothematic image threatens to rupture the bonds that allow the city to remain a place of coexistence. From this perspective, the neighborhood emerges as the preeminent field where the right to the city is reclaimed as a living practice against new mechanisms of urban inequality.

13.title: Touristification and Displacement: The Case of the Commercial Triangle in Athens

authors.name: Konstantinos Marougkas
authors.affiliation: Panteion University of Social and Political Sciences

authors.name: Vasilios Avdikos
authors.affiliation: Panteion University of Social and Political Sciences

13.abstract:
The article aims to investigate the multi-layered impacts of touristification on the urban fabric of Athens, with a particular focus on its historic center. The Commercial Triangle has been selected as a case study, as this area constitutes a representative example of the socio-spatial and economic changes experienced by the broader Athenian center under the influence of tourism and the 2009 crisis.
In recent years, the rapid increase in tourist flows, combined with the spread of short-term rentals such as Airbnb and the growth of tourism-oriented land uses, has significantly contributed to the transformation of the area's character. These changes affect not only land uses but also the social composition and economic dynamics of the city center, leading to a restructuring of the relationships between visitors, residents, and business activities.
Therefore, touristification constitutes a complex process that reshapes the identity of central Athens, influencing both its physical characteristics and its intangible dimensions. The study examines these transformations by analyzing the causes and consequences of touristification, focusing on the shift from a space of production to a space of consumption—particularly the displacement of traditional shops and professions—along with changes in land use and the broader role of tourism in shaping urban space.

14.title: Urban Sprawl and Airbnb Concentration on the Island of Crete
14.abstract:
Short-term rentals, especially Airbnb, have become an important expression of tourism pressure in the Greek islands, reshaping local settlement patterns and increasing demand for built space. Although tourism development is usually associated with coastal zones, many island mountainous areas are also affected by second-home development, short-term accommodation and built-up dispersion. These areas are environmentally and culturally sensitive, often linked with traditional settlements, distinctive landscapes and fragile local communities. In this context, built-up area dispersion in mountainous island areas raises important questions for spatial planning and sustainable tourism management.
This study focuses on the mountainous areas of Crete and investigates how built-up area dispersion is related to the spatial concentration of Airbnb listings. The mountainous zones are delineated through a terrain-based classification that combines elevation and slope, allowing the distinction between moderate, steep and high mountainous environments. The analysis integrates Copernicus built-up data for 2006 and 2018, digital elevation and slope layers, settlement boundaries and Airbnb listings. Through GIS-based overlay analysis, the study examines whether dispersed built-up development is mainly located within established settlements or expands beyond their boundaries. In parallel, Airbnb density is mapped in order to identify areas where short-term rental activity overlaps with patterns of dispersed development.
The results show how urban sprawl and Airbnb activity are spatially related in mountainous island areas. The analysis highlights whether Airbnb concentration is located within existing settlements or extends into outside settlement areas already affected by dispersed development. The study contributes to the discussion on tourism pressure, urban sprawl and spatial planning in mountainous island environments, emphasizing the need for integrated policies that balance tourism development, landscape protection and the resilience of local communities.

14.title: Patterns and spatial dynamics of built-up area dispersion on Sifnos island
14.abstract:
Island landscapes are a key factor in the quality of life for local residents, while also representing important economic resource, as they constitute a primary driver of tourism. Rapid tourism development creates a constant demand for the expansion of built-up areas and changes in land use. When these pressures occur outside a coherent spatial planning framework, they can lead to irreversible transformations of the island landscape, ultimately resulting in unsustainable tourism models.
Pressures for new constructions are particularly strong across the Cycladic islands, not only in internationally renowned tourist destinations but increasingly in smaller islands that have experienced significant growth in recent decades, such as Sifnos. This study aims to provide a quantitative and spatial analysis of the patterns of built-up area dispersion on Sifnos by examining specific spatial dynamics that influence its expansion. To achieve this, remote sensing methods are employed to detect changes in built-up areas over time. Settlement boundaries are used to delineate dispersed development. Then an overlay analysis is applied to estimate the proportion built-up area dispersion occurring in coastal zones, along road networks, and along ridgelines.
The results highlight the increasing pressures on the island’s landscape in recent years, as well as distinct spatial patterns of development. These patterns appear to be closely linked both to existing planning regulations and to the absence of a comprehensive spatial planning framework.

14.title: Spatial Distribution of Tourist Accommodation and the Impact of Short-Term Rentals in Mykonos
14.abstract:
Tourism development constitutes a key pillar of the economy of the Greek island regions, but at the same time it is an activity that exerts significant spatial pressures. The shortcomings at all levels of spatial planning — national, regional, and local — leads to an inability to define clear directions and establish regulatory frameworks for managing tourism pressures and shaping a sustainable tourism model. The present study focuses on Mykonos, an island characterized by particularly intense tourism development. The aim is to examine, in quantitative terms, the spatial distribution of different types of accommodation in relation to areas within settlement boundaries, within traditional settlements, and in the exurban area. Accommodation units in Mykonos were digitized based on listings available on the Booking.com platform, distinguishing between hotels, rental rooms, and short-term rental properties. The boundaries of settlements and traditional settlements were digitized at a scale of 1:5.000. An overlay vector analysis was applied in order to extract quantitative results, followed by the production of the corresponding maps.
The results indicate that more than 60% of the total accommodation stock is located in the exurban area of Mykonos. Although, in the case of both hotels and rental rooms, the largest share is also found outside settlement boundaries, this percentage is lower compared to short-term rental properties. The latter are significantly more numerous than the other types of accommodation, with approximately 79% of them located in the exurban area.
These findings highlight that the exurban area of Mykonos, which was not originally planned for tourism development, has been subjected to intense pressures and has gradually transformed from rural landscape into dispersed urban formations. Short-term rentals, on the one hand, generate unplanned changes in land uses and, on the other, reinforce urban sprawl, constituting a major new challenge for spatial planning.

14.title: Spatial Determinants of Airbnb Distribution in Athens: A Linear Regression Approach
14.abstract: The phenomenon of short-term house rentals has developed rapidly in recent years. The most well-known platform offering primarily short-term rentals is "Airbnb". The factors influencing the demand in terms of location and sets the spatial distribution of Airbnb properties have been the subject of many studies. These factors include, among others, social, economic, and demographic aspects, as well as considerations of accessibility, the location and attractiveness of popular areas, and the characteristics of the available accommodations. The present study aims to identify, examine and evaluate the main factors that shape the spatial distribution of Airbnb accommodations in an urban environment, focusing on the Municipality of Athens. The research focuses on examining the relationship between Airbnb density, used as a dependent variable, and a set of euclidean distances and indicators as independent variables. These include euclidean distances from public transport infrastructure, from points of interest, from entertainment venues, etc., as well as walkability indicators. The methodological approach is based on the application of linear regression analysis, allowing for the exploration of direct relationships between Airbnb concentration and the independent variables. Emphasis is placed on identifying general trends and patterns that can improve the understanding of location choices within the short-term rental market. The results of the study are expected to contribute to a better understanding of Airbnb distribution and to support future research and planning approaches related to short-term rentals.

14.title: Testing the Algorithmic Rent Gap: digital valuation and price formation in European housing markets
14.abstract:
Urban housing markets are characterized by strong spatial differentiation, traditionally explained through factors such as property characteristics, location, amenities and socioeconomic conditions. However, the rapid expansion of short-term rental platforms has introduced new mechanisms of value formation, challenging conventional understandings of how housing prices and rents are determined.

This paper empirically tests the concept of Algorithmic Rent Gap (ARG) as a framework for analysing how digital platforms contribute to the production of housing value. The ARG conceptualises the gap between current and potential rental income as increasingly constructed through platform-mediated processes, including dynamic pricing systems, demand forecasting and algorithmic visibility, particularly in short-term rental markets.

The analysis focuses on four European cities—Copenhagen, Berlin, Madrid and Athens—representing different housing regimes and regulatory contexts. By examining spatial patterns of rental prices, short-term rental activity and neighbourhood-level market dynamics, the paper assesses whether algorithmic valuation processes contribute to housing price differentiation and market segmentation.

The findings suggest that the ARG operates as a significant driver of housing market transformation, particularly in contexts with high levels of tourist demand and limited regulatory control. In Southern European cities, platform-mediated valuation amplifies rental inflation and reinforces spatial clustering of high-value areas, while in Northern European contexts its effects are more unevenly mediated by institutional frameworks.

The paper argues that understanding the geography of housing markets requires incorporating digital valuation processes as a key determinant of price formation. The concept of Algorithmic Rent Gap provides a novel framework for analysing how platform-mediated dynamics reshape housing markets and intensify socio-spatial inequalities across urban contexts.

14.title: Inconspicuous Transformations: The Incremental Transformation of Housing in European cities in Times of Crisis
14.abstract:
Across European cities, housing systems are under growing pressure from affordability crises, demographic change, and the need to adapt existing building stock to new social, economic, and environmental conditions. While academic and policy debates tend to focus on state-led provision or market-driven development, far less attention has been paid to the role of residents themselves in adapting and transforming the existing housing stock, through incremental changes in their homes. Yet, these alterations are widespread and, as we argue, are becoming increasingly relevant in the context of the current housing crisis.

This research adopts the approach of a “multisided individualising comparison” (Hilbrandt et al., 2017), juxtaposing insights from different in-depth case studies to identify shared features and abstract from the specifics of each case. For each case, we examine physical alterations to living spaces, the motivations of residents for altering their homes, the built environment in which these alterations are embedded, and the structure and dynamics of the housing market, as well as the respective regulatory context. Our aim is to document inconspicuous changes to the housing stock, trace the contingencies behind them and reveal the underlying logic of this form of housing production.

The analysis draws on three European settings that vary widely in terms of urban design, housing market structures, and regulatory environments: London and Cardiff (UK); Athens (Greece); and Berlin (Germany). Based on a comparative analysis, this paper offers an alternative perspective on current housing developments by recognizing the role of residents in transforming living spaces and housing practices.

14.title: Evaluating the Impacts of a New Metro Line in Athens through a Quantitative Spatial Model (QSM) and Spatial Accessibility Analysis
14.abstract:
The evaluation of major transport projects is a rather critical component of contemporary spatial and transport planning procedures, particularly in metropolitan areas facing growing mobility demand, spatial inequalities and environmental pressure. In this context, appraisal frameworks are expected to go beyond mere cost-based assessments and adopt more integrated approaches that capture the wider spatial and socioeconomic effects of such major investments. Among the available analytical tools, spatial accessibility analysis and Quantitative Spatial Models (QSMs) have emerged as especially valuable for understanding how transport interventions reshape economic geography, urban structure and spatial interactions.
This study examines the impacts of a new metro line in the Athens Metropolitan Area (AMA) through the combined use of gravity-based accessibility analysis and a QSM framework. Apparently, the novel approach followed, employs these two models separately. The first model measures the improvement in job accessibility and its distributional implications, while the second one, evaluates how the new rail-based infrastructure influences wages, residents’ and workers’ distributions as well as property values. Both models compare the current situation with a three-line metro system and the future scenario, where a fourth metro line is constructed; the key difference assumed between these two scenarios is travel times.
In brief, the results reveal that a new metro line will improve average accessibility by 5.1%, however, the most pronounced changes are found in the Eastern and Northern suburbs (even more than 15%). The QSM predicts that the aggregated welfare level is improved by 2.86% across the city; the most eminent changes regarding wages, residents, workers and floorspace prices could be found again in the same suburbs. The findings are expected to be particularly useful for policymakers and planners seeking to prioritise transport investments that enhance transport inclusion and sustainable urban development.

15.title: Cities Under Pressure: Urban Growth and Socio-Environmental Stress in Delhi
15.abstract:
Urbanization has transformed many megacities, particularly in rapidly expanding urban regions
like Delhi, India. Over the decades, Delhi’s urban growth has been characterized not only by
physical expansion but also by deepening social and environmental inequalities. Patterns of land-use
change, driven by population pressure, infrastructure, and development, has produced a highly uneven
urban landscape in which access to environmental amenities and exposure to environmental stressors are
distributed along socio-economic lines. This study will focus on more than three decades of urbanization
in Delhi using multi-temporal Landsat satellite imagery. By employing the Normalized Difference
Vegetation Index (NDVI) and the Built-up Index (BU), the research will analyze long-term changes in
vegetation cover and built-up areas at both city-wide and district levels. These indices enable a
systematic assessment of how urban expansion has transformed green spaces and intensified built-up areas across different parts of the city, revealing spatial disparities that are closely intertwined with
social vulnerability.
Urban development in Delhi has largely prioritized commercial activity, elite residential zones, and
infrastructure-led growth. As a
result, marginalized and low-income populations are disproportionately concentrated in densely built-up
neighborhoods, informal settlements, and peri-urban areas with limited access to green infrastructure.
Such areas commonly experience higher land surface temperatures, poorer air quality, and increased
exposure to climate-related stresses such as heatwaves and flooding. Reduced access to vegetation has
significant implications for public health, including heightened heat stress and respiratory risks. High built-up density is often associated with overcrowding and inadequate urban services. At the same
time, increases in built-up areas can reflect economic development and infrastructure provision,
highlighting the dual role of urban expansion as both a developmental driver and a source of
environmental stress when unevenly distributed.

15.title: Love and Labour at the Energy Crisis Frontline
15.abstract:
This paper presents the key arguments of my forthcoming book with the same title (University of Toronto Press, 2027), which focuses on the everyday experiences of energy assistance professionals working for cash-strapped civil society and voluntary sector organisations across the Global North. I explore how such workers provide essential resources and advice to address the injustices faced by people who struggle to access adequate levels of energy in the home.

I seek to capture the crucial but often overlooked role of third-sector intermediaries in promoting low-carbon energy access and public engagement in climate policies. Such actors perform infrastructural labour – care, empowerment, advocacy, and sociotechnical work – in shaping low-carbon transformations. Based on evidence from over 100 interviews, survey responses and observations, I explore the institutional nature of such intermediaries, in terms of their place-based impacts and organizational vulnerabilities. I am particularly interested in how third sector energy labour demands a constant negotiation between urgent hands-on action and enduring structural constraints. Amid overlapping pressures and complex trade-offs, frontline workers enact diverse forms of care and solidarity that offer politically powerful intimations of an alternative future beyond the confines of the present order.

I build upon Harb’s (2025) notion of ‘crisis as infrastructure’ to explore how, against the dominant apparatus of vulnerabilization, one finds an extensive, albeit largely unrecognized, counter-infrastructure of public advocacy and practitioner care, primarily led by the third sector. However, efforts to tackle energy-related inequalities may help sustain the very frameworks that drive them. The centring of labour in debates on energy (in)justice and urban infrastructure (Bouzarovski 2022) allows for integrating the socio-political dynamics of energy systems, and unequal access to resources.

15.title: Care as crisis: Reconstruing the carescapes of shelters for unaccompanied minors through politics of place
15.abstract:
Approaching crisis as a sociospatially grounded, everyday-life experience that involves inequalities, politics of governance and resistance (Dimitrakou & Ren, 2025), we explore the interplay of crises, care, and politics of place (Massey, 1993) on a Greek carescape, a hosting shelter for unaccompanied minors that was severely affected by the 2023 Thessaly floods. The shelter is placed on Pelion mountain, 14 km away from the city of Volos, thus isolating unaccompanied minors and posing challenges to their access to education and socializing.
Conceptualizing hosting centers as carescapes, where the practices of care are construed as intertwined with control and discipline (Ticktin, 2011; 2016), we approach ‘care’ as a discursive element produced at the intersection of different crises, humanitarian, health, and environmental. To shed light on this discourse of care, we draw on our ethnographic engagement with the shelter at Pelion mountain in the context of Rhizo-eduscapes project (HFRI, 2025-2028), and we analyze an assemblage of discourses, linguistic landscape elements and digital ethnographic data published in this specific shelter’s facebook page during the floods.
The flood-affected linguistic landscape reveals that the politics of placing shelters in remote areas amplified the unaccompanied minors’ vulnerabilities and insecurity, since they were trapped inside the hosting center and were only saved by the locals’ solidarity. This solidarity breached the isolation and precarity imposed by the biopolitical governing of the multiple crises that feed the structure of institutionalized carescapes (Bowlby, 2012). Created to govern mobility as a humanitarian crisis they pathologize migration (proof of being a minor), thus exercising biopolitical control (Tazzioli, 2019) and integrating bordering dynamics (Angulo-Pasel, 2022). Finally, care in this context becomes a bordering practice that controls rather than protects unaccompanied minors. As a result, these carescapes reproduce them as people-in-need (Merlín-Escorza, Schapendonk, & Davids, 2023) redefining thus care as crisis.

15.title: “We’re like a big family here”: Community-run and public-sector homeless shelters as spaces of care or risk?
15.abstract: Policies intended to support people experiencing homelessness (PEH) can, at times, reproduce or intensify the very vulnerabilities they seek to alleviate. This comparative study examines how homeless shelter environments shape everyday life and substance use among homeless shelter residents (HSRs) in Athens (Greece) and Santiago (Chile), two cities characterised by neoliberal policy reforms and constrained social welfare systems. Drawing on the risk environment framework and employing a mixed-methods design, the study analyses both public-sector and community-run shelters to explore how institutional models structure social relations between HSRs, interactions with staff, coping practices, and access to support. Policy mapping is used to assess how shelter design, regulatory intensity, and policy density influence the organisation and operation of temporary accommodation across the two contexts. The findings indicate that community-run shelters are more likely to foster interpersonal connection, participation, and a sense of belonging, whereas public-sector shelters are more commonly associated with social isolation and marginalisation. These institutional differences have tangible implications for substance use, which emerges both as a coping strategy and as a response to shelter governance and everyday conditions. By foregrounding the lived experiences of HSRs, the analysis demonstrates how shelter policies and practices can generate either harmful or protective social environments. The study concludes by arguing for community-oriented models of temporary accommodation, supported by sustainable funding structures that prioritise dignity, social connection, and wellbeing within homelessness services.

16.title: Pour une onomastique transversale en Algérie : repenser les phénomènes de nomination dans une perspective plurielle
16.abstract:
En Algérie, la recherche onomastique s’est longtemps structurée autour d’approches essentiellement linguistiques, centrées sur la typologie, l’étymologie et la morphologie des noms. Si ces travaux ont permis de constituer un socle descriptif précieux, ils restent encore insuffisants pour saisir les dynamiques complexes qui façonnent les pratiques de nomination dans un contexte traversé par des transformations sociales, économiques, culturelles et territoriales profondes. Cette communication propose d’examiner les voies permettant de dépasser le cloisonnement disciplinaire traditionnel afin de construire une onomastique véritablement intégrée, articulant langue, société, culture et économie.
À partir d’exemples tirés de corpus toponymiques et odonymiques contemporains, ainsi que des noms commerciaux en milieu urbain, nous montrons que les phénomènes de nomination constituent aujourd’hui des indicateurs sensibles des mutations locales : recompositions identitaires, réorganisation des espaces urbains, logiques marchandes, revalorisations patrimoniales, ou encore dynamiques de mondialisation linguistique. L’analyse mobilise une démarche croisée, empruntant à la sociolinguistique, à la géographie sociale, à l’anthropologie de l’espace et à l’économie symbolique.

L’objectif est de démontrer que seule une approche interdisciplinaire permet de rendre compte de la dimension stratégique des noms dans l’Algérie actuelle, en éclairant les enjeux de pouvoir, de visibilité, de mémoire et de légitimité qu’ils véhiculent. Cette perspective ouvre des pistes pour le développement d’une onomastique nationale renouvelée, capable de contribuer à la compréhension fine des transformations socioterritoriales et à la valorisation du patrimoine immatériel.

16.title: Chelas vs Marvila. What disputes over place names say about spatial identities and belonging in a housing estate in eastern Lisbon.

authors.name: Ana Brandão
authors.affiliation: Instituto Universitário de Lisboa (ISCTE-IUL), Centro de Estudos sobre a Mudança Socioeconómica e o Território (DINÂMIA’CET), Lisboa, Portugal.

16.abstract:
The case of Chelas/Marvila, an eastern district of Lisbon, developed around industrial activities and social housing estates, shows how disputes over place names and their meanings evolve over time as different communities appropriate them to expose and defend their spatial identities. In this context, enabled by increased territorial connectivity and its associated socio-spatial dynamics, new residents and younger generations are reshaping the area’s symbolic landscape through culturally grounded visions of belonging.
The communication examines the links between urban development processes and the evolution of place naming in this area, using the specific case of one of its neighbourhoods, Amendoeiras. It aims to reveal how the (recent) conflict over the names Marvila (the administrative district) and Chelas (the area of the social housing urban plan), and their correspondence in terms of neighbourhoods - Amendoeiras / Zona I – came about.
The work draws on the research Homes2Live, which studies and documents the collective squatting process in a neighbourhood still under construction, in the context of the 1974 Portuguese revolution and the acute housing crisis. From this pivotal moment, the research analyses the neighbourhood’s spatial and social transformation, focusing on moments when the importance of place names takes centre stage in internal and external social representation, as well as in residents’ sense of belonging and identity.
The research combines oral histories and ethnographic engagement, interviews with key actors, media text analysis, urban planning and territorial strategies, and documentary records, and traces the discussion around place names and identities triggered by elements such as art festivals, public signage, and films and songs. By situating residents’ views on this dispute within broader urban and social transformations, the Amendoeiras case illuminates how place names are mobilised to anchor personal, collective, and institutional processes of identity formation.

16.title: Territorialisation through Toponymy: Naming and the Geopolitical Transformation of Urban Space in Kavala, 1870–1930

authors.name: Ethan Chandler
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

16.abstract:
This paper examines the role of toponymy in the geopolitical transformation of Kavala between the late Ottoman period and the consolidation of the Greek nation-state. Building on research conducted for a Master’s thesis on urban geopolitical transformations in Southeastern Europe, the paper explores how successive regimes of sovereignty were inscribed not only through commercial and administrative changes in urban development but also through the symbolic practice of naming.

Between 1870 and 1930, Kavala experienced a series of geopolitical ruptures: the decline of the Ottoman Empire, the Balkan Wars, Bulgarian occupation and eventual incorporation into the Greek state. These macro-scale transformations were manifested in micro-scale reconfigurations of the city’s spatial and symbolic landscape. Street names, neighbourhood designations and public place-names functioned as instruments of territorialisation, rearticulating urban space within shifting geopolitical frameworks—from the mahallahs of Ottoman imperial organisation to symbolic performances of the Greek national imaginary.

Drawing on historical maps, municipal records and archival sources, this paper analyses how naming practices reflected broader processes of national territorialisation. Adopting a historical approach to Political Geography whilst building on the spatial turn in Ottoman Studies, particular attention is paid to the ways inherited imperial spatial structures were reinterpreted, replaced or layered with new meanings under Greek administration. Rather than viewing toponymy as purely symbolic, the paper situates language and nomenclature within the material and political production of urban space, demonstrating how naming practices operated as mechanisms through which sovereignty was asserted and normalised in the palimpsest post-imperial landscape of Northern Greece.

By foregrounding the politics of naming in a peripheral yet strategically significant port city, the paper contributes to debates in Political Geography concerning urban manifestations of geopolitical change. In doing so, it highlights how historical, political and geographical transformations in Southeastern Europe were experienced and materialised through everyday urban spatial practices.

16.title: ‘The city’s current name possesses no historical provenance’: Gidas – Alexandreia and the national narrative in early 1950s Greece
16.abstract: On 2 April 1952, the Municipal Council of Gidas unanimously resolved to rename the town ‘Alexandreia,’ a decision ratified by Royal Decree on 16 January 1953. In the resolution of the municipal authorities, it was noted that the name ‘Gidas’ failed to evoke historical associations and, moreover, was cacophonous—evidently because it alluded to the word ‘gida’ (goat in Greek). The tendency to rename places did not originate in Greece in the 1950s; rather, it had a lengthy history that began during the War of Independence in the 1820s. In the first half of the twentieth century, the arduous task of identifying ‘appropriate’ toponyms to replace ‘inappropriate’ ones was overseen by the Toponyms of Greece Committee (1909–1945), staffed by geographers, folklorists, linguists, and senior civil servants. This paper examines the case of Gidas–Alexandria within its historical context, with the aim of presenting the arguments for and against the initiative to rename the town and of elucidating the perspectives of both sides in the ensuing public debate, which was conducted primarily through the press. The association of the small town in Imathia with the name and historical weight of Alexander the Great served both the central national narrative—which sought, through the ideology of the continuity of Hellenism, a vindication of modern Greek identity in a country ravaged by the Second World War and the subsequent Civil War (1945–1949)—and the local aspirations of the newly established municipality, which made its advancement contingent upon an archaizing persona. Conversely, the principal argument of the critics of the renaming of Gidas to Alexandreia—of this ‘toponymic cleansing’—among whom was the distinguished philologist Emmanuel Kriaras, was grounded in the idea that the past may be recovered as a material and visible presence in the Greek nation’s recent past and present, within the language and culture of its people.

16.title: “… but they actually only exist by their names.” The visibility of landscapes through their names – with examples from southeastern Europe

authors.name: Peter Jordan
authors.affiliation: Austrian Academy of Sciences; University of the Free State (South Africa)

16.abstract:
From a cultural-geographical point of view, geographical names are not only linguistic codes for geographical features. They are also social constructs that reflect the cultural, economic and political constitution of a society and play important roles as mediators between humans and space. Based on the cultural-geographical works of Carl SAUER (e.g. 1925, 1941) and Yi-Fu TUAN (e.g. 1974, 1977, 1991) this has more recently been pointed out especially by Derek H. ALDERMAN (e.g. 2000, 2003), Maoz AZARAYAHU (e.g. 1996, 1997, 2012) and Reuben ROSE-REDWOOD (e.g. 2008). In the wake of these pioneers, this field of research has become significantly denser, especially in recent years.
This paper also takes up this approach and describes the symbolic effect of geographical names of cultural landscapes in the sense of historical political units, which are no longer administrative units today. It tries to show that in many cases it is just the name – with the concept it designates, of course – that keeps a cultural landscape in mind and allows it to remain visible. If the name (and the concept it designates) did not exist, there would be little or no evidence for some spatial identities.
Before presenting examples of cultural landscapes in southeastern Europe, the article describes the fundamental roles that geographical names can play in the relationship and as mediators between humans and space in order to better understand the symbolic meaning of geographical names.

16.title: Between governmental projects and popular protests, Syria’s toponymic tendencies since 2024
16.abstract:
This paper aims at exploring and presenting the toponymic changes and tendencies in Syria since the fall of the Assad’s regime. Following an inductive reasoning, based on the hypothesis that toponymy is the expression of political dialectics and on official documents and inquiries, I census post-December-2024 toponymic tendencies from two perspectives: the government-led changes, and the popular acclamations of old or new toponymies.
As early as December 2024, school, hospital and other institution names were changed and were given an Islamist dimension that was rather before. Some other landmarks were given the names of the new heroes (killed during the civil war). Such changes might not be astonishing when seen in an ideological perspective. Yet other official tendencies might be more interesting for future analyses: the first is the continuity in the globalised naming practices. The phenomenon began in Syria in the early 2000 (Damascus Hills) and accelerated during the war (Marota City, Basilia City, etc.). The provisional government continues in the same line with Damascus Towers and The Beaumont, amongst others. The second tendency is the formalised use of the religious connotations of established toponyms: Bab Touma and Bab Sharqi become synonyms for the Christians, Jaramana for the Druzes, and so on. This “singling out” is a novelty is modern Syrian toponymies.
On the popular side, most toponymic tendencies express opposition or to the new government: some neotoponymies, denoting political projects, like Mount Bashan, Ugarit, Sahel, and Rojava, also reflect or urban toponymies and show that protests are expressed through the acclamations of neotoponyms or the refusal of government-imposed ones.
This preliminary reading shows that both formalised connotative use of old toponyms and popular use of political neotoponyms stem from the religious divisions within Syria. What will the consequences of such practices be?

16.title: ‘Unravelling’ development through Omonoia

authors.name: Penny Koutrolikou
authors.affiliation: School of Architecture, National Technical University of Athens

16.abstract:
Development is all over the news and advertisements; as something positive and desirable, as the way forward. But what does development mean? And who does it really benefit? If we examine it a little more closely, we see development as a “canvas” onto which different ideologies, approaches, and images are envisaged. A floating signifier upon which imaginaries of a desired future of a society and a city are projected, as well as the preferred ways that such desired futures are to be realized.
These development imaginaries are shaped both by discourses, policies, and projects, as well as by images and representations of the “desired” new world and the world we must “leave behind.” In today’s world, dominated by the rapid succession of images and grand declarations, development imaginaries and their illustrated “public relations” constitute a machinery of both propaganda and diplomacy. Via their visual rhetoric, these imaginaries define and legitimize not only the modes and aesthetics of development, but simultaneously political strategies demarcating which subjects belong to the visualised future and can benefit from its “gifts,” and which are “erased” or “forgotten” (explicitly or implicitly) from it. Yet, these “desirable” urban futures are often created through displacement and rampant speculation, while the “Others”—both people and materials—are eliminated, save for the necessary quota of diversity that each society defines. Thus, these glamorous development imaginaries often harbour pitfalls, as they tend to reproduce and further entrench segregation, discrimination, and injustices in both physical and imaginary spaces. In the end, resulting often in colonising or erasing of spaces, social infrastructures, memories and bodies – even of alternative, possible future imaginaries.
This contribution aims to explore these questions through a verbal and visual analysis of the various plans and actions concerning the centre of Athens, and particularly the area around Omonoia Square.

16.title: Naming the Industrial City: Toponymy, Symbolic Designations, and Working-Class Identity in Elefsina (Greece)

authors.name: Regina Mantanika
authors.affiliation: PANTEION University/ Department of Social Anthropology

authors.name: Io Chaviara
authors.affiliation: University of Thessaly/ Department of History, Archeology and Social Anthropology

authors.name: Gel Mademli
authors.affiliation: University of Amsterdam/ Amsterdam School for Cultural Analysis

16.abstract:
Elefsina occupies a singular position in Greece's urban history. For nearly a century, two-thirds of the country’s heavy industry was concentrated within this city of 30,000 inhabitants, twenty kilometres from Athens, forging a working-class culture with distinct material and symbolic traces. Today, partially deindustrialized and still renowned as an archaeological site, it is found amid negotiations over the territorialization and exploitation of memory, land, and urban identity.
Understanding toponymy not as a practice rooted in identity representation but as an inscription technology ‘inquiring into modes of existence’ (Latour 2013), our research examines the social imaginary tied to working-class history through name-giving on a double register: Firstly, it focuses on built environment: the neighborhoods of Stafida, Symiaka, Oikimata TITAN, and Rossika, built by and for factory workers, but also Vlycha, the ship scrapping yards, and Kynodontas, a former limestone quarry, landmarks repurposed during the city's tenure as European Capital of Culture; in so doing, it assess how toponyms encode corporate power and collective memory in ways that official cartography rarely acknowledges. Secondly, it turns to documentary, approaching it as a medium par excellence where reality is represented, manifesting the ability of language to visualize relationships in space. Whereas an episode of the series Anazitontas tin hameni ikona ( 1995) frames Elefsina as “the focal city,” projecting an imaginary of industrial modernity and civic pride that actively constructs the city’s identity through language, Takis Papagiannidis’s Elefsina (1986) documents the transitions brought by industrialization (labor struggles), granting the representations of the city some nominal attributes not for social classification, but the formation of a working-class community.

By demonstrating the interrelatedness of these two registers, the paper renders Elefsina a privileged analytical site for the convergence of toponymy and symbolic designation, the vernacular and the institutional, power and memory.

16.title: Linguistic Transformations in Lahore: (Re)Naming and Urban Reconfigurations
16.abstract:
This paper examines how place names in Lahore reflect and influence shifts in identity, occupancy, and urban form across different phases of the city’s development. Lahore has undergone multiple reconfigurations under successive regimes, including Mughal, Sikh, British colonial, and post-partition periods, each reshaping both the built environment and the linguistic landscape.
Prior to the Partition of India, Lahore was marked by religious and cultural diversity, with Muslim, Sikh, and Hindu communities shaping neighbourhood identities. Following partition, demographic change led to a more homogenised population and systematic renaming practices. Neighbourhoods such as Krishan Nagar were renamed Islampura, and colonial-era roads were reassigned to national and religious figures. However, these changes did not fully replace earlier naming systems, many of which persist in everyday use.
These layered naming practices correspond with shifts in urban morphology. In the historic inner city (Androon Shehr), older naming systems are associated with dense, organic, and incrementally developed settlements, where streets and neighbourhoods derive their names from local features, trades, and everyday practices. Areas such as Ichra and Mozang reflect similar conditions. In contrast, colonial and postcolonial expansions introduced more controlled spatial orders. Areas such as the Mall and Cantonment reflect colonial planning, while developments such as the Defence Housing Authority employ standardised systems, including alphabetic sectors and generic terms such as “avenue.” These names often signal aspiration and exclusivity, shaping patterns of use and occupation, even when such developments incorporate older village settlements (pinds), where earlier naming practices persist. Drawing on site surveys, archival sources, and ethnographic observation, the paper shows that naming in Lahore functions as both a planning instrument and a lived practice, revealing how urban space is continuously negotiated rather than fully redefined.

16.title: Urban Political Landscapes – the study of a boulevard
16.abstract:
The role of road network in cities is fundamental, as it serves flows of people, goods, and ideas. In
that way, it shapes not only mobility patterns but also social networks, economic activity, and
political expression. In metropolitan settings, key urban axes operate as spatial condensations
where history, power, economic dynamics, and social practices intersect. As a result, beyond
serving as settings accommodate daily life, they also operate as arenas of symbolic and political
expression, social claims, and shifting urban identities.
Panepistimiou Avenue in Athens constitutes a representative example of such an urban axis. It was
originally conceived as a boulevard by the German architect and painter Leo von Klenze, designed
to link the city’s principal squares with its archaeological sites. Today, this avenue stands as one
of the most emblematic urban axes of the Greek capital, characterized by a complex interplay of
unique design, monumental charge, architectural finds as well as intertemporal political
semiology.
Political expression, in particular, is especially pronounced over time: marches, demonstrations,
confrontations, and celebrations alike become inscribed onto the body of the city through the
occupation of the street. The urban landscape is thus transformed into a stage upon which society
negotiates rights, crises, and collective identities. Periods of tension — including economic crisis,
social unrest, and transformations of the commercial centre — are reflected in changes in land use
distribution, vacant shops, intensified policing, and urban regeneration interventions. Such
regeneration proposals, that have led to a polarization of views among the public in the past, tend
to reveal conflicts between competing visions for the city centre and its function: touristic and
consumption-oriented, historic and monumental, or open and socially inclusive. Panepistimiou
Avenue, therefore, is not a neutral space; it is a terrain of political choice that shapes who has the
right to the city.

17.title: Küçükköy as a Rural Space of Layered Mobilities: Migration, Heritage, and Rural Gentrification in Ayvalık, Turkey

authors.name: Kumru Çılgın
authors.affiliation: Mimar Sinan Fine Arts University, Department of Urban and Regional Planning

17.abstract:
This study examines the spatial and social transformation of Küçükköy, a rural settlement in Ayvalık, in the context of historical migration, cultural heritage, and contemporary rural gentrification. Formerly known as Yeniçarohori, Küçükköy is one of the important rural settlements of the shared Aegean geography. Its Greek cultural heritage, rural architectural fabric, the experiences of communities settled after the population exchange, and the social structure formed by Bosnian migrants have transformed the village into a distinctive space bearing the traces of layered mobilities.

Based on a research project comparing rural settlements in Ayvalık and Lesvos, as well as recent fieldworks in Ayvalık, this paper discusses the transformation of Küçükköy in terms of economic, cultural, symbolic, and spatial restructuring. Traditionally defined by agriculture, olive cultivation, and livestock breeding, the local economy has diversified in recent years through art workshops, cultural tourism initiatives, boutique accommodation, and alternative production methods. This process has transformed Küçükköy into a rural settlement whose value is being redefined through images of rural attractiveness, authenticity, and the “rural idyll.”

However, this process of revaluation also gives rise to tensions, including the transformation of property relations, demographic change, the reorganisation of everyday life, spatial differentiation, and indirect exclusion. In this context, Küçükköy is a prime example of a rural settlement historically shaped by migration and reproduced through new forms of urban-to-rural mobility, cultural economies, and tourism-oriented investments.

While addressing Küçükköy as a transforming rural settlement, this study proposes to conceptualise it as a “geography of mobilities,” in which mobilities from different periods accumulate and gain new meanings through contemporary transformation processes. Considering the shared cultural landscape across the two shores of the Aegean Sea, it discusses the future of rural areas along the axes of mobility, cultural heritage, identity, belonging, and gentrification.

Migration, Rural mobility, Rural tourism, Rural gentrification, Küçükköy

17.title: Tracing Migrant Trajectories: Mobilities, social position, and belonging in rural Greece

authors.name: Loukia Maria Fratsea
authors.affiliation: Senior researcher, Department of Geography, Harokopio University of Athens

17.abstract:
Research on migration in rural Greece has increasingly examined migrants’ incorporation into agricultural labour markets and their contribution to rural economies. However, migrants’ lived experiences of mobility and their social and spatial trajectories remain underexplored. This paper investigates how migrants living in rural Western Greece negotiate mobility, social positioning, and belonging at different stages of their lives and migration journeys.
Drawing on qualitative research conducted between 2017 and 2022 with 30 Albanian, Romanian, and Bangladeshi migrants living in villages and small towns of Western Greece, the paper adopts a biographical perspective to explore migrants’ trajectories across places, labour markets, and social worlds. Through life-story interviews carried out at two time intervals, the analysis examines how aspirations, expectations, and perceptions of social mobility are reconfigured over time through experiences of migration, work, family life, and settlement in rural areas.
The findings show that migrants’ trajectories are shaped by complex forms of spatial mobility, including transnational migration, everyday rural mobilities, and movements between urban and rural labour markets. These mobilities are deeply intertwined with migrants’ efforts to achieve social recognition, economic security, and a sense of stability and belonging. Migrants’ narratives reveal that belonging is not fixed but is continuously produced through everyday practices, social relationships, and emotional attachments to place.
The paper further highlights how migrants assess their life trajectories through relational comparisons between origin and destination contexts, past and present selves, and different social groups. Such comparisons reveal the deeply temporal and spatial dimensions of migrants’ understandings of social mobility and inclusion. By focusing on socio-spatial trajectories and everyday mobilities, the paper argues for a more processual understanding of migrant incorporation in rural areas, one that recognises belonging as shaped through movement, settlement, and the continuous negotiation of place and identity.

17.title: Spatialising Migrant Labour Precarity in Greece

authors.name: Vasiliki Kakosimou
authors.affiliation: Harokopio University of Athens/ Department of Geography

17.abstract:
This paper examines how migrant labour precarity in Greece is shaped by spatial context, focusing on the differentiated conditions of urban and rural reception and settlement. It argues that precarity is not simply the outcome of insecure employment or unstable legal status, but a socio-spatial condition produced through the interaction of labour-market structures, migration governance, access to services, and place-specific opportunities and constraints.

The paper draws on qualitative fieldwork conducted between 2022 and 2023 in four reception facilities: Eleonas and Schisto in metropolitan Attica, and Filippiada and Katsikas in rural mainland Greece. The empirical material consists of 79 interviews, including 52 with Syrian migrants, 23 with staff in reception facilities, and 4 with senior officials from the Ministry of Migration and Asylum. The comparative design enables an examination of how urban and rural settings mediate access to work, everyday survival strategies, and aspirations for onward mobility.

The findings show that spatial location matters not as a single explanatory factor, but as a framework within which different forms of precarity are produced and experienced. In rural areas, migrants encounter limited labour demand, seasonal and uninsured agricultural employment, weaker institutional support, and heightened isolation. In urban areas, access to informal work and services is broader, but employment remains unstable, poorly paid, and marked by intense competition. Across both settings, language proficiency, social networks, and legal-institutional uncertainty play a decisive role in shaping labour-market incorporation.

By foregrounding the spatial dimension of precarity, the paper contributes to debates on migration, rural transformation, and uneven development, showing how urban–rural differences structure migrants’ work trajectories, everyday lives, and sense of future in contemporary Greece.

17.title: Islands as “places that matter” and the role of culture: Exploring the potential of insular cultural strategies

authors.name: Nicholas Karachalis
authors.affiliation: University of the Aegean/Department of Tourism Economics and Management

authors.name: Vassiliki Georgoula
authors.affiliation: University of the Aegean/Department of Tourism Economics and Management

authors.name: Anna Kyriakaki
authors.affiliation: University of the Aegean/Department of Tourism Economics and Management

17.abstract:
The interconnection between cultural infrastructure, cultural activity, and cultural work with vibrant and attractive insular space has been widely discussed, particularly in relation with the so-called "return to the countryside". Supporting cultural development is vital for fostering healthy, inclusive, and sustainable communities. Culture contributes to the formation of identity and local pride while affirming values, embracing diversity, and reflecting the aspirations of the communities it serves. Equal access to culture remains a central objective of cultural strategies, with the coordination of diverse actors—including public, private, and voluntary stakeholders—being a significant challenge.
