Recent critiques of the "cultural industry" concept have highlighted concerns regarding the economic instrumentalization of culture, the precarious conditions faced by cultural workers, and unequal opportunities for local populations in cultural production and consumption (Bell & Oakley, 2016; Mould, 2018; O'Connor, 2024). However, opportunities for cultural participation add to the attractiveness of a place and are, arguably, one of the criteria for choosing life on an island.
This paper critically examines cultural strategies within this context, drawing on extensive field research and a participatory cultural planning meeting/workshop conducted on the islands of Samos and Chios. The study explores whether cultural industries/activities can serve as a developmental pathway and identifies the support mechanisms required for such integration. The fieldwork consisted of two parts: (a) interviews with stakeholders, including representatives and artists active in contemporary culture and key participants in the islands’ cultural events and a questionnaire survey with inhabitants, and (b) a face-to-face participatory workshop involving representatives from public and private institutions, associations, and cultural professionals in each island. This research critically evaluates the synergies and networking opportunities among artists, local institutions, creative and cultural industries, and tourism actors, with a particular focus on the role of participatory processes in shaping cultural strategies.

17.title: Precarious Harvests: Seasonal Migration and Labour Hierarchies in Mediterranean Agriculture
17.abstract:
This paper reflects on seasonal labour migration in Mediterranean agriculture and argues for a more nuanced geographical understanding of mobility, labour, and precarity in rural contexts. While migration studies have traditionally approached labour migration as primarily an urban phenomenon, the increasing dependence of agricultural production on migrant workers across Southern Europe has repositioned rural regions as critical sites of transnational mobility and labour restructuring. Since the early 2000s, international migration to peripheral, agricultural, and remote areas has emerged as a major field of inquiry within migration and rural studies.
Drawing on examples from Greece, Italy, and Spain, the presentation examines how different agricultural systems across the Mediterranean rely on seasonal migrant labour despite important national and regional differences. In Greece, migrant workers have become central to labour-intensive agricultural production under conditions marked by informality and legal insecurity. In Italy, highly segmented labour markets and subcontracting systems have intensified forms of labour exploitation and spatial segregation. In Spain, export-oriented agribusiness and circular migration schemes reveal how mobility is institutionally organised to meet the demands of flexible agricultural production. Despite these differences, common patterns emerge across the Mediterranean: labour shortages in rural areas, the increasing casualisation of agricultural work, dependence on migrant labour, and the production of precarious living and working conditions.
The paper critically repositions the “seasonal” dimension as a constitutive feature of agricultural labour regimes rather than a secondary characteristic of migration. It explores how temporality, mobility, and legal precarity shape labour hierarchies in the fields, while also examining the ways migrant workers exercise agency within restrictive labour arrangements. By connecting migrant mobility to the restructuring of rural labour markets, the paper contributes to broader debates in human geography on migration, rural transformation, and the spatial organisation of precarious labour in contemporary Mediterranean agriculture.

17.title: Differential Emplacement: Migrant Labor, Civic Stratification, and the Future of Rural Greece
17.abstract:
As Greece’s countryside faces demographic decline, it has become structurally reliant on international migrants to fill labor market gaps. Since the influx of migrants from Eastern Europe in the 1990s, these groups have diversified significantly in terms of employment strategies, settlement patterns, network accessibility, legal status, and migration trajectories. This study maps the structural conditions shaping differential emplacement of migrants working in rural Thessaly, exploring how socio-cultural predispositions, labor market structures, civic stratification, and networked social relations jointly shape place-making and social inclusion.

Situated within the session’s focus on "Mobilities, Migration and Rural Transformations," this research explores the lived experience of emplacement of migrants and their role and agency in rural transformation. Countering dominant discourses of displacement, the concept of emplacement reframes migrants not as threats to social cohesion, but as active agents in the process of spatial transformation and place-making.

Employing ethnographically informed mixed-methods—including participant observation, narrative interviews, and GIS-mapping—the multi-sided study analyzes a heterogeneous sample of migrant backgrounds to compare how distinct legal and social positions shape integration.

Preliminary analysis suggests that while economic necessity drives spatial presence, "civic stratification" and varying access to social capital critically determine whether migrants can transition from temporary laborers to active community members. By foregrounding migrant agency within rural power dynamics, this research contributes to underrepresented scholarship on rural migration in Southern Europe. It offers a nuanced geographic perspective on local inclusion mechanisms, providing actionable insights for planners. Ultimately, this work argues that successful integration is not merely a humanitarian goal but a prerequisite for the sustainable future of the Greek countryside, where the long-term viability of the countryside depends most strongly on the mutual flourishing of migrants and local communities.

18.title: Spatial Analysis of Socio-Economic Inequalities in the Municipality of Athens Using Geographic Information Systems (GIS)
18.abstract:
This study investigates socio-economic spatial segregation within the Municipality of Athens, exploring how the urban landscape reflects and reproduces socio-economic inequalities. Athens is characterized by a unique model of "vertical segregation," while the Greek capital is currently facing new spatial challenges. The prolonged economic crisis, rapid gentrification, touristification, and shifting migration flows are actively disrupting traditional urban balances and horizontally reshaping the city's social geography.
The primary objective of this research is to quantitatively and spatially document these emerging disparities across the seven (7) Municipal Districts of Athens. To achieve this, a Spatial Decision Support System approach is adopted, utilizing Geographic Information Systems (GIS) as the core analytical tool. The methodology involves the collection, processing, and integration of open census data and economic indicators for the years 2011 and 2021.
The perspective of this study is to produce a series of thematic maps that visualize the distribution of key demographic, social, and economic variables. Rather than focusing solely on isolated indicators, the spatial analysis aims to identify geographical patterns, trends, and distinct clusters of social and economic segregation over the last decade. Ultimately, the research seeks to synthesize a comprehensive representation of intra-urban disparities, demonstrating the efficacy of GIS in analyzing sociospatial segregation. The findings aspire to provide a vital, evidence-based tool for local authorities to design and implement targeted social and urban planning policies in an increasingly polarized metropolitan environment.

18.title: Spatial distribution of foreigners in Greek Municipalities and its demographic implications, 1991-2021
18.abstract: This research examines the spatial distribution of the foreign population across Greek municipalities over four consecutive censuses (1991, 2001, 2011 and 2021), using municipality-level data on the total and foreign populations, by gender and five-year age group. The aim is to look into the demographic implications of immigration and foreign presence in Greek municipalities over the past four decades, a period marked by persistently low fertility, population ageing, elevated mortality and, consequently, population decline since 2010. The analysis proceeds in two steps. First, it measures and maps the spatial concentration and demographic structure of the foreign population, with a focus on spatiotemporal gender and age differences. Second, it assesses the demographic profiles of the municipalities, according to their foreign population shares in relation to population ageing and fertility. To this end, we employ descriptive statistics and indicators, namely location quotients and spatial autocorrelation, in order to identify clusters and outliers in foreign settlement. The findings are expected to reveal a shift in the long-term trend of foreign settlement from the peripheral municipalities of mainland Greece towards Attica and the Greek islands, persistent spatial concentration in selected urban and peri-urban areas, as well as more diverse age structures in municipalities with higher foreign presence. This work aspires to contribute to spatial demography and population and migration research in Greece, by offering a framework for relating migration patterns to broader demographic change.

18.title: Commuting Distance and Sectoral Structure of Employment: Evidence from Slovakia

authors.name: Štefan Gábor
authors.affiliation: Institute of Geography, Faculty of Science, Pavol Jozef Šafárik University in Košice, Slovakia

authors.name: Loránt Pregi
authors.affiliation: Institute of Geography, Faculty of Science, Pavol Jozef Šafárik University in Košice, Slovakia

18.abstract:
This study addresses daily commuting as a dynamic component of spatial socio-economic stratification in Slovakia. It aims to analyse how commuting distances relate to the sectoral structure of employment and how these relationships vary across spatial scales. In contrast to approaches that rely primarily on static indicators of inequality, the paper emphasises the role of spatial mobility in connecting locations with differentiated employment opportunities. The analysis draws on municipality-level data on commuting flows and examines how commuting distances relate to the sectoral composition of employment defined by SK NACE classifications. A multilevel perspective is applied, comparing patterns at the regional level (functional urban regions) and local level (municipalities). This enables the identification of variations in commuting behaviour across spatial scales and economic sectors. Distance-based measures of commuting are combined with sectoral classifications to explore sector-specific mobility profiles. The analysis examines whether commuting distances differ across economic activities and how these differences relate to the spatial distribution of jobs and labour supply. The study highlights the analytical potential of incorporating mobility into the study of socio-economic differentiation. By focusing on commuting patterns, it aims to provide additional insight into the spatial organisation of labour markets and the processes shaping socio-economic stratification in Slovakia.
Acknowledgement:
This research was supported by the Scientific Grant Agency VEGA under project No. 1/0768/24: Multiscale assessment of spatial variability of social-economic population stratification.

18.title: Spatial approach to mobility in the countryside of Greece: new trends?

authors.name: Stamatina Kaklamani
authors.affiliation: Department of Sociology, University of Crete

authors.name: Konstantinos Zafeiris
authors.affiliation: Department of Humanities, Democritus University of Thrace

18.abstract:
In Europe, the study of geographical mobility, approached from different perspectives, has been the subject of scientific research in the fields of geography, spatial demography and spatial econometrics in recent decades.
In Greece, intense mobility is recorded, which changes the intensity and characteristics of the local populations, with differentiations of urban and rural space, reshapes the physiognomy of the areas and leads to uneven developments and typologies.
In the context of this work focusing on rural space, it is proposed to investigate the levels of phenomenal migration at a low spatial level (municipal units) during the recent inter-census period (2011-2021). The study aims to investigate the intensity of the phenomenon and the possible existence of different and distinct groups of territorial units.

18.title: The Political Geography of Modernity: Social Engineering Through Electricity in Liverpool and the Mapping of Spatial Inequality (1879–1926)
18.abstract:
This paper examines the dramatic urban, social, and demographic movements that Liverpool underwent between 1879 and 1926 from a political geography perspective, using the method of "urban history mapping." It discusses the constitutive role that the city's relationship with electricity played in this spatial and political context. The study analyzes how infrastructure processes, beginning with the 1879 Liverpool Corporation Electric Lighting Act, the UK's first electricity legislation, and centralized by the 1926 Electricity (Supply) Act, were applied selectively and hierarchically in different parts of the city, and how transportation (electric tram) lines affected the city's spatial development. This half-century period represents not only technological advancement but also a political and economic redistribution of urban space through "Private Acts of Parliament."

Methodologically, the study questions the relationship between local council ownership, class, and demographics by mapping the spatial projections of local laws. The wide boulevards and electric tram lines developed by urban engineer J. Brodie increased urban mobility while simultaneously creating a new "hierarchy of accessibility" based on service access capacity. In this context, the electrification and transportation networks in commercially oriented port areas and affluent suburbs will be compared with "slum clearance" operations in low-income neighborhoods. The analysis discusses, through the lens of political geography, for whom access to infrastructure services has become a "right" and for whom it has become a "mechanism of control." Spatial analysis of regulations such as the 1890 Housing of the Working Classes Act and the 1905 Aliens Act investigates how infrastructure, as a tool of social engineering, has pushed poor and immigrant populations to the periphery of the city or isolated them in certain areas. Ultimately, this paper reveals, through maps, how infrastructure and legislative activities have institutionalized urban inequality in Liverpool.

18.title: Mapping Energy Poverty as Socio-Spatial Vulnerability: The Role of Demographic, Housing, and Territorial Inequalities
18.abstract:
This paper approaches energy poverty as a multidimensional form of socio-spatial vulnerability. Its purpose is twofold: first, to identify the key mechanisms that intensify households’ inability to secure adequate and affordable energy services; and second, to examine how these inequalities vary across space. The analysis is built on an investigation of the international literature focusing on the drivers of energy poverty, such as low income, increasing energy costs, poor residential energy efficiency, and the social vulnerability of specific demographic categories.
The study focuses on households with elderly individuals, children, single-parent families, unemployed persons, tenants, and individuals from migrant backgrounds, as these demographics are more susceptible to energy deprivation. It also examines how building standards affect people's fundamental needs. It indicates that older buildings which are not well-insulated require more heating and cooling, that increases the cost of living and negatively impacts the quality of life. Additionally, this work investigates how urban, suburban, and rural areas, as well as small towns, are particularly vulnerable based on energy infrastructure accessibility, housing costs, climate, and population distribution.
In general, energy poverty is not perceived as a distinct economic problem but as an indication of broader socioeconomic and spatial disparities. Its connection with demographic change, housing conditions, and unequal living environments makes it a critical field for understanding contemporary socio-spatial transformations. Identifying its determinants is essential for the design of targeted policies related to social protection, energy upgrading, and spatial justice. Focusing on these aspects can promote the development of more equitable solutions tailored to the specific needs of varied locations and social groups. This can help reduce energy deprivation and strengthen social cohesion during the current energy, economic, and climate crises.

18.title: A Comparative Analysis of Marital Dissolution and Attitudes Toward Divorce in Greece, Italy, Spain, and France

authors.name: Georgios Kontogiannis
authors.affiliation: University of Thessaly, Volos and Democritus University of Thrace, Komotini, Greece

authors.name: Kostas Rontos
authors.affiliation: University of the Aegean, Mytilene Greece

authors.name: Luca Salvati
authors.affiliation: Department of Methods and Models for Economics, Territory and Finance (MEMOTEF), Faculty of Economics, Sapienza University of Rome, Rome, Italy

authors.name: Dimitrios Antonoglou
authors.affiliation: University of the Aegean, Mytilene Greece

18.abstract:
Abstract:
Since the 1970s, family-related behaviours in Southern Europe have undergone significant changes. More specifically, a gradual increase in the frequency of marital dissolution has been observed, accompanied by substantial changes in social attitudes and perceptions regarding marriage and divorce. The present study comparatively examines marital dissolution and attitudes toward divorce in Greece, Italy, Spain, and France, highlighting both similarities and differences among these countries.
The research is based on two main axes of analysis. First, a demographic analysis of the intensity and timing of divorce is conducted from the 1950s to the present, using both period and cohort divorce indicators (marriage cohort analysis). Second, attitudes toward divorce are examined using data from the European Values Study 2017. Descriptive statistics, chi-square tests of independence, logistic regression, and machine learning algorithms (XGBoost, Random Forest, LightGBM, and CatBoost) are employed.
The findings indicate that France and Spain display higher divorce intensity and greater acceptance of divorce compared to Greece and Italy, where changes have occurred more slowly and are closely associated with institutional and legislative developments. Age, sex, religiosity, marital status, and perceptions regarding the institution of marriage appear to play an important role in shaping attitudes toward divorce. Machine learning models further identify age and religiosity as the most important predictors.

Keywords:
marital dissolution, attitudes toward divorce, Southern Europe, religiosity, demographic analysis and machine learning models

18.title: Mapping Socio-spatial Inequalities in Thessaloniki: Emerging Divisions in a Mediterranean Metropolis

authors.name: Apostolos Lagarias
authors.affiliation: Department of Planning and Regional Development, University of Thessaly

authors.name: Aristotelis Vartholomaios
authors.affiliation: Department of Planning and Regional Development, University of Thessaly

18.abstract:
Socio-spatial inequalities in Mediterranean cities have long been understood as producing relatively “soft” patterns of segregation, embedded within dense, compact, and socially mixed urban fabrics. However, emerging evidence suggests that these patterns may, in some cases, be evolving into sharper internal divisions. This paper revisits this question by examining whether contemporary dynamics are reshaping the traditionally cohesive structure of Southern European metropolitan areas, through an original case study in the city of Thessaloniki.
Established literature on Greek cities like Athens, highlights a coexistence of social mixing and micro-scale segregation—including neighborhood-level differentiation and vertical stratification within residential buildings. The research develops a methodological framework combining multivariate statistical analysis with location quotient mapping.
Findings reveal a persistent and longitudinally stable pattern of differentiation between the southeastern and northwestern suburban zones of Thessaloniki, suggesting a gradual consolidation of polarized spatial structures built upon historical procedures and a strong layer of spontaneous urbanization. At the same time, the metropolitan core continues to function as a zone of relative social amalgamation, accommodating diverse populations across income, age, and ethnic lines. Yet this integrative capacity is increasingly under pressure. Processes such as gentrification and the rapid expansion of short-term rental platforms are transforming central neighborhoods, potentially undermining their traditional role as social "connectors" within the urban system.
From a planning perspective, these dynamics unfold alongside a weakening of metropolitan-scale governance and a shift toward localized, project-based interventions, often coupled with large-scale infrastructure developments implemented with limited social consensus and public participation. This transition risks reinforcing existing spatial inequalities, particularly along emerging east–west axes of division. Mediterranean cities may be entering a new phase in which historically diffuse socio-spatial patterns give way to more pronounced and structurally embedded forms of urban fragmentation.

18.title: The relationship between geography and migration in the early decades of scientific activity of the Italian Geographical Society
18.abstract: How is the topic of migration addressed in the texts published by the Italian Geographical Society during its first decades of activity? And from what perspective? This contribution aims to help reconstruct how the discourse on migration within the Italian Geographical Society evolved over time. Since its foundation (1867), in fact, the Society’s attention has also focused on the migrations (or emigrations) of Italians around the world, as well as on the movements of foreign populations toward Italy. Migration, therefore, has consistently permeated the geographical discourse emerging from the Italian Geographical Society’s activities, which can be traced through articles in the Bollettino and other publications, up to the present. The present contribution will focus primarily on the period from the Society’s foundation to the Second World War, while acknowledging the continued relevance of this topic nowadays. The texts, analyses, research and, more broadly, the narratives that emerge from this period of activity can constitute a significant discursive archive for understanding, on the one hand, how migration has contributed to shaping spatial imaginaries, population dynamics and socio-spatial inequalities and, on the other, how migratory experiences have been framed, remembered, narrated, transmitted and embedded within geographical culture of both that time and the present.

18.title: Mapping Rural Depopulation in Greece (1928–2021): Multi-Scalar Socio-Spatial Patterns from the Peloponnese
18.abstract: Rural depopulation in Greece has unfolded unevenly across space and time, producing differentiated settlement trajectories shaped by accessibility, historical contingencies, and shifting administrative frameworks. Capturing these dynamics requires spatially explicit, temporally consistent data capable of supporting multi-scalar comparison across changing administrative geographies. This project draws on a GIS-ready, georeferenced population dataset derived from digitised Greek census records (1928–2021), with a focus on the Peloponnese. By integrating settlement-level population data within a unified spatial framework and linking them to successive administrative geographies, the dataset supports consistent longitudinal analysis despite boundary changes. The analysis highlights distinct socio-spatial patterns of demographic change, including: (i) asynchronous population peaks across settlements, (ii) spatially uneven rates of decline associated with remoteness, connectivity, and differential access to economic opportunities, and (iii) divergent post-decline trajectories, ranging from persistent contraction to partial stabilisation. These patterns reflect broader processes such as post-war urbanisation, mid-twentieth-century emigration, and the reorganisation of administrative structures, but also reveal significant local variation that resists uniform interpretation. Through thematic mapping and multi-scalar visualisation, the presentation demonstrates how long-term demographic transformations can be traced across shifting spatial frameworks, enabling the identification of both regional regularities and localised deviations. While the underlying georeferenced dataset provides the empirical foundation for this analysis, this presentation focuses on its analytical application to mapping socio-spatial transformation and population dynamics over time, as part of a broader project involving the digitization of multi-year census data and the development of a geospatial analytical framework. Ongoing work extends the dataset to the national scale.

18.title: Using spatial autocorrelation as a tool for the identification of migration patterns and socio-economic stratification

authors.name: Loránt Pregi
authors.affiliation: Pavol Jozef Šafárik University in Košice, Faculty of Science, Institute of Geography

authors.name: Ladislav Novotný
authors.affiliation: Pavol Jozef Šafárik University in Košice, Faculty of Science, Institute of Geography

18.abstract:
More than three decades after the collapse of socialism, post-socialist countries continue to exhibit specific spatial patterns of internal migration and socio-economic stratification. However, detailed analyses of the spatial aspects of both processes remain limited. This study uses Slovakia as a case study to demonstrate how spatial autocorrelation methods can be applied to evaluate internal migration by age and educational attainment, as well as socio-economic stratification, across multiple spatial scales. The aim of this study is to identify and interpret spatial patterns of migration processes and socio-economic stratification using a combination of global and local spatial autocorrelation techniques. Global Moran’s I is employed to assess the overall spatial structure of selected indicators, while local indicators (Anselin Local Moran’s I and Getis-Ord Gi*) serve to detect spatial clusters and outliers at local, and sub-local levels. Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (Space-Time Pattern Mining) is further used to capture the temporal dynamics of these processes and to identify stable, emerging, and declining spatial concentrations. The results highlight significant spatial differentiation in intra- and inter-regional migration, including patterns of decentralization and metropolization, as well as clear differences in migration selectivity by age and educational attainment. At the same time, the applied methods reveal clear spatial clustering of socio-economic characteristics, enabling the identification of areas with specific stratification profiles. The study presents a methodological framework for the application of spatial autocorrelation techniques in the assessment of migration processes and socio-economic stratification, offering detailed insights into their spatial organisation and evolution.
Acknowledgement:
Funded by the project VEGA 1/0768/24 “Multiscale assessment of spatial variability of social-economic population stratification”.

18.title: “After different migratory routes and difficulties, Greece as a space and country of temporary or permanent residence for non-European migrants who entered the European Union via Greece ; a quantitative and interview-based survey (2022-2026)”

authors.name: Jean-Luc Richard
authors.affiliation: University of Rennes / Γαλλική Σχολή Αθηνών / Ecole française d'Athènes - French School at Athens

18.abstract:
This paper presents the results of a field and statistical survey conducted primarily in Greece between 2022 and 2026, funded by the French School at Athens and the French Convergences Migrations Institute. The research aims to analyze how initial intentions, perceptions (opinions about Greece and Greeks), the consequences of obstacles (past persecutions, closed borders, discrimination, opinions of Greek people), and opportunities, potentially linked to life events (meetings, relationships, the birth of a child), contribute to determining whether or not Greece becomes the destination for future or permanent settlement. To this end, interviews and analyses of individual trajectories -at least 200- and statistical trends, and observations of political actors will be conducted. Greece represents a crucial stage for migrants (BATHAÏE, 2009). The survey involves interviewing non-European migrants in various regions of Greece (Aegean islands including areas of refugees camps, the Athens’ region, Thessaly, Macedonia, Thrace, and the Cyclades). This article will focus on the satisfactions and difficulties of migrants in different regions of Greece, which may help to explain their past, present and future geographical mobilities. mobilities. They are linked with past, present and expected living conditions and quality of life, so with poverty and socio-spatial inequalities ad discriminations (ARVANITIDIS et al., 2021). We will present methodological insights which led us to use specific statistical models (MCA) with references to others researches mainly published in English, French or Greek by various colleagues (PAPAILIAS / Παπαηλίας Θεόδωρος, 2022 ;
SCHAPENDONK et al, “Re-routing migration geographies: Migrants, trajectories and mobility regimes”, Geoforum, Volume 116, November 2020 ; ARVANITIDIS Paschalis, , PAPAGIANNITSIS George, ZOI DESLI thina, VERGOU Penelope & GOURGOULINI Sofia, « Attitudes Towards Refugees & Immigrants in Greece: a nationallocal comparative analysis », European Journal of Geography, Vol. 12, Issue 3, 2021, pp. 039 - 055

18.title: Rethinking Labour Market Areas: Comparison of the Traditional Commuting Threshold Method with a 3SFCA–Modified Huff Approach

authors.name: Stefanos Tsigdinos
authors.affiliation: Centre of Planning and Economic Research (KEPE), University of West Attica

18.abstract:
Labour Market Areas (LMAs) are increasingly used in regional and transport planning because they can capture the geography and function of labour markets more effectively than administrative boundaries. Traditionally, LMAs are delineated through commuting flows, using fixed thresholds to identify functional integration between municipalities, settlements, etc. Nevertheless, such approaches may overlook variations in spatial interaction potential, competition effects and the heterogenous attractiveness of employment centres. In this context, the present study examines alternative ways of identifying LMAs in the island region of Crete, Greece, by comparing the conventional commuting threshold method with a methodology based on a 3-step floating catchment area (3SFCA) framework combined with a modified Huff model and cluster analysis.
Using data from the 2021 Population Census at the municipal unit (LAU-2) level, the first approach defines LMAs according to the traditional rule that areas are functionally linked when at least 15% of employed residents commute to a neighbouring zone for work. The second approach estimates probabilistic labour market interactions by incorporating both travel impedance, i.e., generalised travel cost, and the relative attractiveness of destinations through the modified Huff model formulation embedded in the 3SFCA method. The resulting interaction patterns are then grouped through clustering techniques to identify spatially coherent labour market areas.
The comparison underscores important differences in the geography, size and internal structure of the resulting LMAs. While the traditional method identifies clear functional linkages based on observed commuting intensity, the alternative approach reveals more nuanced patterns of labour market integration by accounting for competition among destinations and spatial accessibility to employment. The outcomes can contribute to the discussion about the methodology of delineating LMAs. It can further offer useful insights for regional planning and transport policy in insular and peripheral contexts, where labour market interactions are strongly shaped by uneven accessibility and settlement structure.

18.title: Spatio-Temporal analysis of Rural–Urban Migration and Urban Expansion of secondary cities in Sub-Saharan Africa: The Case of Jimma city, Ethiopia

authors.name: Gemechu Debesa Wedajo
authors.affiliation: Jimma University, Ethiopia and KU LEUVEN, Belgium

18.abstract:
Abstract
Sub-Saharan Africa is undergoing a rapid transition from predominantly rural to urban societies, with urban populations projected to exceed 50% by 2050. While existing research has largely focused on capital cities, the dynamics of secondary cities remain underexplored despite their growing demographic and economic significance. This study examines the spatio-temporal expansion and socio-economic dynamics of emerging urban neighborhoods in a secondary city, using Jimma, Ethiopia (population 239,022), as a case study.
The research adopted a mixed-methods approach. First, multi-temporal satellite imagery (SPOT and Sentinel-2) from 2000 to 2022 is analyzed to map urban growth patterns and land-use transformations. The results show significant spatial expansion, with four former rural settlements (Kofe, Bore, Ifa-Bula, and Hora-Gibe) progressively integrated into the urban fabric. Built-up areas more than doubled, increasing from 1,037 to 2,246 hectares, accompanied by declines in agricultural land (−9.56%), forest cover (−1.29%), and wetlands (−1.24%).

In the second phase, a household survey of 384 rural-urban migrants examines migration drivers and typologies. The findings reveal that migration to Jimma is shaped by a combination of push factors, including limited infrastructure, low wages, declining agricultural productivity, and conflict at place of origin, and pull factors, like improved urban services, better livelihood opportunities, and access to markets for small businesses, highlighting the increasing role of secondary cities as alternative urban destinations.

These findings underscore the accelerating transformation of secondary cities and their growing importance in regional urban systems. The study highlights the need for proactive urban planning and infrastructure development to accommodate rapid population influxes and mitigate unplanned spatial expansion.

Keywords: Spatial analysis, Secondary cities, Rural-Urban Migration, Neighborhood-detection, Jimma city

19.title: Geographical dimensions of fertility in Greece during the inter-war period
19.abstract: The 1920s are often described by demographers as a period of "population depression” across Europe. By the end of the decade, many Western and Northern European countries were approaching or had already fallen below replacement level fertility for the first time in recorded history with Total Fertility Rate (TFR) close or below 2.1 children per woman. Greece provides a fascinating and distinct contrast to the Western European trend. While the rest of Europe saw a steady decline in the 1920s, Greece recorded volatile but generally ascending fertility rates. This rise in fertility indexes is often attributed to the arrival of over 1.2 million Greek refugees from Asia Minor following the military defeat in Anatolia It has long been hypothesized that refugees exhibited more prolific reproductive behaviour than the native population. This paper re-examines the reproductive behavior of the Greek population by Geographical Department and ethnic group (refugees and natives) employing established methods of historical demography to derive fertility indexes indirectly, as these cannot be calculated straightforwardly due to data limitations. The findings reveal that the observed rise in fertility was not primarily driven by an increase in marital fecundity, but rather by a shift in nuptiality: women were marrying more frequently and at younger ages. This shift in marriage patterns bolstered the TFRs while leaving the TMFRs only marginally affected. Furthermore, significant regional variations underscore that interwar Greece was a mosaic of populations with distinct cultural, social, and historical identities, particularly within territories that had only recently been annexed into the modern Greek state.

19.title: The Evolution of Marriage, Divorce, and Fertility in Southern Europe: Demographic and Social Approaches

authors.name: Georgios Kontogiannis
authors.affiliation: University of Thessaly, Volos and Democritus University of Thrace, Komotini, Greece

authors.name: Kostas Rontos
authors.affiliation: University of the Aegean, Mytilene Greece

authors.name: Luca Salvati
authors.affiliation: Department of Methods and Models for Economics, Territory and Finance (MEMOTEF), Faculty of Economics, Sapienza University of Rome, Rome, Italy

authors.name: Dimitrios Antonoglou
authors.affiliation: University of the Aegean, Mytilene Greece

19.abstract:
Abstract:
Since the 1970s, significant changes in marriage and divorce patterns have been observed across Southern Europe, following—albeit with a temporal delay—trends that had already emerged in Northern and Western Europe. The present study examines the long-term evolution of primonuptiality, fertility, and divorce patterns in Greece, in comparison with Italy, Spain, and France, emphasising the role of values, religion, gender roles, and institutional transformations.
The analysis is based on data derived from national statistical authorities, EUROSTAT, and the European Demographic Observatory. Methods associated with the Classical French School of Demography are employed, including indicators of primo-nuptiality, fertility, and divorce intensity. In addition, logistic regression analysis is used to investigate the influence of age, gender, and educational attainment on the likelihood of entering marriage or a registered partnership in Greece.
The findings indicate that transformations in family-related behaviours emerged earlier in France, followed by Spain and Italy, while Greece experienced these developments with a more pronounced delay. The postponement of marriage, rising childlessness, and increasing divorce rates are associated with the spread of individualistic values, improvements in women’s educational and occupational status, the diffusion of effective contraception, secularisation processes, and the weakening of social stigma surrounding unmarried, childless, and/or divorced women. Nevertheless, in Greece, strong family ties and traditional attitudes continue to exert substantial influence, resulting in a slower transition toward new family patterns compared to other European countries.
Keywords:
primo-nuptiality, fertility, divorce, demographic analysis, Southern Europe

19.title: Mapping urban restructuring in the EU: Visualizing the underperformance of southern cities
19.abstract:
This paper investigates macro-trends in uneven urban development, focusing on urban restructuring dynamics across the EU. We approach cities comparatively, exploring three key urban restructuring indicators: GDP growth, employment traits and population shifts across the metropolitan area, linking socio-economic performance with urbanization trends. Divergent urban dynamics in the EU, we argue, and the resultant economic disparities they create and reproduce, shape the urbanization trajectories of cities and are reflected on their morphology.
Comparative urban analysis was advanced with the use of web mapping techniques and visualization methods. A cartographic web application named «EU - SET» was designed, using proportional symbols and multivariate visual encoding, enabling the simultaneous depiction of magnitude and direction of change across urban indicators. «EU - SET» consists of three dashboards, each one tracking and visualizing the aforementioned key socio-economic and morphological dimensions of post-industrial urban adaptation and competitiveness in 75 cities in the 2001-2020 period. The analytical and cartographic attention is aimed at the urban south (Portugal, southern Italy, Greece, and Spain), an area with macroregional characteristics that exhibits sustained divergence and declining investment dynamics. Our examination marks the deviating development paths noted in northern and southern urban Europe and discusses the conditions in which socio-economic restructuring processes took place in lagging southern cities.
The distance of southern cities from the emergent cross-border urban hubs that coordinate the European economy, we argue, reflects a new phase of peripheralization in the area with noticeable path-dependent traits, currently defined by the dynamics of EU integration, enhanced competitiveness and austerity preoccupations. The use of geoinfomatics and web mapping methods is a key resource for monitoring spatial disparities, particularly so in the diverse EU urban setting, the absence of which in EU policy making is commented upon.

19.title: Living in Athens: a study of mortality inequalities by cause of death
19.abstract: The literature studying the losses of life expectancy at birth by cause of death is extensive. However, studies investigating the gender, age, and spatial variation of longevity loss in Greece are rare. Rarer are those that focus on Attica. The main goal of this paper is to examine whether there is a variation in longevity losses by cause of death, by gender, by age group, and by the Regional Unit of Attica from 2014 to 2019. Analysis of microdata from the Hellenic Statistical Authority and data from the Eurostat Database showed a spatial dimension in some causes of death, such as circulatory system diseases, neoplasms, and external causes of mortality and morbidity. Additionally, the results show that for specific categories of diseases, the loss of life expectancy also has a gender and an age dimension. Finally, it is worth noting that, overall, Greece exhibits significantly lower life expectancy losses at birth across most categories of causes of death, for both men and women.

20.title: Trends in the reduction of coastal agricultural land.

authors.name: Georgia Karvouniari
authors.affiliation: National Technical University of Athens MSc in Environment and Development

20.abstract:
Rural areas in Greece are undergoing profound socio-spatial transformations associated with demographic decline, ageing, changing agricultural economies, and increasing environmental pressures. In coastal rural regions in particular, these processes are closely linked to the gradual reduction and fragmentation of agricultural land, driven by urban sprawl, tourism-related development, and shifting land-use patterns. These dynamics contribute not only to changes in rural production systems, but also to the transformation of rural landscapes, local identities, and spatial inequalities.
This presentation examines the reduction of high-productivity agricultural land in the Municipality of Ilida (Western Peloponnese), focusing on the coastal zone regulated by the Urban Development Control Zone (ZOE). The study investigates the extent to which spatial planning policies have succeeded in protecting rural space amid increasing development pressures and broader rural restructuring processes.
Drawing on spatial planning analysis and the examination of land-use change over time, the presentation explores the relationship between agricultural land reduction, urban expansion, and the changing socio-spatial character of the countryside. Particular emphasis is placed on how these transformations intersect with long-term demographic decline and the weakening of the productive rural base.
The findings reveal a significant and long-term reduction of rural space, accompanied by increasing pressures on agricultural land and substantial changes in the physiognomy of the area. The study also evaluates the effectiveness and limitations of the existing planning framework, highlighting the challenges of regulating coastal rural areas under conditions of economic transition and uneven rural development.

20.title: Spatial Inequalities in the Regions of the European Union: A Comparative Analysis of Rural Regions in Sweden, Romania, and Greece
20.abstract:
This paper examines recent developments in spatial inequalities across European Union regions with diverse social, political, and geographical characteristics. Moving beyond conventional comparative approaches, it analyses regional disparities, particularly in rural areas, through the lens of Geographical Political Economy and institutional geographical analysis. The study focuses on the regions of Sweden, a mature economy in the European core; Romania, a newer EU member facing structural constraints; and Greece, a semi-peripheral economy marked by pronounced spatial unevenness. Particular attention is given to the role of the agricultural sector, which remains significant in the latter two countries.

From a methodological perspective, quantitative methods are applied at both urban and regional levels for the sub-periods 2015–2019 and 2020–2024, using Eurostat data. Firstly, at the urban level, the urban hierarchy in the three countries under study is analysed using the rank–size rule for cities with populations exceeding 50,000 inhabitants. Secondly, at regional level, the Hirschman–Herfindahl (H–H) index is used to examine the regional and sectoral distribution of the labour force across the two study periods. The analysis is further complemented by calculating the location quotient (LQ) to identify the key productive sectors of each region, detect rural regions, and assess the impact of successive crises on them.

The study concludes that regional disparities have been widening, both between rural and non-rural regions and among rural regions themselves, highlighting the decisive role of path-dependent processes and structural deficiencies in shaping spatial unevenness.

20.title: Tourism-driven spatial fixes and labour flexibilisation: the case of Greece

authors.name: Giorgos Sykas
authors.affiliation: PhD, Department of Geography, University of the Aegean

authors.name: Athina Avagianou
authors.affiliation: Postdoctoral Researcher, Department of Geography, University of the Aegean

authors.name: Kostas Gourzis
authors.affiliation: Postdoctoral Researcher, Department of Geography, University of the Aegean,

authors.name: Stelios Gialis
authors.affiliation: Professor, Department of Geography, University of the Aegean

20.abstract:
This paper examines the dialectical relationship between spatial fixes and labour flexibilisation in Greece, positioning touristification as a key contemporary form of capital's spatial fix. Building on Harvey's spatial-fix theory and the circuits-of-capital framework, the paper draws on a multi-scalar methodology that combines Gross Fixed Capital Formation (GFCF) with employment data to trace capital switching between the primary and secondary circuits of accumulation and to analyse its implications for labour recomposition across sectors and regions.
The findings confirm that the Greek economy has long relied on the built environment as a central site of value extraction. However, in the aftermath of the 2008–2009 crisis, a structural shift occurred from construction-led growth to tourism-oriented accumulation. This transition reflects a reconfiguration of spatial fixes, whereby investment increasingly targets tourism-related land uses, infrastructure, and real estate, signalling the consolidation of touristification within the secondary circuit of capital. Simultaneously, labour markets have undergone intensified devaluation, manifested through the expansion of part-time, temporary, and other forms of precarious employment. These dynamics are particularly evident in tourism and construction, where flexibilisation functions as a mechanism for restoring profitability under conditions of capital devalorisation. The analysis further demonstrates that the contrast between Attica's urban touristification and the South Aegean's resort-based model represents complementary expressions of a single accumulation regime rather than divergent development paths. Touristification operates across both urban and rural contexts, reinforcing uneven geographical development and embedding local economies within transnational circuits of capital.
The paper argues that spatial fixes and labour devaluation function as intertwined crisis-management strategies. While tourism-led growth may temporarily absorb overaccumulated capital and stabilise accumulation, it simultaneously entrenches precarious labour and reproduces structural inequalities, thereby exposing the inherent limits of spatial fixes in resolving capitalist crises.

21.title: Spatial Inequalities in Urban Accessibility: A GIS-Based Analysis of Pedestrian Mobility in Athens
21.abstract: Urban environments often display marked spatial disparities that create accessibility barriers for vulnerable social groups, particularly older adults and people with disabilities. These barriers are embedded in the spatial structure of the city and shape uneven mobility patterns, limiting access to essential services and reducing quality of life. Understanding how such inequalities are distributed and manifested across urban space is critical for promoting more inclusive and sustainable mobility systems. Identifying these issues requires both quantitative evaluation to determine their extent and qualitative spatial analysis to capture their geographical expression and distribution. This study examines accessibility conditions in Athens through GIS-based analysis, focusing on how they vary across urban space. Accessibility indicators are used as analytical inputs to support the interpretation of spatial patterns of pedestrian mobility and inequality. Particular emphasis is placed on the role of urban structure, including the spatial concentration of activities, central land uses, and the organisation of the sidewalk network, in shaping differentiated geographies of access. Three population groups – the general population, older adults, and people with disabilities – are examined to reveal distinct spatial experiences of mobility. The methodology combines geospatial data, GIS analysis, and detailed information on pedestrian infrastructure and land-use patterns. Indicator evaluations are integrated into the spatial analysis to identify patterns, concentrations, gradients, and discontinuities in accessibility across the city. The findings reveal significant spatial inequalities in Athens, with fragmented and unevenly distributed pedestrian infrastructure disproportionately affecting vulnerable groups.

21.title: Decarbonizing the Core, Recolonizing the Periphery: Green Growth and Uneven Development under the EGD
21.abstract:
The European Green Deal (EGD) seeks to transform the EU into a climate neutral economy by 2050, offering both a new growth strategy for the continent and being a
‘just transition’ that leaves no place or person behind. Moreover, from a regional development perspective, the EGD claims potential for regional development through a promise of growth opportunities for these places through renewable energy infrastructure projects. Critiques of the EGD criticize its green growth agenda that focuses on technological improvement which fails to address the root causes of climate change and does not consider the extractivist and ecologically destructive nature of large-scale renewable energy projects. We aim to add to this critique through a political geographical economy perspective. By taking into account the critique of the EGD and its claims of regional development, we argue the EGD is a socio-ecological fix that aims to solve the problem of climate change and uneven development through a capitalist growth strategy. Through the case study of Greece, we aim to demonstrate how the European Green deal policy conceptualizes peripheral areas in an extractivist manner that operates from the European to the national level. We argue that this growth focused approach offers little benefit for regional development, as it is entrenched in the very logics that created their current problems. We conclude by proposing how renewable energy can be implemented for
neo-endogenous regional development, drawing on current debates on post- development energies and community renewable energy ecologies.

21.title: Geographies of Transport Transition in Greece: HGV Driver Shortages, Labor Restructuring, and the Potential Role of Autonomous Driving
21.abstract:
The shortage of Heavy Goods Vehicle (HGV) drivers constitutes one of the most critical challenges for the road freight transport sector in Europe and, more intensively, in Greece, where labor shortages intersect with broader processes of transport transition, regional inequality, and economic restructuring. The ageing workforce, relatively low wages compared to the responsibility and intensity of the profession, prolonged absence from home base, and increased operational pressures related to an ageing vehicle fleet and stricter regulatory controls have significantly reduced the attractiveness of the profession for younger generations.

This study examines the shortage of HGV drivers in Greece through a geographical perspective, focusing on how labor scarcity is distributed across space and how it reflects wider transformations in freight mobility systems. Emphasis is given to spatial disparities between main logistics hubs and peripheral areas where transport accessibility, labor availability, and economic dependence on road freight differ substantially. These spatial inequalities shape both the intensity of driver shortages and the resilience of regional supply chains.

The methodology combines primary data collected through questionnaires addressed to professional drivers, transport company executives, and sector stakeholders, with quantitative spatial analysis of transport activity and regional labor patterns. The objective is to identify the structural causes of the reduced attractiveness of the profession, evaluate their geographical dimensions, and examine whether autonomous driving technologies could function as a strategic response within the ongoing transition of the transport sector.

By linking labor shortages with automation, regional inequalities, and the political economy of freight mobility, the study contributes to the broader discussion on the geographies of transport transition and the future restructuring of transport employment in Greece.

21.title: Wind Farms and Barbed Wire: How Brazil’s Energy Transition is Reshaping Rural Landscapes
21.abstract: In the north-eastern regions of Brazil, wind power has become a priority under the country’s energy policy, with development being driven by private energy companies. As a result, every land suitable for wind power generation is turning into a new El Dorado for capitalism. For the state of Rio Grande do Norte, it represents 3,122 wind turbines located across 302 wind farms. Therefore, we are witnessing a massification of wind parks, with energy companies that are building more and more wind farms, reproducing the extraction model already used for fossil fuels. They exploit the power imbalance in their favor by signing purchase agreements or tenancy contracts directly with local communities, facilitated by a Brazilian state that justifies its lack of regulation for wind farms as part of its energy transition policy and its fight against climate change. At the local level, the consequences of these policies lead to enclosed areas that leave increasingly less room for communal spaces. As a result, in some cases, communities are confined to their villages, connected only by roads that run between barbed-wire fences. The privatization of these spaces alters how people use the land and move around, while also depriving them of their symbolic and cultural values. These landmarks of the territory are now inaccessible to the people. Furthermore, the financial compensation provided under Brazilian law is slow to materialize, as are the public investments expected to accompany a flourishing economy. In conclusion, over the past 20 years, the Northeast region has become a benchmark for the energy transition in Brazil, partly thanks to the purchase and privatization of land that is essential to the survival of local communities.

21.title: Central Asia’s Geopolitics in Energy Transition: Resources, Strategies, and regional Dynamics
21.abstract:
This paper examines the strategic interplay between geopolitics and the energy sector in Central Asia. It focuses on how regional actors navigate great power competition while managing infrastructural, regulatory, and institutional constraints. Drawing on a synthesis of studies and policy analyses from 1999 to 2026, with historical context from the post-Soviet period. It integrates insights on Russia–China dynamics, pipeline politics, and energy diplomacy. It also addresses institutional and governance barriers, as well as emerging energy transition pathways in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan.
Methodologically, the paper employs a comparative meta-analysis of the selected literature. First, geopolitical frameworks from international relations are applied to evaluate the multi-vector foreign policies of Central Asian states and their responses to Russia, China, the EU, and the United States. Second, it develops an infrastructural assessment by synthesizing technical and economic analyses of oil, gas, and pipeline systems, including transit bottlenecks, outdated transmission networks, and capacity constraints. Third, it conducts an institutional review to assess the impact of corruption, regulatory instability, and governance deficits on energy reform and investor confidence. Finally, it performs a cross-sectoral analysis of renewable energy policies and deployment trends, drawing on studies of hydropower, solar potential, green fiscal policy, and legal barriers to decarbonization.
Findings indicate that Central Asia’s fossil-fuel wealth continues to drive geopolitical rivalries, particularly between Russia and China, with pipeline politics reshaping regional alignments. However, infrastructural decay and governance challenges significantly constrain energy security and export diversification. Renewable energy presents growing opportunities but remains hindered by fragmented regulation, insufficient investment, and limited institutional capacity. The results underscore that achieving long-term energy security will require coordinated governance reforms, modernization of energy systems, and balanced engagement with external powers.

21.title: SPATIAL IMPACTS AND THE ENVIRONMENTAL GEOGRAPHY OF WIND ENERGY EXPANSION IN CENTRAL GREECE

authors.name: Apostolos Lagarias
authors.affiliation: Assistant Prof., Department of Planning and Regional Development, University of Thessaly

authors.name: Alisa Miliaeva
authors.affiliation: Biodiversity Conservation Laboratory, Department of Environment, University of the Aegean, Mytilene, Greece

21.abstract: The accelerated deployment of Renewable Energy Sources (RES) across Europe is widely framed as a necessary pathway toward decarbonization. However, its spatial manifestation reveals a growing tension between climate mitigation goals and the integrity of landscapes, ecosystems, and local communities. This paper critically examines the “de facto” industrialization of open and mountainous landscapes in Central Greece, adopting a planning-oriented and critical human geography perspective. A geospatially explicit framework is proposed to assess the cumulative impacts of wind energy on what are conceptualized as Natural-Historical Landscape Ensembles, i.e. spatial entities integrating ecological, archaeological, and perceptual dimensions of space. The methodological approach integrates multiple dimensions of landscape change through a combinatory geospatial framework. Environmental dynamics are monitored using remote sensing indicators, capturing both vegetation/forest condition, land use patterns and structural change; combined with spatial data on renewable energy infrastructure, protected areas (Natura 2000), and cultural heritage sites. Additional layers include elevation-based analysis to isolate impacts on mountain systems, and socio-demographic and qualitative data reflecting local perceptions and responses. Together, these components enable a multi-scalar assessment of landscape transformation, linking biophysical changes with spatial planning processes and socio-political dynamics. Findings indicate that in several cases, particularly within protected areas, infrastructure development is associated with land-cover change, habitat fragmentation, and localized vegetation degradation. These processes unfold in parallel with broader Climate Change pressures, producing compounded risks for already vulnerable ecosystems. Alongside these spatial transformations, a growing number of grassroots movements have emerged across Central Greece These initiatives move beyond generic opposition to renewable energy, foregrounding concerns over landscape degradation, loss of biodiversity, and the erosion of cultural identity and local livelihoods. We need a shift toward place-based, landscape-sensitive planning approaches that recognize the socio-ecological value of rural mountainous regions.

21.title: Sustainable mobility without mobility justice: the proposed metro station in Exarchia, Athens
21.abstract: Athens’ transport network is under increasing pressure, in part due to its poor public transport provision. The construction of a fourth Metro line, already in the making, is generally considered a welcome step towards improving mobility in the city. One of the stations that is to be constructed as a part of the new line is located on Exarchia Square, in the central neighbourhood of Exarchia. The placement of the station on the Square has faced resistance from the local community, has gained media attention and has been the subject of a long-drawn debate. Having a closer look at the events, however, reveals that the placement of the station is far from a case of “some people” being for and some others against it. The introduction of the new metro station provides insights into how decisions that are made as part of or linked to the transition to a more sustainable transport system can raise significant justice issues, especially in places where public deliberation and participation in decision making are limited or under threat. In the case of Exarchia, these justice issues include lack of transparency, insufficient or non-existent consultation, unclear decision-making processes, and the deployment of illegal practices in the public space. Our research uses quantitative tools to examine the location of the new metro station, and qualitative tools to document the residents’ efforts to prevent illegal interventions and maintain their right to the public space. The resulting analysis provides a critical discussion on how transitions are shaped, particularly in their early stages, and into what Mimi Sheller describes as “the unequal capabilities for movement, as well as the unequal rights to stay or dwell in a place”.

21.title: Wind Energy Development and Environmental Pressures in Greece: A Spatial Analysis Using GIS
21.abstract: The rapid development of wind energy projects in Greece during the last decade has significantly transformed the Greek landscape, particularly mountainous and environmentally sensitive areas, intensifying the debate regarding the environmental impacts of the energy transition and the adequacy of the existing spatial planning framework. Although wind energy is promoted as a key pillar for addressing the climate crisis, its development in Greece is often associated with increasing pressure on natural ecosystems, fragmented implementation of environmental legislation, and the growing concentration of projects in areas of high ecological value. This study investigates the spatial distribution of existing and proposed wind energy projects in Greece and examines their relationship with environmentally sensitive areas through the use of Geographic Information Systems (GIS). A GIS-based spatial analysis methodology was developed to map wind energy installations and evaluate their spatial overlap with Natura 2000 sites, Important Bird Areas, roadless areas, and mountainous regions. The analysis is based on the environmental criteria of the existing spatial planning framework for Renewable Energy Sources, while also exploring alternative approaches to spatial restrictions and the protection of sensitive ecosystems. The results indicate that a significant number of wind energy projects are located within or in close proximity to areas of high environmental importance, revealing limitations both in the planning framework and in its implementation. The study contributes to the broader discussion on the spatial limits of wind energy development and the need to strengthen the protection of mountainous and environmentally sensitive areas.

22.title: Cities of Encounter: Everyday Geopolitics of Peace in Nicosia and Xanthi

authors.name: Ethan Chandler
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

22.abstract:
Geopolitical tensions between Greece and Turkey are often framed through elite-level diplomacy, territorial claims and statist narratives. Yet such macro-scale discourses are continuously negotiated, contested and subverted in the everyday spaces of cities situated on Europe’s geopolitical periphery. This paper examines how Nicosia (Cyprus) and Xanthi, (Western Thrace) function as borderland sites where hegemonic geopolitical imaginaries intersect with quotidian practices of coexistence, revealing a “double helix” that binds macro-level narratives to micro-level lived experience.

Nicosia exemplifies a “checkpoint city,” where the legacy of partition, the UN-controlled Buffer Zone and Orientalising discourses of the divided island shape socio-spatial life. By contrast, Xanthi represents an unpartitioned periphery where Muslim communities exempted from the Treaty of Lausanne population exchanges negotiate coexistence within the Greek nation-state. Both cities share histories of imperial governance and subsequent Westphalian nation-state imposition, yet their divergent geopolitical configurations – partition versus coexistence – produce distinct urban geographies of peace-making.

Drawing on critical and feminist geopolitical frameworks as the theoretical foundation of an ethnographic PhD project, this paper conceptualises peace as plural, personal and place-specific – performed through everyday encounters in markets, schools, civic spaces and public institutions. It illustrates how marginal cities are constructed as liminal spaces subverting Westphalian statist territorial logics, whilst simultaneously offering sites of possibility in which local actors can reinterpret dominant geopolitical narratives through embodied everyday practices.

By foregrounding Southeast European cities as sites of geopolitical theorisation, this paper contributes to Critical Geopolitics, Geographies of Peace and Borderland Studies. It demonstrates that geopolitics is not produced at the political core, but negotiated continuously at the margins. By tracing the intersection between discursive geopolitical power and lived geopolitical experiences in cities of Greek-Turkish interaction, this comparative framing demonstrates how the geopolitical configuration of cities actively shapes the production, negotiation and spatialisation of everyday peace.

22.title: Inhabiting the Gaza Strip in the 21st century
22.abstract:
This research examines the issue of inhabiting in Gaza Strip during the 21st century. The investigation focuses on materiality as a central aspect of the experience of inhabiting, in relation to the socio-political conditions of settler colonialism imposed by the Israeli state in the region. In Gaza, urbanization and urbanity are constituted—amid multiple experiences of violent displacement and spatial confinement—as fields of control, precarity, and collective punishment.
The siege of the Gaza Strip and the socio-spatial conditions it created, implicating severe restrictions on basic goods, infrastructure, and public services, had clear effects on the transformation of housing typologies and on the emergence of informality as a necessity through which the Palestinian community develops its own spaces of living. The analysis of this condition includes concepts such as Yiftachel’s “gray spaces,” situated between legality and illegality, as well as the notion of “urban citizenship”, as a means of claiming the right to the city against regimes of spatial inequality and urban apartheid.
Israeli aggression, as it has evolved throughout the 21st century against the Gaza Strip, in conjunction with transformations of contemporary warfare, led to the reuse of the term “urbicide”, understood as the extensive and deliberate destruction of the built environment aiming to the present or future annihilation and/or erasure. Subsequently, by constructing the concept of home as a universal human experience, the investigation turns to the term “domicide”, understood as the intentional destruction of home by humans, causing suffering to its victims for specific purposes—in this case, forced displacement or even genocide.
The destruction taking place in the Gaza Strip must be understood as a process of systematic erasure of a nation from its land, embedded in the fundamental logic of elimination, with intervention in territory and territoriality constituting a central objective of settler colonialism.

22.title: Pushbacks in Greece as enemy under-criminalization
22.abstract: This article examines the practice of illegal pushbacks at Greece's borders through the lens of ‘enemy under-criminalization’. Drawing on field reports, testimonies, and academic analyses, the study identifies three defining characteristics of pushbacks: raw violence, permanent exclusion, and the absence of the law. It argues that, unlike crimmigration, which merges criminal and immigration law, pushbacks operate entirely outside legal frameworks, creating an extra-legal space where unrestrained violence replaces legal procedures, treating irregular border crossers as ‘enemies’. The concept of enemy under-criminalization reflects the exclusion of irregular migrants from both physical territory and legal protection, framing them as adversaries to be removed rather than individuals with rights. By situating pushbacks as a punitive strategy beyond crimmigration, this study underscores their implications for justice, accountability, and the integrity of democratic institutions.

22.title: Critical Cartographies of Border Violence: Migrant Shipwrecks and Biopolitics in the Aegean Sea

authors.name: Nafsika Kretsa
authors.affiliation: Department of Spatial Planning and Development – Aristotle University of Thessaloniki

22.abstract:
This paper was motivated by the shipwreck off the coast of Pylos in June 2023. The aim of this research is to highlight critical cartography as an analytical tool for recognizing migrant shipwrecks in the Aegean as spatial and political phenomena, rather than as isolated, tragic incidents, during the period 2015–2025. The research approaches the sea as a dynamic border space where control, surveillance, and selective intervention produce uneven geographies of protection and exposure.
Methodologically, secondary quantitative data from the IOM – Missing Migrants Project and UNCHR are integrated with principles of critical cartography. The data were processed and visualized using GIS. The mapping comprises a flow map of migratory routes, a heat map of incidents, two maps illustrating the spatial distribution of the dead and missing, and an interactive map enabling temporal exploration of shipwrecks.
The mapping reveals recurring spatial patterns and clusters of shipwrecks, highlighting specific zones of precarity in the Aegean. These patterns confirm that shipwrecks are not random incidents but integral elements of the biopolitical practices implemented within border regimes. The border constitutes a field of continuous negotiation. The Aegean Sea emerges as a “spatio-temporal threshold”, where mobility is intertwined with precarity and surveillance.
This research does not seek to impose a definitive conclusion, but rather to suggest that understanding shipwrecks, as well as the borders within which they are inscribed, requires continuous reflection. Mapping constitutes an ongoing political act that challenges dominant narratives of borders, migration, and humanitarianism.

22.title: Geopolitics of Reception: Refugee Camp Siting and Local Reactions in Lesvos

authors.name: Alexandra Makridou
authors.affiliation: PhD Candidate, Department of Spatial Planning and Development, AUTH

authors.name: Yannis Frangopoulos
authors.affiliation: Professor, Department of Spatial Planning and Development, AUTH

22.abstract: In 2015, Europe faced an unprecedented increase in refugee arrivals, leading to the so-called “reception crisis” (Rea et al., 2019). As part of the externalization of migration governance (Niemann & Zaun, 2018), the EU imposed the establishment of 'hot spots' at its entry points (Greece-Italy) (Kreichauf, 2018). A decade later, despite the significant decline in refugee arrivals and efforts to implement alternative, more sustainable, and inclusive forms of housing, Greek reception policy continues to be based on the logic of siting large refugee camps. The siting of these controversial facilities often provokes reactions from the local community associated with the NIMBY (Not In My Back Yard) movement (Makridou et al., 2024). Lesvos, as an informal gateway to Europe, constitutes a geopolitical space par excellence where supranational strategies of migration governance are embedded at the local level, directly influencing social relations, representations, and spatial practices across urban and peri-urban areas. In this context, the present research focuses on the local reactions that emerged in Lesvos in February 2020 against the creation of a new refugee camp in the Karava area. The hypothesis is that these specific forms of protest constitute fluid, multifactorial, and dynamic phenomena that are shaped in direct relation to central planning practices and geopolitical strategies for immigration management. The theoretical framework draws on Lefebvre (1991) and Rémy (1975), and is enriched by NIMBY reactions and migration governance studies. Following a socio-spatial approach, the methodology is based on qualitative research through semi-structured interviews with experts, stakeholders, and residents of the Regional Unit of Lesvos. The research contributes to a deeper understanding of how geopolitical strategies of migration governance are implemented and challenged at the local level, highlighting spatial planning’s role in shaping social tensions and resistance, as well as the interconnection between supranational, national, and local levels.

22.title: Issues of Geography, Biopolitics & Power in the Turkish Settlement of Northern Cyprus
22.abstract:
Nicosia, the last divided capital in Europe, constitutes a dense geopolitical landscape where sovereignty, population management, and everyday life intersect. Established through the division of the island in 1974, the city operates simultaneously as a site of territorial fragmentation and as a key node in the spatial consolidation of the Turkish settler project in Northern Cyprus. This paper examines the socio‑political dynamics of Turkish settlement through the lens of critical geopolitics and biopolitical governance.

The analysis focuses both on settlers, approached as mobile populations organized and regulated by state power, and on indigenous Turkish Cypriots, whose positioning is marked by tensions between ethnic affiliation and geographically grounded forms of belonging. Drawing on an analysis of legal frameworks alongside demographic and population data, the paper situates settler presence within international legal debates while engaging with the lived realities produced by long‑term population displacement.

Building on Ghassan Hage’s concept of “generalized domestication” (2017), the paper conceptualizes settlers as domesticated subjects: populations governed through intersecting racial, spatial, and political technologies that seek to regulate land, bodies, and social relations. This framing moves beyond treating settlers as mere demographic agents and instead highlights their role within a broader nationalist project that produces hierarchies and exclusions. In Nicosia, this process unfolds through housing allocation, property regimes, restricted mobility, and differentiated access to citizenship and rights, transforming the city into a frontier where national projects are materially enacted.

The settlers’ ambiguous legal status, constrained movement, and structural dependence on the Turkish state reveal the internal contradictions of settler colonial power. By tracing these dynamics across multiple spatial scales—from the urban to the international—the paper contributes to critical discussions on imperialism, racialization, and anticolonial resistance.

Key Words:
Settler Colonialism, Northern Cyprus, Nicosia, Biopolitics, Racialization, Critical Geopolitics, Displacement, Imperialism

22.title: Securitization Strategies in Greek Universities, The case of the National Technical University of Athens (Patision Str. Campus)
22.abstract:
Securitization strategies in Greek higher education institutions involve reframing issues of education and politics as matters of security and public order, thereby justifying increased control and intervention. In recent years, this shift is primarily driven by legislative changes, including the abolition of the academic asylum and the establishment of a university police force, alongside subsequent legislation introducing, among other measures, video surveillance systems, controlled access points and stricter disciplinary legal frameworks, all aimed at securing campus life and the educational process.

At the same time, the dominant narrative promoted by political actors, university administrations and the media, portrays universities as spaces of lawlessness requiring immediate and decisive intervention.
