Within this discourse, security is framed as freedom, while those who oppose such measures are marginalised as a reactive minority acting against public interest. By constructing a sense of urgency and cultivating social consent, political authorities reinforce strategies presented as necessary and inevitable.

The case of NTUA on Patission Street exemplifies this transformation in a historically symbolic context. Situated in the centre of Athens and serving as a landmark of democratic resistance during the 1973 student uprising against the military junta, the campus has been associated with political engagement, social ferment and struggles, openness and public accessibility. Over the past years, however, it has increasingly been subject to surveillance and control, reflecting the broader securitization of Greek universities. Framed as a risk hotspot, it has, following constant police interventions, become an example of the effectiveness of security policies.

This transformation highlights not only a change of policy, but also a spatial and symbolic redefinition of the university. The shift from an open, public and free space to a controlled and monitored environment raises critical questions about the implications for academic freedom, political expression and the overall quality of the educational process.

22.title: The phenomenon of urbicide and models of post-conflict reconstruction and restructuring in zones of limited sovereignty and surveillance: The cases of Mogadishu, Aleppo, and Mosul
22.abstract:
The announcement will highlight the field of urban geopolitics, with emphasis on the phenomenon of urbicide, in liquid modernity/urban pastiche. Synthesizing critical infrastructures, institutional restructuring, international relations, spatial planning, and the reconstruction of megacities, as fields of regional and international conflict poles in the Global South.
The first case will be Mogadishu. This is a city that has been affected by hostilities since 1991, initially in the context of a civil war and then as a field of power for Islamist networks. The city faces structural human-security problems within the institutional framework of a failed state, resulting in successive crises. Since 2023, its reconstruction has been attempted through the projects “Post-Conflict Reconstruction and Development Project” and the “New Mogadishu Project”.
The second case is that of Aleppo. With the beginning of the Syrian civil war, the city found itself at the target of the opposing sides and suffered a multi-year humanitarian crisis. Both its structural infrastructure and its social identity were battlegrounds, leading to the breakdown of its economic and urban structures. Since 2024, the city has been the stronghold of the new Syrian leadership, while ethnocultural neighborhoods are being militarized. The main reconstruction models are "Law 10" and the policy of "selective restoration of emblematic monuments".
The third case, that of Mosul, lies mainly in the three years 2014-2017, when the city was occupied by the Islamic State (ISIS). In this case, there was extensive destruction of monuments and the city's rich cultural heritage, as well as widespread population displacement. The dominant reconstruction model, carried out by UNESCO with international participation, is “Revive the Spirit of Mosul”.
The three case studies reveal the strategic value of cities in contemporary geopolitical rivalries in zones of limited sovereignty and surveillance, and a cognitive mapping of securitization as a geography of polycrisis.

22.title: Mapping Israeli Real Estate Investments in Exarcheia neighborhood
22.abstract:
In the spring of 2026, a large billboard by the Israeli real estate company “Palmo” at Athens International Airport sparked considerable controversy. Addressed to Israelis, the billboard read: “We don’t return home without a home in Greece”. The campaign’s aggressive marketing—particularly striking in a period during which Israel acts as a key organizer of the war while simultaneously continuing to perpetrate genocide. From large-scale tourism investments in central Athens and beyond, to hybrid real estate schemes involving serviced apartments for short-term or mid-term rentals, Israeli capital has established an expanding presence in the city center.
In the contested neighborhood of Exarcheia—both a testing ground for urban securitization policies and a hotspot of touristification—Israeli investments are particularly intense. Based on primary research conducted at the National Cadastre as part of my doctoral project, which examines changes in property ownership in the area between 2018 and 2023, a clear trend emerges: the purchase and conversion of entire buildings. These properties are effectively withdrawn from the available housing stock, thereby significantly exacerbating the housing crisis. Corporate actors account for a substantial share of these transactions, with Israeli-linked investments standing out. More specifically, over half of the properties acquired by companies during the period under study were purchased by firms that are either directly or indirectly connected to Israeli capital.
Building on these findings, this presentation seeks to map Israeli investments in the Exarcheia neighborhood. What specific forms do these investments take, and through which channels are they implemented? Under what conditions do they contribute to the touristification of the neighborhood and to the material and symbolic displacement of its residents? Why do Israeli investments display such intensity, and how is this intensity shaped by the broader geopolitical context, the strategic alliances of the Greek state, and ultimately the war itself?

22.title: Belgrade: The 1999 NATO bombing as urbicide and the politics of collective memory
22.abstract: The city of Belgrade, as the capital of Serbia and former capital of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, has historically occupied a strategic position at the intersection of social, cultural and geopolitical transformations in Southeast Europe. In March 1999, during the Kosovo War and the broader process of Yugoslavia’s dissolution, Belgrade became one of the main targets of NATO’s aerial bombing campaign, known as Operation Allied Force. This study explores whether, and to what extent, the bombing of Belgrade can be interpreted through the concept of urbicide, understood as the deliberately or systematic destruction on the urban environment and the social relations embedded within it. More specifically, it is investigated how this military intervention impacted not only the city’s infrastructure, but also its social life, symbolic identity, and memory narratives. The destruction caused by the bombing is approached not merely as physical damage to buildings and infrastructure, but as an attack on the conditions that allow urban life to function: networks, communication systems, public services, everyday routines, and the sense of security among residents. In this context, Belgrade is examined as more than a passive backdrop to international conflict. It becomes a field where geopolitical power and lived urban experience intersect. Furthermore, the research argues whether the 1999 bombing can be deciphered as a form of violence directed against the city itself. At the same time, the aftermath of the bombing opens up questions of collective memory, concerning how the traces of the intervention are represented, or silenced. The city is therefore highlighted both as a target of geopolitical conflict and a space where its consequences are remembered, negotiated, and reproduced. The case of Belgrade offers an important example for understanding how war, destruction, and politics of memory can shape a city’s contemporary urban landscape and identity.

23.title: Migrant Emplacement as “Spatial Overflow”: Urban Ambiances and Everyday Encounters in Turin, Italy

authors.name: Kumru Çılgın
authors.affiliation: Mimar Sinan Fine Arts University, Department of Urban and Regional Planning

23.abstract:
Drawing on one year of ethnographic observations, informal conversations, fieldnotes, and spatial mapping conducted by two migration researchers in Turin, this paper discusses migrant emplacement through the lens of transforming urban ambiances. Rather than reducing migrant presence to specific neighbourhoods, ethnic infrastructures, or institutional integration, it examines the embodied encounters, tensions, fears, shared practices, and spatial negotiations that emerge in everyday life. Building upon Akhtar’s (1999) psychoanalytic discussion of migration and identity, Bauman’s (1995) reflections on fragmented life strategies and encounters with strangers, and Stavrides’ (2019) approach to urban thresholds and common spaces, the paper reconceptualises the notion of “spatial overflow.”

Spatial overflow refers to the ways migrants move beyond spaces explicitly or implicitly allocated, restricted, or rendered hostile to them through the necessities of everyday life. This process reconstitutes the sensory, economic, aesthetic, and social ambiances of the city. In Turin, marketplaces, tourist squares, ethnic businesses, places of worship, and solidarity spaces reveal how diverse linguistic, religious, labour, consumption, and livelihood practices become visible within urban space. Barriera di Milano, a northern district with a history of working-class life and a contemporary multicultural population, is a key threshold for this discussion.

The paper addresses the three themes of the session: fearscapes, emerging through criminalisation, racialised surveillance, and anxieties associated with transitional urban spaces; ethnoscapes, materialised through food, commerce, worship, language, memory, and embodied practices; and commonscapes, formed through repeated encounters in markets, streets, squares, and solidarity initiatives such as Sermig – Arsenale della Pace, a former military arsenal transformed into a shared space for peace and solidarity.

Akhtar, S. (1999). Immigration and identity: Turmoil, treatment, and transformation. Jason Aronson.
Bauman, Z. (1995). Life in fragments: Essays in postmodern morality. Blackwell.
Stavrides, S. (2019). Towards the city of thresholds. Common Notions.

Migrant emplacement, Urban ambiances, Spatial overflow, Everyday encounters, Turin

23.title: The Curry Mile and Its Shadows: Belonging, Memory, and Unease Among Iranian Immigrants
23.abstract:
How do immigrants navigate the tension between belonging and estrangement in their adopted urban landscapes? Drawing on doctoral research into Iranian immigrants' landscape perception in Manchester, this paper examines how place-making unfolds through embodied, spatiotemporal, and intangible heritage practices within multicultural urban neighbourhoods.
Focusing on Rusholme, a culturally layered and diasporic neighbourhood along Wilmslow Road, this paper presents findings from two walking interview methods: Docent-led interviews and Participatory walking interviews. These methods captured how Iranian immigrants across different generations navigate Rusholme's contested ambiences: a space simultaneously evoking childhood memories of Iranian neighbourhoods, cultural belonging rooted in familiar food, language, and community gatherings, yet also provoking unease through perceived neglect, safety concerns beyond the main artery, and ideological tensions around visible markers of religious identity.
Informed by Gill's (2010) model of immigrant place-making, the analysis reveals that Rusholme occupies an ambivalent position in participants' cognitive and emotional geographies, functioning as both a cultural anchor for transnational identity and a site of contested heritage, where the place-making of earlier immigrant generations can simultaneously affirm and unsettle belonging for newer arrivals. Sensory encounters, familiar smells from Iranian restaurants, sounds of Farsi, the visual rhythm of a street reminiscent of home, emerged as powerful mediators of attachment, alongside negative perceptions shaped by urban planning, safety, and immigration-related anxieties.
By foregrounding the embodied, mobile, and generationally differentiated dimensions of immigrant emplacement, this paper contributes to understanding how multicultural urban neighbourhoods become sites of both heritage inscription and affective negotiation.

23.title: Campscapes and Camp Communities
23.abstract:
This paper begins from the premise that camps are best understood not as isolated or exceptional spaces but as interconnected formations structured by shared logics of governance, control, and humanitarianism. This paper develops the notion of campscapes, conceived as networked formations linking camps across sites, scales, and functions. On a global scale, three overlapping campscapes are identified—a post-war ‘humanitarian’ campscape largely located in the Global South; a ‘crimmigration’ campscape emerging within the Global North from the late 1970s; and a contemporary ‘global frontier’ campscape, a frontline between Global North and South, where practices and processes of care and control converge.
The global frontier campscape is itself a machine of many moving parts; this paper sketches the campscapes of contemporary Greece, both on the mainland and on the islands, before examining one specific camp (Ritsona) in greater detail.
Ethnoscapes and comonscapes in particular are examined in depth; are the same community relations often seen in an urban setting replicated in a camp environment? What are the major similarities and differences? How does ethnicity figure in terms of individual and collective identities in camps? What is 'community' in such an environment?
This paper is multi-scalar in scope, and based on ethnographic field research conducted in Ritsona camps between 2019 and 2022.

23.title: Decolonizing Urban Atmospheres: Solidarity-Based Commoning Practices among Newly Arrived Populations in Thessaloniki
23.abstract:
Scholarship on migration policies and humanitarian action often frames newcomers as passive recipients of services. However, the ways in which migrants claim their right to the city and enact practices of urban commons remain insufficiently explored. This paper examines established urban atmospheres in relation to the newcomers’ collective and solidarity practices, investigating their potential to decolonize the national(istic) urban atmospheres in the case of Thessaloniki.
In the early twentieth century, Thessaloniki was a multiethnic and multireligious Ottoman metropolis. Following its occupation by the Greek army during the Balkan Wars, processes of national homogenization—often implemented through violent means—targeted the city’s population, but also living memory, and the urban space. In recent decades, however, particularly after the fall of the Berlin Wall, new populations from the Balkans and the former Soviet Union have settled in the city. Even more recently, Thessaloniki has emerged as a key transit hub for thousands of people on the move from West Asia and Africa, traveling from Turkey toward central and northern Europe.
Having crossed the violence of national borders, newcomers encounter invisible borders, as “other” bodies are often perceived as not fitting within the city’s established atmospheres. Drawing on urban ethnography conducted in past research endeavours but also in the context of a newly started research project, this paper focuses on instances in which these atmospheric borders are traversed through collective practices, relations, and uses of space. In so doing, newcomers actively contribute to the emergence of new transnational atmospheres that destabilize national atmospheric borders and open up possibilities for the decolonization of the city.

23.title: Exploring migrants' right to ambiance? Methodological pathways of newcomers' experiences of urban atmospheric landscapes?
23.abstract:
Positivist research in migration and urban studies, seeking “objective” truth in observable and measurable “facts”, has long been challenged, complemented or countered through the proliferation of qualitative methodologies. Nevertheless, qualitative research methodologies are still dominated by the prevalence of text, speech, narrative or discourse, as the research process’ “raw material” and hence as primary sources of knowledge production. Yet, in interviews and focus groups, people commonly talk about their experiences, practices, perceptions, or feelings. However important, textual and discursive material alone may not be sufficient enough to methodologically approach and empirically grasp urban ambiances, involving sensorial, emotional and affective dimensions of the urban experience, alongside relational and material ones. Relevant scholarly contributions in recent years (e.g. Mendoza & Morén-Alegret 2013; Desille & Nikielska-Sekuła 2024; Pegorer 2024) have proposed a number of ethnographic fieldwork techniques to complement these, including observational and walking methods, photo/video/audio elicitation/documentation, sketching or drawing, but also non-representational, subjective and participatory cartographic methodologies, as in the tradition of mental maps, psychogeography and counter-mapping.
Drawing on our first encounters with fieldwork in the context of a recently-started research project, this presentation interrogates methods for studying the interconnections between urban ambiances and migrant emplacement in Greek cities. It particularly focuses on the three atmospheric landscapes that lie at the core of the session’s interests - fearscapes, ethnoscapes, and commonscapes – discussing ways of tracking these by “living the field”, alongside and together with research participants, yet under time constraints and resource limitations. It specifically aims at exploring methodological pathways (a) to trace established ambiances in Athens and Thessaloniki, (b) to map how these may be sensed, felt, perceived and lived by newcomers, and (c) to investigate how, in some cases, the migrants’ very presence, practices and relationships interfere, alter and reshape those ambiances, leading to the emergence of new ones.

23.title: In-between Places the case of Ioannina: Invisible Communities and Hybrid Identities in Space through the Lens of Social and Spatial Resilience
23.abstract:
This thesis, entitled "In-between Places the case of Ioannina: Invisible Communities and Hybrid Identities in Space through the Lens of Social and Spatial Resilience", investigates how migrants in Ioannina constitute in-between places of encounter, solidarity, and creation that often operate outside official frameworks. The central hypothesis asks how migrants' spatial and social strategies produce hybrid identities and resilience networks, presenting the city as a dynamic field of continuous social negotiation.
The study is grounded in an interdisciplinary framework combining: a) Henri Lefebvre's critical spatial theory, particularly the socio-spatial dialectic and the distinction between conceived, perceived, and lived space; b) Homi Bhabha's theory of cultural hybridity and the Third Space as a field of identity negotiation; and c) contemporary approaches to socio-spatial resilience, understood not as a return to equilibrium but as a dynamic process of adaptation and transformation.
Methodologically, the thesis adopts a qualitative approach based on the case study of Ioannina. Data collection includes semi-structured interviews with experts, collective members, and residents; on-site observation in gathering places such as squares, informal meeting spots, and local collectives; and secondary analysis of statistical data. Through empirical data analysis, the study aims to highlight the complexity of in-between places as fields of resistance and resilience.
The thesis concludes that official refugee management policies fail to incorporate the lived experience and organic needs of migrants. Instead, informal practices and the in-between places created by communities themselves emerge as critical mechanisms of social and spatial resilience. Finally, it proposes a shift from technocratic population management toward inclusive planning that recognizes Τhe Right to the City and the organic survival strategies of mobile populations.

23.title: Traces, discourses, archive in an abandoned school of the Borderland: re-enacting the affective fearscapes of Evros

authors.name: Sophie Kratidou
authors.affiliation: PhD candidate, Panteion University, Department of Sociology

authors.name: Eirini Dafermou
authors.affiliation: MA in Gender Studies, Panteion University/ Library on Gender and Equality and Historical Archive

23.abstract:
An abandoned school in Praggi, at the northern Evros border, situated directly within the Militarized Zone (ΖΑΠ), becomes a liminal space where refugee and ethnic bodies, objects, and discourses intersect at different times and leave traces. In this location -a transient passage for refugees and part of the militarized border complex of Evros, the Borderland of Europe and topograpgy of fear for the unrecognizable populations- we examine the traces and mobility of the fearscape. We study the embodied presence of people on the move within the school and the ways in which the school-border is produced - discursively and spatially – as a contested site for the culturally intelligible (or unintelligible) subject. We also examine the discursive presence of locals through racist and antifascist inscriptions on the surfaces of the school, as a struggle over sovereignty (and the hospitable or inhospitable nation) enacted in the school space and articulated through the masculinities that (are called upon to) represent it. We ask how newly arrived subjects find refuge in the school, despite technologies of prohibition and death, and how they embody and carry with them the border atmosphere on their way to the city.

In this site, the two researchers meet, examining and reconstructing traces and the affective atmosphere -the remnants of ritual practices through which subjectivities are produced and identities performed. We combine fieldwork findings (photographic archives, narratives, diaries) and analyze the iconography to foreground the lived atmosphere of the border fearscape. Drawing on feminist decolonial border theory and the archive, as well as post-structuralist discourse analysis, we examine the presence of migrants and residents alike: objects, slogans, wall inscriptions, the sticky affect, excretions of the ethnic body, and the exergue of ramparts upon the open archive/body of Evros -unfolding enclosures and resistances within the urban landscape.

23.title: Nostalgic Infrastructures: Domesticity, Tacit Knowledge, and Spatial Attunement in Labour Migrant Housing
23.abstract:
Labor migration is constitutively bound to social reproduction, and the living environments of migrant workers are often conceived merely as sites where labor power is restored: spaces to recover and return to work. As a result, the spatial intelligence through which migrant communities organize collective life within and beyond these constraints remains largely illegible within the planning categories inherited by architecture and urbanism. This contribution proposes domesticity, tacit spatial knowledge, and spatial attunement as reorienting frameworks for reading migrant emplacement through lived urban ambiances.
Drawing on feminist theories of social reproduction and the notion of “life’s work” developed by Mitchell, Marston, and Katz, this contribution asks whether everyday domestic practices exceed capital’s attempts to discipline migrant life under conditions of precarity. It does so by bringing migration housing studies into dialogue with ambiance theory. Central to this argument is nostalgia, understood not as a fixed longing for a lost home, but as a generative spatial condition through which migrants negotiate belonging, continuity, and orientation within unfamiliar urban landscapes. This excess becomes visible through practices of spatial attunement: shared routines, sensory memories, affective gestures, and embodied forms of inhabitation that reconfigure hostile or temporary environments into spaces of care and collective presence.
Mobilising Polanyi’s concept of tacit knowledge, the contribution grounds its argument in the Rotterdam–Venlo logistics corridor (Sgolacchia, 2023), where workers housed in surveillance-governed flexwoningen reorganize domestic space through collective routines and nostalgic spatial practices that exceed the logistical infrastructures designed to contain them. Collectively maintained thresholds, improvised domestic rituals, and spaces charged with sensory memory transform institutionally imposed housing into affectively dense commonscapes. In doing so, migrant presence not only inhabits existing urban ambiances but actively reworks them, generating alternative forms of sociality and emergent claims to the city.

23.title: Solidarities at the Margin of Fortress Europe. The making of Commonscapes in Nicosia
23.abstract:
Urban solidarities around migration are not only produced through moments of public mobilization. They are sustained, more quietly, through everyday spatial practices that hold collective life together at the margins of institutional reach. In Cyprus, a small-state context shaped by unresolved territorial division and deep migrant precarity, grassroots solidarity operates under particular pressure. Networks are informal, alliances unstable, and support for migrants is often politicized. Within this terrain, certain spaces have emerged where migrants and locals produce shared life outside institutional channels. This paper calls these commonscapes.
The work draws on ethnographic and spatial research in Nicosia to examine how commonscapes are produced through grassroots and migrant-led practices. It asks what kinds of spaces and relational arrangements sustain solidarity, and how these remake urban space through inhabitation. Two sites anchor the analysis: assembly and event spaces at Social Space Kaymakkin and Yalla Collective Space, where trust, shared political meaning, and coordination accumulate through recurring encounter; and a sewing project run from a refugee woman's workshop in the city center, where a private business space becomes a site of skills-sharing, care, and community for survivors of violence and displacement.
Across these sites, solidarity operates less as event than as infrastructure, built through introductions, repeated presence, and practical collaboration. These are not spectacular politics. Yet this paper argues they constitute a politics of presence in their own right: one that remakes urban space from within, asserts migrants' right to the city through inhabitation, and binds solidarity to the slower rhythms of urban life that event-centered accounts tend to miss. Commonscapes, in this sense, are not just sites of refuge but spatial arguments about who the city is for.

23.title: Camp ambiances: Affective geographies of dehumanization and solidarity
23.abstract:
The discussion on camps typically prioritizes the structural, managerial and logistical dimensions. Academic inquiry frequently centers on the macro-politics of containment, the spatialities of exclusion, and the economies of deterrence that define camps as spaces of exception. While an emerging body of scholarship highlight the agency of residents in contesting camp regimes, the specific role of ambiance remains critically under-examined. This paper seeks to address this gap by exploring the camp not merely as a physical site, but as a complex affective landscape shaped by intersecting emotions, senses, and intensities.
Drawing upon extensive ethnographic research conducted within various camps in Greece over the past decade, this paper explores how ambiances are deliberately weaponized as tools of governance. I argue that the atmospheric production of the camp often seeks to instill a sensorial racism, emotional despair and corporeal obedience. By modulating fear, anxiety, and sensory deprivation, these environments aim to induce the dehumanization of their inhabitants, rendering them powerless passive subjects of a biopolitical order.
However, atmospheres are inherently unstable and cannot be fully enclosed. This paper demonstrates that the camp’s ambiance is not an absolute, biopolitically sealed space. Instead, it is a site of constant atmospheric struggle. I explore how residents navigate and disrupt the oppressive climates to invent and produce minor everyday atmospheres of solidarity. Through practices of camouflage, sabotage, and commoning, camp residents enact a radical form of care and contestation. These affective maneuvers represent the production of new socialities of solidarity that challenge the dehumanizing intent of the camp. Ultimately, this paper argues that focusing on ambiance reveals the subtle, sensory, and deeply human ways in which the camp is both felt and resisted, offering a more nuanced understanding of the embodied and lived experience of camp residents.

23.title: The sensorium of commonscapes. Migrant presence and the lived ambience of urban thresholds

authors.name: Zacharias Valiantzas
authors.affiliation: PhD candidate in Human Geography, Spatial Planning and Development department AUTH

23.abstract:
This paper focuses on the interconnections between contemporary human geography and ambiance theory in the everydayness of migrant emplacement in the city of Thessaloniki. Beginning with the theoretical framework of the right to the city and urban commons, which enhance our understanding of contested urban neighborhoods[PH1.1], we see migrant inhabitance through the analytical lens of threshold spaces and non-representational geographies. Bridging the gap between materialist and phenomenological approaches, ambiance theory enables us to explore and analyse aspects of urban dwelling beyond theoretical dichotomies, giving also space for the exploration of the sensory perceptions and interpretations of place.
How do specific neighborhoods of the city affect and are affected by migrant communities? How is urban space felt and appropriated? How do atmospheres-ambiences and urban rhythms unfold in the constant rapidly transforming neoliberal urban terrain? In total how do commoning practices challenge the logic of urban enclosures and gentrification? Does care and solidarity unfold both in the local and in the wider metropolitan field, highlighting the possibilities of another lived ambience in the public sphere of the city?
Through our ongoing ethnographical research in three district neighborhoods of Thessaloniki, we propose the notion of commonscapes as a hybrid analytical tool which, through participatory transnational and transcultural practices of commoning, enables urban transformative potentialities. In the ever-changing current turbulent times of exclusion and marginalization of migrant communities, the emergence of multiple commonscapes in urban thresholds actively confronts the neoliberal and commodified logic of the city, proposing forms of collective inhabitance, solidarity and mutuality among the urban dwellers.

24.title: Rhine's landscapes as a socio - natural assemblance

authors.name: Quentin Scherrer
authors.affiliation: Political Sciences student, University of Strasbourg

authors.name: Jarre Ameye
authors.affiliation: BA in Marine Sciences, Wageningen University & Research

authors.name: Christos Bakalis
authors.affiliation: PhD, Cultural and Environmental Sociology, faculty member in the School of Social Sciences, University of the Aegean

24.abstract:
This paper proposes the Rhine River as a key natural component of the formation of both natural and cultural landscapes in regions of western and northwestern Europe. The river conceptualized as an “actant” actively participating in the co-production of social, economic, and political relations across scales, of a transboundary socio-environmental assemblage.
Specifically, the paper explores how Rhine operates as an actor, as well as a cultural and mnemonic infrastructure, deeply embedded in collective memory and identity, while also being mobilised within contemporary economic dynamics, including tourism and cross-border cooperation. By examining Rhine as a relational network connecting rural productive landscapes, urban infrastructures, and institutional frameworks, this contribution highlights how water systems function as both material and symbolic commons. It ultimately argues that understanding Rhine through an assemblage lens allows us to rethink the rigid separation between nature and society, and to better grasp the challenges of managing cultural landscapes in the context of climate change and European integration. The analysis draws on insights from assemblage theory and Actor-Network Theory.
Historically, Rhine has structured settlement patterns, trade routes, and urban development, notably contributing to the emergence of cities as major crossroads within European space. At the same time, it has been profoundly transformed by human interventions, particularly through canalization projects, hydroelectric infrastructures, and flood-control systems, illustrating the hybrid and co-constructed nature of landscapes.
This work discusses the contribution of Rhine upon the Alsatian landscape in parallel with other contexts shaped by the river notably in the Gelderland province landscape. Both regions are deeply influenced by the Rhine’s hydraulic, economic, and symbolic functions. The comparative approach provides a complementary viewpoint, allowing us to examine how similar material infrastructures and environmental constraints are translated into different urban forms, governance models, land management and cultural practices across national settings.

24.title: Rural Water Infrastructures as cultural landscapes: local knowledge, climate adaptation, spatial planning and governance challenges in the mountain area of Pelion-Greece
24.abstract:
Worldwide, extreme events driven by climate change are responsible for the destruction of lives, livelihoods, and property, with particularly acute impacts across urban-rural spaces. In addition, rapid climate change, combined with growing inequalities, pose threats to human existence and well-being, and jeopardize the prospects of communities and future generations to thrive.
Redefining urban-rural relationships as a continuum rather than a strict dichotomy, this paper views rural settlements not as isolated, purely agricultural areas, but as integral components of broader, multi-functional urbanized landscapes linked to urban areas through flows of people, goods, and ecosystem services. Many rural areas face a range of interconnected challenges: shrinking and ageing populations; limited economic opportunities; challenge of balancing agricultural production with environmental conservation and tourism, while maintaining traditions and architectural identities in the face of rapid change.
This paper examines how former agricultural communities and traditional settlements respond to extreme environmental events through locally embedded water management practices. It argues that rural water infrastructures such as irrigation systems and communal water distribution networks, function not only as technical systems but also as cultural landscapes that sustain both productivity, local social networks and thus, resilience. It explores how these local practices adapt to environmental stress while analyzing how fragmented or inconsistent governance and spatial planning can undermine them. Furthermore, it emphasizes the importance of everyday practices of resilience and resistance, the significance of traditional knowledge-sharing, and the various forms of mutual support that operate at different levels.
Using a case study approach, the research highlights the value of traditional ecological knowledge in climate adaptation, focusing on sustainable and holistic strategies that transform neglected or degraded areas into productive, ecological, and culturally vibrant spaces. Mapping and ethnographic research combine quantitative and qualitative approaches to develop a relational and spatial understanding of socio-environmental phenomena across multiple scales.

24.title: A water crisis in the making: Infrastructuring water deficiency in the Greek territory
24.abstract: For over a decade, Greece has stood at the epicenter of a prolonged socioeconomic turmoil, with water emerging as a new frontier of urban inequality. Since 2022, a growing number of national fora on water have taken place, culminating in the introduction of the National Plan for Water by the Greek authorities in June 2025. A familiar discourse of security, scarcity, and emergency has re-entered public debate, shaping water governance via emergency measures and big scale infrastructural projects, intensifying existing vulnerabilities and inequalities. Within this scape, peripheral municipalities face mounting pressures from uneven development and tourism, exposing interdependencies between Athens, the mainland, and the islands. This presentation explores how a “water crisis” is produced, how austerity and privatization reshape infrastructural governance, how tourism and real estate transform access to water, and how grassroot movements contest plumbing poverty and infrastructural injustice while connecting water access to broader claims to the right to the city.

24.title: Building resilience through a culturally-grounded commoning of water: The case of Stagiates

authors.name: Maria-Iris Kotzamani
authors.affiliation: PhD Candidate at Harokopio University of Athens

24.abstract: Water has a pivotal role in humanity’s history and culture, shaping communities’ natural and built environments, and reinforcing the development of social systems and practices. At the same time, the commodification of water resources has led to a global increase in water price rates, and to the depletion of water resources that have been historically managed by local communities. As a direct response to the pathogenies of the neoliberal economy, local communities develop resilient social mechanisms based on traditional knowledge and local know-how, as well as claims of water as a commons. Such mechanisms present an alternative towards a more sustainable water management. This research explores the case of Stagiates, a small community in mountain Pelion Greece, and in close proximity to the city of Volos. In Stagiates the local initiative “Free Waters” emerged upon the abrupt disconnection of the village’s water supply network from the community’s ancestral water resource “Krya Vrysi”, followed by its subsequent connection to the supply network of the neighbor village of Portaria. Drawing from empirical data collected through document review, web research, field visits, and semi-structured in-depth interviews with residents of the community, this research analyzes the case of Stagiates to address the following questions: 1) How can initiatives against water privatization articulate for water as a commons? 2) How can culturally-grounded commons-based initiatives build resilience? and 3) How can a culture of water as a commons preserve collective memory, knowledge, and identity, towards a sustainable water management?

24.title: Hydro-commons in Transition: Socio-technical Water Management Systems as Living Cultural Landscapes
24.abstract:
Rural water infrastructures are complex socio-technical ecosystems encoding collective protocols, embodied territorial knowledge, and more-than-human coexistence. In an era of rapid environmental change, small local communities that function symbiotically with the natural environment face profound transformations, called upon to readjust inherited methods and techniques, reframing them as strategies for climate survival and rural landscape regeneration.
The presentation is based on findings from the transdisciplinary research of the collaborative artistic platform Counterpublics, through two projects on collective water management as a common resource: the peer-to-peer technology of the pumping windmill in the Lasithi Plateau, Crete, and the gravity-fed community irrigation system of the "raised ditch" (Σηκωμένο Αυλάκι) in Kyriakochori, Fthiotida. Both are registered as intangible cultural heritage, occupying the threshold between living practice and its reinvented form. Water commons are among the most complex forms of commons governance, they require a continuous commoning, a living-together organized around the resource.
In both cases, complex environmental and social transformations affect the management of the common resource: on the one hand, changing environmental parameters, water scarcity, shifts in the productive model, and the restructuring of the social fabric that once sustained the socio-technical system. On the other hand, there is the possibility for traditional practices and technologies to acquire a new role within the framework of a new ecological paradigm, combined with new community identities.
Drawing on political ecology, commons theory, and more-than-human approaches, these systems are treated not as historical relics but as living models with direct relevance to climate adaptation. The methodological approach develops a "being-present" practice combining walking as research tool, embodied landscape knowledge, personal narratives as historical evidence, and artistic practice as a mode of inquiry, producing geographies and mappings of both material infrastructure and immaterial protocols, creating space for community voices at the margins of official environmental policy.

25.title: « Save your hood » but not your city ? Multiscalar contradictions of participation in urban cleanliness

authors.name: Clément Dillenseger
authors.affiliation: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique (CNRS), Lyon

25.abstract:
If we generally know why people participate in something (for recognition, sociability, morality), for what purpose (for the environment), and for whom (for oneself, one’s children, neighbors, employer, etc.), answering the questions “for where” and “from where” is much more difficult. In fact, these questions even sound strange because Western individuals, in a context of globalization, are not accustomed to representing—or considering—the spatial consequences of their actions.

Inspired by the concept of urban metabolism, which emphasizes the circulation of materials and the interdependence of territories and scales, I wondered which spatial references justify the unpaid labor of volunteer litter collectors. Based on an ethnography of collective volunteer waste-picking movements (2018–2022) in Athens, Vienna, and Lyon, this reflection situates civic participation in cleanliness across multiple scales, from the polluting molecule to the world itself.

The results show that the places and scales of engagement are primarily those of proximity (my body, my neighborhood) and distance (the world, the ocean, the planet), while never taking into account either the political scale of waste management (at the metropolitan/regional level) or the origin of the waste itself. Put simply, everything happens as though, once collected on Turkovounia or Lycabettus hill, a waste is no longer a problem because it no longer represents, apparently, a risk either to one’s own body or to the planet—“the environment is protected” by "environmental heroes" as the common rhetoric says… albeit at the expense of the bodies of the inhabitants of Fyli ! When i asked people in Athens if they knew where the collected waste goes, they ignored the location of the landfill. Their bourgeoise discursive ecology in the city-center is opposed, in a way, to the embodied ecologies of Fyli inhabitants.

25.title: The limits of Participation and the transition to co-production of space through digital platforms
25.abstract:
This paper examines the limits of institutional and semi-formal participatory practices in contemporary planning and explores the conditions under which participation can transition from passive consultation to meaningful co-production. Drawing on structured interviews with 13 actors, including planning authorities, private practitioners, NGOs, and research intermediaries, the study investigates how participation is implemented through case studies, perceived, and operationalized across institutional contexts.
The findings reveal a persistent structural gap between formal decision-making systems and participatory processes. While participation is embedded within planning frameworks, it is often procedural, compliance-driven, and limited in its capacity to influence outcomes. In contrast, more adaptive and connective actors demonstrate higher engagement potential but lack the institutional authority and capacity to translate participatory input into actionable decisions. This misalignment highlights a critical barrier: decision-making practices are institutionally rigid and linear, while effective participation is produced outside decision-making centers and not translated into actionable information capable of influencing outcomes.
In response, the paper explores the potential of data-enabled participatory methods as a bridging mechanism between qualitative local knowledge and quantitative spatial analysis. Through the presentation and evaluation of a geolocated, workshop-based participatory tool, the research examines how structured digital environments can support the capture, codification, and integration of tacit, place-based knowledge at the neighborhood scale. Particular emphasis is placed on spatial interfaces, iterative feedback loops, and facilitator-led processes in enhancing both the quality and duration of engagement.
The study identifies three key requirements for advancing toward co-production: (1) methodological clarity in structuring participation, (2) technical capacity to translate qualitative input into usable evidence, and (3) institutional readiness to absorb and act upon participatory outputs. Ultimately, the paper argues that the transition to co-production is not solely a technological challenge, but a systemic one requiring alignment between participatory practices, governance structures, and decision-making cultures.

25.title: Urban Morphology, Real Estate and Urban Governance in the 15-Minute City Model

authors.name: Maria Giaoutzi
authors.affiliation: Professor / National Technical University of Athens

25.abstract:
The “15-minute city” model, introduced by Carlos Moreno (2016), is considered as one of the most interesting efforts of the recent years, for promoting sustainable urban planning. This has already been adopted by major cities, such as Paris and Barcelona, in order to promote sustainable urban transitions. The present paper is making an effort to elaborate on the 15-minute city concept, by placing it in a historical context.
In the first part, the present study argues that the 15-minute model concerns of a modern version, of a type of organization which can be met already in ancient Greek cities, e.g. Athens. Such an argument, opens up new possibilities for research and experimentation, in sustainable urban practice.
In the next part, the paper elaborates on the economic aspects of the model under study, by focusing on the implications of the proximity-based models on real estate markets, namely on land prices. These effects are closely related to the added value of mixed land-use areas, but also to urbanization and spatial discrimination.
In the final part, the paper argues that the successful implementation of the 15-minute city model requires a shift towards participatory planning, enriched by appropriate tools such as, multicriteria approaches, geo-visualization tools etc. Finally, some interesting conclusions are drawn regarding the interrelationships among urban morphology, real estate economics and urban governance.

Keywords: 15-minute city, urban proximity, real estate dynamics, participatory design.

25.title: Participation Beyond the Buzzword: Rhetoric, Practices and Funding Logics

authors.name: Alexandra Linardou
authors.affiliation: School of Architecture, National Technical University of Athens

25.abstract:
This paper examines participation both conceptually and empirically through the synAthina programme of the Municipality of Athens, one of the case studies of an ongoing doctoral research. It situates participation within the broader context of neoliberal urban governance, tracing the proliferation of concepts such as sustainable development, good governance and participatory development since the 1980s. These notions have been increasingly embedded within a normative and value-laden discourse, often detached from a critical interrogation of the political and economic imperatives underpinning them (Leal, 2010).
Within this shift, the transition “from managerialism to entrepreneurialism” (Harvey, 1989) redefines the role of cities as competitive actors striving to attract investment, consumption and symbolic capital. In this context, participation acquires a specific instrumental value, functioning as a policy prerequisite for accessing European funding. As such, it operates as a “buzzword” (Cornwall, 2007), whose conceptual and political content is progressively diluted, while urban competitiveness becomes tied to the effective mobilisation of such vocabulary.
At the same time, dominant approaches to participation tend to focus on methods and tools, leaving largely unaddressed fundamental questions concerning who participates, under what conditions, and with what consequences. This critique echoes earlier interventions that have problematised participation as a potentially depoliticised and technocratic practice (Cooke & Kothari, 2001).
Drawing on Critical Discourse Analysis across three levels—textual, discursive and socio-political practices—this paper explores the dialectical relationship between rhetoric and practice in the case of synAthina. Focusing on the period 2013–2019, during which the Municipality of Athens aligned closely with European and international urban agendas, synAthina emerged as a flagship initiative, widely recognised as a best practice within networks and programmes (URBACT, Refill, etc.). However, this paper critically interrogates such narratives of success, highlighting the contradictions, exclusions and power relations that remain obscured within evaluation frameworks primarily oriented towards measurable outputs and deliverables.

25.title: Forest Mapping from Below: Objections and the Limits of Participatory Land Governance in Greece
25.abstract:
Participation has become a central reference in spatial planning and territorial governance. However, its integration into decision-making processes often remains uneven, procedural and contradictory. This paper examines these tensions through the case of forest mapping reform in Greece after 2016, a large-scale project of land administration and environmental mapping implemented in the context of the economic crisis, cadastral modernization, and contradictory policies surrounding the nationalization, privatization and commodification of forest lands. Rather than focusing on formally designed participatory tools, the paper analyses objection and land-acquisition procedures as a form of indirect, conflictual and largely individualized participation in the production of spatial knowledge.

Empirically, the study combines quantitative analysis of forest-map data in Ilia, Western Peloponnese, with qualitative research based on semi-structured interviews with citizens, local actors and technical professionals involved in objection procedures. The findings show that these procedures, officially presented as mechanisms for correcting technical errors, operate in practice as instruments of spatial regulation. Through them, land-use classifications, property claims and interpretations of forest legality are renegotiated “from below”. However, this participation is deeply unequal: access to it depends on geographical inequalities related to the exchange or use value of land, financial capacity, legal knowledge and technical mediation.

The paper argues that objections to forest maps reveal both the democratic potential and the limits of participatory spatial governance. They make local histories, informal relations to land and contested environmental categories visible, while at the same time risking the reinforcement of individualized property strategies and socio-spatial inequalities. The Greek case therefore offers an opportunity for broader reflection on how participatory practices can move beyond consultation, correction or conflict management and contribute to more collective, public and accountable forms of spatial planning.

27.title: Left-Behind Places in an Age of Polycrisis: Political Discontent and Spatial Inequality
27.abstract:
The relationship between polycrisis and spatial inequality remains insufficiently explored, particularly with regard to its political implications. This paper addresses this gap by examining how intersecting crises reshape territorial disadvantage and contribute to the reproduction of ‘left-behindness’, with particular reference to the European Union. It argues that contemporary crises should not be understood as isolated shocks, but as interacting processes whose cumulative effects are spatially mediated and unevenly absorbed across territories. These dynamics carry significant political implications, as the compounded exposure to crises deepens territorially rooted grievances and contributes to the erosion of institutional trust. In this context, regions, cities, and neighborhoods characterized by structural disadvantage are especially vulnerable to these overlapping pressures.
Building on the literature on left-behind places and the geography of discontent, the paper develops an analytical framework centered on a “double dialectic” of disadvantage formation. The first dialectic concerns the interaction among local dimensions of left-behindness, including economic fragility, demographic decline, weak infrastructure, and weakened local governance capacity, conditions that undermine institutional accountability and deepen perceptions of political abandonment. The second concerns the intersection of external crises operating across broader scales, such as economic, geopolitical, environmental, and migration-related shocks. The paper argues that political discontent is often rooted in the interaction between these two processes, as repeated crises intensify territorially concentrated grievances, perceptions of abandonment, and distrust in institutions.
The argument is illustrated by the case of the North Aegean Region in Greece, a peripheral, structurally vulnerable territory where multiple crises have accumulated over time. By linking polycrisis to spatial inequality and political discontent, the paper contributes to current debates on left-behind places and offers a framework for rethinking territorial cohesion and place-sensitive policy in an era of heightened uncertainty.

27.title: How does geographical space shape voting behavior in Greece? A spatial analysis approach
27.abstract:
This paper investigates and aims to prove the relationship between geographic space and electoral behavior in Greece, within the theoretical framework of electoral geography. The study intends to identify and explain spatial patterns in voting behavior, highlighting the extent to which electoral preferences are affected by demographic and spatial factors.

Drawing on electoral, demographic, and socioeconomic datasets, the analysis is based on Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and spatial statistical techniques to map and examine the distribution of voting patterns across regions. Particular emphasis is placed on detecting spatial autocorrelation and identifying clusters of similar electoral behavior, as well as on assessing the influence of variables such as income, education, economic structure, and degree of urbanization.

The research further explores the role of spatial interactions and historically embedded political identities in shaping persistent regional voting patterns. In doing so, it seeks to evaluate the explanatory and predictive capacity of geographic space in relation to electoral outcomes.

Preliminary findings suggest that electoral behavior in Greece is not randomly distributed, but instead exhibits significant spatial structuring, reflecting underlying social and economic inequalities as well as enduring territorial identities. The study contributes to the broader discussion on the spatial dimensions of political behavior, highlighting the importance of integrating spatial analysis into electoral studies.

27.title: Regional Discontent and the Reconfiguration of the Greek Far-Right after Golden Dawn
27.abstract:
This study examines the post-crisis reconfiguration of the Greek far-right through a regional lens, focusing on the rise of populist radical right parties following the collapse of Golden Dawn. While existing accounts of far-right support in Greece have been dominated by demand-side explanations, this paper develops a more integrated framework that brings together demand-side conditions, supply-side dynamics, and historical electoral legacies. More specifically, it argues that the resurgence of far-right support after 2019 cannot be understood solely in terms of socio-economic grievances but must also be linked to the fragmentation of the populist radical right party space and to territorially embedded legacies of earlier far-right voting.
Empirically, the paper analyses spatial variation in the increase in populist radical-right electoral support across Greek regions between the 2019 and 2023 national elections. The analysis combines electoral geography with econometric modeling at the regional level, using indicators of socio-economic conditions, historical support for Golden Dawn, and the effective number of populist radical right parties as a proxy for supply-side structure. The findings suggest that the recent surge in populist radical-right support in Greece was not spatially uniform. Rather, it was shaped by the interaction of regional socio-economic disadvantage, inherited far-right legacies, and a more fragmented PRR supply structure that widened the range of available political options.
The paper contributes to the growing literature on the geography of discontent by showing that the transformation of the Greek far right is deeply territorialized. More broadly, it argues that uneven regional development and place-specific political legacies are central to understanding how political discontent is translated into new forms of radical right mobilization. In doing so, it highlights how geographically uneven political outcomes can erode trust in mainstream institutions and reshape democratic competition.

27.title: Unequal distribution of natural resources as a cause of international conflict
27.abstract: It is a fact that natural resources have always been among the conflict-triggers not only within a state but also between or among states. In several cases, international political discontent is the result of political dissatisfaction and unrest within the state. From water and crops to diamonds and rare earths unequal distribution of natural resources due to the geographic characteristics of a region can trigger conflict and/or even multiply and intensify existing ones. Using the lens of securitization, this paper examines two cases studies: a) how the unequal distribution of economically viable rare earth deposits has led to state-level political discontent – especially among great powers such as the US and China– which is further being exacerbated by the ‘race’ in the green technology sector, where rare earths are indispensable parts and b) how the unequal distribution of water has led to conflict over the Nile Basin among Egypt, Sudan and Ethiopia. Finally, the paper summarises the main findings and suggests fields of further research.

27.title: Aid Fragmentation, Health Governance, and the Geography of Discontent: The Protracted Refugee Reception Crisis in the North Aegean Islands (2013–2020)
27.abstract:
This paper examines how the refugee health governance in the North Aegean Islands (re)produced socio-spatial inequities related to access to health services, as well as distrust in domestic institutions.

Drawing on a mixed-methods retrospective health policy case study—including 58 semi-structured interviews with officials from the governments of the time, international organizations and NGOs, as well as a secondary analysis of funding data— the presentation analyzes aspects of refugee health governance and social tensions within a context of fiscal austerity, foreign aid fragmentation and securitization of migration.

The findings indicate that the EU-led governance configuration prioritized emergency humanitarian interventions aimed at ensuring the survival of asylum seekers and their immobilization near their homelands, rather than pursuing their equitable social integration and universal access to health as a public good. This approach was supported by largely emergency-based, fragmented European aid, which was channelled mainly through international organizations and NGOs, creating thus a quasi-market of social services often competing with the depleted public health sector.

The socio-spatial inequities and the related discontent were not merely due to administrative failures, but rather constituted a by-product of securitization policies that repeatedly sparked protests —some in solidarity to refugees, some by refugees themselves, and some racist. Unequal access to services, combined with the prolonged detention of asylum seekers in unsuitable and overcrowded facilities, reinforced perceptions of neglect and exclusion among both refugees and host populations, creating political tensions and legitimizing the camp-based confinement of refugees.

Connecting health governance, socio-spatial inequalities, and political discontent, the paper seeks to contribute to discussions on local governance and the spatial foundations of contemporary democratic challenges.

27.title: Geospatial Analysis of Migration and Refugee Flows in Europe for the Formation of a Modern Geopolitical Landscape

authors.name: Konstantina Pervolaraki
authors.affiliation: National Technical University of Athens (NTUA), School of Rural and Surveying Engineering and Geoinformatics

27.abstract: This study investigates the geographical dynamics of migration and refugee flows into Europe and their subsequent impact on the continent’s geopolitical architecture. By mapping specific transit routes and entry points, the research evaluates the demographic shifts and socio-spatial implications inherent in contemporary displacement patterns. The analysis further scrutinizes European Union integration policies and the efficacy of international migration management agreements. Utilizing a robust methodological framework, this paper employs advanced data visualization tools, including cartographic mapping and statistical charting, to interpret complex flow patterns. The findings provide critical insights into how migratory movements are actively redefining European geopolitical compositions and cross-border relations.

27.title: The Italian Geography of Discontent: Beyond the North-South Divide?
27.abstract:
Across Europe, economically stagnating regions have become increasingly associated with political discontent and the rise of far-right parties. This trend is particularly evident in Italy, a country with a historically fraught political history and characterised by pronounced spatial inequalities, most notably the persistent North–South divide. The September 2022 general election, which brought Giorgia Meloni and her far-right coalition to power, signaled a critical moment in the mainstreaming of these political forces.

While regional disparities in Italy are well documented and manifested in differences in income, productivity, infrastructure, and access to services; recent research moves beyond this binary framework to focus on “dissatisfied regions”. This presentation argues that discontent is not confined to economically disadvantaged areas but is also present in more affluent regions, driven by disillusionment with the political system. Rather than being fuelled by hardship per se, such discontent reflects a sense of relative loss: the perception that neighbouring countries or regions are prospering while one’s own fortunes stagnate or decline. This dynamic suggests that political behaviours are steadily shaped by a sense of loss of voice, posing a significant challenge for policymakers seeking to address declining institutional trust and restore a sense of political inclusion.

28.title: A MICMAC-Based Analysis of Urban Accessibility: Interdependent Infrastructure and Public Space Factors Affecting Older Adults and People with Disabilities
28.abstract: Access to transport systems, public buildings, healthcare, education, and daily activities is a fundamental social right that underpins autonomy and social inclusion. Despite significant technological advancements that offer new opportunities to improve accessibility, major barriers persist in the urban environment, often reinforcing social inequalities and exclusion. Older adults and people with disabilities continue to face physical, sensory, and cognitive obstacles in everyday urban life, including inaccessible transport systems and inadequate infrastructure that generate a hostile environment for them, keeping them isolated within their houses and without the opportunity to be seen by the rest of the population, to interact with them, and the city. Using a solid participatory planning methodology such as Structural Analysis–MICMAC, this study identifies and evaluates the factors in the urban environment that shape the everyday experiences and inclusion of vulnerable social groups. Through experts' consultation, this research maps and organizes in order of importance the interdependencies among critical social, built environment, and spatial variables, focusing specifically on urban infrastructure and public space elements that shape how vulnerable populations navigate and experience urban space. The paper aligns these factors with existing urban and social policy frameworks and proposes actionable recommendations, including targeted investment in accessible transport, inclusive public infrastructure, and user-centred technological innovation. This work provides valuable insights for shaping urban environments that respond more effectively to social vulnerability and promote resilient, inclusive, and human-friendly cities.

28.title: How to govern mobility hubs for integrated transport and urban planning
28.abstract:
Mobility systems today reflect territorial inequalities. While metropolitan areas are typically characterized by congestion, environmental pressures, and overburdened infrastructure, rural and peri-urban regions often experience limited connectivity and inadequate public transport provision. These uneven conditions restrict access to opportunities and raise critical questions of spatial justice in contemporary planning.
Within this context, mobility hubs have gained attention as integrated nodes that combine public transport, shared mobility services, and complementary non-mobility functions in a single location. Beyond their operational role, mobility hubs can act as spatial instruments to rebalance accessibility and improve first- and last-mile connectivity across different territorial settings.
This study explores how governance structures can support the effective integration of mobility hubs into existing transport systems, with a particular focus on their potential to address spatial disparities. Drawing on evidence from good practices and desktop research in six Mediterranean countries (Greece, Spain, Italy, Malta, Cyprus, and Bosnia and Herzegovina), the study examines institutional arrangements, coordination mechanisms, regulatory frameworks and public–private collaboration models that influence implementation.
The analysis highlights the importance of context-sensitive and participatory governance approaches, capable of aligning diverse stakeholders while responding to local spatial characteristics. Special attention is given to how planning and governance decisions shape accessibility outcomes, user inclusion and the integration of mobility and non-mobility services.
By linking governance structures with transport and urban perspectives, the study contributes to ongoing debates on inclusive and integrated mobility systems. It argues that well-designed governance frameworks are critical not only for enabling the operational success of mobility hubs, but also for enhancing territorial cohesion and supporting more equitable mobility patterns across urban and rural areas.

Keywords: mobility hubs, governance structures, integrated transport planning, multimodal integration

28.title: Governing the Urban Periphery: TOKİ as an Apparatus of Neoliberal Governmentality in Turkey
28.abstract: Over the past decades, the Mass Housing Development Administration in Turkey (TOKİ) has radically transformed the Turkish urban landscape, facilitating a massive transition from informal squatter (gecekondu) settlements to standardized, high-rise social housing complexes. While existing scholarship predominantly critiques TOKİ through the lenses of political economy and neoliberal urbanism, there is a notable gap regarding the subtle mechanisms of power that regulate the daily lives of residents. My presentation will address this gap by employing Michel Foucault’s concept of governmentality to analyze TOKİ not merely as a provider of shelter or an instrument of neoliberal urban policies, but as a sophisticated apparatus for the “conduct of conduct.” In this regard, I will employ a critical Foucaultian discourse analysis of official TOKİ policy documents and a meta-synthesis of existing ethnographic case studies. By re-evaluating this secondary-data through this framework, I will argue that TOKİ neighborhoods function as laboratories of conduct for this transition from informality to state-sanctioned housing necessities the production of a specific neoliberal subject who is he disciplined, modernized and indebted homeowner. Accordingly, I will explore how spatial normalization, architectural uniformity, and long-term mortgage obligations act as technologies of the self, prompting these homeowners to self-regulate in alignment with state and market interests. Ultimately I will attempt to illustrate that how the biopolitical management of populations founded mostly within the urban periphery is exercised through TOKİ policies.

28.title: Mobility and the production of inequality: an intersectional reading of everyday movement
28.abstract: Urban mobility unfolds as a relational practice shaped through intersecting positions of gender, cultural background, linguistic fluency, socioeconomic position and bureaucratic accessibility, and this paper draws on travel diaries from international students in Florence to examine how movement takes form within these overlapping conditions. The analysis follows how a set of pressures reconfigure mobility by narrowing spatial reach, fixing certain areas as off-limits, and orienting everyday travel around anticipation and embodied memory, so that the city is encountered through a continually adjusted map of where one can go and how. Within this field, movement is sustained through strategies that both enable and reveal its conditions — cycling is mobilised as an anti-harassment technology, valued for the possibility of remaining in motion and limiting unwanted interaction, while the reshaping of self-presentation, including the projection of a more masculine presence, allows some travellers to pass through space with reduced scrutiny, effectively borrowing a different position within the social order of the street. Mobility thus becomes the terrain through which uneven urban participation takes shape, as the capacity to move and remain present in the city depends on how exposure, information and administrative access are organised across different bodies. For planning, this directs attention towards the interactional and institutional arrangements that structure mobility environments, raising questions about how exposure is distributed in space, how information circulates across linguistic boundaries, and how administrative procedures condition access to movement, and it is at this level that the paper locates its contribution, in showing how close attention to everyday mobility can inform planning approaches that address inequality at the level where it is generated.

28.title: Inclusive Routes, Uneven Cities: Accessibility Mapping and Spatial Justice in the Municipality of Athens
28.abstract: This research presents an accessibility mapping initiative in the Municipality of Athens, focusing on the development of inclusive routes and points of interest across the urban environment. The project integrates spatial data on public transport, sports facilities, municipal services, and other key urban amenities. The initiative is developed through a collaborative framework that brings together diverse forms of expertise, including local knowledge, user-informed perspectives, and geospatial analysis. To operationalize this spatial data, the project utilizes Mapbox technology, as its primary web-mapping platform, selected for its advanced customization capabilities and superior performance in rendering complex interactive maps. It results in the creation of curated routes that support more inclusive navigation and engagement with the city, enhancing both everyday mobility and the urban experience of residents and visitors. Beyond its technical dimension, the project engages with broader questions of spatial justice and urban inclusion. It highlights uneven geographies of accessibility within the city and demonstrates how mapping practices can contribute to identifying gaps and informing more inclusive urban planning strategies. In this sense, accessibility is approached not only as a technical issue but also as a socio-spatial condition embedded in everyday urban life. The study contributes to discussions on inclusive urban mobility and tourism, offering a practical example of how digital tools and collaborative processes can support more equitable and inclusive cities.

28.title: Spatiotemporal perspectives on road safety. Geo-statistical analysis of road accidents in the Attica Region, Greece
28.abstract: Road safety remains a pivotal concern in urban areas, regardless of their size. Among different types of road accidents, fatal road accidents (FRAs) pose critical challenges, especially in Greece, where their incidence is notably higher than in Northern European countries. The present study examines FRAs within the Attica Region of Greece using geostatistical methods and shedding light on three categories of casualties: total casualties, non-pedestrian casualties, and pedestrian casualties. It should be mentioned that variables related to road infrastructure, land use, and socioeconomic factors were evaluated, with optimal models determined through exploratory regression analysis. Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) and Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR) techniques were employed to compare model performance and explore the impact of key predictors in detail. Notably, the findings indicate that the proportion of residen-tial roads and the density of traffic lights significantly affect accident occurrence. What is more, socioeconomic disadvantage, represented by limited internet ac-cess and low vehicle ownership, was evidently associated with higher accident rates. Although GWR only outperformed OLS in modelling non-pedestrian cas-ualties, it highlighted spatial variability across all casualty types, urging the need for geographically targeted road safety policies and interventions.

28.title: Investigation Gentrification Typologies for the Perspective of Urban Development in Attiki Basin
28.abstract: Despite positive effects, there is evidence of gentrification causing segregation and displacement in urban population. This study investigates gentrification in the Attiki basin, its categorization in three different typologies (marginal, mainstream and super gentrification) and potential and development in the future. We believe that Athens embodies the role model of a “Touristic City” and it is indicated from previous authors that touristification is most likely the prominent urban typology in touristic areas. A combination of sociodemographic data and Space Syntax methods were applied to determine the influence of certain points of interest (bicycle lanes, squares, subway stations, pedestrian areas, archaeological monuments) in the urban fabric. The findings show that (i) marginal gentrification is to be found in the western areas, mainstream gentrification near the City Center and super gentrification in the northern and southern suburbs, which are linked to the specific demographics of the population in each area. (ii) Moreover, the metro lines influence in a great level the development of gentrification. (iii) Finally, touristification is likely to have developed in the historical center rather than mainstream gentrification.

28.title: The 15-minute city in spatial analysis: A GIS methodology for measuring, visualizing, and analyzing accessibility through proximity and public transport
28.abstract: The 15-minute city can offer a meaningful framework for measuring and analyzing accessibility to basic urban functions, if proper theoretical and methodological choices are made. This paper develops a comprehensive methodology and presents the steps for measuring, visualizing, and analyzing x-minute accessibility by proximity (walking accessibility) and accessibility by public transport supply (accessibility potential created by nearby public transport services) using geographic information systems (GIS). Five sequential steps are presented: project definition, data preparation, measuring accessibility, visualizing accessibility and insufficient accessibility, and analyzing accessibility using spatial statistical analysis and modeling. The proposed approach is applied to Copenhagen. Results indicate that, even in a city where sustainable mobility is prominent, there are spatial clusters of lack of accessibility and insufficient accessibility, lying mainly in suburban locations. Proximity-based accessibility and accessibility by public transport supply are found to highly overlap across space. Moreover, density was found to largely predict both 15-minute walking accessibility to local destinations and accessibility to other areas via public transport. This approach can be used as a guide by those aiming to understand the patterns and drivers of accessibility across space, reveal socio-spatial inequalities, and identify locations for potential interventions that improve walking accessibility and reduce car dependence.

28.title: The Polycrisis and the Mediterranean City: Prospects for a Spatially Just Transition in Athens
28.abstract: Athens, one of Europe’s hottest cities, is home to over 3.7 million people in its metropolitan area, putting it among the ten largest agglomerations in the EU. Athens’ core is also one of Europe’s densest urban areas.
