These conditions, along with the challenges of the polycrisis era, underscore the urgency of pursuing a just transition towards an ecologically, economically and socially sustainable urban model. Greece has experienced the deepest economic recession of any developed country in peacetime, while extreme weather events have led to increasing incidences of wildfire, drought and flash flooding in the city. Against this backdrop, we examine the prospects for a spatially just transition in Athens: one that ensures the benefits of climate adaptations and economic interventions are fairly distributed in the city. Drawing on qualitative research with key local stakeholders, this study explores perceived barriers and opportunities for achieving such a just transition. By providing contemporary insights on a major European city that remains relatively understudied, this paper contributes to debates on urban transitions and spatial justice in Mediterranean urban contexts. The findings have broader relevance for cities across the Mediterranean, one of the planet’s most vulnerable regions in the climate crisis.

28.title: Urban form types and centralities as an analytical framework for integrated urbanism: An open data approach
28.abstract:
Contemporary cities are characterised by complex spatial structures that require comprehensive approaches capable of linking urban geography, spatial analysis and planning. Therefore, framing this session, this contribution discusses the findings of doctoral research on the role of urban form types and centres as an analytical geospatial framework integrating geography and planning for reading, understanding and discussing urban issues.

Patterns and nodes have long functioned as the conceptual tools to this end; however, their translation into a geospatial analytical framework for integrated urbanism-mobility planning remains limited. This presentation outlines the development of a methodological framework that combines composite urban form types with walk-oriented centrality clusters as the main analytical vehicle for integrated urbanism. The proposed framework builds on quantitative typo-morphology and centrality analysis, using open geospatial data to describe the city through two complementary dimensions. First, composite urban form types are developed for built density, functional mixture and network configuration, providing a modular spatial language for interpreting urban form. Second, walk-oriented centres are identified through a multi-dimensional centrality approach that combines the density and diversity of centrality components, including activity concentration, network centrality, public transport accessibility and access to urban green and active leisure spaces.

The framework is implemented in Athens, offering a detailed reading of the geography of urban form types and centrality clusters. Its contribution is twofold. First, it provides a replicable, transferable (and scalable towards comparative analysis) way to interpret the spatial structure of the city through its form, functions and centralities. Second, it supports planning by translating spatial analysis into legible, actionable outputs relevant to walk-oriented, integrated urbanism. In doing so, this contribution argues that types and centres can be utilised as a shared analytical language for linking spatial analysis and early-stage spatial strategy, with a view towards participatory approaches.

28.title: Pilot investigation of data availability for the adoption of automated disaggregated travel demand models in Athens, Greece

authors.name: Natalia Seltsioti
authors.affiliation: Department of Surveying and Geoinformatics Engineering, University of West Attica

authors.name: Panagiotis G. Tzouras
authors.affiliation: Department of Surveying and Geoinformatics Engineering, University of West Attica | School of Rural, Surveying and Geoinformatics Engineering, National Technical University of Athens

28.abstract: The development of disaggregated travel demand models constitutes an innovative approach to addressing contemporary challenges in the transport sector. These models are based on representing the activities that a “synthetic” traveler is expected to perform. Major European cities, such as Berlin, Germany and Paris, France have already advanced in developing agent-based transport simulation models. In Athens, however, current practice remains limited to aggregate transport models. As a result, spatiotemporal demand variations are neither adequately captured nor predicted. This study examines the availability of data necessary for developing disaggregated travel demand models in Athens, Greece. Building on this, it provides a qualitative evaluation of the suitability of four, already utilized, modeling frameworks: CEMDAP, the Equasim pipeline, Creario, and PAM. To meet this objective, a workshop with a heterogeneous group of 10 experts, coming from various disciplines of planning studies, was organized in February 2026. The workshop was structured around a sheet, through which experts reported their knowledge of dataset availability based on four levels: (i) openly accessible data, (ii) data available upon request, (iii) data not available, and (iv) unknown availability. In addition, data requirements were organized into five main categories: population data, trip and activity data, empirical data, spatial data, and measurements. A key output of this process is the development of the final mobility data map that sheds light on availability, ownership, and provides direct links for downloading and inspecting open sets. Furthermore, the data map includes experts' views regarding the challenges arising from the quality and accessibility of each set, as they were discussed in the workshop. Of course, the map highlights significant gaps, particularly in dynamic data such as trip diaries and traffic flow data in Athens neighborhoods, as well as the absence of standardized protocols for integrating these datasets.

28.title: Pedestrian Infrastructure, Spatial Justice, and Healthcare Mobility for Older Adults
28.abstract:
As urban population age, pedestrian infrastructure emerges as a critical dimension of urban mobility justice. This study investigates how micro-scale sidewalk conditions shape healthcare accessibility for older adults in Egaleo, West Athens, which is a municipality experiencing pronounced demographic aging, with direct implications for inclusive urban planning.
Using a GIS-based methodology, sidewalk conditions within a 500-meters catchment around the Health Center were assessed through a Virtual Audit of 12 accessibility factors, scored via a standardized composite index. A novel based routing algorithm prioritized the "easiest" path over the shortest distance, reflecting the spatial cognition and constraints characteristic of older adults. A total of 841 origin points, derived from census block grid and the pedestrian network grid, served as the basis for route-level analysis.
The findings revealed a statistically significant accessibility gap between routes to the Health Center (mean score 2.76), compared to the broader study area (mean score 3.17). Moreover, a negative spatial correlation (r = -0.20, p < 0.001) confirmed that urban blocks with the highest concentrations of older residents consistently present the poorest infrastructure. The LISA analysis, identified spatially clustered "Accessibility Deserts" where a 92.5% absence of crosswalks and an 81.7% obstruction rate, was present. In parallel, a Global Moran's I of 0.912 confirmed near-perfect spatial autocorrelation, demonstrating that infrastructure failure is not random but structurally embedded in the urban fabric of the city.
These results show a planning paradox, where the areas that need walkable, accessible streets, are lacking infrastructure. The current pedestrian environment functions as a spatial barrier, reproducing mobility inequity and reinforcing socio-spatial disadvantages for the city's most vulnerable residents. This study highlights the need for a transition toward age-sensitive urban design. Moving beyond mere functional utility, the proposed framework addresses the specific needs of older adults to foster inclusive and spatially just urban environments.

29.title: Circular Economy and Regional Development: Territorial Governance, Strategic Planning, and Spatial Dimensions of Circular Transition
29.abstract:
Environmental crisis has been growing over the last years, bringing into the spot the need for alternative models for the development of the society and the economy. On this basis, Circular Economy has emerged as a central approach for addressing the environmental challenge. Unlike the traditional model of Linear Economy (take-make-dispose) Circular Economy is aiming to create more sustainable and resilient production and consumption systems. In addition, the scientific dialogue around Circular Economy is moving from environmental and technological aspects to its spatial and governance dimensions.
In this context, regions and cities are increasingly at the forefront for the implementation of circular transition since many circular dimensions and practices are connected to local economic structures and capacities. As a result, the principles of Circular Economy need to be integrated into local and regional development strategies, constituting an important objective of national policy.
This paper examines the connection between Circular Economy and regional development through the study of strategic planning and governance frameworks developed within the THESEUS Project, a European initiative aimed at establishing Greece’s first Hub for Circularity (H4C). The research focuses on the Region of Attica, the project’s main pilot region, which represents a complex urban and industrial environment facing significant environmental pressures, making it a particularly relevant case study for circular transition policies. The paper studies key regional strategic frameworks, in order to assess the degree of integration of Circular Economy principles within them. Emphasis is given to the role of regional governance and policy coordination in supporting circular transition. By focusing on Attica, the paper contributes to the discussions on the geographies of circularity and highlights the importance of place-based approaches to the transition and implementation of Circular Economy.

29.title: Vacancy as Resource: A Framework for Understanding Stakeholder Dynamics in the Circular Reuse of Residential Buildings

authors.name: Lamiaa Ghoz
authors.affiliation: TU Dresden; leibniz institute of ecological urban and regional development

29.abstract:
As circular economy agendas gain traction in urban policy and planning, the persistence of high housing vacancy across densely populated cities presents a striking global paradox. The reuse of vacant residential buildings offers a dual opportunity: addressing housing demand while advancing urban circularity by extending the life cycle of existing material stocks. However, such processes are frequently hindered by complex and often conflicting stakeholder interests.
This paper conceptualises vacant housing as part of urban material flows and positions its reuse as a key—yet underexplored—circular strategy. It develops an analytical framework to capture the challenges and priorities of stakeholders involved in vacancy reuse. The framework is constructed through empirical research in Cairo, a rapidly growing non-European city with a housing vacancy rate of 33% (2017), and subsequently applied and refined in Athens, Greece, a European context characterised by high vacancy under different regulatory and socio-economic conditions.
The analysis draws on semi-structured interviews with key stakeholders in both cities, including government representatives, investors, property owners, NGOs and building professionals. Thematic analysis is used to identify core challenges as well as context-specific variations in how these challenges manifest.
The findings show that while fundamental stakeholder concerns—particularly economic viability—are consistent across contexts, their relative importance and operationalisation differ significantly. Regulatory environments and socio-cultural perceptions play a decisive role in shaping reuse practices and outcomes.
By tracing both recurring patterns and contextual divergences, the proposed framework provides a transferable diagnostic tool for policymakers to identify barriers, navigate competing interests, and design context-sensitive strategies. In doing so, the paper grounds circularity in practice and contributes to a more spatially and institutionally embedded understanding of urban circular transitions.

29.title: Rethinking digitally enabled circular and sharing economies
29.abstract:
Circular economy paradigms are being implemented (and contested) worldwide across economic sectors, policy domains, and geographical scales, including local communities and the everyday practices of individuals, groups, and local authorities. This contribution focuses on local recycling, upcycling, and repair, as well as on sharing and reuse practices that foster community relations as alternatives to individualism and consumerism. Specifically, we address circular and sharing economies that are supported or enabled by digital platforms.
We aim to investigate how digital tools can contribute to shaping new forms of governance and of economic exchange that are socially just, place-sensitive, and meaningful for local communities.
Our experimental case study is a blockchain-based wallet app through which cryptographic tokens can be created to represent values that are relevant to local communities. Its overall goal is to enable tokenized economies oriented toward the public good and collaborative logics, in contexts such as makerspaces, libraries of things, and community currencies.
This research relates to recent geographical studies that critically investigate the potentials and limits of non-corporate digital platforms and civic technologies for local democratic participation and collaborative governance (Chiappini, 2020; Cardullo, Kitchin, 2019, 2025), grassroots urbanism and practices of care (Vadiati, 2025; Cenere, 2025), and solidarity and sharing economies (Lekan, Rogers, 2020; Leontidou, 2020; Santala, McGuirk, 2022)—the latter being particularly relevant for tokenized systems and (circular) economic exchanges. Bridging these literatures with economic sociology accounts on the embeddedness of money (Zelizer, 1994), and reading these economic and digital practices through the lens of diverse economies (Gibson-Graham, 2008; Certomà, 2023), we advance an interdisciplinary method for co-designing tokenized social economies in local communities.
Our case study provides an example of how digital geographies matter not only for critically investigating sociotechnical practices, but also for rethinking and remaking them in novel, place- and context-sensitive ways (Lynch, Farrokhi 2022).

30.title: Spatial correlation of freshwater pollution with pollution sources and economic inequalities: the case of Epirus, Greece
30.abstract: In the present paper, it is attempted to correlate the position of critical spots of waterbodies of the mountainous region of Epirus, in terms of pollution, with the ones of possible point pollution sources. Furthermore, in this work, freshwater pollution is to be correlated with the income of the local inhabitants. Who pollutes Epirus’s waters? Are the polluted municipal localities, poor? These daring questions are tried to be answered using primary data from a series of official state organizations. Freshwater quality documentation is provided by Epirus’s River Basin Management Plan of the Greek Ministry for Environment and Energy (YPEN). Possible pollution sources documentation is given by the Hellenic Survey of Geology and Mineral Exploration (EAGME). Local GPD per capita documentation is granted by the Hellenic Statistical Authority (ELSTAT). Conclusions are drawn using a spatial approach of the forementioned data. River and lake parts’ ecological and chemical condition, possible pollution sources and local GDP per capita are placed on their actual location using Q-GIS program. The study of these three layers lets us figure out what the relation between them is and, thus, ascertain whether our initial hypotheses are confirmed.

30.title: New Forms of Dwelling in the Mountain Settlements of Epirus. Spatial and Social Practices as a Response to Peripheralisation

authors.name: Mara Bousi
authors.affiliation: Department of Urban Planning, Regional Planning and Development, School of Architecture, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki

30.abstract:
This paper investigates new forms of dwelling emerging in the mountain settlements of Epirus in Greece, under conditions of peripheralisation. Focusing on the mountainous areas of Zagori and Tzoumerka, the study examines how the spatial and social practices of local communities shape new models of habitation and collective organisation, highlighting alternative responses to the pressures of demographic shrinkage, tourism monoculture and institutional marginalization, as characteristics of neoliberal spatial planning.
The theoretical framework is organised around the concept of peripheralisation as a dynamic process rooted in asymmetric urbanisation, producing deep socioeconomic and ecological restructuring. Four research dimensions are analysed: the traditional built environment as a bearer of local identity and community regeneration; the gender dimension and the role of women in the production of space; social innovation and the reactivation of traditional productive practices; and public space through placemaking as a field of community cohesion and resistance.
These dimensions are connected through the concept of "socio-ecologies of care" — the ways in which communities care for their place, built environment and members, as an active act of resistance to peripheralisation. In Epirus, these practices are historically expressed through the stewardship of the architectural heritage, the role of women shaped by the historical tradition of male emigration and the traditional agropastoral activities that have largely disappeared, whose underlying potential for sustainable community regeneration this research seeks to explore.
Methodologically, the study combines fieldwork, interviews, ethnographic research, GIS mapping and participatory design workshops. Keywords: Peripheralisation, Mountain Settlements, Traditional Built Environment, Gender Dimension, Socio-ecologies of Care

30.title: Urban Sprawl in the Mountainous Areas of Greece, 2006-2018
30.abstract:
Greece is a country characterized by strong mountainous terrain, as mountainous areas cover a significant share of its territory and contribute to the intense geographical fragmentation of space. These areas, located both in mainland Greece and on the islands, are associated with distinct natural, cultural and settlement characteristics. At the same time, they constitute environmentally sensitive areas facing multiple spatial pressures, including population decline, abandonment of traditional activities and increasing built-up area dispersion. In the Greek context, mountainous areas are not governed by a unified planning framework, but rather through a combination of environmental, forest, spatial planning and regional policies.
This paper examines built-up area dispersion in the mountainous areas of Greece during the period 2006–2018. Mountainous areas are defined using geomorphological criteria that combine elevation and slope. Three categories are identified: moderately mountainous areas (400–800 m elevation and 4–10% slope), steep mountainous areas (400–800 m elevation and slope above 10%) and high mountainous areas (above 800 m elevation). The analysis is based on Copernicus built-up data for 2006 and 2018 and elevation and slope datasets. Spatial overlay techniques are used to combine these datasets and examine the distribution and changes in built-up areas across the three mountainous categories.
The results show the spatial distribution and intensity of urban sprawl in mountainous Greece, highlighting differences in built-up area dispersion across the three mountainous categories. The paper contributes to the understanding of spatial transformations in mountainous environments and underlines the need for systematic monitoring and more effective spatial planning policies in environmentally sensitive areas.

30.title: Factors Affecting Plant Cover in Shrublands Grazed by Greek Shorthorn Cattle in the Pindus Mountains

authors.name: Dimitrios Oikonomou
authors.affiliation: Dept. of Forestry, Wood Sciences and Design, University of Thessaly

authors.name: Michail Vrahnakis
authors.affiliation: Dept. of Forestry, Wood Sciences and Design, University of Thessaly

authors.name: Maria Yiakoulaki
authors.affiliation: Dept. of Forestry and Natural Environment, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki

authors.name: Gavriil Xanthopoulos
authors.affiliation: Hellenic Agricultural Organization “Demeter”, Institute of Mediterranean & Forest Ecosystems

authors.name: Yannis Kazoglou
authors.affiliation: Dept. of Forestry, Wood Sciences and Design, University of Thessaly

30.abstract:
The decline of human populations in the settlements of the Pindus mountain regions of Aitoloakarnania and Evrytania, western Greece, has resulted in significant changes to the adjacent land cover types. Numbers of goats and sheep have decreased, while EU subsidies have favored the increase of the population of the Greek shorthorn cattle breed. Because of these changes, it is important to assess the impact of cattle grazing on plant structure and composition, as this can influence fire risk and hazards, which are serious threats for the sub-Mediterranean regions of Greece. In this contribution, the results of our ongoing research on this topic will be presented. We will assess the impact of grazing regimes and environmental factors on plant cover, focusing on shrublands near cattle sheds. This assessment will consider both total plant cover and cover of the functional plant groups. Particular attention will be given to the kermes oak (Quercus coccifera) because of its abundance in the region. We will consider factors such as stocking rates, the distance from animal sheds and watering points, as well as topographic and soil conditions. Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) will be used to examine the impact of each factor.

Keywords: Greek shorthorn cattle, cattle grazing, Mediterranean shrublands, kermes oak, fire risk

30.title: Small Tunnels, Deep Returns: Accessibility and Revitalisation in Mountainous Greece

authors.name: George Panagiotopoulos
authors.affiliation: Metsovio Interdisciplinary Research Center - National Technical University of Athens

30.abstract:
Mountain regions across the Mediterranean face persistent depopulation, as younger residents migrate to cities in search of employment and services. Conventional infrastructure-evaluation frameworks, which weigh benefit by population served, tend to deprioritise small-scale interventions in sparsely populated upland areas, even when those interventions deliver order-of-magnitude improvements in accessibility for the communities they reach. This paper examines the contrasting accessibility impact of two classes of road infrastructure in mainland Greece: a major motorway spine connecting the principal cities of the north, and a set of small mountain tunnels that bypass the most isolating terrain in the country's central massifs. Using a settlement-level accessibility index computed over the full census-settlement network, we compare the breadth and the per-settlement depth of benefit delivered by each class.
Results show that the motorway spine reaches the much larger beneficiary set, consistent with its intended national role. However, the per-settlement accessibility improvement delivered by mountain tunnels — for the relatively small number of upland communities they serve — is substantially deeper than that of the spine, in some cases reducing journey times to neighbouring market towns and service centres several-fold. Population-weighted welfare measures, while appropriate for aggregate economic accounting, systematically obscure this threshold effect.
We argue that targeted, small-scale infrastructure of this kind deserves a distinct evaluation framework. By making routine access to employment, education and health services tractable from villages that have spent decades effectively cut off, such interventions create the conditions under which return migration becomes viable, local enterprise can scale beyond subsistence, and the demographic decline of mountain communities can begin to reverse. The accessibility benefits visible in our results, though modest in aggregate population terms, identify these tunnels as instruments of regional development rather than merely transport-cost reductions, with implications for how mountain-area infrastructure is appraised and prioritised.

30.title: Participatory Assessment of Barriers to the Environmentally-friendly Tourism Accommodation Management in Mountainous Regions – The Case of Metsovo Settlement, Epirus, Greece
30.abstract: Based on their outstanding natural and cultural assets, mountainous regions are globally perceived as attractive alternative tourism destinations. However, in order for such a developmental direction to keep track with sustainability objectives, cooperatively-driven bottom-up policy decisions, delineating particular alternative tourism pathways that ensure integrity of those assets and are in alignment with local values and traditions need to be in place. In addition, the deployment of relative tourism accommodation infrastructure – supply side – that values these assets and attempts to minimize its environmental footprint has to be embedded in the management spirit and practice of the respective entrepreneurial community. The latter is the focus of this work, aiming to establish and implement a participatory methodology for exploring, through stakeholders’ engagement, the extent to which tourism accommodation businesses in a specific mountainous destination – the settlement of Metsovo, Epirus, Greece – integrate environmental management systems or generally adopt relevant actions with the aim of reducing their environmental footprint in the study area. This methodology follows a two-step stakeholders’ engagement approach, namely: a questionnaire, distributed through a Google form to relevant local tourism businesses, aiming to realize the current state of environmental management as a practice for handling tourist accommodation businesses in the study region; and a Focus Group discussion, building upon questionnaire’s results and seeking to identify potential barriers or deficits applying towards an environmentally-responsible tourism accommodation management. Results of such an effort demonstrate a certain gap that crosscuts both the policy and the entrepreneurial community, being roughly sketched as the lack of a certain future vision for sustainable tourism as a pillar for local development and related policy measures for its implementation; and the knowledge gap as well as the lack of incentives, technical and financial support for adopting environmental management schemes at the business level.

30.title: From the ‘Intermediate Mountain Range’ to the ‘Decisive Battleground’: How Sporting Events Contribute to the Recognition of Mid-Mountain Regions
30.abstract:
The evolving role of mid-mountain ranges—here, the Vosges and the Massif Central—within the route of the Tour de France lies at the heart of this proposal. The aim is to understand how a sporting event can become a driver of development for regions facing a form of marginalization.

Historically, mid-mountain ranges were regarded merely as intermediaries between the plains and the high mountains, crossed without any major sporting ambition. Since 2007, however, a paradigm shift has taken place: race organizers have made the routes more demanding, increased the number of summit finishes (La Planche des Belles Filles, Markstein, Le Lioran), and positioned these stages at decisive moments in the race. Mid-mountain terrain has therefore moved from being a transition zone to becoming a true “decisive battleground” for the general classification.

This sporting valorization has been accompanied by territorial appropriation by local authorities. Departmental councils, in partnership with municipalities and intermunicipal bodies, finance the hosting of stages and develop long-term strategies: marking cycling tourism routes that follow Tour de France stages, organizing large cyclosportive events (L’Alsacienne, Les 3 Ballons), and creating greenways. These initiatives aim to capitalize on spectators’ desire to imitate sporting practices and to build lasting tourist appeal.

The observed impacts—increased cycling tourism, longer tourist seasons, and greater visibility—illustrate how sporting events can become a territorial resource for rural mid-mountain areas facing demographic and economic decline. These territories, often affected by deindustrialization or agricultural decline, find in cycling a path toward economic transition that highlights their geographical specificity: accessibility, selective slopes, and usability outside the winter season.

The objective, therefore, is to demonstrate that mid-mountain regions are increasingly asserting themselves as mountains in their own right, with temporalities and potentialities distinct from those of high mountains.

30.title: What is a patrimonial sport event ? Reflections on the Tour de France
30.abstract:
Sporting events are now seen as tools for territorial promotion, relying on media coverage and local anchoring to highlight the places where they are held. Among them, major events such as the FIFA World Cup or the Olympic and Paralympic Games seem to stand apart, as they occur less frequently over time and their territorial anchoring is more diffuse and debatable. By contrast, events that take place in the same locations year after year become more deeply rooted among local populations and appear to benefit the local economy more, which is largely residential and partly based on tourism.
Through these heritage events, the aim is to showcase a wide range of skills, the culture of the host location, and beyond that, a broader “event culture” that indirectly embeds the event within the local heritage. This can be observed both in their integration into the landscape and the local calendar, as well as in the highlighting of the territories’ heritage elements—though still far removed from very large-scale events.
The case of the Tour de France is nevertheless unique. As the third most visible sporting event in the world, it is held annually and brings visibility to a consistently large number of places thanks to its geographical variability. In this sense, it promotes an ever-growing array of local expertise, regional cultures, and a search for authenticity through the lens of a heritage sporting event—a concept that is constantly evolving.

30.title: Development Disparities and Development Dynamics in Europe’s Mountain Regions: A Comparative Analysis from the Alps to the Balkan Mountains
30.abstract:
Mountain areas account for approximately 30% of the European Union’s territory and are home
to 17% of its population. European mountain landscapes are cultural landscapes that reflect the
long-standing interactions between human societies and natural systems. Nevertheless, within the
framework of European social and economic cohesion, mountain regions are recognised as
disadvantaged areas due to their specific characteristics, particularly the natural constraints
associated with altitude and topography, which limit their development potential.
Stretching from the Arctic to the Mediterranean, Europe’s mountain regions exhibit considerable
topographical diversity, ranging from high mountain ranges, such as the Pyrenees, the mountains
of southern Norway, the Alps and the Romanian Carpathians, to lower-altitude or “mid-mountain”
areas, which cover a substantially larger geographical extent. Accordingly, morphological
characteristics, such as elevation and slope, influence local microclimatic conditions and play a
crucial role in shaping ecosystems and determining existing and potential land uses.
Mountain regions across Europe exhibit varying levels of economic development and distinct
employment structures. More specifically, northern mountain regions include prosperous
communities with strong tourism-based or industrial economies, in contrast to those in Southern
Europe, where economic diversification tends to be more limited. Furthermore, these regions
display divergent demographic trends and varying rates of demographic change, as well as
differences in land cover, vulnerability to climate change and infrastructure provision.
Overall, the European mountain environment cannot be regarded as a homogeneous category in
terms of regional development, but rather as a multidimensional geographical space characterised
by pronounced spatial inequalities and diverse development prospects. Although some mountain
regions are economically viable and well integrated into the EU economy, the majority face
development challenges and require targeted support. Understanding these regional disparities is
essential for designing effective policies that promote the sustainable and balanced development of
mountain areas.
This study examines the spatial distribution of mountain regions in Europe and subsequently
seeks to synthesise their diverse characteristics and development dynamics. By bringing together
geographical, demographic, economic and environmental dimensions, the study seeks to establish
a framework for understanding the heteroge

31.title: Expert-Based vs. GenAI-Assisted Landscape Character Assessment: A Comparative Multi-Scale Geospatial Framework.

authors.name: DImitrios Alexakis
authors.affiliation: Institute for Mediterranean Studies, Foundation for Research and Technology Hellas

authors.name: George Lampropoulos
authors.affiliation: Institute for Mediterranean Studies, Foundation for Research and Technology Hellas

authors.name: Eirini Paraskevaki
authors.affiliation: School of Chemical and Environmental Engineering, Technical University of Crete

authors.name: Androniki Tsouchlaraki
authors.affiliation: School of Chemical and Environmental Engineering, Technical University of Crete,

31.abstract:
This study presents an integrated framework for Landscape Character Assessment (LCA), comparing an expert-based GIS approach with a Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI)-assisted approach across two spatial scales. The aim is to explore how GenAI can support the delineation, interpretation, and communication of landscape character, while critically comparing its outputs with those produced through conventional expert-based geospatial analysis.
The expert-based methodology follows a hierarchical structure, beginning with the delineation of Land Description Units (LDUs) based on geomorphological and land cover attributes, and progressing to the synthesis of Landscape Character Types (LCTs) through spatial aggregation and expert interpretation. The overall analysis integrates spatial datasets related to morphology, land cover, vegetation condition, and population density, capturing both natural and anthropogenic dimensions of the landscape.
In parallel, a GenAI-assisted LCA methodology is applied using the same spatial datasets as input. Through a structured prompt-based workflow, GenAI supports the interpretation of spatial classifications, the formulation of landscape character descriptions, and the development of scenario-based narratives. The comparison is conducted at two spatial scales: a detailed local-scale analysis of the Akrotiri Peninsula, Chania/ Crete (Greece), and a broader regional-scale assessment covering the Prefecture of Chania. This multi-scale design allows the evaluation of how landscape classification and interpretation vary according to spatial resolution, territorial extent, and analytical scale.
Overall, the framework demonstrates the potential of GenAI to enhance the efficiency, consistency, and communicability of LCA documentation, while underlining the continued importance of expert validation for local specificity, landscape meaning, and contextual interpretation.
This research was funded by the European Union’s Horizon Europe MSCA Staff Exchanges 2022 (HORIZON-MSCA-2022-SE-01), project “Towards Democratic Landscape Observation Through Geoinformatics and Public Participation (TOPIO)”, under grant agreement No 101131109.

31.title: From water systems to hybrid landscapes: integrating Historical GIS and PPGIS into a Heritage Potential Index for Mediterranean landscapes

authors.name: Claudio Sossio De Simone
authors.affiliation: Institute of Heritage Science (Italian National Research Council)

authors.name: Christos Polykretis
authors.affiliation: Department of Surveying & Geoinformatics Engineering, University of West Attica

authors.name: Magdalini Angeli
authors.affiliation: Institute for Mediterranean Studies, Foundation for Research and Technology Hellas

31.abstract:
Mediterranean rural landscapes are shaped by long-term interactions between water management,
agrarian practices, and local knowledge, generating hybrid environments where ecological
functions, land-use patterns, and heritage values are tightly interwoven. This paper proposes a
spatial decision-support framework that combines Historical GIS with Public Participation GIS
(PPGIS) to construct a Heritage Potential Index capable of identifying areas of high heritage value
and landscape fragility, with a specific focus on case studies in Italy and Greece.. Geo-historical
layers (multitemporal land-use/land-cover change, historical hydrography, archaeological records,
traditional rural features) are integrated with participatory and volunteered geographic information
(community-mapped landmarks, perceived values and conflicts, PPGIS data, OSM-based
contributions) within a GIS-based Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) workflow. Criteria and
indicators are structured into ecological, historical, and socio-cultural dimensions; they are
weighted through an expert–stakeholder procedure and aggregated via a weighted linear
combination to derive a continuous Heritage Potential Index. The framework is designed for
application across Mediterranean contexts, enabling the identification of “core” zones where
historical continuity, ecological connectivity, and community meanings converge, as well as
contested areas where land-use pressures and perceived values diverge. By explicitly integrating
geo-historical reconstruction and participatory spatial knowledge, the paper contributes to
democratic landscape monitoring and offers a transparent, replicable tool to support heritage-
oriented planning in Mediterranean landscapes.

31.title: An AI and Participatory GIS Framework for Visual Quality Assessment of Rural Landscapes: A Case Study from Falasarna, Crete, Greece
31.abstract:
This study introduces an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based framework for assessing the visual quality (“scenicness”) of rural landscapes by integrating geospatial data, landscape ecology principles, and participatory evaluation processes. The approach is grounded in the Information Processing Theory developed by Rachel Kaplan and Stephen Kaplan, which explains landscape preference through four key perceptual dimensions: coherence, complexity, legibility, and mystery. The methodology incorporates participatory data collected from local communities, stakeholders, and visitors, alongside image-based inputs, to support democratic landscape monitoring and inclusive landscape quality assessment. A dataset of images from diverse rural case studies is used to train Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs), specifically Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) models, to predict scenicness. The system employs a pipeline including semantic segmentation of landscape elements (e.g., vegetation, water, built environment), combined with feature extraction based on spatial composition, and a constrained optimization model to align outputs with human perception. The framework is demonstrated through a case study in Falasarna, Crete, Greece, a Mediterranean coastal landscape of high ecological and cultural value. Results show that the AI-based approach provides more accurate scenicness predictions compared to traditional regression models. The results were evaluated against human scenicness assessments, demonstrating strong agreement between the AI-based outputs and participants’ perceptions. By integrating cognitive theory with machine learning and participatory GIS principles, the proposed framework enables scalable, transparent, and user-informed landscape monitoring. Its application within digital twin environments supports real-time, human-centered evaluation, contributing to more inclusive landscape planning, sustainable tourism management, and evidence-based policy-making.

This research was funded by the European Union’s Horizon Europe MSCA Staff Exchanges 2022 (HORIZON-MSCA-2022-SE-01), project “Towards Democratic Landscape Observation Through Geoinformatics and Public Participation (TOPIO)”, under grant agreement No 101131109.

Kaplan, Stephen, Kaplan, & Rachel. (1981). Cognition and environment: functioning in an uncertain world. https://www.hse.ru/data/2019/03/04/1196348207/%5BRachel_Kaplan,_Stephen_Kaplan%5D_The_Experience_of_(b-ok.xyz).pdf

31.title: THE GREAT WILDFIRES OF 2007 ΙΝ PELOPONNESE AND THE REGENERATION OF FORESTS
31.abstract:
The fires of the summer of 2007 in Greece have been recorded as the most destructive in Europe in recent decades. The total area burned exceeded 250,000 hectares, of which 30,132 were located within the Natura protected areas 2000 network. Furthermore, for the first time, the damage report included not only burned forests and agricultural land, but also entire villages, civil infrastructure and the loss of 57 lives.
This research thoroughly investigates and examines the short, middle, and long term impact of these catastrophic wildfires. It estimates the severity of the impact and the time needed for regeneration of the forests, regeneration implying that the forests returned to their previous extends and syntheses before the fires. The study is conducted using remote sensing data and methods, i.e., satellite images and products from NASA's MODIS satellites, namely the products MOD09A1 and MCD64A1.
Seven different polygons (burned areas) were singled out as Regions of Interest (ROIs) and their evolution was monitored for the entire period of satellite data (2002-present) with the construction of the time series of the NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index) and NBR (Normalized Burn Ratio) ratios. The post-fire yearly evolution of these ratios was compared with the averaged pre-fire values leading to some first conclusions. It is noted that the NBR index is normally used as the difference pre-fire to post-fire (dNBR) but the particular point in time that is considered pre-fire can be varied to conform with the scope of the study. Additionally, the concurrent examination of the two indices can provide useful input for the timely growth of the forest vegetation.
Given the uncertainties inherent in remote sensing methods the results were compared with other similar studies, especially those that included field examinations, and the comparisons were favorable.

31.title: Mapping the dynamics of urban green-blue spaces and ecosystem health indicators in Varanasi, India

authors.name: Kiran Kumari Singh
authors.affiliation: Department of Geography, University of Allahabad, Prayagraj, India.

31.abstract: One of the key elements of urban sustainability and resilience is ensuring that natural components in cities, such as green and blue spaces, are managed and protected. The rapid transformation of Varanasi and its built-up expansion have caused the loss and fragmentation of urban green and blue spaces, negatively affecting urban ecosystem health and threatening long-term sustainability. This study derived and mapped ecosystem health indicators from 1993 to 2026 for Varanasi city. Multi-temporal Landsat imagery is employed to derive urban green and blue spaces dynamics, and landscape fragmentation metrics are used to characterise structural changes. The Ecosystem Vigor Index (EVI) is derived from four spectral indices (Normalised Difference Vegetation Index, Normalised Difference Water Index, Normalised Difference Built-up Index, and Modified Bare Soil Index), and the Ecosystem Structure Index (ESI) is derived from landscape shape, connectivity, and heterogeneity indices using FRAGSTAT v4.2.1. The results showed noticeable decreases in green and blue spaces over the past three decades, along with increased fragmentation, particularly in the periphery of the city. These indicators can help assess ecosystem health, provide evidence-based data to improve it, and support effective governance of green and blue spaces in Varanasi city.

31.title: Mapping Cumulative Anthropogenic Pressures in the Marine Environment of Cyprus: A High-Resolution Modeling Approach Using GIS and Python
31.abstract:
The coastal and marine zone of Cyprus is under increasing pressure from multiple anthropogenic activities, making the accurate spatial assessment of their impacts imperative. This study presents a comprehensive Cumulative Impact Assessment (CIA) methodology for Cypriot marine ecosystems, building upon the established Halpern model. The objective is the high-resolution mapping of environmental degradation hotspots by integrating advanced Geographic Information Systems (ArcGIS Pro) techniques with programming algorithms (Python, GeoPandas).

Spatial analysis was conducted across three grid scales (1x1km, 500x500m, and 250x250m resolutions), examining the interactions between diverse anthropogenic pressures (e.g., shipping, port facilities, aquaculture, military operations) and sensitive marine habitats, with a focus on Posidonia meadows (Seagrass), Reefs, and MSFD Benthic Broad Habitat Types (BBHT). The geospatial data was subsequently fed into a custom Python script, which applied a specific vulnerability matrix to compute the final CIA index.

The results highlight areas of maximum accumulated pressure in Cypriot waters, providing a realistic and quantified representation of the environmental status. To facilitate broad accessibility and practical decision-making, the final research outcomes have been visualized and integrated into an interactive web application. The proposed methodology offers a powerful, scientifically validated decision-support tool, directly applicable to Marine Spatial Planning (MSP) for the sustainable management of Cyprus's marine environment.

32.title: Assessment of road network connectivity using GIS-based spatial analysis to enhance organized preventive evacuation planning.
32.abstract:
The climate crisis and the escalating frequency of natural disasters necessitate a comprehensive reassessment of civil protection strategies, especially in regions facing demographic pressure driven by tourism in both urban and insular environments. This influx of visitors, coupled with spatial heterogeneity, exacerbates the challenges of timely and efficient evacuation during emergencies such as seismic events, wildfires, or floods. Consequently, the formulation of targeted preventive measures and adaptive evacuation scenarios has become more critical than ever.
This study leverages GIS capabilities and spatial network analysis to evaluate road topology as a pivotal factor in evacuation efficacy. The research aims to establish an integrated geospatial framework for assessing accessibility to emergency shelters, grounded in fundamental metrics such as intersection density, clustering coefficients, link-node ratios, and the distribution of Points of Interest (POIs).
Utilizing spatial modeling within a GIS environment, the study investigates how intersection density modulates evacuation dynamics by offering redundant routing options. Concurrently, clustering analysis identifies zones of high local connectivity that bolster resilience at the neighborhood scale. Furthermore, the interplay between links and nodes is employed to map network permeability, pinpointing critical bottlenecks and culdesacs that impede the flow of civilians and emergency response units.
The application of GIS facilitates the precise spatial pinpointing of network vulnerabilities and their spatial correlation with shelter locations. The findings indicate that geospatial connectivity analysis enables dynamic population rerouting and the prioritization of structural interventions. The study culminates in specific policy recommendations for refining civil protection protocols, proposing a robust decision-making tool to enhance urban safety and preparedness against emergencies.

32.title: Estimating care and support needs of older people at the small-area level: The case of Athens

authors.name: Alexandros Alexiou
authors.affiliation: Panteion University of Social and Political Sciences

authors.name: Angelos Mimis
authors.affiliation: Panteion University of Social and Political Sciences

authors.name: Thomas Georgiadis
authors.affiliation: Panteion University of Social and Political Sciences

32.abstract:
Population ageing poses significant challenges for health and social care planning, particularly when policy decisions require granular, sub-national data that national surveys rarely provide. This study addresses the data gap by generating high-resolution, small-area estimates of care and support needs among older people in Athens.
We draw on data from the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), alongside the decennial Census of the population to produce neighbourhood-level estimates of local need. Iterative Proportional Fitting (IPF) is employed to construct synthetic populations whose sociodemographic profiles are constrained to match census track records. We apply spatial microsimulation techniques in order to estimate neighbourhood-level values of health and care indicators, such as limitations in daily activities, out-of-pocket care expenses, and perceived physical and mental health.
We combine indicators and construct a multi-dimensional index, describing care and support needs among local older populations. We map results and explore resulting patterns, illustrating the intra-urban variation presented. We further analyse results by exploring the relationships between the observed level of need and sociodemographic characteristics of neighbourhoods.
This work carries important implications for policy, particular within local government contexts. Local decision-making requires access to granular data for effective policy planning, and the resulting heterogeneity across neighbourhoods underscores the limitations of aggregate-level planning approaches. High-resolution care need estimates can be leveraged for more efficient resource allocation, targeted service delivery, and inform overall local government strategies, enabling authorities to identify priority areas, and plan interventions accordingly.

32.title: DigiFarm: Covering the digital training needs of agricultural advisors in Europe

authors.name: Alessandro Lachetti
authors.affiliation: Confagricoltura – General Confederation of Italian Agriculture

authors.name: Diofantos Hadjimitsis
authors.affiliation: Eratosthenes Centre of Excellence / Cyprus University of Technology (CUT)

authors.name: Menelaos Stavrinides
authors.affiliation: Eratosthenes Centre of Excellence / Cyprus University of Technology (CUT)

32.abstract: With the development and expansion of smart and/or digital farming, geoinformatics is becoming increasingly central to agriculture. Yet, the effective uptake of Earth Observation, spatial data, sensors and decision-support tools into everyday farm practices remains slow and uneven. DigiFarm, an Erasmus+ project, addresses this gap by developing an open online training programme targeted to agricultural advisors, designed to strengthen spatial intelligence, digital literacy and sustainability-oriented advisory capacity. Building on a previous needs assessment of agricultural advisors in four European countries (Cyprus, Greece, Italy and Ireland) and on an extensive review of 26 existing digital-agriculture training initiatives/ courses, we present the development of DigiFarm’s modular training scenarios through the Cultivate Academy e-learning platform. The programme is organised around four interconnected modules: remote sensing technologies and applications; tools and data for smart farming; green and soft skills; and business development for digital agriculture. These modules place GIS, satellite imagery, sensor data, farm-management systems and decision-support workflows within real advisory contexts. Our pedagogical approach combines self-paced online learning, scenario-based examples, interactive quizzes, certification and quality-assurance indicators, and is aligned with vocational and adult-learning principles. We place emphasis on translating spatial and environmental data into practical recommendations concerning crop monitoring, phenology, soil and water conditions, resource efficiency, climate adaptation, and farm-level decision making. A common thread linking the modules of the programme is the integration of ethics-and-society concerns. This addresses data governance, trust in recommendations, digital tool access inequalities, AI and transparency, and the social role of advisors as mediators between technological innovation and farmers’ situated knowledge. By embedding these issues within geoinformatics training, DigiFarm frames spatial intelligence as a socially accountable advisory practice and not merely as a technical competence. We argue that this type of capacity-building is essential for useful and responsible geospatial applications in European agriculture.

32.title: Mapping Apartment Housing in the Eastern Mediterranean

authors.name: Athanasios V. Argyriou
authors.affiliation: Institute for Mediterranean Studies, Foundation for Research and Technology-Hellas, 74131 Rethymno, Greece

authors.name: Konstantina Kalfa
authors.affiliation: Institute for Mediterranean Studies, Foundation for Research and Technology-Hellas, 74131 Rethymno, Greece

authors.name: Angelos Hliaoutakis
authors.affiliation: Institute for Mediterranean Studies, Foundation for Research and Technology-Hellas, 74131 Rethymno, Greece

authors.name: Nikos Papadopoulos
authors.affiliation: Institute for Mediterranean Studies, Foundation for Research and Technology-Hellas, 74131 Rethymno, Greece

32.abstract: This research is part of the ERC-funded project MCH-EsMed: How the Middle Class Housed Itself in the Eastern Mediterranean, based at IMS, FORTH, which explores how inhabitants, in key Eastern Mediterranean cities, located themselves in the building environment and constructed their ordinary apartment buildings. Most of these cities are dominated by common apartment buildings, not grand landmarks, indicating the type of residential structures most people actually live. Examining the emergence and formation of such buildings requires analyzing large amounts of data collected during long periods of time, since thousands of contractors, architects, developers and residents all were actively involved in shaping the urban landscape. This study highlights the methodological framework to study this process utilizing GIS and other geospatial approaches. Using untapped demolition and building permit data, a combination of digital tools (GIS, photogrammetry) and traditional tools (censuses, surveys, aerial photography) was employed. Through these methods we can visualize and analyze the spread of apartment buildings over time, identify the contractors and key actors involved in their construction, and trace the architects who signed these permits. By bringing all of this together, what once appeared as an anonymous collection of identical buildings starts to reveal identifiable patterns, processes, and agents. It is possible to identify who build what, where and when by answering the following so far unaddressed questions: how was the wealth of the housing market in these cities distributed? Were there monopolies? What were the main strategies of developers in these real estate markets? Only by leveraging, we suggest, large-scale data in an iterative process can be meaningfully to understand how the Eastern Mediterranean cities were produced.

32.title: Unknown Ownership as a Spatial Indicator of Territorial Abandonment: Evidence from the Hellenic Cadastre

authors.name: Sevasti Chalkidou
authors.affiliation: School of Rural and Surveying Engineering, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki

authors.name: Konstantinos Tsiouplakis
authors.affiliation: School of Rural and Surveying Engineering, Aristostle University of Thessaloniki

authors.name: Angeliki Tsorlini
authors.affiliation: School of Rural and Surveying Engineering, Aristostle University of Thessaloniki

authors.name: Themistoklis Roustanis
authors.affiliation: School of Rural and Surveying Engineering, Aristostle University of Thessaloniki

32.abstract: Cadastral registration in Greece was designed to produce a definitive record of property rights. It also produced an unintended, geographically uneven map of properties for which no one submitted valid tenure documentation. These "unknown ownership" entries are not randomly distributed. Their concentration at the municipal and regional level tracks patterns of rural depopulation, inheritance fragmentation, and the long absence of formal property documentation in peripheral areas. This paper treats unknown ownership as a spatial proxy for territorial abandonment. The analysis is based on the spatial data infrastructure of the Hellenic Cadastre (Ktimatologio) to calculate unknown-ownership shares for each administrative unit and to map the resulting concentrations. These patterns are then overlaid with CORINE Land Cover data to examine whether unknown ownership clusters disproportionately occur on agricultural and forest land, where property values are lower and incentives for formal registration are weaker. Census population data are integrated to test the association between unknown-ownership rates and demographic decline. Sequence matters here. Urban areas were surveyed first; rural and semi-urban areas came last. Recently surveyed non-urban zones are therefore expected to exhibit higher unknown-ownership rates, partly as an artefact of the cadastral process itself rather than ownership conditions alone. The paper also examines the structural reasons behind non-registration. In many rural areas, property deeds simply do not exist. Inheritance chains remain unresolved across generations. Informal tenure persists. And a problem that receives too little attention: the chronic lack of geometric documentation means that owners may hold a valid deed, yet cannot locate their property on a map. Ownership without spatial identity, in cadastral terms, amounts to no ownership at all. The findings speak to land governance failures and the geography of institutional neglect across southern Europe.

32.title: Mapping dissolved oxygen (DO) spatial distribution of coastal aquaculture environment based on remotely sensed data and machine learning algorithm
32.abstract: Monitoring dissolved oxygen (DO) in marine environments where aquaculture operates is crucial for ensuring aquaculture productivity and preserving the ecological status of the surrounding ecosystem. This study aims to present and evaluate a methodological approach for predicting DO in a semi-enclosed cove, where floating cage farming is carried out. It integrates in situ measurements and remotely sensed data to develop a machine learning regression model. The study area is located in the southeastern part of Pagasitikos Gulf (Eastern Mediterranean). Surface DO measurements were carried out over six seasons, between summer 2021 and spring 2024, recording 152 measurements in total, using a CTD (Seabird-19plus). Atmospherically corrected Multispectral Sentinel-2 MSI images were selected close to the sampling dates. Based on the coordinates received during sampling, pixel-to-point matching was performed, and remote sensing reflectance (Rrs) was extracted using SNAP (v.13.0). A selected number of bands from the satellite data was imperative for applying machine learning models to remove collinearity. For this purpose, two criteria were utilized: (a) the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF ≤ 10) index and (b) the correlation coefficient (rho) between spectral bands and DO, using IBM SPSS Statistics (v.31). The support vector regression (SVR) model was developed using the Python scikit-learn library with 5-fold cross-validation. SVR was selected as it demonstrates better performance compared to other regression-based machine learning (ML) models and neural network (NN) architectures under limited data availability. The SVR was trained using five of the six sampling campaigns. The remaining season was utilized for validation, comparing the actual in situ measurements with the extracted predicted values. The model performance was examined with different statistical indices. The resulting map shows the spatial distribution of DO across the entire study area. This approach could serve as a basis for the systematic monitoring of DO in coastal aquaculture environment.

32.title: Spatial Analysis and Local AI for Smart City Digital Twins: A Framework for Real-Time Urban Risk Monitoring

authors.name: Dimitris Kavroudakis
authors.affiliation: University of the Aegean, Department of Geography

32.abstract:
Compound risks are growing in urban environments: infrastructure strain, crowd pressure, microclimate variability and operational disruptions. City planners need evidence-based, real-time tools to promote resilience and adaptive management. In this paper we propose a smart city framework that integrates IoT sensing, local (on-premise) AI for time series anomaly detection, spatial analytics, and Digital Twin models for enhanced urban monitoring and decision making.
The framework assumes the deployment of IoT devices in urban spaces to capture variables such as temperature, humidity, CO2, vibration and population density. Data is sent in near real-time with lightweight protocols and stored locally in time-series and GIS-enabled spatial databases. A local-first architecture provides low latency, operational autonomy, and satisfies data governance and privacy requirements.
We formulate an end-to-end anomaly detection pipeline that includes data ingestion, data validation, pre-processing, feature engineering, and model inference. It allows for different analytical approaches, from statistical baselines to machine learning and neural models (e.g. autoencoders, LSTM) to detect complex and non-linear patterns in urban dynamics.
Anomaly outputs are integrated in a Digital Twin environment, combining 3D visualizations of buildings or districts with dynamic layers, such as environmental conditions, mobility flows and scenario simulations. Spatial AI methods (e.g., spatio-temporal clustering, hotspot detection) translate anomalies into actionable insights such as risk maps and vulnerability indices.
In general, the framework allows smart city management to transition from reactive monitoring to predictive, interpretable decision support, allowing early warning systems, optimized urban operations, and better resilience planning.

32.title: A Geospatial Data Integration Framework for Urban Mobility Analysis in Small Island Cities: The Case of Mytilene, Greece

authors.name: Nikoleta-Nefeli Kofou
authors.affiliation: Laboratory of Spatial Analysis Geographic Information Systems and Remote Sensing (SAGISRS), Department of Geography, University of the Aegean, University Hill, 81100 Mytilene, Greece

authors.name: Dimitris Kavroudakis
authors.affiliation: University of the Aegean, Department of Geography

32.abstract:
Urban mobility analysis increasingly relies on the integration of heterogeneous geospatial datasets that describe the physical structure, functional characteristics, and population dynamics of cities. However, in many small island cities, mobility research is constrained by fragmented datasets, limited availability of traffic information, and the absence of integrated geospatial data infrastructures. These limitations hinder the systematic analysis of urban mobility patterns and the development of evidence-based planning strategies.
This study proposes a geospatial data integration framework designed to support urban mobility analysis in small island cities. The framework combines multiple spatial datasets, including road network topology, pedestrian infrastructure, land use distribution, population patterns, and mobility-related observations, within a unified GIS environment. By harmonizing data from different sources and spatial resolutions, the proposed approach enables the creation of a comprehensive geospatial database suitable for advanced spatial analysis.
The methodological workflow includes spatial data preprocessing, network structuring, attribute harmonization, and the integration of spatial indicators that describe accessibility, connectivity, and urban activity patterns. The framework is applied to the island city of Mytilene (Lesvos, Greece), a representative example of a small island urban system characterized by spatial constraints and heterogeneous mobility dynamics.
By addressing challenges related to data fragmentation and interoperability, the study contributes to the development of geoinformatics methodologies for urban mobility research and demonstrates how integrated geospatial data infrastructures can enhance spatial intelligence applications in urban analysis and planning.

32.title: Optimizing Spatial Decision-Making: Integrating Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) and GIS for Robust Site Selection

authors.name: Vasiliki Konstantinidou
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

32.abstract: Contemporary spatial planning faces the challenge of balancing economic goals with environmental and social needs. This paper presents an application that combines Geographic Information Systems (GIS) with Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) to provide a clear and scientific way to select the best possible sites for specific land uses. The methodology focuses on a screening stage that uses Boolean logic to apply "hard constraints" - such as legal restrictions and safety zones. This process effectively filters out unsuitable areas, leaving only the land that meets all necessary requirements. Within this framework, the criteria are evaluated to ensure the final decision is logical, consistent, and mathematically sound. This approach is demonstrated through a case study in Naxos, Greece. The analysis incorporates various parameters, including administrative boundaries, proximity to infrastructure, urban patterns, and environmental zones like NATURA 2000. Using official open data (from ELSTAT, GET SDI Portal, and Corine Land Cover), the entire workflow is automated within ArcGIS Pro using ModelBuilder to ensure the process is fast and easy to repeat. Ultimately, the results show that the combination of MCDA and GIS provides a reliable way for stakeholders to make objective, data-driven spatial decisions instead of relying on subjective judgment.

32.title: Assessment of urban green spaces and development of a vegetation cooling index using PRISMA hyperspectral data
32.abstract: The management of urban ecosystems is a critical challenge in today's geographical research to ensure the quality of life in cities. Climate change and the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect are changing the microclimate, making it essential to accurately map vegetation. This study focuses on Heraklion, Crete, a typical Mediterranean island city that experiences intense heat and persistent drought during the summer. This study aims to propose a methodology for assessing vegetation conditions and recommending targeted cooling measures. To this end, hyperspectral data from the PRISMA satellite were used for two dates (at the beginning and the end of summer). After preprocessing, the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) was applied to detect pixel density of vegetation, as well as the Normalized Difference Infrared Index (NDII) utilizing NIR (820nm) and SWIR (1650nm) bands, to assess the water status and health of the plants. Next, using the Linear Spectral Unmixing (LSU) method, density maps were created for five categories (ground, buildings, roads, water, vegetation). Finally, a cooling index was developed as the combination of vegetation density and vegetation health. The analysis revealed a significant deterioration in terms of health and a decline in the presence of vegetation during the summer months. In late summer, the number of pixels identified as “live vegetation” decreased significantly (~6.3 hectares), while those requiring immediate care increased, indicating severe dehydration. The study's findings highlight the fragility of urban green spaces under Mediterranean drought conditions. The resulting “Red Alert” map serves as a valuable decision-making tool for urban planners and stakeholders. As it is based on satellite data and vegetation indices, this methodology can be easily applied to any comparable urban center in the Mediterranean or Southern Europe facing similar climate challenges.

32.title: Immersive Geovisualization of the Moria Refugee Camp in Virtual Enviroments
32.abstract:
The aim of this study is to present the development of a digital twin of the Moria Refugee Camp on Lesvos Island, Greece, documenting its spatial transformation from 2017 to 2026 as an educational tool to enhance students understanding of spatial change in territories through geovisualization. Even though recent developments in geospatial technologies, digital twins, and immersive environments are available, there is still limited research concerning geovisualization methods for the effective representation of such complex spatiotemporal datasets. The Moria Refugee Camp is a suitable case for investigation, as it constitutes a dynamic case study characterized by continuous spatial transformations, shifting configurations, and changing land-use patterns over time.

An innovative methodology was developed, integrating: 1. high-resolution UAV imagery and 360° panoramas, 2. image-based 3D modelling techniques, and 3. immersive visualization approaches. To represent the temporal evolution of the refugee camp, separate reconstructions corresponding to selected years between 2017 and 2026 were created and implemented within a game-engine environment. Due to restricted access during earlier operational phases of the camp, systematic field-based data collection was not feasible. To address this limitation, archival aerial imagery and journalistic visual material were additionally utilized to approximate the spatial organization and infrastructure density of earlier periods.

The resulting application provides an immersive environment which allows users to navigate through the Moria Camp spatiotemporally. It allows the users to select different temporal stages in the evolution of the Moria camp and it can assist as a visual and conceptual aid towards the understanding of the concept and phenomenon of territorialization. Particularly, how state policies and practices organize space in order to control movements of people. Moreover, to assess the interaction of the above with the initiatives and actions of different organizations, asylum seekers and refugees in shaping the reality of space, power relations and human movements.

32.title: A Methodological Framework for Assessing Tourism Hotspots at Fire and/or Flood Risk – Implementation in Four Greek Islands

authors.name: Angeliki Papazoglou
authors.affiliation: Dept. of Geography and Regional Planning, School of Rural, Surveying and Geoinformatics Engineering, National Technical University of Athens

authors.name: Anastasia Stratigea
authors.affiliation: Dept. of Geography and Regional Planning, School of Rural, Surveying and Geoinformatics Engineering, National Technical University of Athens

32.abstract: In the Climate Change (CC) era, frequency and intensity of wildfire and flood occurrences are predicted to further amplify, resulting in severe socio-economic and environmental implications for the affected areas. Repercussions of such occurrences are expected to be more intense in the Mediterranean highly-urbanized, tourist-overloaded insular territories, highlighting the necessity for proactive –e.g. local/regional plans, land use etc.– but also reactive planning –e.g. Disaster Management Plans – in, mainly, tourism overloaded areas. In both proactive and reactive planning, efforts have to be carried out on the ground of the combined assessment/mapping of tourism hotspots and the spatially-defined fire/flood risk. In order for such a task to be accomplished, this work develops a framework for identifying tourism hotspot zones that are prone to fire and/or flood risk; and implements this framework in four Greek islands – Evia, Lesvos, Chios and Rhodes – as examples of different types of Mediterranean insular territories, exposed to both CC and (over)tourism. This framework integrates: i) a pool of fifteen literature-based, wildfire-related subcriteria that fall into four major criteria/factors, i.e. Topography, Climate, Environment and Urban Space, and are used as input to the Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) for producing, with the support of the Geographical Information Systems (GIS), Fire Risk maps for the study areas; ii) burned areas in the study islands in the time span 2000-2024 for validating fire risk assessments; iii) the officially-delineated flood-prone zones for identifying flood risk in the areas at hand; iv) tourist hotspots in the study regions, identified by means of tourist accommodation distribution. Results obtained by implementation of this framework demonstrate the urgent need for setting up proactive/reactive strategies/plans since coastal urban sprawl due to tourism pressure in the studied islands is steadily leading to the expansion of built up space in areas of high fire and/or flooding risk.

32.title: Urban Informatics for Spatial Inequality: Making 3D Land Administration Accessible for Mapping Vertical Environmental Injustice
32.abstract:
Keywords: 3D Land Administration; LADM Edition II; Vertical Inequality; Urban Informatics; Spatial Justice; Environmental Justice; Voxel-Based Models;

Traditionally, geoinformatics has focused on horizontal analysis at the neighborhood level, often overlooking how environmental factors such as air pollution fluctuate between different building floors. This study introduces a new workflow that connects geographic theory with practical technology by shifting from broad area analysis to detailed, parcel level assessment. Using the updated ISO 19152:2024 standard (LADM Edition II), we present a 3D Land Administration framework that incorporates atmospheric data directly into property records.
Our approach uses high resolution 3D models of city structures and voxel-based pollutant dispersion models to measure air quality within dense urban areas. A voxel is a three dimensional unit, much like a digital building block that allows for detailed mapping of pollution as it moves and accumulates in the air. These models simulate the flow of pollutants through each "block," helping planners understand which parts of buildings or floors are most affected.
By integrating these environmental datasets with the Unique Immovable Property Number (KAEK), the official cadastral identifier, we identify systematic vertical inequalities. In Athens, Greece, a city of dense apartment blocks, residents on lower floors typically experience poorer air quality due to pollutants trapped at street level within urban canyons. The implementation of a 3D Cadastre by authorities facilitates the identification of affected floors and the subsequent implementation of targeted interventions, such as enhanced air filtration, with the objective of reducing exposure. This framework transforms the Cadastre from a static registry into a dynamic tool for Spatial Intelligence. This approach ultimately empowers stakeholders to identify and address hidden vertical disparities, thereby upholding the "Environmental Right to the City" and promoting fair urban planning for all.

32.title: Towards Alternative Indicators of Touristification: An Approach based on GeoAI and ML
32.abstract: This study presents a reproducible GeoAI-based framework for detecting and spatially analyzing swimming pools as proxy indicators of touristification in tourism-intensive island environments. The methodology combines pre-trained and custom-trained deep learning models optimized for small-object detection in high-resolution imagery, enabling automated, large-scale extraction of swimming pool features across Rhodes, Greece, for the period 2017–2024. Spatiotemporal analysis of the detected pools reveals a significant increase in their total number over the study period, with expansion extending well beyond established coastal resort zones into semi-rural and inland areas — a pattern that mirrors broader tourism and accommodation growth. To assess the touristic character of this expansion, detected pools are spatially associated with hotel and short-term rental locations; results confirm strong proximity, indicating that pool proliferation is predominantly tourism-driven. Further spatial analysis identifies considerable overlap between pool concentrations and active private groundwater extraction points, suggesting that tourism-induced landscape transformation is directly intensifying pressure on the island's already scarce freshwater resources. The study's principal contribution lies in documenting the intensification of touristification across Rhodes through the spatial diffusion of swimming pools, while addressing a methodological gap in Tourism Studies by demonstrating how GeoAI-derived datasets can serve as a foundation for spatial intelligence workflows that support environmental monitoring and the identification of touristification processes. Given the post-COVID rebound of tourism with limited sustainability transitions, and amid growing concerns over global freshwater depletion, the proposed framework offers a transferable approach applicable to other socio-spatial contexts facing analogous pressures.

32.title: Integrating Disaster Event Records and Earth Observation Data: A Geospatial Database for Spatial Intelligence in Southern Europe

authors.name: Olga Roussou
authors.affiliation: University of the Aegean, Department of Geography

authors.name: Kiosa Irint
authors.affiliation: University of the Aegean, Department of Geography

authors.name: Eftychia Sorligka
authors.affiliation: University of the Aegean, Department of Geography

32.abstract:
A complex panorama of natural hazards, including wildfires, floods, heatwaves, earthquakes and landslides, is increasingly prevalent in Southern Europe. However, effective disaster management is often constrained by fragmented and heterogeneous datasets.
