Global databases such as EM-DAT provide essential standardized information on disaster types and impacts, yet they frequently exhibit significant temporal and spatial gaps, particularly for localized or small-scale catastrophes. To address these limitations, this study proposes a geoinformatics framework for the development of an extensive geospatial database of natural disasters in the Mediterranean region.
The proposed methodology adopts a multi-source data fusion approach, integrating high-resolution satellite-derived datasets from NASA, harmonized infrastructure datasets, and official event records from EM-DAT. The study improves the geographical completeness of traditional records by utilizing Earth observation (EO) data, enabling more accurate identification of the extent and frequency of hazard events. A strict harmonization and integrated process carried out in a PostgreSQL/PostGIS environment, that guarantees consistency across many spatial reference systems, temporal resolutions, and danger classification methods, is essential to this strategy.
The resulting geodatabase highlights the critical role of geoinformatics in standardizing disaster records and serves as a critical decision-support tool. It facilitates multi-hazard risk assessment, supports climate change adaptation strategies, and provides the spatial intelligence required for evidence-based urban planning and cross-border emergency management in Southern Europe. Overall, the study presents a scalable framework for improving disaster data integration, enhancing vulnerability analysis, and strengthening disaster resilience across the region.

32.title: Time Series Analysis in Geographical Data: (Seasonality) and (Cyclicality)

authors.name: Nikolaos Sorkos
authors.affiliation: Laboratory of Spatial Analysis Geographic Information Systems and Remote Sensing (SAGISRS), Department of Geography, University of the Aegean, University Hill, 81100 Mytilene, Greece

authors.name: Nikoleta-Nefeli Kofou
authors.affiliation: Laboratory of Spatial Analysis Geographic Information Systems and Remote Sensing (SAGISRS), Department of Geography, University of the Aegean, University Hill, 81100 Mytilene, Greece

authors.name: Dimitris Kavroudakis
authors.affiliation: University of the Aegean, Department of Geography

32.abstract: This study aims to analyze the time series of the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) using the technical analysis indicators MACD (Moving Average Convergence Divergence) and RSI (Relative Strength Index), with the objective of detecting, identifying, and interpreting changes in vegetation dynamics during the five-year period 2018–2022. The research was conducted in the selected study area through the utilization of high spatial and temporal resolution satellite data obtained from the Sentinel-2 platform, enabling the monitoring of vegetation dynamics at both seasonal and multi-annual temporal scales.The methodological approach was initially based on the calculation of mean monthly NDVI values for the study period, followed by the application of the MACD and RSI indicators in order to examine the temporal variability of vegetation. Specifically, the MACD indicator was employed to identify turning points and shifts in vegetation dynamics through the convergence and divergence between moving averages, while the RSI indicator was applied to capture the intensity and rate of change of NDVI values, allowing the distinction between periods of vegetation strengthening (increased greenness) and weakening (reduced greenness).The results demonstrate the effectiveness of both indicators in the temporal monitoring of vegetation and their ability to capture variations primarily associated with the seasonal and cyclical behavior of vegetation. The MACD proved to be more effective in identifying long-term trends and points of trend reversal, whereas the RSI showed greater sensitivity in detecting short-term fluctuations and distinguishing periods of relatively strong or weak vegetation activity. Overall, the findings indicate that technical analysis indicators such as MACD and RSI can provide a complementary and innovative approach to the analysis of vegetation time series. Their application to satellite-derived and geospatial data contributes to a better understanding of NDVI temporal patterns, particularly in relation to seasonality and cyclicality, and supports the interpretation of vegetation dynamics over time.

32.title: Geospatial Analysis of the Energy Landscape in the European Union with emphasis on Electricity
32.abstract:
The ongoing energy crisis and the transition towards sustainable energy systems have highlighted the need for comprehensive spatial analysis of energy patterns across the European Union (EU). This study presents a geospatial approach to evaluating the energy landscape of EU member states, with a particular emphasis on electricity.

The main objective of this research is to identify spatial patterns and disparities in energy production, consumption, and efficiency, and to propose a representative energy model that could guide future policy decisions. The study integrates multiple datasets from international energy organizations and statistical sources, incorporating key indicators such as energy intensity, electricity production by source, and the contribution of fossil fuels and renewable energy.

A Geographic Information Systems (GIS)-based methodology is applied to process, analyze, and visualize the data. Spatial indicators are developed to enable comparative evaluation among EU countries. The results are presented through thematic maps and statistical visualizations, allowing for a clear interpretation of spatial trends and temporal variations.

The analysis reveals significant differences in energy profiles across member states, reflecting diverse economic structures, policy frameworks, and levels of energy transition. By evaluating these differences, the study identifies best-performing countries and highlights potential pathways for improving energy efficiency and sustainability across the EU.

The research contributes to the field of geoinformatics by demonstrating the value of spatial analysis in understanding complex energy systems. Furthermore, it provides a decision-support framework for policymakers, supporting the development of a more integrated and sustainable European energy strategy.

32.title: A Spatiotemporal Pipeline for Detecting and Visualizing PM2.5 Pollution Events Using Low-Cost Sensors

authors.name: Martin Dolejš
authors.affiliation: Jan Evangelista Purkyně University in Ústí nad Labem

authors.name: Dimitris Kavroudakis
authors.affiliation: University of the Aegean, Department of Geography

32.abstract:
Urban growth has made air quality issues harder to overlook, especially in dense cities where emissions tend to build up rather than disperse. That shift seems to place new pressure on monitoring systems, not only to collect data but also to interpret it quickly enough to flag meaningful pollution episodes. This study focuses on Athens, Greece, using hourly PM2.5 data collected through a network of low-cost sensors. While these sensors are becoming more widespread, integrating their data into a consistent analytical workflow is still not straightforward. Despite the volume of available data, there is no widely used framework that combines cleaning, event detection, and spatial analysis at a fine temporal scale, which can limit how effectively the data is used. The approach developed here includes preprocessing, event detection, and spatiotemporal analysis. Between 2018 and 2022, more than 400 pollution events were identified. Many of these occurred during winter evenings and are likely linked to residential heating, along with atmospheric conditions such as temperature inversions. The framework does appear to capture large-scale events as well, including the wildfires in August 2021. Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) was used to estimate pollution levels between sensor locations. Tracking the movement of event centroids provided a way to examine how these episodes expand, shift, or dissipate over time. While this method involves certain assumptions (for example, IDW may smooth local extremes), it offers a useful representation of spatial dynamics.
Taken together, the results suggest that low-cost sensor networks, when handled carefully, can yield fairly detailed and reliable insights into urban air quality. They are perhaps best understood as a complementary layer, which adds granularity and responsiveness. With further refinement, the framework could be adapted for near real-time use, potentially informing local environmental management and public health responses.

33.title: An Engineering Approach to Environmental Resource Assessment and interactive web-based Geospatial Communication: The Case of Nisyros Geopark

authors.name: Varvara Antoniou
authors.affiliation: National Technical University of Athens/School of Rural, Surveying and Geoinformatics Engineering/Laboratory of Physical Geography and Environmental Impacts

authors.name: Maria Papadopoulou
authors.affiliation: National Technical University of Athens/School of Rural, Surveying and Geoinformatics Engineering/Laboratory of Physical Geography and Environmental Impacts

33.abstract:
Understanding the environment as an integrated system of natural and human resources is a key requirement for engineering practice, yet environmental interpretation often remains descriptive rather than analytical. This paper proposes an engineering-oriented approach to the assessment and communication of environmental resources, combining structured evaluation with map-based documentation and public-oriented communication.
The proposed framework is based on the identification, description, and prioritization of environmental resources in terms of their significance, constraints, and development potential, under the additional pressure of the climate crisis. Emphasis is placed on the use of geospatial information not for advanced spatial analysis, but as a means to support interpretation, substantiate evaluation, and organize environmental knowledge within a system-oriented perspective.
A central component of the approach is results communication to non-specialist audiences. Interactive, web-based geospatial environments, such as Story Maps, are used to translate complex environmental information into accessible spatial narratives, enabling user engagement and exploration, while bridging the gap between expert knowledge and public understanding.
The methodology is demonstrated through the case study of Nisyros, a UNESCO Global Geopark. The island provides a representative environment where diverse natural and human resources can be examined in relation to geomorphological processes, volcanic activity, and climate-related pressures. The case study illustrates how the proposed framework can be applied in practice, supporting both structured environmental assessment and effective communication.
Implemented within an educational context, the approach supports place-based learning and the development of environmental narratives grounded in spatial evidence. The paper contributes to current discussions in geography and engineering education by linking environmental analysis with communication practices and societal relevance.

33.title: Web Application for Multivariate Visualization of the Coastal Vulnerability Index

authors.name: Margarita Kokla
authors.affiliation: National Technical University of Athens / School of Rural, Surveying and Geoinformatics Engineering

authors.name: Dimitrios Vasilelis
authors.affiliation: National Technical University of Athens / School of Rural, Surveying and Geoinformatics Engineering

authors.name: Loukas Katikas
authors.affiliation: National Technical University of Athens / School of Rural, Surveying and Geoinformatics Engineering

33.abstract:
The coastal zone constitutes one of the most dynamic and complex geographical environments, concentrating intense human activity, rich ecosystems, and significant infrastructure. In recent years, due to climate change, sea-level rise, and increasing pressure from human interventions, the issue of coastal vulnerability has come to the forefront, leading to a wide range of scientific studies and applications focusing on the identification, prediction, and management of the impacts of these phenomena.
Within this context, the assessment and mapping of coastal vulnerability constitute a critical issue, both for the protection of human societies and economic activities and for the preservation of natural heritage. This study focuses on calculating and mapping the Coastal Vulnerability Index (CVI) for the island of Lesvos to evaluate the vulnerability of its coastline. Three different spatial analysis methods were applied: a fine-resolution fishnet grid (200m x 200m), a coarser fishnet grid (1,000m x 1,000m), and a transect-based approach. The analysis incorporated eight critical variables that significantly influence coastal vulnerability. Results highlighted specific coastal segments with high and low vulnerability, while comparisons among the methods revealed important differences in spatial accuracy and level of detail.
In addition, an interactive web mapping application was developed using the Mapbox platform, integrating the outputs of all three methods. The application visualizes the CVI and its underlying parameters and provides tools for data filtering, thematic analysis, and comparison of different spatial datasets. Moreover, the application’s interactive environment facilitates a deeper understanding of coastal vulnerability at both the island-wide scale of Lesvos and the local scale of individual coastal segments. By enabling dynamic visualization, thematic exploration, and comparative spatial analysis, the platform supports informed decision-making and contributes to the development of well-founded conclusions for the effective management of the study area.

33.title: Web mapping and open satellite data for associating crop drought stress with fire severity assessment
33.abstract:
As the frequency of climate-related environmental disasters increases, the need for accessible geospatial intelligence becomes vital for effective land management and disaster response. This study presents a practical workflow for developing a WebGIS prototype that incorporates satellite data into a functional decision-making tool. By leveraging open-access multispectral imagery from the Sentinel-2 satellite, the proposed system offers a comprehensive approach to crop health monitoring, combining continuous monitoring of water stress with the subsequent assessment of fire damage.
The methodology relies on the processing of spectral indices within the QGIS environment. Specifically, the platform visualizes spatial patterns of crop vigor and water stress through indices like NDVI and NDWI, enabling the detection of areas requiring irrigation or intervention. Additionally, the dNBR index is used to generate detailed damage assessment maps, which categorize prone areas into different severity levels providing a clear overview of a fire’s impact. The core innovation of the study lies in the integration of these complex datasets into a simplified web interface. This allows users without specialized knowledge to monitor environmental risks, such as crop drought or fire damage, using an interactive map.
By using open-source software and publicly available data, the system ensures broad applicability, for various areas of interest and time periods. The results demonstrate that the combination of satellite remote sensing and web-based mapping can bridge the gap between research and practice. Ultimately, this tool helps small farmers as well as larger agricultural communities make evidence-based decisions by providing easy access to accurate maps and supporting them address contemporary environmental risks.

33.title: A Methodology for Determining Prospective Hazard Interactions through Spatio-Temporal Dependency Graphs

authors.name: Michail-Christos Tsoutsos
authors.affiliation: • School of Rural, Surveying and Geoinformatics Engineering, National Technical University of Athens, National Observatory of Athens,

authors.name: Vassilios Vescoukis
authors.affiliation: School of Rural, Surveying and Geoinformatics Engineering, National Technical University of Athens, 9 Iroon Polytechneiou Street, Zographos, 15780 Athens, Greece

33.abstract:
Hazard interactions are increasingly recognized as a central component of Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR), due to their unforeseen and amplified consequences. Different types of interdependency networks exist, particularly when a secondary hazard is triggered immediately after a primary event, manifests in the aftermath through increased probability induced by the primary event, or occurs in parallel as a concurrent hazard within overlapping spatial and temporal domains.
Despite the growing body of literature on multi-hazard assessment and predefined hazard interaction scenarios, a significant gap remains in the development of dynamic computational tools that enables the systematic exploration of hazard interrelations based on historical event data. To address this gap, this study develops a web-based geospatial tool that represents diachronic hazard events in Greece as nodes within a spatio-temporal framework. The dataset consists of officially recorded hazard events, which were extracted from authoritative text sources and integrated into a geodatabase through AI-assisted processes for data extraction, normalization, and standardization of spatial and temporal attributes (place, date, and time). Hazard interactions derived from the literature are encoded as edges within a dependency graph structure, with distinct interaction types (e.g., triggering, increased probability, and concurrent occurrence) explicitly represented. The tool enables the selection of individual hazard events so as their potential secondary interconnections to be explored within user-defined spatial distance thresholds and temporal constraints. As the spatial radius is adjusted, additional potentially related hazard events become visible, enabling a progressive exploration of multi-hazard dependencies, and the construction of dynamic dependency graphs across hazard sequences.
The proposed framework provides a novel decision-support and exploratory tool for multi-hazard analysis, which contributes to risk assessment and dynamic interdependency modeling by bridging theoretical hazard interaction knowledge with empirical geospatial data.

33.title: Transforming Spatial Datasets into Dynamic Web Platforms: A Cost-Free, Open-Source WebGIS Blueprint

authors.name: Alexandros Liaskos
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

authors.name: Evangelos Spyrou
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

authors.name: Konstantina Lymperopoulou
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

authors.name: Eleni Achmakidou
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

authors.name: Georgia Kakoura
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

authors.name: Giannis Saitis
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

authors.name: Anna Karkani
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

authors.name: Niki Evelpidou
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

33.abstract: This initiative presents an open-source WebGIS architecture for publishing spatial datasets as interactive, free and open web platforms. The framework will be demonstrated through Coastal Lagoons of Earth (lagoons.vercel.app), an interactive, web-based repository of coastal lagoons, structured as a dynamic, node-based geoinformatics system. The WebGIS framework consists of 3 major layers: the Leaflet-based map, the Supabase (Postgress, PostGIS) database, and the vanilla Javascript, alongside the custom User Interface (UI) components. The frontend is lightweight and fast, providing an appealing user experience through the interactive map, nodes, modals, filters, statistics, etc.. Through the example project, at macro scales, lagoons are visualized as discrete nodes color-coded to denote their projected 2100 inundation risk under varying climatic scenarios, while upon high-resolution zoom, these nodes transition to reveal precise polygon geometries. Interacting with any individual lagoon node triggers a detailed modal interface exposing its underlying data. The platform excels in real-time spatial, statistical and analysis, allowing users to refine datasets via multi-criteria filtering that utilizes interactive categorical lists alongside dynamic sliders for numerical variables. Based on these active filters, the system automatically calculates dynamic interactive plots per variable, while at the same time supporting global searches, variable-specific database queries, and advanced filtering. Client-server communication follows a standard HTTPS request–response pattern through parameterized calls to a web API of predefined functions. Additionally, the entire infrastructure is version-controlled via GitHub and deployed through Vercel. As a proof of concept, the application currently hosts a dataset of 152 Greek lagoons, while similar projects utilizing this scalable framework, like Historic Floods (HistoricFloods.org), seamlessly support 2,000+ flood events as nodes. Ultimately, this architecture provides a highly reproducible, cost-free blueprint for converting complex datasets into visually engaging, dynamic web platforms.

33.title: Developing an Interactive Web-Based Platform for Map Projection Exploration

authors.name: Aikaterini-Maria Kyriakou
authors.affiliation: University of West Attica, Faculty of Engineering, Department of Surveying and Geoinformatics Engineering, Geoinformatics & Computer Vision Lab - GeoInVision

authors.name: Vassilios Krassanakis
authors.affiliation: University of West Attica, Faculty of Engineering, Department of Surveying and Geoinformatics Engineering, Geoinformatics & Computer Vision Lab - GeoInVision

authors.name: Giorgos Sfikas
authors.affiliation: University of West Attica, Faculty of Engineering, Department of Surveying and Geoinformatics Engineering, Geoinformatics & Computer Vision Lab - GeoInVision

33.abstract: This paper describes the ongoing development of an interactive, web-based platform designed for effective exploration of map projections. This web-based tool aims to serve mainly as a robust educational resource, helping university students better understand and interpret the mathematical foundations of map design. Specifically, a dynamic, user-friendly interface is introduced that enables users to compare and visualize different map projections in real time, supporting a more intuitive understanding of their properties and differences. The platform supports the core categories of map projections, including equidistant, conformal, and equal-area projections, alongside representative examples of transverse projections. Furthermore, it is designed to be extensible, allowing the future integration of additional geospatial datasets, utilizing well-known file formats, as well as new projection types, ensuring long-term adaptability within evolving digital learning environments. The platform is developed using the Julia programming language, which was selected for its high-performance numerical computing capabilities and suitability for scientific applications. The web tool allows users to interactively adjust map projection parameters, switch between projection types, and immediately observe the resulting spatial distortions through Tissot’s indicatrix. This capability fosters a deeper understanding through direct visual feedback and interactive experimentation. In practice, our web tool bridges the gap between theoretical concepts and practical application, encouraging self-directed learning through side-by-side comparative visual analysis. We anticipate that its public release will significantly enhance user engagement and facilitate a deeper understanding of the complex mathematical concepts involved in map creation. In a nutshell, this work advances geospatial education by combining modern programming practices with an extensible and interactive learning framework for academic use. Future work involves evaluating the platform in real-world settings through usability studies, aiming to assess its effectiveness in supporting geospatial education and improving learning outcomes.

33.title: Open building datasets: analysis and comparison for Greece in a web geovisual application
33.abstract:
Buildings constitute a critical geospatial data layer that can be used to calculate construction density and distribution, assess urbanization, and evaluate land use corresponding to urban coverage. At the same time, in the context of civil protection, they constitute valuable data for assessing cities' vulnerability and resilience.
In this work, building data for Greece is derived from three sources of open data: official geospatial data provided by the Digital Building Stock Model (DBSM) of the Joint Research Center (JRC) of the European Commission, Volunteered Geographic Information provided by OpenStreetMap, and data collected with artificial intelligence from satellite images provided by Microsoft Global ML Buildings. Each dataset has different characteristics. OSM Buildings are VGI collected by citizens; DBSM includes data from official and VGI sources that have been harmonized and checked; and Microsoft ML Buildings are collected using machine learning tools with minimal human intervention.
For comparison and evaluation of the datasets, several measures are applied, including Total Building Area, Coverage Percentage, Average Building Area, Total building area ratio and the Overlap Index based on building areas or on buildings' centers of gravity between two datasets. The results are presented in a geovisual analysis environment implemented with a map-centric dashboard that includes indicators, graphs, selectors and maps. The analysis and visualization of the data are implemented at multiple levels: at the three administrative divisions of Greece (regions, regional units and municipal units) and at a larger scale across three hexagonal grids (10 km², 5 km² and 1 km²). The web application (https://tinyurl.com/buildingsgr) is a valuable tool for acquiring information and evaluating open data for buildings in Greece. Several conclusions are derived regarding the distribution of buildings and the data sources.

33.title: Web-GIS for X-Minute Cities: Challenges and Opportunities in Proximity-Based Accessibility Tools
33.abstract: In this work, we explore the development of Web-GIS tools for proximity-based planning and X-minute city analysis, focusing on both their potential and inherent challenges. We present a suite of open-access tools—CThood, CTstreets, and CTwalk—that capture accessibility to services and amenities, as well as street-level walkability, using network-based methods and open datasets (e.g., street networks, points of interest, elevation, and street-level imagery). Applications in European cities, including Amsterdam, Athens, and Stockholm, illustrate how such approaches can generate high-resolution insights into spatial accessibility patterns. Building on the development and application of these tools, we transfer key lessons learned regarding the design, implementation, and use of Web-GIS-based accessibility systems. In particular, we reflect on challenges related to data quality, modelling assumptions, and the difficulty of capturing complex and context-dependent aspects of urban experience. Drawing on recent work on walkability tool design, we further discuss issues of interpretability, alignment with planning needs, and the translation of analytical outputs into meaningful insights. Overall, the presentation highlights how proximity-based accessibility tools can support planning practice, while emphasizing the need for informed, context-aware, and user-oriented development.

33.title: Designing Indoor Maps for University Environments
33.abstract:
Indoor Mapping is a rapidly growing field of modern cartography, primarily focusing on the representation of complex, multi-level building structures (such as universities, hospitals, airports, shopping malls, etc.). Compared to traditional cartography, cartographic visualization of interior spaces has to face additional challenges such as high scale geometric detail, the resulting increased complexity of spatial layout and the need for clear thematic organization of the information regarding each building.
This paper examines the cartographic representation of interior spaces, with an emphasis on cartographic design and visualization of spatial information within a university building complex, and more specifically, the buildings of the School of Rural, Surveying & Geoinformatics Engineering, at the National Technical University of Athens. In order to create an online web map of the school’s facilities, architectural drawings of the buildings were utilized; these were appropriately processed and updated through on-site inspections to accurately reflect the current condition and use of the buildings. The design methodology was based on the cartographic principles of generalizing the geometry of the original architectural plan, thematically categorizing the spaces and developing a visual hierarchy. The final cartographic representation is achieved through a combination of area and point symbolization, aiming at a clear distinction among uses and functions of space, as well as ensuring optimal readability by the user. At the same time, the ability of actual built environment representation is provided as a supplemental feature, preserving its basic structural characteristics.
The final result of this work is a coherent cartographic model for the visualization of interior spaces, which can serve as the basis for creating maps of more complex building environments, as well as for navigation applications.

33.title: From Ottoman Property Registers to Interactive Web Mapping: Database Design, Geocoding, and Cartographic Integration of the 1832/33 Property Survey in Cyprus
33.abstract:
This presentation introduces a Historical GIS (HGIS) approach for transforming the 1832/33 Ottoman Property Survey of Cyprus into an interactive web application. Developed as part of the ECOLAND project, it focuses on the technical and methodological processes required to convert property survey records into a structured geospatial dataset suitable for analysis and web-based visualization. The research involves data modeling, the design and implementation of an object-relational spatial database, the transcription of archival material, and the systematic treatment of historical terminology and toponymy, including property categories and ownership information. Settlement names recorded in the Ottoman registers were geocoded using multiple sources, including historical maps and modern gazetteers. The resulting database is integrated into an interactive web application built with open-source technologies, supporting advanced text search and filtering of property records based on multiple criteria, such as property type, land use, and settlement affiliation, as well as map-based visualization. These functionalities facilitate the exploration and interpretation of spatial patterns.
The paper outlines the workflow from transcription to web deployment, highlighting challenges related to spatial uncertainty and data interoperability. By linking database design, historical data processing, and web application development, the study demonstrates how Ottoman property surveys can be integrated into modern geospatial infrastructures, contributing to the broader use of archival sources in digital cartography and geospatial research. A short live demonstration will be included.

33.title: Interactive Cartography and Digital Humanities: The Case of N. Kazantzakis' Geographies

authors.name: Spyros Ntzouropanos
authors.affiliation: University of West Attica / Department of Surveying and Geoinformatics Engineering

authors.name: Kleomenis Kalogeropoulos
authors.affiliation: University of West Attica / Department of Surveying and Geoinformatics Engineering

authors.name: Ioannis Katsios
authors.affiliation: University of West Attica / Department of Surveying and Geoinformatics Engineering

authors.name: Andreas Tsatsaris
authors.affiliation: University of West Attica / Department of Surveying and Geoinformatics Engineering

33.abstract: The present study explores the implementation of ArcGIS Online as a powerful digital tool for the interactive mapping and public dissemination of Nikos Kazantzakis' extensive travel history. By leveraging the cloud-based capabilities of the ArcGIS platform, the project transitions static geographical data into dynamic web-based environments, facilitating a deeper understanding of the spatial dimensions of the author's work. A central component of this application is the creation of Web Maps and Web Applications, which allow for the seamless visualization of travel routes and significant stops across different continents. Through the integration of Story Maps, the project effectively combines cartographic precision with narrative depth, incorporating multimedia elements such as photographs and textual excerpts to create an immersive biographical experience. Furthermore, the platform’s interactive analysis features, including advanced filters and queries, enable users to explore specific chronological periods or geographical regions of interest, offering a personalized engagement with Kazantzakis’ journeys. The use of Web Services ensures that the mapping data remains scalable and updatable, while the inherent accessibility of ArcGIS Online promotes the widespread sharing of this "cultural map" for educational and research purposes. Ultimately, the application of these digital humanities tools provides an innovative framework for analyzing the intersection between geography and literature, highlighting how the physical landscapes Kazantzakis traversed influenced his intellectual and artistic evolution. By providing an open-access interactive viewer, the study democratizes geographical knowledge and offers a modern pedagogical approach to studying one of Greece’s most significant literary figures through the lens of modern Geoinformatics.

34.title: “Together for life” ? Acts of hindrance in contemporary workers’ struggles: a labour geography perspective
34.abstract: Amid ongoing economic restructuring, increased labour precarity, and the erosion of social and labour rights, it is necessary to analyse the role of spatially-informed labour agency and the spatiality of contemporary workers’ struggles. Workers are often studied from the perspective of capital, which overlooks the agency labour possesses to shape its politico-economic landscape. This work places workers and their struggles at the centre to analyse their agency as they shape the economic geography of countries with semi-advanced capitalism, specifically Greece. We focus on the 2022 labour struggle of Malamatina’s workers (Thessaloniki, Greece) and examine how they attempted to produce spatial fixes both in collaboration with and in opposition to capital, the state, unions, and local, national, and international actors in solidarity. We employ a mixed-method research design, combining primary and secondary qualitative and quantitative data with mapping techniques. Our research on labour actions and strategies through workers’ inquiry contributes to scientific debate and enhances understanding of the conditions under which labour may produce specific landscapes that serve workers’ interests, and the role negative forms of labour agency – termed acts of hindrance – may play in constraining successful struggles.

34.title: Racial Capitalism and the Multiplication of Labour: Towards Migrant Workers’ Inquiry
34.abstract:
This contribution contends that if labour is central for organising and struggling, then workers’ inquiry that wants to intervene in the politics of knowledge must grapple with how conditions of racial capitalism intersect with the multiplication of labour.

First, it takes the starting point of precarious migrant labour in urban contexts in European welfare states as a possibility to bring analytical refining to the much-contested relationship between race and capitalism. I will probe into Black Marxist debates that argue that race helps to ‘reproduce labour’ in an ‘internally divided form’, and thus create sections of the working class which might be subject to greater forms of exploitation and to forestall ‘the unity of the [working] class as a whole’ (Hall et al., 1978: 346). By connecting these predominantly North-American debates to that of the ‘differential inclusion’ (Mezzadra & Neilson, 2013) of precarious migrant workers in European cities, I aim to analyse how the multiplication of labour (incl. new labour regimes) produce diverse subject positions.

Second, if class is a social relation forged through struggle, then we must pay attention to how the multiplication and racialised division of labour can give rise to multiple struggles. In this sense, I tackle how precarious migrant workers’ inquiry can reveal how labour unions have long occupied a paradoxical position within Marxist theory, both essential for working-class formation, but also part of corporatist state apparatuses which reproduce classed, raced, and gendered orders of capital-labour relations. Hence, finally, I argue that if we truly want to grasp how precarious migrants inhabit and organise around the racialised exploitation of their labour in urban contexts, we need to adopt an infrastructural lens.

34.title: Critical monitoring: A workers’ inquiry into socio-legal workers’ casefiles in support of an anti-displacement agenda in Brussels
34.abstract:
This paper examines housing precarity in Brussels through a workers’ inquiry into socio-legal case files, situating frontline social workers within broader transformations in welfare and housing regimes. In a context marked by austerity, political fragmentation, and the erosion of welfare infrastructures—exemplified by prolonged governmental deadlock in the Brussels Region—households face intensifying legal and material insecurity. These dynamics are mirrored in the working conditions of social and legal professionals tasked with safeguarding the right to housing within a fragmented policy landscape.

The contribution draws on an action research collaboration with Bonnevie, a regionally subsidised housing aid organisation in Old Molenbeek-Saint-Jean. It mobilises social workers’ case files as situated data, demonstrating how such institutional archives can compensate for the lack of systematic eviction data while offering a grounded entry point to conceptualise displacement. Methodologically, the study combines quantitative classification of eviction types and causes with qualitative analysis of case files and working conditions, informed by institutional ethnography. This approach foregrounds how “texts”—case files, legal documents, and administrative procedures—mediate ruling relations and shape housing trajectories.

Positioning this inquiry within a broader network of socio-legal actors, including engaged lawyers, the paper conceptualises social workers as frontline agents navigating and extending institutional mandates. Drawing on a Marxist-feminist understanding of work, it highlights how these actors exceed formal job descriptions to contest processes of socio-legal precarisation. Empirical material includes interviews, workshop recordings, and field notes, capturing both the negotiation of legal frameworks and emergent strategies of resistance.

By centring eviction and displacement, the paper advances the notion of “critical monitoring” as a method of knowledge production. It argues for displacement-based eviction monitoring grounded in frontline perspectives, contributing to anti-displacement struggles while critically interrogating the institutional production of precarity.

34.title: Precarity and Dual Power: The Political Composition of Ireland’s Working Class
34.abstract:
This paper presents ongoing PhD research examining how migrant and non-migrant communities navigate precarity through informal care infrastructures in two Irish localities, Blanchardstown-Mulhuddart and Letterkenny. Drawing on Census analysis and preliminary fieldwork, the research investigates how state withdrawal from housing, healthcare, and social services, combined with rising living costs, produces distinct geographies of vulnerability. These conditions generate restless temporalities: prolonged waiting for social housing, accelerated evictions, and the relentless circulation of marginalised populations through temporary accommodations. These arrangements are actively produced through deregulated housing markets, austerity, and welfare conditionality, while anti-migrant discourse blames racialised communities for scarcity.
Insisting on labour's continued centrality, I carry out social investigation in and beyond workplace organising to reconceptualise care as socially reproductive labour through which class composition and its political capacities are forged. This is compounded with my own militant research interests as being involved in tenant and trade union organising. Within these conditions, care emerges as contested practice. Initial fieldwork identifies "shadow care infrastructures" of community gardens, language exchanges, tenant organising through which communities build collective capacity. In Blanchardstown, engagement revealed cross-community work to claw back public services. In Letterkenny, residents' associations unified Irish and non-Irish tenants against evictions and far-right mobilisation.
Methodologically, the research develops a two-phase "care-tography" as a contribution to workers' inquiry. Phase 1 maps structural conditions "from above" through demographic analysis, positioning the researcher's local subjectivity within capitalist relations. Phase 2 employs spatial ethnography: participatory mapping, focus groups, interviews documenting how communities collectively respond, treating knowledge production as a weapon of organising. By tracing care labour's uneven distribution and transformation through collective power, this paper posits that care operates beyond reproductive labour, instead as a political means. The inquiry orients toward communties’ capacities to act upon shared findings, seeking to turn experiential knowledge into a weapon for collective resistance.

34.title: Conflict as method: tenants’ organising and the making of a housing subject in Greece
34.abstract:
This contribution departs from a practical and theoretical paradox encountered in organising tenants in Greece: a severe housing crisis does not automatically produce a housing movement. In a context shaped by the hegemony of small property, housing insecurity is still often experienced as private failure, temporary misfortune or individual maladjustment, rather than as a shared political condition. Organising, therefore, does not simply aggregate pre-existing identities. It contributes to the formation of a collective subject capable of naming its position, identifying its adversaries and acting upon the relations that produce insecurity.
When the home, the neighbourhood and the public square become fields of exploitation and struggle, workers’ inquiry can be transposed from the workplace to the terrain of rent, debt and social reproduction. The landlord–tenant conflict is not merely a political dispute, but a method for producing knowledge. Rent disputes, eviction threats, negotiations, heated public exchanges, but also internal organisational tensions and disagreements, do not merely provide empirical material. They make visible the moral, legal and economic architecture of the Greek housing property regime. They uncover actors, logics, alliances, patterns. They reveal how property common sense operates, how tenants are individualised and moralised, and where this hegemony begins to fracture.
Research can thus move beyond detached observation and become a situated, conflictual process embedded in organising. Assemblies, mutual aid, public discourse and strategic reflection become sites where experience is collectivised, concepts are tested and revised and dispersed grievances are translated into shared claims. Nevertheless, the process remains incomplete. The analytical framework must be disconnected from the researcher/organiser and enter a collective cycle of analysis, planning, action, evaluation and reflection.
Such tenants’ inquiry blurs the lines between methodology and politics. It produces knowledge on property relations, while contributing to the construction of a housing subject beyond the property imperative.

34.title: Tenants’ Inquiry: Knowledge production and class recomposition under rentier capitalism

authors.name: Nikolaos Vrantsis
authors.affiliation: Institute for Housing and Urban Research

34.abstract:
The ongoing reconfiguration of capitalism, marked by the growing centrality of rent extraction
and housing assetization, demands a reorientation of inquiry itself. As accumulation shifts from
production toward rents and finance, new terrains of struggle emerge. Labor remains central,
but must now be traced across the fragmented relations that bind tenants, debtors, and urban
populations to circuits of capital.
This contribution argues for the development of tenants’ inquiry as a contemporary extension of
workers’ inquiry. Emerging from operaismo and militant research, workers’ inquiry was a
political wager that knowledge production can aid class recomposition, and that research must
be embedded within collective struggle. Today, this wager must be reactivated under conditions
where exploitation is increasingly organised through rent, credit, and asset-based accumulation.
Such a shift requires a rupture with the self-referential tendencies of academic research. Rather
than producing knowledge for institutional circulation, inquiry must become a situated practice
that strengthens movements and contributes to collective capacities for action. This entails
moving from studying housing struggles to producing knowledge with tenants as political
subjects.
Grounded in work with the Thessaloniki Tenants’ Union and the European Action Coalition, this
paper points to emerging infrastructures of tenants’ inquiry from collective mapping of rents
and evictions to shared analysis of legal and financial mechanisms and the circulation of
knowledge across struggles. At stake is the possibility of transforming dispersed experiences of
dispossession into coordinated practices of resistance.

35.title: Digitalizing Geography in the Classroom: methods to make it more appealing to young learners
35.abstract: Geography is a school subject that is not always given the appropriate attention. There is lots of research and examples showing that students are not familiar with the term of "Geography" and the many different aspects it contains. Sometimes they may even face difficulty in distinguishing their own country. Furthermore, the rapid evolution of digital technologies can definitely be a strong asset for teachers in order to help them reshape how geography is taught, learned and experienced. That is what educators have to learn more about, get trained and used to. This research shows that this is a first but crucial step in order to change the way people think of “Geography” and how much important it finally is for developing geospatial knowledge in the modern era. At an empirical level, presenting Geography to 9–13-year-old students in a more digitalized way can make it more appealing and conceivable. In a globalized world Geography should be considered as crucial knowledge that young children should be exposed to and learn in the most enjoyable way.

35.title: Designing Inclusive Geography Learning: A Digital Toolkit and AI-Driven Lesson Planning Framework

authors.name: Angeliki Papazoglou
authors.affiliation: Department of Geography and Regional Planning, School of Rural, Surveying and Geoinformatics Engineering, National Technical University of Athens

authors.name: Maria Pigaki
authors.affiliation: Department of Geography and Regional Planning, School of Rural, Surveying and Geoinformatics Engineering, National Technical University of Athens

authors.name: Yannis Paraskevopoulos
authors.affiliation: Department of Geography and Regional Planning, School of Rural, Surveying and Geoinformatics Engineering, National Technical University of Athens

35.abstract:
Geography education, a discipline associated with the spatial, social, cultural and environmental diversity shaping the modern word, provides a particularly fertile ground for the development of inclusive pedagogical approaches. At the same time, technological advancement expands opportunities for differentiated didactic material and the support of multiple learning pathways, enhancing participation of students with diverse background, learning needs and abilities. However, the meaningful pedagogical integration of digital tools requires the integration of pedagogical, technological, and design expertise and often increases teachers’ cognitive and organisational workload, particularly in the planning of inclusive learning experiences.
This study presents an integrated framework for designing inclusive teaching in Geography and Science education, based on two complimentary digital tools: (a) a digital toolkit that supports teachers in the structured selection of educational software aligned with pedagogical strategies, learning objectives, and student accessibility needs, incorporating a glossary of inclusion-related concepts and an AI-assistant navigation system for real time pedagogical decision support; and (b) an AI-driven lesson plan template that enables the generation of multiple instructional scenarios, differentiated learning pathways, and alternative forms of assessment.
The development and evaluation of the framework follow a design-based research approach and are grounded in pilot implementations of instructional scenarios, enabling iterative refinement through systematic feedback. In addition, the framework is interpreted through the principles of Universal Design of Learning (UDL), with emphasis on multiple means of representation, expression, and engagement, as well as the reduction of barriers to participation in learning processes.
Preliminary findings suggest that the proposed framework can reduce teachers’ instructional design workload, strengthen pedagogical differentiation, and support the development of more accessible and participatory learning environments. Overall, the study highlights the potential of combining structured digital tools with artificial intelligence to meaningfully contribute to the transformation of geography education towards a more inclusive, flexible and pedagogical grounded practice.

35.title: Enhancing Spatial Thinking in Lower Secondary Geography through Artificial Intelligence-Supported Learning Activities
35.abstract: The growing permeation and integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education are reshaping teaching practices and opening new possibilities for meaningful learning. AI has emerged as a powerful tool for both teachers and students alike. In Geography education, in particular, the development of spatial thinking is a focal objective, as it enables students to interpret maps, understand spatial relationships, and analyze geological and geographic phenomena. The current Greek curriculum for lower secondary Geography (Grades 7–8) emphasizes inquiry-based learning, the use of maps and geospatial tools, and the connection of geographic knowledge with real-world issues, including sustainability and environmental challenges. Within this context, this paper explores the pedagogical potential of AI as a supportive tool for enhancing spatial thinking in geography classrooms. It presents examples of AI-supported learning activities that combine traditional geographic resources, such as maps and spatial representations, with digital tools that facilitate questioning, exploration, and discussion. The proposed activities aim to support students in identifying spatial patterns, understanding relationships between natural and human systems, and promote more active engaging with geographic concepts. Through the integration of AI, students are encouraged to develop critical thinking and spatial reasoning skills while participating in learner-centered and interactive learning processes. Moreover, such approaches can support educational practices aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly those related to quality education, environmental awareness, and sustainable development, by fostering students’ understanding of global challenges through spatial analysis. The paper highlights how the thoughtful use of AI can enrich geography education and align with contemporary curricular goals, while also addressing key pedagogical considerations, including the responsible and effective integration of emerging technologies in the classroom.

35.title: Gamification and Immersive Technologies in Geography Education: Pilot Findings from the AcademIa of ARistarchus AI/AR Serious Game

authors.name: Anastasia Georgiou
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, School of Education, Department of Pedagogy and Primary Education

authors.name: Apostolia Galani
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, School of Education, Department of Pedagogy and Primary Education

authors.name: Christina Koutouveli
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, School of Education, Department of Pedagogy and Primary Education

35.abstract:
This research project focuses on the development of AcademIa of ARistarchus, a serious game that integrates Augmented Reality (AR), Artificial Intelligence (AI), and hybrid digital–board-game mechanics. The game is designed as an inquiry-based learning experience in which students actively explore scientific questions through gameplay. Through a narrative inspired by Aristarchus of Samos, students investigate planetary atmospheres and the greenhouse effect by comparing environmental conditions on Earth, Mars, and Venus. The gamified structure incorporates challenge-based tasks, narrative progression, immediate feedback, and collaborative problem-solving to enhance curiosity, engagement, and interdisciplinary thinking.
A pilot implementation was conducted with twelve students, divided into a control group receiving traditional instruction and an experimental group using the AR/AI-supported game. Pre- and post-testing provided initial insights into the feasibility and pedagogical value of the gamified intervention. Preliminary findings indicate that students in the experimental group demonstrated higher motivation and stronger engagement in learning about atmospheric processes than those in the control group. The pilot also revealed positive attitudes toward integrating AR and AI into geography learning.
By placing gamification at the center of the learning design, this pilot study contributes to current discussions on the emerging trend of integrating immersive technologies and game-based approaches in geography education. It demonstrates how game mechanics, combined with immersive technologies, can support meaningful, learner-centered learning, enhancing spatial reasoning and comparative analysis of planetary environments, in alignment with contemporary global challenges such as climate change and sustainability.

35.title: Disrupting automated thinking in geography education
35.abstract: Geography education cannot escape what Hannah Arendt called thoughtlessness: self-reinforcing patterns and practices that offer comforting shortcuts and a shared sense of purpose yet often fail to address the very infrastructures—ideational and material—within which academic thinking takes place. Drawing on N. Katherine Hayles’ concept of cognitive assemblage, this paper asks how geography students might interrogate dominant infrastructures of thought and their ongoing transformation in the context of artificial intelligence and automated media. In particular, it examines pedagogical approaches that critically address the entanglement of educational technology and knowledge production with carbon-intensive processes that perpetuate colonial asymmetries through forms of resource extraction and labour exploitation. Engaging the field of speculative design, the paper then offers strategies for rendering tangible—and ultimately disrupting—the often-imperceptible mediations that structure thinking. Through the friction generated by experimental practices of making, speculative design can be deployed to unsettle unnoticed—and unsustainable—infrastructures that continue to shape the thinkable within and beyond geography.

35.title: Students’ spatial thinking and use of maps in developing country: Nigeria
35.abstract: Geography is a branch of inquiry that focuses on spatial information on Earth. This paper examines spatial thinking, awareness and use of maps among post-secondary institution students in Nigeria. The data used in the paper were from administration of two hundred and eleven questionnaires to post-secondary institution students. Descriptive statistics were used to analyse the data. The study shows among others that majority of the students have situations in their daily lives or specialty that require spatial thinking; the top three situations in which they require spatial thinking were walking, identification of places, and route planning. Majority of them were aware of maps, majority of them could read maps, majority of them have interest to learn more how to read maps. Policy implications of the findings towards enhancing capacity building in the development and use of digital earth and geospatial information technologies are discussed in the paper.

35.title: From Embodied Movement to Early Programming: Enhancing Spatial Orientation through Bee-Bot Activities in Kindergarten

authors.name: Christina Zisi
authors.affiliation: Principal of the 7th Kindergarten, Mytilene, Lesvos

35.abstract:
Spatial orientation is a fundamental cognitive ability, closely associated with everyday functioning and later academic achievement, particularly in STEM related domains. In early childhood education, the integration of educational robotics provides innovative opportunities to cultivate these skills through experiential, inquiry-based, and play-oriented learning environments. Bee-Bot, a child-friendly programmable robot, introduces young learners to fundamental concepts of directionality (e.g., left–right, forward–backward), sequencing, and problem-solving, while also supporting the development of early computational thinking. The present study investigates the role of embodied movement in enhancing spatial programming performance among kindergarten children. The sample consisted of 35 preschoolers who participated in structured Bee-Bot activities involving route planning and prediction of the robot’s final position. Two experimental conditions were implemented: (a) tasks preceded by bodily enactment of the route on a floor grid, and (b) tasks completed without prior motor engagement. The activities incorporated both visual representations of routes and scaffolded planning frameworks, enabling children to construct and test their own navigation sequences. The findings reveal that children who engaged in embodied route enactment achieved significantly higher programming accuracy, made fewer directional errors, and demonstrated greater competence in predicting outcomes. These results highlight the importance of sensorimotor experience as a cognitive scaffold, facilitating the internalisation of spatial concepts and supporting the transition from concrete action to abstract representation. Overall, the study underscores the pedagogical value of integrating embodied learning strategies within educational robotics. Such approaches can meaningfully enhance spatial reasoning and early programming skills, offering developmentally appropriate and effective practices for fostering cognitive growth in kindergarten education.
Keywords: spatial orientation; embodied learning; educational robotics; Bee-Bot; early childhood education; spatial reasoning; programming skills

35.title: Evaluating a Serious Educational Computer Game on Terraced Landscapes: Evidence from 7th-grade Students
35.abstract: This study evaluates the effectiveness of an educational computer game on terraced landscapes, as perceived by 7th-grade students. It focuses on student responses following the implementation of a serious game specifically designed for secondary education. The research adopts an empirical approach, informed by a review of the literature on digital game-based learning. Data were collected through structured questionnaires administered after students engaged with the game. The sample consisted of 58 7th-grade students from the Greek island of Leros in the Dodecanese; therefore, the findings should be considered indicative rather than broadly generalisable. The results suggest that the serious game developed for this study was positively received by the participating students. Furthermore, most students demonstrated improved knowledge, as well as enhanced attitudes and perceptions regarding terraced landscapes. These findings indicate that well-designed, user-friendly, and engaging digital educational tools can contribute meaningfully to learning outcomes when effectively integrated into teaching practice. The study also highlights the importance of active student participation in fostering awareness and supporting the transition toward a more sustainable future. In this context, the integration of innovative digital game-based learning approaches into school curricula—particularly within geographical and environmental education—is strongly recommended. To enhance the generalisability of future research, it is suggested that larger and more diverse samples be employed, including students from both island and mainland regions of Greece. Such expansion would provide a more comprehensive understanding of the educational potential of serious games in sustainability education.

35.title: Mapping practices for educational commons. Re-imagining the city of Poznań as a space for play and education
35.abstract:
Over the past decades, outdoor spaces—often characterized by fluidity, ephemerality, and everyday practices—have functioned as critical sites for the production, exchange, and negotiation of knowledge beyond formal institutional frameworks. However, outdoor play has progressively been displaced from the street and confined within enclosed and regulated environments. This shift has contributed to forms of topographical disorientation, diminished engagement with urban life, increased spatial segregation, and fragmentation in governance structures.

Grounded in the concept of educational commons, and informed by "school streets" urban strategy, the notion of the “city for children” fundamentally reconfigures the understanding of public space as a site of learning. Rather than conceiving education as a process confined within school boundaries and administered exclusively by professionals, this perspective positions the urban landscape itself as a shared and collective resource for learning.

This paper presents a workshop conducted in March 2026 at the Faculty of Architecture of the Poznań University of Technology in Poland, which focused on exploring urban voids as potential educational spaces. The workshop was structured in three phases: an introductory exercise designed to familiarize participants with the concept of educational commons; a series of exploratory walks centered on selected schools as reference points; and a mapping exercise employing collective, analogue collage techniques mixed with satellite cartography and digital media.

Through situated practices, participants collected sensory, social, and spatial data that informed the collage-making exercise. Such fieldwork cultivates attentiveness to lived experience, fostering an embodied understanding of place that extends beyond passive observation to active participation. When translated into collage maps, these experiences have been rearticulated as visual compositions that synthesize empirical observation with interpretive insight. In this context, collage mapping emerges as a critical methodological tool for documenting and interpreting dynamic urban environments, revealing the pedagogical dimensions embedded in everyday life.

35.title: Transforming Education for Sustainable Development through Geospatial Technologies and Spatial Thinking: The GEO-Academy Approach
35.abstract: Green, digital, and spatial competences are increasingly recognized as essential components of contemporary education, reflecting the growing importance of sustainability, technological literacy, and spatial awareness across multiple disciplines and professional sectors. Numerous school subjects contribute to the acquisition and integration of these competences, highlighting the need for interdisciplinary and innovative educational approaches. In this context, GEO-Academy, an Erasmus+ Teacher Academy project, has aimed to develop a blended competence-based framework for teaching sustainable development through the use of innovative geospatial technologies and modern pedagogical methodologies. The project has sought to deliver a comprehensive training framework supporting both pre- and in-service teachers in their professional development, with the broader objective of fostering holistic sustainability education for future European citizens. At the core of GEO-Academy lies the integration of advanced geospatial tools and concepts, including Geographic Information Systems, Cartography and Spatial Thinking, Remote Sensing and Earth Observation, Map Storytelling, and Coding for Urban Sustainability, enabling educators to incorporate sustainability-related topics into their daily teaching practices in a meaningful, interdisciplinary, and practice-oriented manner. The project’s principal outcomes are grounded in the development of specialized training courses (E-modules) addressing the aforementioned thematic areas, alongside the establishment of the GEOBSERVE Platform as the GEO-Academy central hub. The platform hosts GEO-Hubs (National Communities), educational tools and training and teaching resources implemented at local, national, and international levels in seven European countries. These outcomes are expected to contribute to the development of an expanding network of teachers and teacher trainers at the institutional level (GEO-Labs), empowered through access to innovative teaching tools and methodologies.

35.title: Enhancing Education on Climate Change–Related Natural Hazards through Interactive Storymaps: Evidence from the CRISEPAC Erasmus+ Project
35.abstract: Climate change is increasingly amplifying the frequency, intensity, and spatial distribution of natural hazards across Europe, with floods, storms, and wildfires posing significant risks to ecosystems, infrastructure, and communities. These evolving threats highlight the urgent need for effective educational approaches that not only communicate scientific knowledge but also develop risk awareness, preparedness, and resilience among students. The CRISEPAC Erasmus+ project addresses this need by developing innovative pedagogical strategies and tools focused on climate change–induced natural hazards. The project is structured around three main objectives: (1) designing and implementing training and support programs for educators on natural hazards and risk prevention; (2) developing interdisciplinary and innovative educational resources that integrate environmental, geographical, and digital competencies; and (3) enhancing understanding of local climate-related risks while promoting active community involvement in prevention and adaptation measures. A key outcome of the project is the creation of three interactive Storymaps that present representative case studies of climate change impacts, floods and storms, and wildfires across the European Union. These Storymaps function as multimedia, geospatial learning tools that combine maps, scientific data, narrative elements, and visual content. By linking climate processes with real-world hazard events and their local impacts, they make complex information accessible, engaging, and relevant to learners. The Storymaps support place-based and inquiry-driven learning by enabling students to explore spatial patterns, analyze cause–effect relationships, and reflect on vulnerability and risk at multiple scales. Furthermore, they integrate scientific knowledge with local perspectives, encouraging learners to consider context-specific solutions for risk reduction and climate adaptation. Freely accessible and adaptable, these resources empower educators to incorporate local hazard contexts into their teaching. The CRISEPAC approach demonstrates the potential of Storymaps as powerful tools for advancing education on climate change–induced natural hazards and fostering a more informed, prepared, and resilient society.

35.title: Designing Resilience: An Immersive Game-Based Approach to Flood Risk Awareness and House Protection

authors.name: Olga Roussou
authors.affiliation: University of the Aegean, Department of Geography

authors.name: Aikaterini Klonari
authors.affiliation: University of the Aegean, Department of Geography

35.abstract:
Floods have increased in both frequency and severity due to the combined effects of rapid urbanisation and climate change. Despite this escalating risk, public awareness and readiness continue to be disproportionately low, especially among younger populations. Addressing this gap necessitates a shift from traditional, passive educational approaches to more engaging, immersive, interactive and experiential forms in learning to capable of fostering deeper understanding and sustained behavioural change.
This paper presents a game-based pedagogical tool developed within the CRISEPAC project (see: www.crisepac.eu), aimed at enhancing flood risk awareness and strengthening resilience at the household level. The suggested tool places students in an interactive virtual environment in which they challenged to protect a house under a range of simulated flood scenarios. To enable users to investigate the spatial determinants of flood risk, the gameplay integrates important geographic aspects such as topography variability, water flow dynamics, and built environment features. Through iterative decision-making processes, players assess the effectiveness of various mitigation measures, such as structural adaptations and land-use practices, while observing their outcomes in real time.
In addition to its instructional design, the study outlines a comprehensive evaluation framework to assess the pedagogical effectiveness of the tool following its implementation. This framework includes pre- and post-game knowledge assessments, analysis of user engagement, interaction patterns and qualitative feedback from both teachers and students. By integrating game-based learning principles with flood risk education, this study contributes a scalable and innovative approach to enhancing flood risk literacy. Ultimately, the tool aims to support the development of a proactive risk perception informed decision-making, and resilience-oriented behaviours among young learners, while also providing valuable insights for teacher training and curriculum development.

35.title: Teaching Climate Change with GIS and Satellite Imagery Urban Heat Islands and Game‑Based Learning in Secondary Geography
35.abstract:
This paper explores an innovative approach to teaching climate change in secondary geography through the integration of Geographic Information Systems (GIS), satellite imagery, and game-based learning. As climate change increasingly impacts both global systems and local environments, geography education plays a crucial role in helping students understand spatial patterns and processes. However, traditional teaching methods often struggle to make these complex dynamics tangible and engaging. This study addresses that gap by presenting a classroom-based learning design centered on the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect.
The proposed teaching model combines real-world geospatial data with an interactive “City Climate Challenge” scenario, in which students assume the roles of urban planners. Using GIS tools and satellite imagery, learners investigate temperature variations, identify urban heat hotspots, and analyze land-use patterns such as vegetation cover and built surfaces. Through collaborative inquiry, students explore the causes of urban heating and evaluate the impact of materials like asphalt and concrete, as well as the cooling potential of green infrastructure.
Students then design and propose evidence-based solutions, including urban forests, green roofs, reflective surfaces, and sustainable mobility strategies. The activity culminates in presentations where teams defend their proposals, simulating real-world decision-making processes. This approach fosters not only climate literacy and spatial thinking, but also critical skills such as data interpretation, collaboration, and problem-solving.
The paper also discusses key challenges, including unequal access to digital tools, the need for teacher training in GIS, and the importance of developing students’ data literacy. Despite these challenges, the integration of GIS, satellite imagery, and game-based learning offers a powerful framework for engaging students in meaningful, inquiry-based climate education. The findings suggest that such approaches can effectively bridge the gap between theoretical knowledge and real-world application, preparing students to better understand and respond to contemporary environmental challenges.

36.title: Neighbourhood Social Identity and the Sociospatial Production of School Segregation in Athens
36.abstract:
This paper examines the sociospatial production of school segregation in the urban context of Athens, focusing on how neighbourhood-level social dynamics shape the functioning and social positioning of schools. Despite the institutional uniformity and centrally prescribed curriculum of the Greek educational system, significant geographical disparities in student outcomes persist, as schools are embedded in unequal urban environments that contribute to patterns of school segregation. These environments influence student composition, academic performance, infrastructure, and informal school choice practices.
The study investigates the relationship between urban space and school differentiation across areas with distinct sociospatial profiles. It explores how the social identity of neighbourhoods contributes to the hierarchical positioning of schools within the local educational field. The empirical analysis is based on qualitative data from semi-structured interviews with parents and teachers in public lower secondary schools in the inner city of Athens and its suburbs.
Findings show that schools in socially and ethnically heterogeneous areas, particularly in the city center, are subject to territorial stigmatization, which is associated with higher concentrations of disadvantaged students, lower academic performance, and increased dropout rates. In contrast, schools in higher-status areas, such as the Northern suburbs, benefit from spatial advantages that enhance their perceived value and attract students beyond their designated catchment areas. These dynamics contribute to the formation of socially and ethnically homogeneous school populations, reinforcing patterns of school segregation and broader sociospatial inequality in Athens. In this context, urban space operates as a structuring force that actively produces differentiation, segregation, and unequal educational opportunities.
Keywords: Territorial Stigmatization, School Segregation, Sociospatial Inequality, School Choice Practices, Athens

36.title: The Geography of School Choice: Spatial, Socioeconomic, and Institutional Dynamics in the Educational Trajectories of the Filipino Second Generation in Athens
36.abstract: This paper examines the educational experiences of the Filipino second generation in Athens, with a focus on the spatial, socioeconomic, and institutional dimensions that shape their schooling trajectories. It explores how urban space and parental labour conditions influence educational decision-making and structure young people’s access to different school regimes. Drawing on ethnographic research, the analysis develops around three main axes. First, it highlights the significance of geographical distance. The location of the Philippine School in Greece in Vyronas, at a distance from major areas of Filipino residential concentration such as Ampelokipoi, combined with parents’ demanding work schedules, often resulted in children attending the local Greek public school. At the same time, the paper identifies a socioeconomic and spatial paradox: the attendance of some students at high-status English-medium private schools in the suburbs, financed by their mothers’ employers within the context of live-in domestic work arrangements. Second, the paper approaches the school as a legal and administrative border. Attendance at Greek public schools often functioned as a strategic pathway towards the acquisition of Greek citizenship, whereas exclusive attendance at international schools was, in some cases, associated with bureaucratic obstacles and delayed institutional recognition. Third, the paper traces emerging transnational educational geographies and forms of educational mobility. Linguistic barriers and the avoidance of the Greek national entrance examinations frequently directed members of the second generation either towards private English-medium colleges in Greece or towards university studies in the Philippines. Overall, the paper argues that the spatial organisation of the city, labour dependencies, and legal-institutional requirements actively produce unequal educational geographies, reshaping access to both education and urban belonging.

36.title: Online schooling during the COVID lockdowns in Greece
36.abstract:
The paper examines online education in Greece during the COVID-19 lockdowns through a spatial lens, focusing on learning, students’ socialisation, and the emerging ethics of a digitalised society, which prioritises technologically-mediated interactions in education and social life.
The presentation takes the form of a thinkpiece based on personal observations (2020–2022), combining parental experience with insights from social geography, philosophy, and education theory, alongside engagement with sociopolitical developments. During the lockdowns, online education was implemented across all levels—from kindergarten to university. Schooling was conducted through digital platforms, where microphones and cameras replaced physical co-presence, marking a shift from embodied, collective learning environments to digital ‘non-places’.
