This spatial reconfiguration generated multiple challenges. The relocation of schooling into the home blurred boundaries between public and private realms, disrupting domestic routines and giving rise to new forms of absenteeism and reduced participation. Students were present and absent—digitally connected yet mentally disengaged, as interaction was constrained by technological mediation. These effects were particularly evident among younger pupils and among socially and economically disadvantaged groups lacking learning resources.
The loss of school as a social space affected students’ mental health and development. Prolonged confinement within the home, combined with the absence of peer interaction, contributed to withdrawal, irritability, and increased screen dependency. The erosion of spatial conditions supporting collective engagement and concentration resulted in learning outcomes falling below expected standards.
While authorities maintain that remote schooling allowed for continuity and digital skills, it can also be seen as part of a shift toward dematerialised and mediated environments, where social and educational life are increasingly detached from physical co-presence. Hence, the experience of remote schooling underscores the importance of defending education as an embodied, spatial practice grounded in shared material environments, which remain essential for meaningful learning and the formation of social relations.

36.title: Embodied Spaces of Learning through Theatre-based Inquiry
36.abstract:
Neither social research nor pedagogy is neutral; both are political practices, entangled in power relations and intertwined. Educational spaces emerge through spatial inequalities and everyday socio-spatial practices, while reproducing and contesting these dynamics. Processes of identity formation, spatial belonging, and justice are inseparable from the environments where learning takes place. Yet education also holds transformative potential - not only reflecting existing conditions, but reconfiguring them.
Drawing on one author's work with improvisational theatre in social research (Hostniker & Meyer 2024), we argue for methodological approaches that access what conventional methods overlook: the implicit, the affective, and the embodied. To amplify voices muted in public discourse, we conceptualize theatre as an art-based methodology that redistributes epistemic authority and enables the co-creation of knowledge, echoing Paulo Freire's (1968) pedagogical philosophy. Augusto Boal (1974) extended this liberatory project into embodied techniques for social transformation.
Building on this tradition and drawing on Massey's (2005) understanding of space as relational and always in the making, we propose theatre-based methods as a vital tool for engaged pedagogy in the sense of bell hooks (1994). Space, in this view, is not a neutral backdrop but a constitutive force in identity formation: the everyday spaces young people inhabit – neighbourhoods, schools, streets – are sites where social identities are produced, contested, and negotiated. Theatre-based methods make these spatial identity-making processes visible and open them to collective reflection, disrupting the "culture of silence" that marginalized youth often internalize.
This dialogue, however, is not one-sided. A critical pedagogical understanding of learning as transformative and relational can also inform social research, where participants engage reflexively with their own socio-spatial conditions. In this way, we hope to contribute to conversations about how research and pedagogy – as inherently spatial and political practices – can work together toward greater epistemic and spatial justice.

36.title: Between two worlds. Spaces and identities of three Roma women

authors.name: Xanthippi Konstantinou Sgourou
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

36.abstract:
A spatial perspective on education offers me a different lens through which I can (re)approach concepts that, thanks to my studies in education, seem more familiar. This allows me to question them again and ultimately design a small-scale research for my undergraduate thesis. The theoretical tools used to formulate questions and analyze research material are drawn from the intersection of two fields: geography and education. When the concepts of identity, power relations, and educational inequalities are viewed through a spatial lens, they highlight how space influences them and vice versa.
More specifically, the resulting thesis concerns the relationships, spaces, and identities produced by three women who come from Roma communities and have pursued higher education -thus following an upward social trajectory- and who now occupy a position of social distance both from their community of origin and from the dominant group. They find themselves in an intermediate spatiality from which they (re)negotiate their relationships with Roma communities and the dominant group, as well as their sense of belonging and their identities. Through thematic analysis of three semi structured interviews, the study highlights the liminal it’s that characterise the life paths of the three women, who are also the founders if an organisation that works to combat school dropout while simultaneously constituting a space of support and solidarity -one that is continuously built alongside the ever evolving identities of each members.

36.title: Notes from a teacher's informal diary: documenting with the children the transformations of Kypseli

authors.name: Niki Konstantinou-Sgourou
authors.affiliation: αναπληρώτρια δασκάλα / μεταπτυχιακό στην κοινωνική ανθρωπολογία

36.abstract:
For the past two school years, I have been working as a substitute primary school teacher in a large school in Kypseli, and through the children’s experiences I have come to know their neighborhood — a neighborhood that is being transformed, changing, dug up: “here, miss, there used to be a playground,” “when I first came and didn’t know Greek well, I thought it was a dead dog under the statue.” Through an informal diary of my experiences, which records the pedagogical practices and activities I implemented as a teacher in both the general classroom and the reception class, that were centered around space, I reflect and observe how space functions as common ground for communication, storytelling, and claiming. With what words do children describe their neighborhood? How does a multilingual poem about Kypseli look like? What do street names tell us? How do we map through the birdsong of blackbirds on Fokionos Negri and Agias Zonis? What do the routes of swallows and the desert dust settling in the schoolyard mean?
By drawing on interdisciplinary approaches and teaching practices, space, neighborhood, and everyday life become intertwined with the subjects taught in primary school. The examples I choose ultimately speak about the right to history and to the city: as I document the children’s perspective, I wonder what connections are formed with the past and present of a dense neighborhood with an uncertain future.

36.title: Creativity as Spatial Practice: Exploring the Interplay of Space, Time, and Materials in the School Classroom
36.abstract:
Recently, there has been a growing interest in the study of creativity in education. Previous research (Kyritsi, 2018) suggests that within school settings and other collaborative learning environments, creativity is not merely an individual trait. Rather, creativity is experienced as a dynamic process that extends beyond the individual and is shaped by interactions among participants, space, learning materials, and the relationships and interdependencies that develop among them.

Responding to the ‘spatial turn’ in education, this presentation offers a theoretical contribution that frames the study of creativity in education as a geographical concern. More specifically, it proposes a pedagogical approach that conceptualises creativity through the interplay of space, time, and materials. Within such a framework, space is understood as a dynamic process constituted through embodied interactions between human and non-human entities.

The presentation also draws on preliminary findings from a case study conducted in two primary school classrooms in Achaia, Greece. Using semi-structured interviews and classroom observations, the study explores how children’s creativity is embodied and enacted within collaborative processes. It also examines how children interact not only with other children but also with space, time, and materials.

By bridging geographical and educational theory and practice, the presentation argues that attention to the interrelationships among space, time, and materials can contribute to rethinking creativity in spatial terms, in ways that foreground embodied experience, support inclusive and participatory practices, and promote spatial justice.

36.title: School differentiation, spatial dynamics and parental practices in a socioeconomically mixed neighborhood: A Case Study in Athens

authors.name: Vasiliki Soltatou
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

authors.name: Nelli Askouni
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

36.abstract: This presentation examines how social divisions are constituted within public education by analysing the school map of a mixed urban area in central Athens. It draws on research into divergences in parental educational practices and informal school choice strategies. The study focuses on neighbouring public primary schools with different social profiles due to the uneven distribution of students in terms of ethnic and social characteristics, as well as differences related to the neighbourhood context. We argue that school differentiation at the local level is shaped by spatial variations, distinct school identities, and diverse parental educational practices. The research was conducted in an ethnically and socially heterogeneous area comprising two neighbourhoods with contrasting social and built-environment characteristics. The analysis places particular emphasis on spatial dynamics at the micro-scale: we examine the socio-demographic profile of the area, as reflected in its class and ethnic composition. As enrolment in Greek public schools is determined by residential address, the social and ethnic characteristics of the local population are consequently reflected in school populations. Moreover, we investigate the symbolic dimension of the neighbourhood. Drawing on interviews with parents, this study explores their perceptions of both the local area and the school. The findings suggest that spatial heterogeneity and differentiated school spaces (in terms of infrastructure and facilities) interact to produce diverse school contexts. At the same time, neighbourhood morphology and the profile and status of the local school activate specific forms of parental agency.

36.title: Geography Education and the Educational Commons: Towards an integrated pedagogical framework
36.abstract:
How can primary schools become a space where children not only learn about places, but also understand, decide for, and co-design the environments they inhabit? This paper argues that bringing Geography Education into dialogue with the Educational Commons offers a powerful pedagogical response.
Grounded in critical geographies and the ‘spatial turn’, we approach Geography Education as a socio-spatial practice constituted through spatial imaginaries, relational processes, and lived experience. The Educational Commons are understood as the creation of inclusive, participatory learning spaces that challenge hierarchical and market-based models of education.
In this paper, we explore an integrated pedagogical framework that combines methodologies from both fields: collaborative mapping and participatory planning from Geography Education, alongside sociocratic practices and active listening from the Educational Commons. Collaborative mapping is understood as a collective process through which learners critically engage with and re-imagine their environments, while participatory planning further extends this by positioning them as active agents and co-creators of shared spaces. Sociocratic practices -such as circle-based dialogue and decision-making by consent- combined with active listening, establish the conditions for inclusive participation, mutual care, and shared responsibility. Together, these approaches enable learners to critically engage with their environments, participate in collective decision-making, and co-design shared spaces.
The paper draws on work in Greek primary education across three interconnected fields: doctoral research in human geography (University of the Aegean) and teaching in Geography Didactics (University of Thessaly), the HORIZON 2020 SMOOTH project (UTH) on educational commons in diverse educational settings and, applied participatory planning initiatives developed with schools and community partners, including the ‘Parko ton Rodon’ project, in collaboration with the Department of Planning and Development (AUTH) and the Municipality of Kalamaria. Through these examples, we propose an integrated pedagogical framework for Geography Education in primary school contexts.

36.title: Tools and Practices for Spatial Exploration in Situated Critical Pedagogy
36.abstract:
This contribution examines methodologies drawn from the fields of critical geography and critical pedagogy, which enrich school education with tools for exploring place and understanding the situatedness of learning. Tools such as mapping practices, neighborhood walks, discussions of everyday life, and connections between place and broader historical events provide children with the opportunity to engage in an ongoing reflection on their self-in-place, through conscious, continuous practice and observation of their embodied geography. At the same time, these tools equip them with creative means to invent their own cognitive pathways, fostering personal and collective modes of learning that inherently enact their own here-and-now.
Drawing on research material collected over the past eight years through outdoor teaching programs and workshops on mapping, reflection, and participatory design with elementary school students in Athens, this study offers a review of how tools and activities that move beyond the strictly structured spatiotemporal boundaries of the school curriculum create essential connections between the generalized and siloed approach to taught material and the developments in children’s lives. These connections—between the spatiotemporal micro-scale of children’s embodied experience and the theoretical framing of the school curriculum—not only enhance the learning process itself, but more importantly highlight the political dimension of education, strengthening awareness of everyday realities and revealing the power relations inherent in both the school and the broader social context of their existence.
The analysis of activities that engage children with spatial concepts through the processing of their lived experiences provides valuable research directions for changes and developments in educational practices and primary education curricula, with the aim of approaching learning as a free and transformative process.

36a.title: The Importance of Geography in the Digital Age: Fostering Critical Spatial Thinking through GIS in Primary Education

authors.name: Nikolaos Voudrislis
authors.affiliation: Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, Department of Spatial Planning and Development

36a.abstract:
The rapid advancement of digital technologies and the widespread availability of geospatial data underscore the importance of Geography as a critical field for understanding the complex socio-spatial phenomena of the 21st century. In this context, spatial thinking and spatial literacy emerge as key competencies, closely associated with critical analysis, problem-solving, and informed decision-making. Geographic Information Systems (GIS) play a pivotal role in this transformation by enhancing spatial abilities through the active engagement of students in processes of data analysis, interpretation, and synthesis, thereby moving beyond passive learning and rote memorisation.
This paper presents the research design of an ongoing postdoctoral study that investigates the role of GIS as a pedagogical tool in primary education. The study aims to support the transition from a descriptive approach to Geography towards an inquiry-based model, emphasizing the interpretation of spatial phenomena and their underlying causal relationships. Adopting a quasi-experimental design and a mixed-methods approach, the research implements instructional scenarios using ArcGIS Online and Google Earth in primary school classrooms with diverse socio-economic backgrounds, including students with refugee experiences.
More specifically, the study seeks to explore the contribution of geospatial tools to the development of critical spatial thinking, evaluate their pedagogical effectiveness, and examine the attitudes of both students and teachers towards their use. Preliminary findings from the pilot phase suggest that the integration of GIS enhances student engagement and facilitates an understanding of space as a socially constructed concept. The study is expected to contribute to the formulation of educational policy recommendations for the meaningful integration of digital geospatial tools into the curriculum, promoting inclusive spatial literacy and fostering the development of active and informed citizens in the digital age.

36a.title: AR Sandbox in Geography Education: Effects on Topographic Map Skills

authors.name: Gerasimos Konstantakatos
authors.affiliation: Department of Pedagogy and Primary Education, Νational and Kapodistrian University of Athens, Greece

authors.name: Tryfon Sivenas
authors.affiliation: Department of Pedagogy and Primary Education, Νational and Kapodistrian University of Athens, Greece

authors.name: Georgios Bampasidis
authors.affiliation: Department of Pedagogy and Primary Education, Νational and Kapodistrian University of Athens, Greece

authors.name: Georgios Markogiannakis
authors.affiliation: Department of Pedagogy and Primary Education, Νational and Kapodistrian University of Athens, Greece

36a.abstract:
Reading and comprehending topographic maps is a fundamental skill in geography education that presents considerable learning difficulties, as it requires advanced spatial skills for mental three-dimensional visualization.
The purpose of this study is to evaluate the effectiveness of a STEM educational intervention, using the Augmented Reality Sandbox (ARS), in developing topographic map reading and comprehension skills among higher education students. To address the research objective, a three-hour pilot STEM educational intervention was designed and implemented. A quasi-experimental design with pre-test/post-test measurements was adopted, involving a sample of 14 undergraduate university students. The intervention was designed based on Kolb's Experiential Learning Model, integrating principles of inquiry-based and design-based learning through three structured problem-solving activities focused on topography, hydrology, and flood risk management. The Topographic Map Assessment (TMA) by Newcombe et al. (2015) was selected as the evaluation instrument, assessing six skill domains: path, water flow, slope, visibility, elevation points, relief, and profile.
The findings indicate a statistically significant improvement in participants' topographic map reading and comprehension skills. Mean scores rose from 12.00 at pre-test to 17.36 at post-test, representing a mean gain of 5.36 points. A paired samples t-test confirmed the significance of this change, and the effect size (d=1.003) was classified as large according to Cohen's (1988) criteria. These findings are consistent with embodied cognition theory, which suggests that physical interaction with objects representing spatial relationships enhances conceptual understanding (Wilson, 2002). The ARS allows learners to perceive the three-dimensional nature of terrain in a tangible and interactive way, effectively bridging the gap between two-dimensional representation of a topographic map and the three-dimensional physical reality it represents. These findings have direct educational implications, suggesting that integrating ARS into STEM interventions is an effective approach to teaching geoscience concepts.

36a.title: Outdoor Education and Digital Technologies in Geographical Learning: Enhancing Spatial Thinking, Engagement and Environmental Understanding

authors.name: Christina Koutouveli
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, School of Education, Department of Pedagogy and Primary Education, Athens, Greece

authors.name: Anastasia Georgiou
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, School of Education, Department of Pedagogy and Primary Education, Athens, Greece

authors.name: Eirini Chatzara
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, School of Education, Department of Pedagogy and Primary Education, Athens, Greece

36a.abstract:
This study examines how outdoor education and new technologies combine to enhance geographical learning in primary and secondary education. Contemporary pedagogical approaches, such as experiential learning and place based education, highlight that direct engagement with natural and built environments strengthens spatial thinking, observation, embodied understanding and emotional connection to place. Outdoor learning enables students to transform abstract geographical concepts into lived experiences, fostering deeper comprehension of spatial processes and human–environment interactions.
At the same time, new technologies act as amplifiers of the outdoor learning experience. Tools such as Geographic Information Systems (GIS), satellite imagery, mobile devices and digital storytelling allow students to collect, document and analyse spatial data in the field. The use of GIS supports the interpretation of spatial patterns and the development of cartographic skills, while mobile applications facilitate inquiry based activities and authentic geographical investigation. Digital storytelling transforms outdoor experiences into multimodal geographical narratives, connecting cultural, historical and environmental dimensions of place.
Research evidence indicates that the combination of outdoor learning and technology enhances cognitive outcomes (spatial reasoning, mapping skills), affective outcomes (place attachment, environmental empathy) and behavioural changes (pro environmental actions, active participation in local communities). Technology does not replace the outdoor experience; rather, it functions as a complementary tool that expands opportunities for observation, documentation and critical analysis.
Finally, the study highlights challenges such as inequalities in access to green spaces and digital tools, as well as the need for teacher training in hybrid geographical practices that effectively integrate field based learning with technological tools. Overall, the synergy between outdoor education and technology creates a powerful, multimodal framework for geographical learning that supports knowledge development, emotional engagement and environmental responsibility.

36a.title: Geography Matters, from Observation to Action: Remote Sensing, Hazard Understanding, and Climate Action Orientation in Pre-Service Teacher Education

authors.name: Eirini Chatzara
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

authors.name: Apostolia Galani
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

36a.abstract:
As climate risks intensify, geography education is uniquely positioned to connect scientific knowledge, spatial thinking, and civic engagement. This study examines the impact of two inquiry-based STEM laboratory sessions on pre-service teachers' understanding of environmental hazards and their orientation toward climate action. The intervention integrated remote sensing and physical computing to investigate two real-world events: the 2023 Kleon heatwave and Evros wildfires, enabling participants to engage with satellite-derived data across spatial and temporal scales.
A pre-to-post questionnaire design was employed with 304 pre-service teachers, measuring changes across three constructs: climate literacy, spatial and environmental hazard understanding, and climate action orientation. Composite scores were compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test; effect sizes are reported as Cohen's d.
Results indicate statistically significant improvements across all three dimensions (all p < .001). The largest gains emerged in spatial and environmental hazard understanding (d = 0.54) and climate action orientation (d = 0.68), with more modest but meaningful growth in climate literacy (d = 0.28). At the item level, the strongest effects were found in participants' understanding of forest fire dynamics and the climate-wildfire relationship, suggesting that satellite-based inquiry is particularly effective at linking atmospheric processes to landscape-scale hazard outcomes. Gains in action orientation were more pronounced for structural and collective strategies such as building insulation, public transportation, and renewable energy transition than for individual lifestyle behaviors.
These findings suggest that geography education, grounded in real-world spatial data and place-based inquiry, can serve as a powerful bridge between scientific understanding and climate agency. The stronger effect sizes for hazard comprehension and collective action orientation point to the potential of remote sensing pedagogy to foster systemic environmental thinking in future educators.

36b.title: Fragmented Crises, Fragmented Knowledge: Content Analysis of the New Geography Curricula and the Need for Critical Geoliteracy

authors.name: Maria Christoforaki
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

authors.name: Athina Karatza
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

authors.name: Apostolia Galani
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

36b.abstract:
This study examines the extent to which geography curricula (2021) enable spatial reasoning that engages with polycrisis, understood as the entanglement of environmental, economic, political, and social disruptions whose effects are reinforcing, distributed, and historically produced (Tooze, 2022). Framed within a critical geography education perspective, the study explores how curricular knowledge shapes students’ understanding of, and capacity interrogation with polycrisis complexity. It analyses primary and secondary education curricula through content analysis, guided by an interpretive framework attending to epistemic framing, generative logics, temporal sedimentation, differential exposure, and crisis representation (Huckle, 2023, 2024; León, 2024; Morgan, 2024; Moore et al., 2025).
Findings reveal curricula that are structured yet uneven in their capacity to support spatial reasoning aligned with critical geography. Across educational levels, epistemic framing predominates, with geography enacted through representation, description, and classification. While supporting geoliteracy, this orientation positions knowledge as stable, constraining engagement with it as situated, contested, and socially produced.
A partial shift toward process-oriented reasoning emerges in secondary education, where generative logics appear through environmental systems, production processes, and spatial networks. However, these remain descriptive and weakly connected to socio-political relations.
Temporal sedimentation is constrained, limiting understanding of how present spatial configurations emerge through layered historical processes. Differential exposure to crises is acknowledged, but remains under-theorized, often detached from questions of power, inequality, and responsibility. Crisis representation appears fragmented, limiting opportunities to grasp the interconnected nature of polycrisis.
Overall, the curriculum moves beyond descriptive geography, but only partially supports relational, historical, and systemic reasoning central to critical geography education. The study advances the notion of the critical geoliterate student as an educational aim, a learner who interprets spatial representations while critically interrogating how space is historically produced, politically contested, and unevenly experienced. It calls for epistemic reorientation toward fostering learners capable of engaging with a polycrisis world.

36b.title: When social issues become spatial problems: Geography education and socially acute questions in primary school

authors.name: Marco Lupatini
authors.affiliation: Scuola universitaria professionale della Svizzera italiana (SUPSI)

36b.abstract: This paper presents the research framework of GEOCIVIS, a Swiss–Italian project examining how geography education can support primary teachers in engaging socially acute questions (SAQs) through disciplinary geographical inquiry that frames contemporary social issues as spatially structured problems. Although democratic citizenship features prominently in many contemporary curricula, guidance on how socially contested questions can be approached through geographical reasoning remains limited. In classroom practice these issues frequently appear as themes for discussion, while the spatial processes through which they emerge and unfold receive far less systematic attention. GEOCIVIS explores how teachers can mobilise pupils’ spatial experiences as entry points for geographical inquiry that connects lived environments with wider socio-spatial processes, with particular attention given to the pedagogical conditions under which teachers can transform socially acute questions into objects of geographical investigation within the primary classroom. The research combines literature review, institutional policy analysis, and classroom-based case studies with primary teachers in Switzerland and Italy in order to examine how curricular expectations surrounding democratic citizenship are interpreted in teacher education and translated into teaching practice. Through the development of pedagogical guidelines and practical teaching tools, GEOCIVIS contributes to ongoing debates on how geography education can support teachers in fostering democratic engagement and critical spatial thinking from the earliest stages of schooling.

36b.title: Comparing the ‘Self’ and the ‘European Other’: A Critical Discourse Analysis of Greek pre-service teachers’ representations

authors.name: Athina Karatza
authors.affiliation: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

36b.abstract:
Identities and otherness in Europe have been central topics in contemporary research, particularly following the recent migration and humanitarian crises. Critical approaches to European identities are essential for addressing social inequalities in increasingly multicultural societies. Education plays a key role in shaping individuals’ representations of European identities. Consequently, examining the representations of future teachers, who will, in turn, influence and co-construct their students’ perceptions, is of particular importance.
This study aims to: (1) investigate how pre-service primary school teachers in Greece construct, through discourse, representations of the Self/in-group in relation to the ‘European Other’/out-group; (2) identify potential barriers that reinforce the reproduction of dominant power relations and hinder their critical contestation; and (3) propose ways to overcome these barriers towards social well-being.
Thirty-three students from the Department of Primary Education at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens participated in the study. Data collection was conducted through a Serious Game, a questionnaire, and semi-structured interviews.
Participants’ discourse was analyzed across three levels using Critical Discourse Analysis, as proposed by Fairclough, in combination with Systemic Functional Grammar.
The analysis revealed two themes: (1) the Self/in-group represented as possessing more positive characteristics compared to the ‘European Other’ (e.g., ‘we’ as more open-minded and considerate, versus ‘others’ as passive, aggressive or fanatical), and (2) the construction of equal and reciprocal relationships between the Self and the ‘European Other’.
The findings highlight barriers that facilitate the reproduction of power relations and hinder their contestation, including representations drawing on ethnocentric and racist discourse, racial essentialism, and discourses of intra-regional homogeneity alongside the emphasis on inter-regional heterogeneity.
Finally, the study proposes ways to address these barriers, contributing to ongoing discussions on socio-spatial inequalities and spatial justice, and the role of geography education in fostering more inclusive and critical understandings of European identities.

36b.title: Climate Change in Greek School Curricula – A Comparison with Respective Curricula of Representative Foreign Countries

authors.name: Nelly K.M. Marosi
authors.affiliation: University of Groningen/ Centre for Learning and Teaching

36b.abstract:
This paper presents a content analysis of the curricula of four countries – Greece, Cyprus, the United Kingdom, and Australia – examining the integration of Climate Change (CC) as a cross-curricular theme in primary and secondary education. The study focuses primarily on the newly enacted Greek curricula (2023), situating them within a broader international context through systematic comparison with three representative foreign educational systems selected for their geographic, cultural, and curricular diversity.
Key CC-related terms were systematically identified within curriculum texts across all four countries, and both their frequency and contextual usage were recorded and analyzed. The analysis explores how CC is addressed horizontally across educational levels and vertically within individual subjects, following a spiral curriculum approach – that is, examining whether and how CC concepts are revisited and deepened as students progress through their schooling.
To enable meaningful comparisons across subjects taught for varying numbers of years, a normalized frequency index (f) was introduced. This index is defined as the number of CC-related terms identified in a given subject's curriculum divided by the number of years that subject is taught, thereby providing a more objective and comparable measure of CC integration across disciplines and educational systems.
As expected, environmentally oriented subjects emerged as the primary carriers of CC content across all countries examined. Notably, however, several non-environmental subjects (eg. Home Economics, History) showed a surprisingly high frequency of CC-related terms in certain national curricula, suggesting broader and more interdisciplinary approaches to CC education in those contexts. These findings point to meaningful differences in how countries conceptualize the role of CC across the school curriculum, beyond the boundaries of the natural sciences.
The findings highlight both the strengths and gaps in the Greek curriculum's treatment of CC, offering insights and practical implications for future curriculum design and reform.

37.title: The Work of Staying: Domesticity as Infrastructure of Care in Labor Migrant Housing
37.abstract:
Labor migrant housing is a site where the crisis of care is rendered structurally invisible. Drawing on the feminist notion of "life's work" (Mitchell, Marston, and Katz), this paper asks whether the reproductive labor of migrant workers is fully recuperated by capital under conditions of neoliberal restructuring and increasing precarity — or whether everyday domestic practices within labor migrant housing environments constitute a reproductive commons that exceeds institutional and economic attempts to organise migrant life through regimes of control and managed dependency.
The paper argues that shared cooking, care networks, and the negotiation of thresholds operate as socio-spatial practices that reorganise space beyond the formal logics of labor management. These are acts of maintenance and repair — the unglamorous, ongoing labor of keeping collective life going against institutional neglect and material depletion. Drawing on feminist STS scholarship on care and maintenance (Puig de la Bellacasa), and from an architectural perspective centred on domesticity, this contribution proposes labor migrant housing as an infrastructure of care rather than merely a site of labor reproduction.
The contribution places in dialogue two contexts of labor migrant housing: agricultural settlements in the Piana di Gioia Tauro in Southern Italy and logistical housing systems along the Rotterdam–Venlo corridor in the Netherlands. Although embedded in different labor regimes, both contexts reveal a shared structural condition in which the right to domesticity is suspended by the very systems that house labor migrants — and both reveal forms of self-organisation and spatial production that exceed this suspension.
Attending to everyday practices of spatial solidarity, this contribution makes visible the reproductive commons already emerging within conditions of urban precarity. At the same time, it asks how these practices can be recognized politically without romanticizing the conditions of exhaustion, neglect, and deprivation that make such forms of collective labor necessary.

37.title: Reproductive Commons and Collective Mental Wellbeing in the Squatted Prosfygika of Alexandras Avenue, Athens

authors.name: Vassia Fragkaki
authors.affiliation: Department of Architecture, Roma Tre University

37.abstract:
The contribution explores how reproductive commons emerge as socio-material infrastructures capable of sustaining collective mental wellbeing within conditions of urban precarity. Drawing on the case of the Community of Squatted Prosfygika — a self-organised community occupying a 1930s social housing complex in central Athens — I examine how place-based practices of care, mutual aid, and commoning constitute an assemblage (McFarlane, 2011) that reconfigures the relationship between social reproduction, mental wellbeing, and urban space.
In a context shaped by polycrisis — austerity, housing and commons dispossession and a deepening crisis of care (Fraser, 2016) — the community has developed twenty-two collectively managed structures, including a healthcare structure, a self-organised school, spaces for women and gender non-conforming subjects, and an oncology patient hosting facility. I read these not as service provisions but as infrastructures of care-in-common: spatially embedded socio-material arrangements through which reproductive labour is collectivised, interdependence is practised, and psycho-physical wellbeing is sustained beyond individualised frameworks of health. These infrastructures operate as sites where mental wellbeing emerges as a collective capacity cultivated through everyday relational and affective labour.
Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork — participation in community assemblies, situated conversations, and spatial mapping — and engaging feminist social reproduction theory (Fraser, 2016; Katz, 2001) alongside critical urban infrastructure thinking (McFarlane, 2011; Marvin, McFarlane and Rutherford, 2026; Simone, 2004), I argue that the Prosfygika assemblage produces a political imaginary of reproductive commons grounded in embodied, place-based practice — forging commoning subjectivities through the material reworking of shared space. Yet this imaginary remains under threat: institutional plans for restoration-through-eviction enact a form of slow violence (Nixon, 2011) that renders inhabitants unaccountable and their care labour invisible. The paper asks what is at stake — materially, affectively, politically — when place-embedded infrastructures of collective wellbeing are dismantled in the name of urban regeneration.

37.title: The Architectural Type of the Panigyrospito as a Collective Spatial Practice in the Aegean: The Example of Saint Antonios in Santorini
37.abstract:
This research focuses on the spatial clarification of the architectural type known as the panigyróspito, approached as a fragile yet enduring collective expression of dwelling, still in continuous use across the islands of the Aegean. The panigyróspito, a collectively produced and shared space, forms part of church complexes, accommodating the communal meal and acting as a “vessel” that brings together the spiritual and the secular. Communal dining within a religious context constitutes an archaic condition, traceable to early Christian traditions and monastic refectories.

As a distinct architectural type within anonymous vernacular heritage, the panigyróspito exhibits significant diversity in its spatial configuration. Its capacity for transformation—depending on construction systems, available materials, environmental and social conditions—reveals it as a highly adaptable spatial type. This spectrum, ranging from ephemeral to more permanent or even naturally formed structures, reflects not only morphological variation but also the function it serves within each specific social context.

The research is grounded in in-situ architectural survey and the production of original measured drawings of structures that majority of which had not been previously recorded, conducted across five islands—Chios, Tinos, Mykonos, Kea, and Santorini—— as case studies, where through critical observation and discussions with local inhabitants, church complexes across different places and time periods were documented.

Although rooted in insular contexts, the panigyróspito offers insights into how small-scale spatial infrastructures can sustain collective life through shared practices of care. Within these constructions the fundamental human need to “assemble” (ἀγείρειν) is expressed. In the societies of the Aegean, harmonious coexistence constitutes a core element of social structure. Therefore, the panigyróspito should not be understood solely as a vernacular architectural form, but as a living spatial condition of collective life.

Based on this broader research, the presentation focuses on a selected case study: Saint Antonios in Santorini.

37.title: Producing a place of care: everyday practices at an outdoor market on the urban margins
37.abstract:
This paper examines how an outdoor market in Tor Bella Monaca, Rome, becomes a place of care through mundane, routine interactions. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork, it focuses on small, often overlooked acts—such as conversation, repeated encounters, informal exchanges, and gift-giving—that shape the market as a space where people feel recognised, connected, and momentarily relieved from the pressures of everyday life. A specific combination of material and social practices over time produces a situated place of care that is generally overlooked by researchers, policymakers, and even non-market users in the neighbourhood itself.

Building on feminist work on social reproduction, the paper argues that these practices constitute a form of uncoordinated cooperation through which individual acts of sociability accumulate into a collectively sustained infrastructure of care. In this sense, the market can be understood as a reproductive commons in practice: a shared resource that emerges through everyday relational labour.

At the same time, these forms of care remain fragile and limited. The market itself is a precarious infrastructure based on human labour and thus vulnerable to change and external pressures, such as declining profits and limited institutional support for vendors. Moreover, as a temporary and periodic space, its caring functions are confined to specific times and rhythms. While the market provides meaningful moments of care and connection, it does not offer a solution to the broader, ongoing crises shaping everyday life in the urban margins.
By foregrounding both the generative and limited nature of mundane social relations, the paper contributes to debates on reproductive commons by showing how care is enacted through low-intensity, informal practices that sustain urban life while remaining inherently unstable and incomplete.

37.title: Everyday care as a field of gendered and representational contradictions in public space: Geographies of reproductive labour in the historic center of Thessaloniki.
37.abstract:
This paper explores how everyday care practices are inscribed in public space, focusing on the historic center of Thessaloniki and, more specifically, the axis of Dimitriou Gounari Street. Drawing on feminist urban geography and the concept of “geographies of care,” the study approaches care not as a private or individual matter, but as a spatially and socially embedded practice that actively shapes urban space.

The research is guided by two main questions: (a) how are women’s everyday care practices expressed and dispersed within public space, and (b) which spatial and social mechanisms render these practices often invisible? Within this framework, care is understood as a form of reproductive labour that extends beyond the household, permeates public space, and is closely linked to issues of access, mobility, safety, and urban infrastructure.

Methodologically, the study adopts a qualitative, feminist approach, employing time-use diaries completed by women living or working in the area and relevant mappings. Through the recording of daily routes and routines, micro-practices, and lived experiences, the research highlights the fragmented, non-linear, and often invisible forms of mobility that constitute care within the urban tissue. The analysis focuses on spatial trajectories as well as on obstacles, disturbances, and other difficulties, coping strategies, and relationships with both material and social infrastructures.

The paper contributes to ongoing debates on “reproductive commons” by foregrounding care as a critical yet under-recognised urban infrastructure and as a site of political claim-making, particularly in the context of the contemporary urban polycrisis, in the Greek socio spatial context.

37.title: “Carrying Children”: The Intergenerational Care on Streets in Urban China
37.abstract:
Throughout months of ethnographic observation in a residential neighbourhood in Beijing, I repeatedly encountered a familiar yet under-theorised urban phenomenology: elderly guardians—most often grandparents—occupying urban streets adjacent to residential compounds to take care of their grandchildren. In Chinese, everyday childcare is commonly described by the phrase dài háizi—literally “to carry children.” The practice of dài (carrying), understood in my research as a feminist spatial practice, foregrounds the embodied and relational labour of care that enacts and sustains intergenerational relationships in public space.

Tracing these carrying practices, the paper discusses how intergenerational childcare on urban streets materialises and spatialises the contemporary configuration and struggles of social reproduction in urban China. It raises critical questions: whose bodies carry the burdens of social reproduction, and where is this labour spatially performed? While such arrangements enable urban households to cope with intensifying economic pressures, they remain informal, unpaid, and marginalised both socially and spatially.

The paper positions the urban street as a key infrastructure of social reproduction. Engaging feminist and critical geographic debates, it conceptualises these practices as emergent forms of reproductive commons: socio-material and embodied arrangements through which care is collectively organised and urban life made liveable under conditions of precarity. These commons are not formalised or explicitly politicised; rather, they are fragile, everyday achievements sustained through routine co-presence, mutual recognition, and shared rhythms of care. They are embedded within longer trajectories of Chinese feminist thought and struggle, in which the visibility, valuation, and distribution of care have been continually negotiated across socialist legacies, market reforms, and contemporary gender politics.

Integrating the notion of carrying, the paper reconceptualises urban infrastructure as a gendered, relational process, foregrounding how social reproduction is continually produced through embodied care practices.

37.title: Time to Care? Caring Commons in Vienna’s Institutional Childcare Provisioning

authors.name: Lisa-Mo Seebacher
authors.affiliation: Wirtschaftsuniversität Wien (Vienna University of Economics and Business), Austria

37.abstract:
The suggested article centres the care crisis from within the spatial-temporal infrastructures of urban institutionalized childcare by focusing on the struggles and contradictions, but also the potential of Viennese parent-led nurseries. Since 1969 parents collectively rent spaces, hire educators, and organize childcare in their free time. These groups can be considered childcare
commons (Zechner 2022), striving to collectively rework and sustain the material, physical and emotional work involved in early childhood education and care in the urban environment of Vienna. Understanding cities as both, reproducing neoliberal capitalist structures, as well as a potential lever for social-ecological transformations (Dengler et al. 2025), the suggested article links the cyclical, situated and relational concepts of temporalities for generative social-ecological processes (“timescapes”, Adam 1998) with the becomings of childcare commons (García-López et al. 2021). An intersectional feminist ecological economics perspective is used to investigate the research question how parent-led nurseries reproduce and persist capitalist logics in their daily social-ecological provisioning of childcare. A qualitative empirical analysis foregrounds the perspective of
parents, educators and children of selected parent-led nurseries, as well as the broader institutional
context of childcare provisioning in Vienna.

Adam, B. (1998): Timescapes of Modernity. The environment and invisible hazards. Routledge.

Dengler, C.; Völkle, H.; Ware, S. (2025). Time and space for social-ecological transformation: Care-full commoning in and beyond the ecofeminist city, Environmental Politics, 34(5), 861-881.

García-López, G.A.; Lang, U.; Singh, N. (2021). Commons, Commoning and Co-Becoming: Nurturing Life-in-Common and Post-Capitalist Futures. EPE: Nature and Space, 4(4); 1199-1216.

Zechner, M. (2022). Childcare commons: Of feminist subversions of community and commune in Barcelona. Ephemera, 22(2), 19-50.

37.title: Children as commoners: Intergenerational care across housing crises in Nairobi, Istanbul, and Berlin

authors.name: Claudia Mock
authors.affiliation: Georg-Simmel-Center for Urban Studies (Humboldt University of Berlin) & Collaborative Research Centre “Refiguration of Spaces” CRC 1265 (Technical University of Berlin)

37.abstract:
This paper examines the collectivization of care within diverse care and housing constellations across Nairobi, Istanbul, and Berlin, positioning children as central actors in reproductive commoning under conditions of urban housing crises. Challenging dominant framings of children as either care recipients or passive victims of neglect, the paper advances an adult-critical perspective that foregrounds children’s active participation in shaping, sustaining, and contesting everyday practices of care.

Drawing on feminist and critical geographical scholarship on social reproduction and care ethics, the paper conceptualizes housing as an intergenerational site of care and a socio-material infrastructure through which commoning practices are constituted beyond the nuclear family. It interrogates the role of children as commoners across varied socio-spatial arrangements, including extended family households in lower-middle-class housing estates in Nairobi, precarious housing conditions among minority groups in Istanbul, and care relations extending beyond single-parent households through neighbourhood-based kinship networks in Berlin. Through these cases, the paper asks how specific configurations enable or constrain children’s capacities to act as caring subjects, and how children’s practices, in turn, actively reconfigure forms of living-in-common.

By situating children as solidaristic contemporaries rather than future urban subjects in different urban housing crises, the paper intervenes in debates on urban commons, social reproduction, and the right to the city. It argues for a reconceptualization of urban care infrastructures and relations as intergenerational, contested, and co-produced by young actors often marginalized in urban debate.

37.title: Time as a Commons: Collective temporal practices and the making of urban care infrastructures
37.abstract: The contemporary care crisis has prompted a surge of scholarly attention to urban care commons and bottom-up care infrastructures, with particular emphasis on their socio-spatial dynamics. By contrast, the temporal dynamics through which such formations are sustained have received limited attention. While previous research has engaged urban and institutional temporalities in relation to processes of commoning, the commoning of time itself remains underexplored as a pathway toward care-full urban transformation. This article turns to the urban co-production of time, focusing on the temporal patterns that sustain one of the largest self-organised collective kitchens in crisis-ridden central Athens. The kitchen mobilises dozens of residents in daily food provisioning and redistribution, preparing and sharing hundreds of warm meals six days a week. The scale and continuity of the initiative provide a unique empirical lens for understanding the organisational and meaning-making practices, at the temporal level, that make informal urban care infrastructures possible. Drawing on ten months of ethnographic fieldwork, the article illuminates both the temporal resources (clock-time hours) and the temporal orientations (valuations of time beyond clock-time) that underpin alternative arrangements of social reproduction. The findings introduce the concept of collective time work to describe how otherwise temporally fragmented urban communities pool time and remake temporal norms to create cohesive community care. Conceptually, the article advances time as a relational, co-produced good, rather than an individually managed resource, to foreground the politics of time as a vital vector for transforming how care is organised and sustained in cities.

37.title: Situating Urban Feminist and LGBTQI+ Movements in Greece: Genealogies of Struggle, Geographies of Care
37.abstract:
Drawing on archival and empirical research into feminist and LGBTQI+ activism against gender-based violence in Athens and Crete, this paper explores the mapping of genealogies, practices, and political infrastructures within distinct urban contexts. Our intervention highlights the articulations and tensions between trans-locality and emplacedness in contemporary Greek movements. In doing so, we critically engage with the politics of knowledge by acknowledging the inherent multiplicities within the feminist “archive.”
This research is situated within a conjuncture defined by an escalation of GBV, increasingly normalized by “anti-gender” ideologies targeting decades of feminist struggle. The rise of far-right and authoritarian politics—reintroducing white supremacism as a dominant sociopolitical technology—has rendered public space a “danger zone” for femininities, LGBTQI+ communities, racialized groups, and those standing in solidarity. Simultaneously, feminist and queer initiatives have gained significant momentum, functioning as a vital counter-response to the encroachment on rights and safety.
Our research identifies distinct activist dynamics in each location. Athens functions, materially and symbolically, as a "metropolis" of activism—a site of convergence where diverse voices, practices, and political trajectories intersect, and where precarity and intersectional discrimination are highly visible. Crete, conversely, is characterized by a cultural divide between a progressive urban milieu and a staunchly patriarchal hinterland where GBV remains deeply normalized. Consequently, the impact of feminist and queer mobilizations in Crete is often more pronounced, representing a direct rupture with the status quo. These smaller-scale urban collectivities exhibit greater long-term continuity, relying on close-knit social networks that serve as both a political base and a vital source of personal support.
By attending to these diverse histories, we emphasize the situated nature of the politics of care. We argue that activists draw on specific socio-cultural resources and political infrastructures unique to each context; these form shifting yet sustained webs of affective and material resistance and solidarity.

37.title: Governing Care in Polycrisis: Social Reproduction, Marginalisation, and the Politics of Urban Care Infrastructures
37.abstract:
From homelessness criminalisation to hostile immigration environments, urban governance consistently produces the very marginalisation it claims to address. Placing critical urban geography in dialogue with debates on care, democracy, and infrastructure, this paper interrogates the governance of care as an urgent yet undertheorised site of democratic struggle in the crisis city. Drawing on qualitative research conducted across Manchester, Athens, and Santiago with communities experiencing homelessness, problematic drug use, and extreme poverty, I contend that who holds decision-making power over care infrastructure: who designs it, funds it, and is consulted in its making, has profound material and democratic consequences for making space for those whose lives are rendered liveable.
This paper analyses questions of authority, accountability, and exclusion, recognising how care governance becomes entangled with the material realities of urban precarity. For example, service architectures built around the traditional single homeless man can render women's homelessness structurally invisible. Criminalisation of drug use compounds vulnerability rather than enable treatment. Hostile border regimes layer onto already fragile care entitlements for refugees and migrants increasingly constituting the urban homeless population. These are not policy failures at the margins but diagnostic of how democratic governance reproduces the socio-spatial inequalities it purports to resolve.
Care governance can be situated within intersecting crises as the unravelling of formal welfare infrastructures under austerity intersects with deepening crises of housing, health, and belonging. In light of this, this paper asks whether mutual aid networks, harm-reduction collectives, and commoning practices can constitute insurgent democratic forms: place-based challenges to the terms on which care is made available, and to the question of who gets to decide?

37.title: Feminist urban planning and guidelines for the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki Campus: A sociol-spatial study using qualitative and quantitative methods

authors.name: Eirini Balamatsia
authors.affiliation: Department of Spatial Planning and Development, Faculty of Engineering, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki

authors.name: Aikaterini Alexiou
authors.affiliation: Department of Spatial Planning and Development, Faculty of Engineering, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki

authors.name: Yannis Frangopoulos
authors.affiliation: Department of Spatial Planning and Development, Faculty of Engineering, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki

authors.name: Dimitrios Kourkouridis
authors.affiliation: Department of Spatial Planning and Development, Faculty of Engineering, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki

authors.name: Eirini Kostaki
authors.affiliation: Department of Spatial Planning and Development, Faculty of Engineering, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki

37.abstract:
This study examines how gendered inequalities manifest in the spatial experience of the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki campus and investigates how feminist spatial planning can effectively address them, contributing to geographical debates on spatial justice and inclusive urban environments. Grounded in a socio-spatial approach, the research explores the interplay between gender, everyday mobility, and the organization of space, emphasizing how built environments reproduce or challenge social inequalities.
The study adopts a mixed-methods methodology, combining qualitative and quantitative tools, including interviews, on-site experimental observation, map analysis, and a survey of approximately 400 participants. This methodological triangulation enables a comprehensive understanding of how different users perceive, navigate, and appropriate campus space in their daily routines.
Findings highlight pronounced disparities in perceived safety, accessibility, and belonging, with women and other marginalized groups reporting heightened insecurity, exclusion, and reduced autonomy, particularly in poorly lit or transitional areas and during nighttime use. These patterns demonstrate that spatial inequalities are both socially constructed and materially embedded in the physical and institutional configuration of the campus.
The results reveal structural and institutional gaps in managing gender-based discrimination, highlighting the limited integration of gender-sensitive planning within existing governance frameworks. Importantly, the study emphasizes the critical role of lived experience in shaping spatial justice and everyday campus life, uncovering hidden geographies of exclusion often overlooked in conventional planning practices.
The study concludes with design guidelines grounded in feminist principles, including care, inclusivity, accessibility, and participation, demonstrating how such approaches can create safer, more vibrant, and socially cohesive university environments and contribute to contemporary debates on embedding gender perspectives into urban planning and reimagining public spaces through equitable, community-centered strategies.

37.title: Reclaiming public space in the crisis era: The case of Thessaly, Greece.

authors.name: Evangelia Maria Kouvara
authors.affiliation: Phd Candidate at the Department of Urban Planning and Regional Development, School of Architecture, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki.

37.abstract:
The paper examines the notion of crisis as a process, in relation to the production of public space. During period of crisis, public space is reconfigured not only through the formal institutional framework –invoked by emergency governance- but also through new methods devised by the local residents, who experience the crisis in question.

The paper reviews the spatial and social dimensions of successive and overlapping crises in Thessaly, as a way for residents to reclaim and redefine public space. Thessaly is a Greek region that during the last decade has been severely affected by successive crises such as the financial crisis, Covid-19, successive floods and the social crisis raised by the fatal rail accident at Tempi. Public spaces in Thessaly have been heavily impacted by these events, leading residents to develop their own mechanisms and resume everyday life. Within this context, streets and squares have been served as sites of dissent and solidarity, fostering new urban qualities and establishing the conditions for reclaiming public space. This response to crisis is based, on the one hand, on the residents themselves -their lived experience and empirical local knowledge- and on the other hand, on the necessity created by the crisis itself, which frequently disrupts “normality” and necessitates a “state of exception”.

The paper argues that residents are not merely passive recipients of a crisis but they constitute key actors in the production of space. Their empirical knowledge and understanding of their everyday public space and their direct engagement with this are crucial factors in the production of space before, during and in the aftermath of a crisis.

37.title: Urban environmental movements and the "green" vote in the 2010 municipal elections. Case studies of the Municipality of Athens and the Municipality of Elliniko-Argyroupoli.

authors.name: Polina Prentou
authors.affiliation: PHD Researcher, National Technical University of Athens

37.abstract:
This paper examines the role of movements for the defense of public open spaces in shaping the electoral results of the 2010 municipal elections. The research focuses on two distinct fields of study that highlight the significance of environmental stakes in the local political arena: the Municipality of Athens and the Municipality of Elliniko-Argyroupoli.
In the case of the Municipality of Athens, the analysis focuses on the importance of local-level resistances (with the Cyprus & Patision Park as a characteristic example), where the claim for public space was directly linked to changes in electoral geography. In the Municipality of Elliniko-Argyroupoli, the mobilization for the creation of a Metropolitan Park on the site of the former airport is examined—an issue that polarized the local community and served as a central axis of the pre-electoral debate.
Through the spatial analysis of the results, this study documents how environmental demands were transformed into political action at the ballot box. The findings demonstrate that in both cases, despite their differences, the environmental movement functioned as a decisive factor for the political activation of citizens, establishing the protection of open spaces as a dominant demand of the period.

37.title: Reproductive commoning as climate adaptation: the neighborhood ecosystem of La Florida (Barcelona)

authors.name: Sergio Ruiz Cayuela
authors.affiliation: Institute of Environmental Science and Technology (ICTA-UAB)

37.abstract:
The neighborhood of La Florida, in the Barcelona metropolitan area, has been subjected to processes of urban dispossession since its development in the 1950s to host migrant workers. As a result, La Florida is currently enmeshed in a chronic crisis of social reproduction exacerbated by several intersecting factors such as recent attempts to “sanitize” the neighborhood, restrictive migration policies and stigmatization of the area. These and other processes intersect with climate change to make La Florida one of the areas with the highest climate-vulnerability index of the whole Barcelona metropolitan area.

In this context, and after more than a decade of organizing and building popular power, neighbors have built what they call a “neighborhood ecosystem”: a network of projects, organizations and spaces that seek to collectivize social reproduction. The ecosystem includes a daily-functioning community kitchen, an editorial lab, a seed bank, a popular school and a housing cooperative among many other initiatives; and is driven by mutual care and collective commitment. We characterize the neighborhood ecosystem in La Florida as an ecology of popular infrastructures weaved together through commoning practices and relations sustained by the everyday involvement of hundreds of people.

In this presentation we explore the potentialities and challenges of the neighborhood ecosystem in La Florida to bring about just climate adaptation from below. We look at everyday commoning practices and heat-coping strategies in La Florida to argue that, by collectivizing reproductive activities and infrastructures, neighbors are building adaptive capacity. In opposition to municipal plans that reproduce marginalization processes, heat adaptation through commoning responds directly to the immediate needs of the community and challenges the stigmatization of the neighborhood. In this way, commoning for climate adaptation builds popular power and collective autonomy in a daily prefiguration of emancipatory social relations from the margins in a heating world.

37.title: Infrastructural Labour and the (Re)making of Reproductive Commons
37.abstract:
Geographical scholarship foregrounds infrastructures as the socio-material systems through which social reproduction is secured unevenly across classed, gendered, and racialised lines and becomes politically contested. This paper develops infrastructural labour as a lens for rethinking reproductive commons. By infrastructural labour, we refer to both the formal, paid, acknowledged and the informal, unpaid, unacknowledged work through which people access, use, repair, improvise, bypass, and rework the infrastructures necessary for sustaining life. Infrastructural labour allows us to follow reproductive work across sites and practices and foreground the devalued relations and work that make life possible and worth living.
Drawing on our work in Thessaloniki over the past decade, we trace infrastructural labour in the everyday work of stretching bills, sharing food, organising education, managing debt, and securing access to warmth, shelter, and electricity. We also trace it in repairing pipes, reconnecting water or electricity, maintaining squats and collective kitchens, or sharing bureaucratic knowledge. In this sense, we argue, infrastructural labour brings reproductive commons into life and use: it is the work through which shared resources, spaces, and capacities are maintained, contested, and made available for collective life-making.
Our focus on infrastructural labour allows us to foreground mutual aid as a material and relational praxis through which reproductive commons are produced, organised, and politically imagined. We, thus, rethink mutual aid through reproductive labour and recentre it as a practice of infrastructuring: a way of collectively securing access to housing, food, water, electricity, shelter, and knowledge when dominant infrastructures exclude, extract, or fail. In reorganising the material conditions of reproduction, mutual aid carries a collective desire for different ways of living in common. It works as a form of political translation, connecting struggles often treated separately — around housing, utilities, migration, food, debt, and education — and making alternative reproductive futures thinkable and realisable.

37.title: Assembling the commons: (Re)production and urban solidarity infrastructures in Athens and Berlin

authors.name: Dimitris Pettas
authors.affiliation: Technical University of Berlin, Insitute of Urban and Regional Planning

37.abstract:
Within an environment of recurring and overlapping crises, the reproduction of everyday life is increasingly organized beyond and in tension with state and market provision. This paper explores how urban commons of various legal forms and sectors of activity in Athens and Berlin assemble urban solidarity infrastructures, namely socio-material configurations through which horizontal practices and relations of production and social reproduction (i.e. housing, food networks, care, media and culture, digital tools and infrastructure) are collectively organized and embedded in urban environments and circuits.

Drwaing on 54 interviews across a diverse set of initiatives operating in the highly differentiated contexts of Athens and Berlin, this presentation approaches the commons not as bounded entities and institutional forms, but as constantly becoming assemblages constituted through heterogenous relations between human and non-human actors, resources and organizational practices. In this frame, production and social reproduction are understood as overlapping, ongoing processes through which labour, care, solidarity and democratic governance models are coninously negotiated and provisionally stratified under conditions of urban precarity. Through bringing together the Deleuzoguattarian concepts of assemblage, desire, and molar/molecular formations with the autonomist lens of the commons theory, I argue i) that these initiatives do not operate in isolation but, rather, they constitute broader infrastructural assemblages by sharing people, infrastructures, material and immaterial resources, and collective desires and ii) they continuously adapt their repertoires of action to fluid and contested urban conditions, assuming multiple and shifting roles, from protest and resistance to the creation of alternative economies and egalitarian forms of social reproduction.

By foregrounding the infrastructural and processual dimensions of (re)production, the paper contributes to debates on social reproduction as a terrain of urban struggle and repositions the commons as a dynamic and contested field of assembling life-sustaining relations in the city.

37.title: Who Sustains Life in the Platform Economy? Migrant Domestic Work and Urban Struggles in the age of Platform Capitalism

authors.name: Ana Santamarina
authors.affiliation: Critical Urban Studies Research Group, Universidad Nacional de Educación a Distancia (Madrid, Spain)

37.abstract:
In recent years, the intensification of platformization has become a defining feature of contemporary capitalism, increasingly embedded within—and constitutive of—an ongoing urban polycrisis (Sequera et al., 2026). This process is both reshaping key domains of social reproduction—e.g. access to housing and labour—and also expanding into the very activities that sustain everyday life, including care, cleaning, and health services (Barrial et al., 2025). Despite their marginal position in dominant accounts of platform capitalism, these sectors have experienced some of the most rapid forms of platform expansion in recent years (Rodríguez-Modroño & Agenjo-Calderón, 2024; Huws, 2018).
Situated within historically feminised and racialised labour markets, platform-mediated reproductive work relies structurally on migrant women, whose labour underpins multi-scalar care chains (Bhattacharya, 2024). Platforms operate not merely as intermediaries but as infrastructures of extraction, driving renewed processes of the recommodification of social reproduction (Strüver & Bauriedl, 2022). This reconfiguration intensifies existing regimes of exploitation through labour flexibilisation and fragmentation, the amplification of informality, the externalisation of risks, and the consolidation of on-demand temporalities, deepening precarity and exposure to intersecting forms of violence (Santamarina & Fernández-Trujillo, 2025).
Drawing on qualitative fieldwork based on over 40 interviews with migrant women platform domestic workers in Madrid, Rome, and Buenos Aires, this paper moves beyond accounts that focus on how platformization restructures domestic labour markets and their socio-spatial organisation to engage with social reproduction as a contested terrain of agency, commoning, and collective organisation. Foregrounding workers’ experiences, the paper traces practices that challenge platform atomisation, from everyday survival strategies to collective forms of organising and mutual support, building collective infrastructures and logistics that help to navigate life in exclusionary urban contexts. These practices are deeply shaped by bordering regimes and migratory trajectories, highlighting social reproduction as a key site of struggle and a generative space for collective resistance.

37.title: Solidarity, Equivalence, and the Limits of Self-Organised Reproduction: Some Reflections on Urban Infrastructures of Care

authors.name: Dimitra Kotouza
authors.affiliation: University of Edinburgh / Labour Research Department

37.abstract: This paper examines the contradictions that emerged within grassroots efforts to collectively reproduce everyday life under conditions of acute economic crisis, drawing on the experience of neighbourhood assemblies and solidarity initiatives in Greece during the debt crisis. It focuses on the structural tensions that shape attempts to construct collective infrastructures of care outside — or against — capitalist social relations. Self-organised initiatives for reproduction face a constitutive tension between two logics: one premised on formal equivalence and exchange, and one premised on solidarity understood as mutuality beyond equivalence. Alternative currency networks, time banks, and other exchange-based projects presuppose property and individual capacity as given while leaving underlying inequalities unaddressed. Where initiatives do exceed the logic of equivalence, however — in collective kitchens, solidarity health centres, or unmediated forms of mutual aid — they can remain circumscribed by the poverty they seek to alleviate, dependent on surplus labour-power rather than surplus wealth. The paper argues that the spatial form of neighbourhood-based organisation compounds these tensions. The presumption of a pre-existing community of equals, united by proximity, can obscure the class, racial, and gender hierarchies that traverse urban space and constitute its residents unequally. The democratic form, premised on the formal equality of participants, cannot address what it cannot recognise. Solidarity is thus not simply a moral disposition that can be declared, but a social relation whose possibility is structurally conditioned. Without directly confronting the social relations that make equivalence necessary, infrastructures of care risk reproducing — rather than contesting — the conditions of their own insufficiency. Yet the possibility of confronting such relations is there, in forms of collective action that expropriate infrastructures while simultaneously questioning the ways social relations penetrate group relations within movements.

38.title: THE GREAT WILDFIRES OF 2007 ΙΝ PELOPONNESE AND THE REGENERATION OF FORESTS
38.abstract:
The fires of the summer of 2007 in Greece have been recorded as the most destructive in Europe in recent decades. The total area burned exceeded 250,000 hectares, of which 30,132 were located within the Natura protected areas 2000 network. Furthermore, for the first time, the damage report included not only burned forests and agricultural land, but also entire villages, civil infrastructure and the loss of 57 lives.
This research thoroughly investigates and examines the short, middle, and long term impact of these catastrophic wildfires. It estimates the severity of the impact and the time needed for regeneration of the forests, regeneration implying that the forests returned to their previous extends and syntheses before the fires. The study is conducted using remote sensing data and methods, i.e., satellite images and products from NASA's MODIS satellites, namely the products MOD09A1 and MCD64A1.
Seven different polygons (burned areas) were singled out as Regions of Interest (ROIs) and their evolution was monitored for the entire period of satellite data (2002-present) with the construction of the time series of the NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index) and NBR (Normalized Burn Ratio) ratios. The post-fire yearly evolution of these ratios was compared with the averaged pre-fire values leading to some first conclusions.
