It is noted that the NBR index is normally used as the difference pre-fire to post-fire (dNBR) but the particular point in time that is considered pre-fire can be varied to conform with the scope of the study. Additionally, the concurrent examination of the two indices can provide useful input for the timely growth of the forest vegetation.
Given the uncertainties inherent in remote sensing methods the results were compared with other similar studies, especially those that included field examinations, and the comparisons were favorable.

38.title: Connections between natural disasters and population displacement in the context of Solar activity influence

authors.name: Milica Langović
authors.affiliation: Institute of Physics Belgrade, University of Belgrade

authors.name: Vladimir A. Srećković
authors.affiliation: Institute of Physics Belgrade, University of Belgrade

authors.name: Marko Langović
authors.affiliation: Faculty of Geography, University of Belgrade

authors.name: Zoran Vidović
authors.affiliation: Faculty of Education, University of Belgrade

38.abstract: Natural disasters represent an increasingly significant factor in population mobility patterns, capable of transforming migration directions. Simultaneously, natural disasters and solar activity relation has gained broad recognition in the academic community, with supporting evidence emerging. Using the influence of the sun on geospatial elements as a starting point, this paper examines the connection between natural disasters and population displacement in the context of solar activity. Specifically, the objective is to investigate the relationship between solar activity characteristics and population displacement induced by natural disasters in Southern Europe. The research addresses different population mobility types triggered by wide range of natural hazards to provide a comprehensive analysis. To achieve the research objectives, data were analyzed using various statistical methods in R. The results indicate a close relationship between the observed categories, especially regarding population mobility induced by weather related hazards, primarily during periods of solar maximum. This research provides new insight into issues related to natural disasters and human mobility, contributing to a better understanding of the Sun-Earth system.

38.title: Spatializing Rural Vulnerability: Flooding, Displacement, and Relocation in the Thessalian Plain
38.abstract:
In recent years, the Mediterranean region has experienced an intensification of extreme weather events, with significant and uneven impacts on human settlements. These phenomena foreground the increasingly conflictual relationship between anthropogenic spatial production and natural ecosystems under conditions of accelerating climate change. The Thessalian Plain in Central Greece constitutes a critical case. The catastrophic flooding of September 2023, which caused widespread damage to settlements, infrastructures, and productive systems, exposed the long-term consequences of agricultural and urban development policies that have systematically disregarded hydrological and ecological processes, thereby amplifying rural vulnerability.

This paper examines the case of Metamorfosi Palamas, an agrarian settlement in Central Thessaly that is currently subject to relocation planning in the aftermath of the floods. Situating the case within broader debates on spatialized vulnerability, displacement, and rural precarity, the study investigates both the historical formation and prospective transformation of the settlement. The research draws on four interrelated studies conducted during Design Studio at the Department of Architecture, University of Thessaly. The methodological approach integrates multiple qualitative and quantitative tools: (a) an extensive literature review spanning archaeological records to media discourse on relocation; (b) fieldwork, including site visits and household surveys; (c) interviews and participatory activities with residents, capturing lived experiences of loss, risk, and uncertainty; and (d) multi-layered cartographic analysis combining digital datasets, archival maps, and photographic material.

Findings indicate that conventional infrastructural and technocratic responses are increasingly inadequate in mitigating risk. Spatial vulnerability emerges from the intersection of geomorphological conditions, climate-induced hazards, and market-oriented agrarian policies, while social vulnerability is compounded by housing deprivation, economic disruption, and emerging displacement pressures. By foregrounding the entanglement of environmental and socio-spatial processes, the paper contributes to ongoing discussions on energy poverty, housing precarity, and climate-induced displacement, highlighting the need for more context-sensitive and ecologically attuned spatial planning strategies.

38.title: Green energy infrastructure and Earth heritage conservation : The Akrocheiras wind farm in the Lesvos petrified Forest as a case study

authors.name: Ilias Valiakos
authors.affiliation: Natural History Museum of the Lesvos Petrified Forest

authors.name: Konstantina Bentana
authors.affiliation: Natural History Museum of the Lesvos Petrified Forest

authors.name: Stratis Zgournios
authors.affiliation: Natural History Museum of the Lesvos Petrified Forest

authors.name: Parthenopi Panidou
authors.affiliation: Natural History Museum of the Lesvos Petrified Forest

authors.name: Nikolaos Grammenopoulos
authors.affiliation: Natural History Museum of the Lesvos Petrified Forest

38.abstract:
The Petrified Forest of Lesvos, located in the western part of Lesvos Island, Greece, is a unique natural monument of international significance formed during the Lower Miocene by intense volcanic activity in the North Eastern Aegean region. The Petrified Forest was declared a "Protected Natural Monument" in 1985, covering an area of 15,000 hectares. The modern history of its protection was shaped significantly in the 1990s, when the installation of the first wind turbines in the Akrocheiras area raised serious concerns regarding the safety of the region's fossils highlighting the absence of implementation of the a legal protection framework at the time. Since the foundation of the Natural History Museum of the Lesvos Petrified Forest in 1994, its global importance has been consistently reaffirmed.: it became one of the first four Geoparks in 2000, and a key feature of the Lesvos Island UNESCO Global Geopark in 2015. Most recently, it was recognized by the International Union of Geological Sciences (IUGS) as one of the first 100 geological heritage sites in the world.
During works for the replacement of the old wind turbines remarkable fossil sites with impressive fossilized tree trunks were unearthed. The Museum realized a major geoconservation project monitored the construction work to detect and protect fossils, conducting rescue excavations during the construction, mapping and protecting the newly discovered fossil sites, collecting and conserving the tree trunks , transferring and storing the movable fossils, and protecting and preserving in situ the standing fossil trees. This rescue excavation project, which lasted three years (2018-2021), represents a major paleobotanical excavation in Greece. The main fossil assemblages, the most prominent fallen tree trunks, and the majority of the standing tree trunks were preserved in their original positions.

39.title: Stray Cats and Cat Ladies: leftover ecologies of urban care in Athens, Greece

authors.name: Dimitris Bormpoudakis
authors.affiliation: Callisto - Wildlife and Nature Conservation Society

39.abstract: This paper explores the infrastructures that people (mainly older women or “cat ladies”) build for stray cats on the streets of central Athens, using leftovers: cardboard boxes, old plastic bags, discarded furniture, food containers, and other residual materials of everyday urban life. I approach these small, improvised constructions as socio-material and affective infrastructures of more-than-human care, produced within conditions of urban crisis, depletion, and a deepening crisis of care. Built in marginal spaces (a pavement in front of a derelict building, a former café currently in ruins, a small overgrown lot, the space around an urban tree) these infrastructures sustain everyday life for both cats and humans alike. The paper focuses on the relations developed between stray cats and the women who care for them. In Athens, caring for stray cats is a highly gendered and often stigmatised activity, frequently rendered invisible or dismissed as insignificant. Yet this discredited labour can be understood as a city-sustaining and potentially transformative practice. Through the lens of feminist and more-than-human geography, I argue that these relations of care illuminate how urban space is continuously remade through multispecies forms of social reproduction. Humans care for cats, cats care for humans, and leftovers mediate this relationship, becoming the material basis through which urban conviviality, attachment, and survival are organised. Methodologically, the paper draws on mapping and photography to document the micro-sites where these relationships unfold. Photography is used not simply to record these spaces, but to attend to the textures, materials, and spatial improvisations through which care becomes visible. In doing so, the paper proposes these leftover infrastructures as reproductive commons: fragile yet vital socio-ecological formations through which more convivial urban futures are sustained.

39.title: Larissa as a Cultural Landscape: Memory, Identity, and Lived Experience through the Interconnection of the Katsigras Collection with the Wider Surrounding Space
39.abstract:
This study conceptualizes the city of Larissa as a cultural landscape, focusing on the interrelations between memory, identity, and lived experience as mediated through visual art and spatial practice. Drawing on selected paintings from the Katsigras Collection, housed in the Municipal Art Gallery of Larissa, the research investigates how artistic representations can be mobilized as interpretive entry points for understanding and re-experiencing the urban landscape. The central objective is to develop a framework for cultural routes that connect the museum collection with the broader urban environment, thus facilitating a transition from passive visual consumption to active, embodied engagement with place.

The methodological approach integrates theoretical and applied perspectives from cultural geography and experience design, particularly focusing on key dimensions such as memory–identity–spatiality, authenticity, and carrying capacity. The Katsigras Collection is treated as a visual archive that encapsulates the symbolic and material dimensions of the local landscape, enabling thematic categorization and interpretive mapping. Concurrently, selected landmarks of Larissa are analyzed as multisensory nodes within the cultural landscape, linked conceptually and experientially to specific artworks.

Based on this synthesis, the study proposes the design of structured cultural routes organized around thematic stations and tailored to diverse user groups, including residents, students, and visitors. These routes aim to enhance participatory engagement and foster a deeper, experiential understanding of the landscape, bridging the gap between representation and lived reality.

The expected outcomes include: (a)a systematic categorization of the Katsigras Collection as a landscape-oriented visual corpus; (b)the identification and interpretation of key urban landmarks through a cultural landscape lens; (c)the design and documentation of cultural routes as tools for cultural tourism and landscape education; and (d)the formulation of a collaborative governance framework involving the museum, local authorities, and stakeholders. Ultimately, the study contributes to the integration of cultural heritage, spatial experience, and sustainable local development.

39.title: Strategic autonomy and regional development: The contribution of regional foresight to addressing geopolitical challenges
39.abstract:
The new geopolitical environment, as it is shaping up brings back to the fore the debate on the strategic autonomy (Lippert, Ondarza, & Perthes, 2019) of the European Union. However, strategic autonomy is neither a self-evident nor a fully achievable goal in absolute terms, especially in an environment of interdependencies. The question, therefore, could concern whether regions are able to chart sustainable development paths within conditions of geopolitical uncertainty.
The presentation formulates a research agenda that links the geopolitical dimension to regional development through foresight (Gavigan & Scapolo, 2001). Central questions are: (a) can the region be understood as a geopolitical actor with a distinct strategic capacity? and (b) under what institutional and methodological conditions does foresight function as a form of governance capable of managing systemic uncertainty?
Our aim is to examine whether strategic autonomy can be considered as an outcome of regional anticipatory governance(OECD, 2021). In this context, regional foresight is proposed as a strategic navigation tool, capable of linking development policy to changing geopolitical conditions.

References

Gavigan, J. P., & Scapolo, F. (2001). A practical guide to regional foresight FOREN Netowork. Luxemburg: European Commision Research Directorate General.
Lippert, B., Ondarza, N. v., & Perthes, V. (2019). European strategic autonomy: actors, issues, conflicts of interests.
OECD. (2021). Foresight and Anticipatory Governance in Practice. Lessons in effective foresight institutionalisation. Strategic Foresight Unit. Office of the Secretary-General: OECD.
